title: Orphic Argonautica
subtitle: Greek Text with English Translation
description: Complete text of the Orphic Argonautica with line-by-line English translation and scholarly commentary

text.greek: Ὦναξ Πυθῶνος μεδέων, ἑκατηβόλε, μάντι,
text.english: O lord, ruler of Pytho, Far-shooter, prophet,
text.note: Invocation is to Apollo, identified by epithets: Pytho = Delphi; hekatēbolos = “Far-shooter”; mantis = “prophet/seer.”

text.greek: ὃς λάχες ἠλιβάτου κορυφῆς Παρνασσίδα πέτρην
text.english: who by lot attained the Parnassian crag of the sun-bathed peak,
text.note: laches = “you obtained (by lot),” echoing divine allotments; ēlibatos = “sun-bathed/sun-blest”; “Parnassian rock” is the crag at Delphi on Mt. Parnassus.

text.greek: σὴν ἀρετὴν ὑμνῶ· σὺ δέ μοι κλέος ἐσθλὸν ὀπάσσαις·
text.english: your excellence I hymn; and do you grant me noble fame;
text.note: aretē = “excellence” (divine prowess); kleos esthlon = “goodly/noble fame.”

text.greek: πέμπε δ' ἐπὶ πραπίδεσσιν ἐμαῖς ἐτυμηγόρον αὐδήν
text.english: send upon my breast a truth-declaring voice,
text.note: prapides = “midriff/breast,” seat of thought; etymēgoros = “truth-declaring, truth-speaking.”

text.greek: ὄφρα πολυσπερέεσσι βρότοις λιγύφωνον ἀοιδήν
text.english: that to far-scattered mortals I may proclaim a clear-voiced song
text.note: polysperes = “much-sown,” used metaphorically of mankind as widely scattered over the earth; ligyphōnos = “clear-voiced”; ēpysō = “I cry aloud/proclaim.”

text.greek: ἠπύσω Μούσης ἐφετμαῖς καὶ πηκτίδι πυκνῇ.
text.english: at the Muse’s behests and with the close-strung pectis.
text.note: ephetmai = “behests/commands”; pectis (πηκτίς) is a stringed instrument akin to the lyre; pyknē = “close-set/closely strung.”

text.greek: - Νῦν γάρ σοι, λυροεργὲ, φίλον μέλος ἀείδοντι
text.english: For now, to you, lyre‑working one, as I sing the beloved lay,
text.note: λυροεργέ (“lyre‑working”) is an elevated epithet, likely addressing either Hermes (inventor of the lyre) or, by self‑address, the poet as master of the lyre; σοι … ἀείδοντι “to you … as I sing” frames the invocation.

text.greek: θυμὸς ἐποτρύνει λέξαι τάπερ οὔποτε πρόσθεν
text.english: my spirit urges me to tell the very things which never before
text.note: τὰ περ (“the very things”) uses περ as an intensifier; λέξαι is the aorist infinitive “to tell, relate.”

text.greek: ἔφρασ' ὅταν Βακχοῖο καὶ Ἀπόλλωνος ἄνακτος
text.english: I declared when I proclaimed the deeds of Bakchos and of lord Apollon.
text.note: ἔφρασ’ “I declared”; ὅταν here functions as “when” (epic/poetic usage), and an object such as ἔργα (“deeds”) is understood with φράζω; Βακχοῖο is the epic genitive of Bakchos; ἄνακτος “lord” preserves the epic epithet for Apollon.

text.greek: κέντρῳ ἐλαυνόμενος, φρικώδεα κῆλ' ἐπίφαυσκον
text.english: Driven on by the goad, I was bringing to light dread afflictions,
text.note: κέντρῳ ἐλαυνόμενος is a vivid metaphor of compulsion/inspiration. ἐπίφαυσκον (imperfect with -σκ-) = “kept revealing/was bringing to light.” φρικώδεα κῆλ’: κῆλα can literally be “arrows,” but here likely “afflictions/ills,” pairing with ἄκη (“remedies”). Some take κῆλα as “spells,” but the medical antithesis favors “ills.”

text.greek: θνητοῖς ἀνθρώποισιν ἄκη· μετὰ δ' ὅρκια μύσταις·
text.english: remedies for mortal men—and thereafter oaths for initiates;
text.note: ἄκη is the poetic plural of ἄκος (“remedy”). ὅρκια μύσταις refers to the vows/bindings of initiates in Orphic rites, indicating Orpheus’ role as mystagogue.

text.greek: ἀρχαίου μὲν πρῶτα χάους ἀμέγαρτον ἀνάγκην
text.english: first of all the implacable Anankē of ancient Chaos.
text.note: ἀμέγαρτον is rare and debated; here rendered “implacable/inexorable.” The phrase presents personified Anankē associated with primordial Chaos (ἀρχαίου χάους). Some have proposed nuances like “unsociable” or “unwedded,” but “implacable” suits Anankē’s force.

text.greek: καὶ Κρόνον ὃς ἐλόχευσεν ἀπειρεσίοισιν ὑφ' ὁλκοῖς
text.english: and Kronos, who engendered beneath boundless birth‑pangs
text.note: Κρόνον in Orphic cosmogony is best understood as Chronos (Time), not the Titan Cronus. ἐλόχευσεν (“engendered/bring to birth”) suits cosmogonic begetting. The phrase ἀπειρεσίοισιν ὑφ’ ὁλκοῖς is difficult; many emend ὁλκοῖς to ὠδῖσι(ν) (“birth‑pangs”), which the translation reflects.

text.greek: Αἰθέρα καὶ διφυῆ περιωπέα κυδρὸν Ἔρωτα
text.english: Aither and the two‑formed, far‑seen, glorious Eros,
text.note: διφυῆ (“two‑formed”) is an Orphic epithet of Eros/Phanes, indicating androgyny; περιωπέα can mean “far‑seen” (conspicuous from afar) or “all‑seeing,” both fitting the luminous, manifest nature of Phanes.

text.greek: Νυκτὸς ἀειγνήτης πατέρα κλυτόν· ὃν ῥα Φάνητα
text.english: renowned father of ever‑born Nyx; whom indeed they call Phanes,
text.note: ἀειγνήτης is problematic in case and form; it is often taken as an epithet of Nyx meaning “ever‑born/everlasting,” and some editors emend to ἀειγενής. ὃν ῥα Φάνητα is elliptic for “whom indeed they call Phanes,” a common epic idiom. The line reflects the Orphic notion that Eros/Phanes is father of Nyx.

text.greek: ὁπλότεροι καλέουσι βροτοί· πρῶτος γὰρ ἐφάνθη·
text.english: The later‑born mortals call him Phanes; for he first shone forth;
text.note: “Hoplóteroi” = “later(-born)” or “younger.” The referent (supplied from context) is Protogonos/Phanes; πρῶτος γὰρ ἐφάνθη (“for he appeared/shone forth first”) etymologically explains the name Phanes. I supply “Phanes” in translation though the name is implicit in this line.

text.greek: Βριμοῦς τ' εὐδυνάτοιο γονὰς, ἠδ' ἔργ' ἀΐδηλα
text.english: and the child of Brimo of exceeding might, and the baleful deeds
text.note: Brimo is an epithet (often of Persephone, sometimes Hekate); “the child of Brimo” in Orphic myth is Zagreus-Dionysos. γονάς (plural) functions as “offspring/child”; εὐδυνάτοιο = “of mighty power.”

text.greek: Γηγενέων, οἳ λυγρὸν ἀπ' οὐρανοῦ ἐστάξαντο
text.english: of the Earth‑born, who from Heaven dripped the woeful blood.
text.note: Γηγενέων (“Earth‑born”) refers to the Giants. ἐστάξαντο is used intransitively/middle, with ellipsis of the noun “blood”; λυγρόν qualifies the omitted αἷμα. The line compresses the myth of Ouranos’ blood dripping from Heaven, from which the Earth‑born arose.

text.greek: σπέρμα γονῆς, τὸ πρόσθεν ὅθεν γένος ἐξεγένοντο
text.english: the seed of generation, whence aforetime the race sprang forth
text.note: σπέρμα γονῆς = “seed of begetting/procreation.” The plural verb ἐξεγένοντο with γένος (sg.) is awkward; many editors emend to γένε᾽ (pl.), “races,” to match the verb: “whence aforetime the races of mortals sprang forth.”

text.greek: θνητῶν, οἳ κατὰ γαῖαν ἀπείριτον αἰὲν ἔασι·
text.english: of mortals, who ever abide throughout the boundless earth;
text.note: Error: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'translations'

text.greek: θητείαν τε Ζηνὸς, ὀρεσσιδρόμου τε λατρείαν
text.english: and the service of Zeus, and the worship of the Mountain-roaming One.
text.note: θητεία and λατρεία are both cultic ‘service,’ here rendered as “service” and “worship” for nuance. ὀρεσσιδρόμου (“mountain‑roaming,” fem. gen. sg.) is a substantive epithet; the referent is debated (often taken as the Mother of the Gods, Rhea/Cybele, though Artemis is also possible).

text.greek: μητρὸς ἅτ' ἐν Κυβέλοις ὄρεσιν μητίσατο κούρην
text.english: as in the Kybelian mountains he contrived the Mother’s maiden,
text.note: Κυβέλοις ὄρεσιν = the mountains sacred to Kybele (the Phrygian/Rhean “Mother”); μητρὸς … κούρην = “the Mother’s maiden (daughter)”; μητίσατο (“contrived/devised”) has an understood subject from the prior context. The ‘Mother’ here is likely Demeter, syncretized with Kybele.

text.greek: Φερσεφόνην περὶ πατρὸς ἀμαιμακέτου Κρονίωνος·
text.english: Persephone, in regard to her father, the resistless Kronion;
text.note: Κρονίων (“Kronion”) is Zeus; ἀμαιμακέτος means “irresistible, unyielding.” The phrase περὶ πατρὸς indicates “with respect to (her) father,” reflecting the Orphic genealogy in which Zeus is Persephone’s father.

text.greek: εὐμήλου θ' Ἡρακλῆος περίφημον ἄμυξιν·
text.english: and the far‑famed wounding by Heracles at the fair‑fruited [garden].
text.note: εὐμήλου = “fair‑fruited,” commonly of the Hesperides’ garden (κῆπος understood elliptically); ἄμυξις = “gash, wounding,” here of Heracles’ blow against the guardian serpent (Ladon) when taking the apples.

text.greek: ὅρκιά τ' Ἰδαίων, Κορυβάντων τ' ἄπλετον ἰσχύν.
text.english: and the oaths of the Idaeans, and the boundless might of the Korybantes.
text.note: “Idaeans” probably means the Idaean Dactyls/Curetes, attendants of Rhea; ὅρκια can denote solemn, oath-bound rites; “Korybantes” are divine dancers/guardians; ἄπλετον = “boundless, measureless.”

text.greek: Δήμητρός τε πλάνην, καὶ Φερσεφόνης μέγα πένθος,
text.english: Demeter’s wandering, and Persephone’s great grief,
text.note: πλάνην alludes to Demeter’s search for Persephone; the “great grief” evokes Persephone’s abduction.

text.greek: θεσμοφόρος θ' ὡς ἦν· ἠδ' ἀγλαὰ δῶρα Καβείρων,
text.english: and how she was Thesmophoros; and the splendid gifts of the Kabeiroi,
text.note: Thesmophoros is Demeter’s epithet and the name of her festival; the Kabeiroi are Samothracian mystery deities.

text.greek: χρησμούς τ' ἀρρήτους Νυκτὸς περὶ Βάκχου ἄνακτος,
text.english: and the ineffable oracles of Nyx concerning lord Bakchos,
text.note: ἀρρήτους = “unspeakable,” i.e., esoteric; Nyx (Night) is linked with Bacchic mysteries; Bakchos = Dionysos.

text.greek: Λῆμνόν τε ζαθέην ἠδ' εἰναλίην Σαμοθράκην,
text.english: and holy Lemnos and sea‑girt Samothrace,
text.note: ζαθέην = “very holy”; εἰναλίην = “sea‑girt”; both islands were famed for mystery cults.

text.greek: αἰπεινήν τε Κύπρον, καὶ Ἀδωναίην Ἀφροδίτην
text.english: and steep Cyprus, and Adonaean Aphrodite,
text.note: Adonaean Aphrodite = Aphrodite in connection with Adonis; αἰπεινή is an epic epithet meaning “steep/lofty.”

text.greek: ὄργια Πραξιδίκης, καὶ ἀρείνης νυκτὸς Ἀθήνης
text.english: the orgies of Praxidikē, and of warlike Night‑Athena,
text.note: ὄργια = sacred rites; Praxidikē is a chthonic justice/avenger figure (or one of the Praxidikai). The phrase ἀρείνης νυκτὸς Ἀθήνης is textually uncertain; “Night‑Athena” is an obscure cult‑title, and ἀρείνης is often taken as “warlike.”

text.greek: θρήνους τ' Αἰγυπτίων καὶ Ὀσίριδος ἱερὰ χύτλα.
text.english: and the laments of the Egyptians and the sacred pots of Osiris.
text.note: θρῆνοι = ritual laments; ἱερὰ χύτλα (rare plural of χύτρα) are sacred earthen pots used in Osirian rites.

text.greek: Ἀμφὶ δὲ μαντείης ἐδάης πολυπείρονας οἴμους
text.english: And of divination you learned the much-tried pathways,

text.greek: θηρῶν οἰωνῶν τε καὶ ἣ σπλάγχνων θέσις ἐστίν·
text.english: of wild beasts and of birds, and that which is the disposition of the entrails;
text.note: θήσις σπλάγχνων: the “setting/arrangement of the entrails,” i.e., extispicy; θηρῶν οἰωνῶν distinguishes omens from beasts and from birds.

text.greek: ἠδ' ὅσα θεσπίζουσιν ὀνειροπόλοισιν ἀταρποῖς
text.english: and whatever they foretell on the dream-ways,
text.note: ὀνειροπόλοισιν ἀταρποῖς: literally “on dream-plying paths,” an instrumental dative for the channel/medium of revelation (“on the dream-ways”).

text.greek: ψυχαὶ ἐφημερίων, ὕπνῳ βεβολημέναι ἦτορ·
text.english: the souls of mortal men, their heart smitten by sleep;
text.note: ἐφήμεροι (“men of a day”) = mortals; ὕπνῳ βεβολημέναι ἦτορ “their heart struck by sleep” is an epic idiom for trance-like receptivity in dreams.

text.greek: σημείων τεράτων τε λύσεις, ἄστρων τε πορείας·
text.english: the unravellings of signs and portents, and the courses of the stars;
text.note: λύσεις (“untyings”) = interpretations/explanations; τέρατα = prodigies/portents.

text.greek: ἁγνοπόλον τε καθαρμὸν ἐπιχθονίοις μέγ' ὄνειαρ·
text.english: and the pure-working purification, a great boon to those upon the earth;
text.note: ἁγνοπόλος (rare) = “pure-working” as epithet of καθαρμός (purificatory rite); ἐπιχθόνιοι “earth-dwellers” = the living.

text.greek: ἱλασμούς τε θεῶν, φθιμένων τ' ἐπινήχυτα δῶρα.
text.english: and propitiations of the gods, and the gifts poured over the dead.
text.note: ἱλασμοί = propitiatory rites; ἐπινήχυτα δῶρα “gifts poured over,” i.e., libations/offerings for the dead (funerary choai).

text.greek: Ἄλλα δέ σοι κατέλεξ' ἅπερ εἴσιδον ἠδ' ἐνόησα,
text.english: Moreover, I have recounted to you the things I saw and understood,

text.greek: Ταίναρον ἡνίκ' ἔβην σκοτίην ὁδὸν, Ἄϊδος εἴσω,
text.english: when I went to Taenarum, the shadowy path within Aïdos,
text.note: Taenarum (Cape Tainaron) was famed as an entrance to the Underworld; Aïdos (genitive) here denotes the realm of Hades. “Shadowy path” renders the conventional epic σκοτίη ὁδός.

text.greek: ἡμετέρῃ πίσυνος κιθάρῃ δι' ἔρωτ' ἀλόχοιο·
text.english: trusting in my own kithara, for love of my wife;
text.note: πίσυνος with the dative means “trusting in.” “For love of my wife” alludes to Orpheus’ descent for Eurydice.

text.greek: ἠδ' ὅσον Αἰγυπτίων ἰερὸν λόγον ἐξελόχευσα,
text.english: and how much of the Egyptians’ sacred lore I ferreted out,
text.note: ἐξελόχευσα is a rare verb meaning “to spy out, ferret out, eavesdrop,” fitting the notion of esoteric Egyptian lore.

text.greek: Μέμφιν ἐς ἠγαθέην περάσας, ἱεράς τε πόληας
text.english: having crossed to glorious Memphis and the holy cities
text.note: ἠγαθέην is an epic epithet; “glorious”/“august” suits Memphis’ sacral prestige. πέρασας is aorist participle, “having crossed/after crossing.”

text.greek: Ἄπιδος ἃς πέρι Νεῖλος ἀγάρροος ἐστεφάνωται·
text.english: of Apis, which the loud‑rushing Neilos has wreathed about;
text.note: Ἄπις is the Egyptian bull‑god; “cities of Apis” points to cult‑centers around Memphis. ἀγάρροος = “loud‑rushing”; ἐστεφάνωται (“is wreathed”) metaphorically of Neilos encircling them.

text.greek: πάντα μάλ' ἀτρεκέως ἀπ' ἐμῶν στέρνων δεδάηκας.
text.english: all these things you have learned most exactly from my breast.
text.note: “From my breast” is a formula for “from my inmost understanding,” underscoring the accuracy of the report (μάλ’ ἀτρεκέως).

text.greek: - Νῦν δ' ἐπεὶ ἀερόφοιτος ἀπέπτατο δήϊος οἶστρος,
text.english: Now, since the baneful gadfly, air-roving, has flown off,
text.note: “δήϊος οἶστρος” is literally the “destructive/baleful gadfly”; οἶστρος can denote both the literal insect (cf. Io) and a god-sent frenzy or goad. “ἀερόφοιτος” (“air-roving”) underscores its wandering, inspired character.

text.greek: ἡμέτερον δέμας ἐκπρολιπὼν εἰς οὐρανὸν εὐρύν,
text.english: leaving our body behind and betaking itself to the broad heaven,
text.note: “ἡμέτερον δέμας” (“our body/frame”) uses the poetic first-person plural for a single speaker. “ἐκπρολιπών” intensifies “leaving utterly.” The phrase indicates the frenzy has departed the poet and gone heavenward.

text.greek: πεύσῃ ἀφ' ἡμετέρης ἐνοπῆς ὅσσα πρὶν ἔκευθον.
text.english: you shall learn from our voice all that before I kept concealed.
text.note: “ἐνοπή” means “sound, voice” (often of battle or song); here “voice/utterance.” “ὅσσα” = “all that.” “ἔκευθον” is epic imperfect 1sg of κεύθω, “I kept concealed,” fitting Orphic motifs of prior silence/secrecy.

text.greek: Ὥς ποτε Πιερίην Λειβήθρων τ' ἄκρα κάρηνα
text.english: Thus once he traversed Pieria and the towering peaks of Libethra,
text.note: Pieria and Libethra are Thracian/Macedonian haunts of the Muses; ἄκρα κάρηνα = “lofty peaks.”

text.greek: (ἡρώωντε καὶ ἡμιθέων πρόμος ἐξεπέρησε)
text.english: (foremost among heroes and demigods, he crossed over),
text.note: πρόμος = “foremost, champion, leader.” The verb ἐξεπέρασε supplies the motion for line 50; the referent is Jason as leader of the Argonauts.

text.greek: λισσόμενός μ' ἐπίκουρον ἑοῦ νόστοιο γενέσθαι
text.english: beseeching me to become an ally of his homecoming,
text.note: νόστος is the technical epic term for “homecoming.” ἐπίκουρος = “ally/helper.”

text.greek: ποντοπόρῳ σὺν νηῒ πρὸς ἄξενα φῦλ' ἀνθρώπων,
text.english: with a sea‑faring ship toward the inhospitable tribes of men,
text.note: ἄξενα (“inhospitable”) alludes to the Pontos Axeinos (later Euxinos), i.e., the Black Sea region.

text.greek: ἔθνος ἐς ἀφνειὸν καὶ ἀτάσθαλον ᾧ ἐνὶ κραῖνεν
text.english: to a wealthy and reckless nation, wherein ruled
text.note: ἀφνειός = “wealthy, rich”; ἀτάσθαλος = “reckless, overweening.” κραίνειν in epic can mean “to rule, hold sway.”

text.greek: Αἰήτης υἱὸς φαεσιμβρότου ἠελίοιο.
text.english: Aeëtes, son of Helios, light‑bringer to mortals.
text.note: φαεσιμβρότου = “light‑bringing to mortals,” an epithet of Helios; Aeëtes is the Colchian king, son of Helios.

text.greek: - Θέσφατα γὰρ Πελίας δειδίσσετο μή οἱ ὄπισθεν
text.english: For Pelias quailed before the oracular decrees, lest hereafter
text.note: - θέσφατα: “oracular decrees.” δειδίσσετο: iterative/imperfective ‘was in dread.’ ὄπισθεν here is adverbial = ‘in future, hereafter,’ not strictly spatial ‘from behind.’

text.greek: χειρὸς ὕπ' Αἰσονίδα καθέλῃ βασιλήϊον ἀρχήν.
text.english: the Aisonid by his hand should cast down his kingly rule.
text.note: - Αἰσονίδα = “the Aisonid,” i.e., Jason. The phrase χειρὸς ὑπ’ Αἰσονίδα is taken as ‘by the hand of the Aisonid’; the construction is slightly compressed (some would expect a genitive with ὑπό). βασίληϊον is the epic adjective ‘royal’; καθέλῃ ‘cast down, depose’ suits ἀρχή ‘rule, sovereignty.’

text.greek: Καί οἱ ὑπὸ πραπίδεσσι δόλου τρίβον ἠπερόπευε·
text.english: And within his heart she was plying the track of guile;
text.note: prapídes (“midriff, heart”) is epic for the seat of thought; dólou tríbon (“track/path of guile”) is a cognate-accusative phrase with ἠπερόπευε “was practising deception/beguilement,” here of the goddess instilling crafty counsel.

text.greek: τάσσε γὰρ ἐκ Κόλχων χρύσειον κῶας ἐνεῖκαι
text.english: for she was enjoining him to bring from the Kolchians the Golden Fleece
text.note: tásse (“array, set in order”) commonly = “enjoin, order” in epic; eneîkai is the aorist infinitive of enenkein “to bring/carry off.”

text.greek: Θεσσαλίην εὔπωλον. Ὁ δ' ὡς κλύεν ἔκνομον αὐδήν
text.english: to horse-rich Thessaly. And when he heard an out-of-measure voice,
text.note: éknomon (“out of rule/mode,” esp. of music) conveys a strange, unearthly quality to the voice—i.e., a divine manifestation.

text.greek: χεῖρας ἐπαντείνας ἐπεκέκλετο πότνιαν Ἥρην·
text.english: stretching forth his hands he called upon Lady Hērē;
text.note: pótniā “Lady” is a reverential epithet regularly used of goddesses; Hērē is transliterated.

text.greek: τήνδε γὰρ ἐκ μακάρων περιώσια κυδαίνεσκεν.
text.english: for among the Blessed he was wont to glorify her beyond the rest.
text.note: makárōn (“the Blessed”) = the gods; periósia “beyond the rest, especially”; the -sk- of kudaínasken marks customary/repeated action (“used to honor”).

text.greek: Ἡ δὲ παρ' εὐχωλῇσιν ἐφέσπετο κηδομένη περ·
text.english: But she attended upon the vows, being indeed full of care;
text.note: παρ’ εὐχωλῇσιν = “amid/along with (their) prayers/vows.” ἐφέσπετο here means “attended (to), was at hand for.” The pronoun “she” is Athena, anticipated and then named in line 66.

text.greek: ἔξοχα γὰρ μερόπων ἠγάζετο καὶ φιλέεσκεν
text.english: for above all mortals she admired and was wont to love
text.note: μερόπων = “mortals (men),” the Homeric term for articulate-speaking humans. ἠγάζετο conveys “admired/held in awe”; φιλέεσκεν (iterative) = “used to love/was wont to love.”

text.greek: δεινοβίην ἥρωα, περικλυτὸν Αἴσονος υἷα,
text.english: the dread-in-might hero, the far-famed son of Aison,
text.note: δεινοβίην (epic compound) ≈ “terrible/formidable in might,” modifying ἥρωα. περικλυτός = “far-famed.” Αἴσονος υἷα identifies Jason by his patronymic.

text.greek: καί ῥα καλεσσαμένη ἐπετέλλετο Τριτογενείη.
text.english: and, having called him, Tritogeneia gave her command.
text.note: Τριτογενείη is Athena’s epithet. καλεσσαμένη (“having called/summoned”) has an implicit object, naturally understood as the hero just mentioned; ἐπετέλλετο (middle) = “gave her command/charge.”

text.greek: Καί οἱ φηγινέην πρῶτον τεκτήνατο νῆα,
text.english: And for him she first fashioned an oak‑built ship,
text.note: φηγινέην from φηγός: in epic commonly ‘oak’ (not ‘beech’); τεκτήνατο (middle) with the dative οἱ = ‘she fashioned for him’; the subject (implied from context) is Pallas Athena.

text.greek: ἣ καὶ ὑπ' εἰλατίνοις ἐρετμοῖς ἁλιμυρέα βένθη
text.english: which also, beneath fir‑wood oars, the briny depths
text.note: εἰλατίνιος = ‘of fir’; hence ‘fir‑wood oars’. The phrase ὑπ’ … ἐρετμοῖς ‘under … oars’ is a standard epic way to mark propulsion by rowing; ἁλιμυρέα βένθη = ‘briny depths’ is formulaic.

text.greek: πρώτην ἐξεπέρησε, τρίβον δ' ἤνυσσε θαλάσσης.
text.english: was first to traverse, and made a track upon the sea.
text.note: πρῶτην ἐξεπέρασε = ‘was first to cross/traverse’; τρῖβον ἤνυσσε ‘made/achieved a track (path)’, i.e., opened a sea‑lane, stressing the ship’s pioneering voyage.

text.greek: - Ἀλλ' ὅτε δὴ συνάγειρεν ἀγακλειτοὺς βασιλῆας,
text.english: But when indeed he had gathered the illustrious kings together,
text.note: συνάγειρεν is epic aorist “gathered together”; ἀγακλειτούς = “very famed, illustrious,” an epic epithet.

text.greek: Θρῄκην εἰς εὔπωλον ἐπείγετο δῖος Ἰήσων,
text.english: to horse-rich Thrace hastened godlike Iason,
text.note: εὔπωλον = “rich in horses”; δῖος = “godlike” (Homeric epithet); ἐπείγετο imperfect middle “was hastening/pressed on.”

text.greek: καί μ' ἔκιχεν κιθάρην πολυδαίδαλον ἐντύνοντα,
text.english: and he came upon me as I was preparing the cunning-wrought kithara,
text.note: μ’ ἔκιχεν = “he came upon me” (aorist of κιχάνω); πολυδαίδαλον = “cunningly wrought, much-wrought”; ἐντύνω of instruments can imply “stringing/tuning.”

text.greek: ὄφρα κέ σοι μέλπων προχέω μελίγηρυν ἀοιδήν,
text.english: so that, singing, I might pour forth for you a honey-voiced song,
text.note: ὄφρα κέ introduces a purpose clause (“so that I might”); προχέω “pour forth” is idiomatic of song; μελίγηρυν = “honey-voiced.”

text.greek: κηλήσω δέ τε θῆρας ἰδ' ἑρπετὰ καὶ πετεηνά.
text.english: and enchant wild beasts, and creeping things, and winged creatures.
text.note: κηλέω = “enchant, bewitch (by song)”; θῆρας = “wild beasts”; ἑρπετά = “creeping things, reptiles”; πετεηνά = “winged creatures,” i.e., birds.

text.greek: Ἡνίκα δ' εἰς ἄντρον πολυήρατον εἰσεπέρησε,
text.english: But when he entered a much‑loved cavern,

text.greek: μείλιχον ἐκ λασίων στέρνων ἀνενείκατο φωνήν·
text.english: he lifted up a honey‑sweet voice from his shaggy breast;
text.note: Lasion sternon is a poetic plural (“shaggy breasts”); rendered as singular “breast” in English idiom. Meilichos means “gentle, honey‑sweet.”

text.greek: - "Ὀρφεῦ Καλλιόπης τε καὶ Οἰάγρου φίλε κοῦρε,
text.english: - "Orpheus, dear son of Kalliope and Oiagros,
text.note: Kalliope and Oiagros are Orpheus’ parents; phile koure is “dear son/child.”

text.greek: Βιστονίῃ Κικόνεσσι πολυρρήνοισιν ἀνάσσων
text.english: ruling in Bistonia over the Ciconians rich in flocks,
text.note: Bistonia is a Thracian district; the Kikones (Ciconians) are a Thracian people. Polyrrhēnoisin means “rich in flocks (many‑sheep).”

text.greek: χαῖρ' ἐπεὶ Αἱμονίους ὀχεὰς πρώτιστον ἱκάνω,
text.english: hail, since for the first time I arrive at the Haemonian watercourses,
text.note: Haemonian here refers to Mt. Haemus (Aimos) in Thrace, not Thessaly; ocheai are “channels, watercourses.” Prōtiston = “for the first time.”

text.greek: Στρυμονίους τε ῥοὰς, Ῥοδόπης τ' αἰπεινὰ πρὸς ἄγκη.
text.english: and the Strymonian streams, and toward the sheer glens of Rhodope."
text.note: Strymon is the Thracian river; Rhodope is the neighboring mountain range. Ankē are “glens,” aipeina “steep, sheer.”

text.greek: Εἰμὶ δ' ἐγὼ Μινύαισι πανέξοχον αἷμα λελογχώς
text.english: And I, among the Minyans, have inherited blood preeminent above all.
text.note: Minyans: the Minyan people/Argonauts. “Blood” (haima) = lineage; πανέξοχον “preeminent above all”; λελογχώς is the perfect participle of λαγχάνω, “to obtain by lot, inherit,” conveying inherited nobility.

text.greek: Θεσσαλὸς Αἰσονίδης· ξεῖνος δέ τοι εὔχομαι εἶναι.
text.english: A Thessalian, Aisonides; and I declare myself your guest‑friend.
text.note: Aisonides = “son of Aison” (Jason). εὔχομαι here means “profess/avow,” not “pray”; ξένος denotes a formal guest‑friendship; τοι is the ethical dative “to you.”

text.greek: Ἀλλὰ, φίλος, πρόφρων μ' ὑποδέχνυσο καὶ κλύε μῦθον
text.english: But, friend, receive me with ready heart and hearken to my word
text.note: ὑποδέχνυσο is likely an epic/morphological variant for ὑποδέξαι/ὑποδέχου “receive”; many editors print a form of ὑποδέχομαι. κλύε μῦθον is a conventional epic formula “listen to my word.”

text.greek: μειλιχίαις ἀκοαῖς, καὶ λισσομένῳ ὑπάκουσον
text.english: with gentle ears, and, as I entreat, give heed,

text.greek: Ἀξείνου Πόντοιο μυχοὺς καὶ Φᾶσιν ἐρυμνόν
text.english: to draw near the inmost recesses of Axenos Pontos and the stout Phasis
text.note: Axenos Pontos is the “Inhospitable Sea” (older name of the Black Sea). μυχοί = “innermost recesses.” ἐρυμνός (“stout, well-defended”) is applied unusually to Phasis (river/region), conveying strength or fortified character.

text.greek: νηῒ σὺν Ἀργῴῃ πελάσαι δεῖξαί τε θαλάσσης
text.english: with the ship Argo, and to point out the maiden paths of the sea,
text.note: “maiden paths” (παρθενίης ἀτραπούς) = untraveled, virgin sea-ways.

text.greek: παρθενίης ἀτραποὺς, ἐπιήρατον ἡρώεσσιν,
text.english: dear to the heroes,

text.greek: οἵ ῥα τεὴν μίμνουσι χέλυν καὶ θέσφατον ὀμφήν
text.english: who indeed await your chelys-lyre and god-ordained voice,
text.note: χελύς here denotes the tortoise-shell lyre (chelys-lyre). θέσφατος ὀμφή = “god-ordained/prophetic voice,” of inspired song.

text.greek: ἐλπόμενοι ξυνὸν πελάγει ἐπαρηγόνα μόχθων.
text.english: hoping for common succor in their labors upon the sea.
text.note: ξυνὸν … ἐπαρήγονα = “common aid/helper,” i.e., a shared succor to all the heroes; πελάγει is a dative of sphere (“upon the sea”).

text.greek: Οὐ γὰρ δὴ πλῶσαι πρὸς βάρβαρα φῦλα μέδονται
text.english: For indeed they do not purpose to sail toward barbarian peoples
text.note: “Barbarian peoples” = non-Greek nations, here likely the Colchians; μέδονται = “intend, have in mind”; πλῶσαι = “to set sail.”

text.greek: νόσφι σέθεν· καὶ γάρ ῥα ποτὶ ζόφον ἠερόεντα
text.english: apart from you; for even toward the misty gloom
text.note: νόσφι σέθεν = “apart from you [singular],” probably addressed to Jason; ζόφον ἠερόεντα is a Homeric formula for “misty gloom” (often of the underworld or far west); the thought is enjambed into the next line.

text.greek: νείατον εἰς κευθμῶνα, λιτῆς εἰς πυθμένα γαίης,
text.english: into the nethermost recess, by supplication to the very base of the earth,
text.note: λιτῆς is best taken as a genitive of means (“by supplication/prayer”); νείατον κευθμῶνα and πυθμένα γαίης evoke the underworld as the earth’s lowest hidden place and very foundation.

text.greek: μοῦνον ἀπ' ἀνθρώπων πελάσαι καὶ νόστον ἀνευρεῖν·
text.english: to draw near, alone among men, and to discover a return;
text.note: νόστος here implies a return from the underworld; μοῦνον ἀπ’ ἀνθρώπων = “alone among mortals,” stressing uniqueness.

text.greek: ὧν ἕνεκεν ξυνήν τε δύην Μινύαισιν ἀρέσθαι
text.english: for which cause he undertook a shared distress to gratify the Minyae.
text.note: ξυνήν τε δύην = “a common/shared woe” (ξυνήν ‘shared’ + δύη ‘woe, distress’). ἀρέσθαι can be understood either as ‘to choose/undertake (for oneself)’ or ‘to please/propitiate’ with the dative; the translation renders a mediating sense (“undertook … to gratify”). Μινύαισιν = the Minyae, i.e., the Argonauts.

text.greek: καὶ κλέος ἀνθρώποισιν ἐπ' ἐσσομένοισι πυθέσθαι."
text.english: and that renown may be heard among men in generations yet to come.
text.note: κλέος = “renown, fame”; πυθέσθαι (aor. mid.) = “to learn, hear of”; ἐπ’ ἐσσομένοισι (dat. pl.) = “among/for those yet to come,” i.e., future generations.

text.greek: Τὸν μὲν ἐγὼ μύθοισιν ἀμειβόμενος προσέειπον·
text.english: Him then I, answering with words, addressed:
text.note: Epic formula: μύθοισιν … προσέειπον “addressed with words”; ἀμειβόμενος = “in reply.”

text.greek: - "Αἰσονίδη, τί με ταῦτα παραιφάμενος ἐρεείνεις,
text.english: “Aisonides, why, coaxing me, do you ask me these things?”
text.note: Αἰσονίδη (voc.) = “son of Aison,” i.e., Iason/Jason. παραιφάμενος carries the nuance “coaxing, trying to draw me out” (also “beguile” in Homeric usage). ἐρεείνεις is Homeric for “you question/ask closely.”

text.greek: ὄφρα κεν ἐς Κόλχους Μινύαις ἐπιήρανος ἔλθω,
text.english: so that I might come to the Colchians, well-pleasing to the Minyans,
text.note: ὄφρα κεν with subjunctive expresses purpose (“so that I might”). ἐπιήρανος = “well-pleasing/propitious, serviceable.” Μινύαις (“the Minyans”) is a poetic designation for the Argonauts.

text.greek: νηῒ σὺν εὐσέλμῳ πλεύσας ἐπὶ οἴνοπα πόντον;
text.english: sailing in the well-benched ship over the wine-dark sea?
text.note: νηῒ σὺν εὐσέλμῳ = “in/with the well-benched ship” (epic formula for a well-rowed vessel). οἴνοπα πόντον = “wine-dark sea.” The transmitted punctuation makes this a rhetorical question.

text.greek: ἤδη γάρ μοι ἅλις καμάτων, ἅλις ἔπλετο μόχθων,
text.english: for already for me there is enough of toils, enough there has been of hardships,
text.note: ἅλις + genitive = “enough, in plenty.” ἔπλετο functions existentially (“has proved to be/has been”). The pairing καμάτοι/μόχθοι is a traditional hendiadys for “toils/hardships.”

text.greek: ὧν ἱκόμην ἐπὶ γαῖαν ἀπείριτον ἠδὲ πόληας
text.english: to whose boundless land and cities I came,
text.note: ὧν (gen. pl.) picks up an antecedent from the broader context (“those” among whom/whose), yielding “to whose land and cities.” ἀπείριτον = “boundless, limitless”; ἐπὶ + acc. with ἱκόμην expresses motion “to/upon.”

text.greek: Αἰγύπτῳ Λιβύῃ τε βροτοῖς ἀνὰ θέσφατα φαίνων.
text.english: in Egypt and in Libya, revealing to mortals the divine oracles.
text.note: ἀνὰ with θέσφατα is adverbial/intensive (“abroad, all around”), here best rendered simply as “revealing” or “showing forth.” θέσφατα = “divine oracles/utterances.” The datives Αἰγύπτῳ Λιβύῃ function locatively (“in Egypt and Libya”), while βροτοῖς is the indirect object (“to mortals”).

text.greek: Καί με ἀλητείης τε καὶ ἐξ οἴστρου ἐσάωσε
text.english: And she delivered me both from wandering and from the gadfly’s goad,
text.note: οἶστρος literally “gadfly,” emblematic of maddening goad (cf. Io), hence also “frenzy”; ἐσάωσε is an epic form meaning “saved/delivered.”

text.greek: μήτηρ ἡμετέρη καί ῥ' εἰς δόμον ἤγαγεν ἄλλον
text.english: my mother; and then she led me into another house,
text.note: εἰς δόμον ἄλλον = “into another house/household”; the object “me” is supplied from the previous line; καί ῥ’ conveys “and then.”

text.greek: ὄφρα τέλος θανάτοιο κίχω μετὰ γήραϊ λυγρῷ.
text.english: so that I might attain the term of death amid grievous old age.
text.note: τέλος θανάτοιο (“the end/term of death”) is a formula for life’s end; κίχω = “reach/attain” (epic); μετὰ with dative = “amid/with”; λυγρός = “grievous, baleful.”

text.greek: Ἀλλ' οὐκ ἔσθ' ὑπαλύξαι ἃ δὴ πεπρωμένα κεῖται.
text.english: But there is no escaping what indeed lies appointed by fate.
text.note: ὑπαλύξαι = aorist infinitive ‘to escape’ (Homeric); πεπρωμένα = ‘things fated/appointed’ (perf. part. of the verb underlying πέπρωται); κεῖται adds the sense of being fixed/established; δὴ is an intensifier (‘indeed’).

text.greek: Μοιρῶν ἐννεσίῃσιν ἐπείγομαι· οὐ γὰρ ἄτιμοι
text.english: I hasten under the promptings of the Moirai; for not dishonored
text.note: ἐννεσίῃσιν = “promptings/instigations”; Moirai = the Fates. The litotes “not dishonored” preserves the elevated tone.

text.greek: ἱκεσίου Ζηνὸς κοῦραι Λιταί· ἵξομαι ἤδη
text.english: are the Litai, maidens of Zeus Hikesios; I shall now come
text.note: Litai (“Prayers”), personified daughters of Zeus; “Zeus Hikesios” = Zeus of Suppliants. The phrasing recalls Il. 9.502–12.

text.greek: ὁπλοτέροις βασιλεῦσι καὶ ἡμιθέοις ἐνάριθμος."
text.english: as one numbered among the younger kings and the demigods.
text.note: ὁπλοτέροις = “younger,” i.e., of a later generation; ἐνάριθμος = “counted among, reckoned with.” The younger “kings and demigods” are the Argonautic cohort.

text.greek: - Καὶ τότε δὴ λίπον ἄντρον ἐπήρατον ἠδ' ἐπέρησα
text.english: And then indeed I left the lovely cave and crossed beyond,
text.note: τότε δὴ marks a narrative transition; ἄντρον ἐπήρατον = a conventional epic epithet “lovely cave.”

text.greek: αὐτῇ σὺν φόρμιγγι καὶ εἰς Μινύας ἀφίκανον
text.english: with my very phorminx, and I came to the Minyae
text.note: φόρμιγξ (phorminx) is the epic lyre; αὐτῇ emphasizes “the very” instrument. ἀφίκανον is an epic 1st-sing. aorist (“I came”).

text.greek: λαιψηροῖσι πόδεσσιν, ὑπὲρ Παγασηΐδας ἀκτάς.
text.english: with nimble feet, over the Pagasaean strands.
text.note: ὑπέρ with the accusative here = “over/along.” “Pagasaean” refers to Pagasae, the harbor of Iolkos, point of Argonautic departure.

text.greek: Ἔνθα δ' ἀριστήων Μινυῶν λόχος ἠγερέθοντο
text.english: There then the band of the best of the Minyans assembled,
text.note: λόχος “band, company”; ἀριστήων is a partitive genitive “of the best.” The plural verb ἠγερέθοντο with the collective singular λόχος is an epic synesis (“the company assembled”).

text.greek: στεῖνον δὴ ψαμάθους ὁμάδῳ, ῥηγμῖνα τ' Ἀναύρου.
text.english: upon the narrow sands with a roar, and at the surf of Anauros.
text.note: στεῖνον is a substantivized adjective “narrow (strip),” here best taken with the following accusatives as an accusative of place attained with ἠγερέθοντο (“they assembled to the narrow sands … and to the surf”). ὁμάδῳ is instrumental dative “with a din/roar.” ῥηγμῖνα (acc. sg.) is “surf, breaker”; Ἀναύρου is the Thessalian river Anauros near Iolkos.

text.greek: Ἀλλ' ὅτε δή μ' ἐνόησαν ἀταρπιτὸν ἐξανύοντα,
text.english: But when indeed they perceived me making my way by a trackless path,
text.note: ἀταρπιτὸν (“trackless”) is used substantively/adverbially; ἐξανύω here = “to make good, win through (a route).” Hence “making my way by a trackless path.”

text.greek: ἀσπασίως ἤγερθεν· ἐγήθεε δ' ἦτορ ἑκάστῳ·
text.english: they rose gladly, and the heart in each rejoiced;
text.note: ἀσπασίως = “gladly, with welcome”; ἤγερθεν is intransitive aorist passive “rose up.”

text.greek: αὐτὰρ ἐμυθεόμην, ἐρεείνων ἄνδρας ἀρίστους.
text.english: but I spoke, questioning the noblest men.
text.note: ἐμυθεόμην is the formal epic “I spoke/uttered words”; ἐρεείνων = “inquiring closely, questioning.” ἄνδρας ἀρίστους can mean “the chiefs/leading men.”

text.greek: - Πρῶτα δὲ εἶδα βίην Ἡρακλῆος θείοιο
text.english: First I beheld the might of divine Herakles,

text.greek: ὃν τέκεν Ἀλκμήνη Ζηνὶ Κρονίωνι μιγεῖσα
text.english: whom Alkmene bore to Zeus Kronion, having mingled with him,

text.greek: ἦμος ὅτε τρισσὴν μὲν ἐλείπετο Σείριος αἴγλην
text.english: when Helios was leaving the threefold blaze of Seirios,
text.note: Seirios is the Dog‑star; “threefold blaze” (trissēn aiglēn) is obscure—often taken as an intensive for the dog‑day glare; the juxtaposition with night “creeping” marks the onset of evening.

text.greek: Ἠέλιος, δολιχὴ δ' ἐπεμαίετο πάντοθεν ὄρφνη·
text.english: and long darkness was creeping on from every side;

text.greek: Τῖφύν τ' Ἀγνιάδην, δολιχῆς ἰθύντορα νηός·
text.english: and Tiphys Agniades, steersman of the long ship;
text.note: Agniades = “son of Agnias” (often transmitted as Hagnias); ithyntōr = technical term for “steersman.”

text.greek: Θεσπιέων δ' ὅγε τῆμος ἐφ' ὕδασι Τελμισσοῖο
text.english: who then was upon the Thespian waters of Telmissos,
text.note: Θεσπιέων … Σιφάεσι places the scene in Boeotia (Siphae was the port of Thespiae). Τελμισσοῖο is problematic; many emend to Τιλφυσσοῖο (of Tilphousa) or posit a local Telmissos. Translation retains the transmitted reading.

text.greek: ἄγχουρος λαοῖς Σιφάεσι ῥεῖθρον ἄμειβεν·
text.english: traversing the shore-hugging current among the Siphaean folk;
text.note: ἄγχουρος = “near‑shore, coast‑hugging”; ῥεῖθρον here “current/stream” of the harbor.

text.greek: ὃς περὶ μὲν βύκταισι καὶ ἀργήεσσιν ἀέλλαις
text.english: who, amid choppy seas and gleaming squalls,
text.note: βύκταισι is rare; likely “short, steep seas/choppy billows.” ἀργήεσσ(ι) ἀέλλαις = “gleaming/bright squalls,” i.e., spray‑flashing gusts.

text.greek: νῆα κατιθύνειν δέδαεν πολυμήτιδι τέχνῃ·
text.english: knew to set the ship straight by resourceful craft;

text.greek: Κάστορά θ' ἱππόδαμον Πολυδεύκεά τ' εἰσενόησα
text.english: and I beheld horse‑taming Kastor and Polydeukes,

text.greek: καὶ Μόψον Τιταρῆθεν, ὃν Ἄμπυκι νυμφευθεῖσα
text.english: and Mopsos from Titarēssos, whom, once wedded to Ampyx,
text.note: Τιταρῆθεν = “from Titarēssos,” the Thessalian river (cf. Il. 2.751–5).

text.greek: Χαονίην ὑπὸ φηγὸν Ἀρηγονὶς ἐξελόχευσε·
text.english: Arēgonis bore beneath a Chaonian oak;
text.note: “Chaonian oak” evokes the sacred oaks of Dodona in Epirus; ἐξελόχευσε is epic for “bore (in childbirth).”

text.greek: Πηλέα τ' Αἰακίδην, Αἰγίνης ἀγλαὸν υἱόν
text.english: and Peleus the Aiakid, glorious son of Aigina,
text.note: Aiakid = descendant of Aiakos; Aigina is mother of Aiakos, hence Peleus is his son.

text.greek: ὃς Δολόπεσσιν ἄνασσεν ἐνὶ Φθίῃ ἐριβώλῳ.
text.english: who ruled the Dolopes in much‑nourishing Phthia.

text.greek: Τρισσὴν δ' Ἑρμείαο κλυτὴν εἰσέδρακα γένναν,
text.english: And thrice have I seated on board the illustrious stock of Hermes,
text.note: εἰσέδρακα (“I have seated [on board]”) is a cataloguing formula in this poem; τρισσὴν … γένναν indicates that three sons of Hermes are among the crew.

text.greek: Αἰθαλίδην, ὃν ἔτικτε περικλυτὴ Εὐπολέμεια,
text.english: Aithalides, whom far-famed Eupolemeia bore,
text.note: Eupolemeia (otherwise obscure) is here the mother of Aithalides; her parentage is specified in the next line.

text.greek: Μυρμιδόνος θυγάτηρ, Ἀλόπῃ ἐνὶ πετρηέσσῃ
text.english: daughter of Myrmidon, in rocky Alope;
text.note: Alope (Ἀλόπη) is a rocky locale, likely the Thessalian/Phthiotian Alope; πετρηέσσῃ = “rocky.”

text.greek: ἠδ' Ἔρυτον, καὶ καλὸν Ἐχίονα, τούς ποτε Νύμφῃ
text.english: and Erytos, and fair Echion, whom once
text.note: τούς refers specifically to Erytos and Echion (not to Aithalides). The name Ἔρυτον here is often elsewhere Εὔρυτον (Eurytos).

text.greek: Λαοθόῃ Μενετοῖο παρευνηθεὶς ἐλόχευσε
text.english: lying beside the Nymph Laothoë, daughter of Menetos, he fathered,
text.note: παρευνηθείς ἐλόχευσε: with a male subject (Hermes), “to bring to birth” = “to beget/father” after lying with; Laothoë is styled a Nymph and daughter of Menetos.

text.greek: Κυλλήνης μεδέων χρυσόρραπις Ἀργειφόντης.
text.english: the golden‑wanded Argeiphontes, lord of Kyllene.
text.note: Κυλλήνης μεδέων = “lord of Kyllene,” a standard Hermes title; χρυσόρραπις = “golden‑wanded”; Ἀργειφόντης is the epithet “Argeiphontes.”

text.greek: Αὐτίκα δ' Ἀκτορίδης καὶ βουφάγος ἦλθε Κόρωνος.
text.english: Straightway came the Aktorides and ox‑devouring Koronos.
text.note: Aktorides is a patronymic, ‘son of Aktor’ (often taken to refer to Menoetius of Opus in Argonautic catalogues). The syntax is awkward: the singular ἦλθε with two apparent nominatives (Ἀκτορίδης and Κόρωνος) suggests that Ἀκτορίδης and βουφάγος may function as appositive epithets to Κόρωνος; alternatively some emend ἦλθε to plural ἦλθον. βουφάγος literally means ‘ox‑devouring.’

text.greek: Ἴφικλος αὖ Φυλάκου δῖον γένος ἀντετόρησεν
text.english: Iphiklos too, illustrious scion of Phylakos, stepped forth in turn.
text.note: The verb ἀντετόρησεν is rare; likely built on τορέω (“to bore; to set forth distinctly”). In this catalogic context it is best taken as “answered/stepped forth in turn.” Some editors suspect a corruption and have proposed verbs like ἀντεβόλησεν (“met, came forward to meet”). “δῖον γένος” preserves the epic formula “illustrious/divine-born.”

text.greek: Βούτης τ' Αἰνειάδης, ἴκελος χρυσάορι Φοίβῳ.
text.english: And Boutes, son of Aineias, like unto gold-sworded Phoibos.
text.note: Αἰνειάδης is a patronymic; Orphic Argonautica differs from Apollonius (who makes Boutes son of Teleon). Whether the patronymic points to Aineias (chronologically problematic) or a figure Aineus is debated. ἴκελος governs the dative (“like unto”), and χρυσάωρ is the traditional epithet of Phoibos (“gold-sworded”).

text.greek: Κάνθος δ' Εὐβοίηθεν Ἀβαντιάδης ἐπέρησεν
text.english: But Canthus, Abantiades, sailed across from Euboea.
text.note: “Abantiades” = ‘son of Abas’; the Euboeans were called Abantes. ἐπέρησεν means ‘sailed across/crossed by sea’.

text.greek: ὃν δὴ μοῖρ' ἐδάμασσε, τέλος δ' ἐπέθηκεν ἀνάγκη
text.english: whom indeed Moira subdued, and Ananke imposed his doom.
text.note: Moira and Ananke are personified Fate and Necessity; τέλος ἐπέθηκεν = ‘imposed/appointed his end (doom)’.

text.greek: φθίσθαι ὑπὲρ Λιβύης, νόστον δ' οἴκοιο λαθέσθαι.
text.english: to perish off Libya, and to be bereft of the homecoming to his house.
text.note: ὑπὲρ Λιβύης = ‘off (the coast of) Libya’; νόστον … λαθέσθαι means ‘to miss/lose the homecoming,’ not mere mental ‘forgetting.’

text.greek: Ἄλκωνος δὲ Φάληρος ἀπ' Αἰσήποιο ῥοάων
text.english: And Phaleros, son of Alkon, from the streams of Aisepos,
text.note: Aisepos is the river in the Troad/Mysia; ῥοάων (“streams”) is a poetic genitive plural. The Orphic poet here departs from the common Athenian origin of Phaleros attested elsewhere.

text.greek: ἤλυθεν, ὃς Γύρτωνος ἁλιστεφὲς ἔκτισεν ἄστυ.
text.english: came, who founded the sea-crowned city of Gyrton.
text.note: ἁλιστεφές (“sea-crowned”) is a conventional epic epithet for coastal places; its application to Gyrton (usually the inland Thessalian city, Γυρτών/Γυρτώνη) is problematic and may be formulaic or reflect a different/local Gyrton-tradition. ἔκτισεν ἄστυ is the standard “founded a city” formula.

text.greek: Ἴφιτος αὖ μετὰ τοῖσιν ἐφέσπετο Ναυβόλου υἱός
text.english: Iphitus in turn followed with them, the son of Naubolus.
text.note: ἐφέσπετο (middle) “followed in their train”; the phrase μετὰ τοῖσιν is Homeric/formulaic.

text.greek: Φωκίδος ὅς ῥ' ἤνασσε καὶ εὐπύργοιο Τανάγρης.
text.english: who was lord over Phocis and well‑towered Tanagra.
text.note: ἤνασσε (“was lord over”) governs the genitive (Φωκίδος, Τανάγρης). Tanagra is Boeotian; the poet credits Iphitus with rule over both Phocis and well‑towered Tanagra, reflecting fluid regional attributions in epic geography. εὐπύργοιο is a stock epithet for fortified cities.

text.greek: Λαοδόκος, Ταλαὸς καὶ Ἀρήϊος, υἱοὶ ἄμωμοι
text.english: Laodokos, Talaos, and Areios, blameless sons,
text.note: The three are presented as the blameless sons of Pêrô (by Bias); Areios (Ἀρήϊος, with diaeresis marking hiatus) is a lesser‑attested brother alongside Talaos (well known as Adrastos’ father). The epithet “blameless” (ἄμωμος) is a standard epic honorific.

text.greek: ἦλθον Ἀβαντιάδαι περιώνυμοι οὓς τέκε Πηρώ.
text.english: came, the renowned Abantiads, whom Pêrô bore.
text.note: “Abantiads” (Ἀβαντιάδαι) is a patronymic/ethnic for Argives, i.e., descendants of Abas; thus the phrase marks them as Argive nobles. Pêrô is the daughter of Neleus, traditionally the wife of Bias and mother of these sons.

text.greek: Ἰφιδάμας δ' Ἀλέου παῖς ἤλυθε· πέμψε γὰρ αὐτόν
text.english: And Iphidamas, son of Aleus, came; for his stalwart sire sent him forth
text.note: ἴφθιμος is a Homeric epithet (“stalwart, mighty”); γενέτης = “begetter, father.” Aleus is the Arcadian king of Tegea; naming Iphidamas as his son is a distinctive Orphic genealogy (elsewhere Aleus is chiefly father of Ancaeus and Cepheus).

text.greek: ἴφθιμος γενέτης, Τεγέης ὅρια προλιπόντα.
text.english: after leaving the bounds of Tegea.
text.note: ὅρια = “bounds, borders” of the land; προλιπόντα (acc. masc. sg.) modifies αὐτόν and is temporal: “after leaving/when he had left.”

text.greek: Ἤλυθε δ' Ἐργῖνος, Βράγχου πολύπυρον ἄρουραν
text.english: And Erginus came, leaving the grain‑rich ploughland of Branchus,
text.note: Branchus is the eponymous hero of the Branchidae, the prophetic clan at Didyma near Miletus; aroura = cultivated/ploughland, here “grain‑rich” (polypyros). The passage marks Erginus’ origin in the Milesian territory.

text.greek: ἐκπρολιπὼν καὶ τύρσιν ἐρυμνῆς Μιλήτοιο,
text.english: and the turreted citadel of well‑fortified Miletus,
text.note: Tyrsis is an archaic epic word for “citadel, towered town”; erymnos means “strong, well‑fortified.” The phrase denotes the city of Miletus.

text.greek: ἔνθα ῥοαὶ κλύζουσι πολυπλανέος Μαιάνδρου.
text.english: where the streams of much‑wandering Maeander wash about.
text.note: Polyplanes (“much‑wandering”) is the traditional epithet of the winding river Maeander. Rhoai klyzousi literally “the streams wash/surge,” i.e., around the site of Miletus at the Maeander’s mouth.

text.greek: Ἐν δὲ Περικλύμενος Νηλήϊος εἰσαφίκανεν,
text.english: And among them Neleïan Periklymenos arrived,
text.note: “Neleïan” (Nēlēïos) = son/descendant of Neleus; Periklymenos is the famed Pylian hero. The verb “arrived” renders eisa-phíkanen, the standard epic verb for coming to the muster/ship.

text.greek: ἀγχόθι Πελλήνης τε καὶ εὐύδροιο Λιπάξου
text.english: close by Pellene and well-watered Lipaxos,
text.note: ἀγχόθι governs the genitive (“near to”). Pellene is the Achaean city; Lipaxos is otherwise obscure—likely a local river or site—here marked by the epic epithet “well‑watered.”

text.greek: ἄστυ λιπὼν ἀφνειὸν ὀρειονόμους τε Κολώνας.
text.english: having left the wealthy city and the mountain‑pastured Kolonai.
text.note: ὀρειονόμους (“mountain‑pastured”) is a rare compound qualifying Kolonai (acc. pl.). The phrase “near Pellene and Lipaxos” most naturally modifies “the wealthy city,” with Kolonai as an additional locality left behind. Identification of Kolonai in this context is uncertain.

text.greek: Ἐκ δὲ λιπὼν Καλυδῶνα θοὸς Μελέαγρος ἔβαινεν.
text.english: And, leaving Kalydon, swift Meleagros set out.
text.note: θόος is a stock epic epithet (“swift”); Kalydon is Meleagros’ Aitolian city. The imperfect ἔβαινεν (“was going”) in catalog style conveys the action of setting out; in some epic contexts βαίνω can imply “go aboard,” but here it is general ‘set out/went.’

text.greek: Οἰνεὺς τόν ῥ' ἐλόχευσε καὶ Ἀλθαίη ῥοδόπηχυς.
text.english: Oineus was his sire, and Althaia, rosy‑armed, bore him.
text.note: ἐλόχευσε (“bore”) is a Homeric/epic genealogical formula used of the mother; the father’s name is coordinated in the nominative though the singular verb agrees notionally with the mother. Hence the idiomatic rendering supplies “was his sire” for Oineus. ῥοδόπηχυς = “rosy‑armed,” an ornamental epithet. The pronoun τόν refers to the hero named in the preceding line (traditionally Meleager).

text.greek: Ἴφικλος αὖτ' ἐπέρησε λιπὼν Ἀτρακηίδα λίμνην,
text.english: Iphiklos in turn crossed over, leaving the Atracian lake,
text.note: “Atracian lake” likely refers to the Thessalian region around Atrax (cf. the Boebeian lake near Iolkos); the exact hydronym is debated. ἐπέρασε with the participle λιπών conveys departure (“crossed over, having left…”).

text.greek: σύγγονος Ἀλθαίης· περὶ δ' αὖ τίεν ἔξοχα πάντων
text.english: a kinsman of Althaia; and he honored, above all others, the fair‑formed Meleagros,
text.note: σύγγονος Ἀλθαίης identifies this Iphiklos as Althaia’s brother (a Thestiad), hence Meleagros’ maternal uncle—distinct from the Thessalian Iphiklos son of Phylakos found elsewhere. The intensifying περὶ … ἔξοχα πάντων underscores the superlative honor.

text.greek: εὐειδῆ Μελέαγρον, ἰδ' ἀγλαὰ ἔργ' ἐδίδασκεν.
text.english: and he taught him glorious deeds.
text.note: ἰδ’ = ἠδέ (“and”). ἀγλαὰ ἔργα is a formula for “glorious exploits,” especially martial prowess. The imperfects τίεν and ἐδιδάσκεν suggest habitual action (“he used to honor/teach”).

text.greek: Ἀστερίων δ' ἐπέρησε πάϊς κλεινοῖο Κομήτου,
text.english: And Asterion crossed over, the son of renowned Komētus,
text.note: ἐπέρησε (“crossed over”) is the conventional epic verb for setting out across the sea; παῖς here = “son.”

text.greek: Πειρεσίην ὃς ἔναιεν ἐπ' Ἀπιδανοῖο ῥεέθροις·
text.english: who dwelt in Peiresiae by the streams of the Apidanus;
text.note: Πειρεσίην is a poetic accusative of place for “in Peiresiae”; the Apidanus is a tributary in Thessaly.

text.greek: Πηνειὸς μίσγων ξυνὸν ῥόον εἰς ἅλα πέμπει.
text.english: Peneus, mingling them, bears their common current into the sea.
text.note: ξυνὸν (“common”) is the older form of κοινόν; the line describes the confluence of Apidanus with Peneus, which then carries the joined waters to the sea.

text.greek: Εὐρυδάμας δ' ἐπόρευσε λιπὼν Βοιβηΐδα λίμνην,
text.english: And Eurydamas set forth, leaving Lake Boibeïs,
text.note: Boibeïs (Lake Boebeis) is the Thessalian lake near Pherae; ἐπόρευσε is epic active used intransitively, “went/advanced.”

text.greek: ἀγχόθι Πηνειοῖο καὶ εὐπελαγέος Μελιβοίης.
text.english: near the Peneios and fair‑open‑sea’d Meliboia.
text.note: ἀγχόθι governs both genitives (Πηνειοῖο, Μελιβοίης). εὐπελαγέος literally “of good/open sea,” here marking Meliboia’s exposure to the open Aegean; hence “fair‑open‑sea’d.”

text.greek: Αὐτὰρ ἔπειτ' Ἐλάτοιο πάϊς Πολύφημος ἵκανεν
text.english: But then the son of Elatos, Polyphemos, arrived,

text.greek: ὅς σφιν ἐν ἠνορέῃσι μετέπρεπεν Ἡρώεσσιν·
text.english: who among the Heroes was preeminent in manly prowess;
text.note: “manly prowess” renders ἠνορέαι, the epic term for valor/virility.

text.greek: Ἠνειὸς Καινῆος ἀφίκετο, τόν ῥά τε φασί
text.english: Aineios, son of Kaineus, arrived, whom they say
text.note: Ἠνειὸς Καινῆος is problematic: the relative clause that follows gives the famous fate of Kaineus, not of a son. Many emend to read the nominative ‘Kaineus’ himself, or replace Ἠνειός with ‘Koronos, son of Kaineus’ (cf. Apollonius Rhodios 1.57). I translate the transmitted text as ‘Aineios, son of Kaineus,’ while the following clauses refer to Kaineus’s myth.

text.greek: μισγόμενον Λαπίθαις ὑπὸ Κενταύροισι δαμῆναι,
text.english: when he joined with the Lapiths, was subdued by the Centaurs,
text.note: μισγόμενον with the dative “Lapiths” means “joining battle with,” not “mingling” in a general sense.

text.greek: θεινόμενον πεύκαισι τανυφλοίοις τ' ἐλάτῃσι,
text.english: being struck with pines and with long‑needled firs,
text.note: τανυφλόιος = “long‑leafed/long‑needled,” of conifers (fir ἐλάτη; pine πεύκη).

text.greek: καὶ οἱ ἀνατλῆναι καὶ ἀκαμπέα γούνατ' ἐρεῖσαι
text.english: and that he endured and planted his unbending knees,
text.note: ἀκαμπέα “unyielding, inflexible,” highlighting Kaineus’s invulnerability and immovability.

text.greek: ζῳόν τ' ἐν φθιμένοισι μολεῖν ὑπὸ κεύθεα γαίης.
text.english: and, alive among the dead, went down beneath the depths of the earth.
text.note: “alive among the dead” (ζῳόν τ’ ἐν φθιμένοισι) alludes to Kaineus’s peculiar end: crushed and pressed into the earth alive, he descends beneath the hidden depths (κεύθεα) of the earth.

text.greek: Ἄδμητος δ' ἀφίκανε Φεραιόθεν, ᾧ ποτε Παιὰν
text.english: And Admetos came from Pherai, to whom once Paian
text.note: ἀφίκανε is an epic/poetic 3rd sg aorist for ἀφίκετο; Paian is Apollo under his healing epithet.

text.greek: θητεύων ὑπόεικε· Διὸς δ' ἠλεύατο μῆνιν
text.english: —serving for hire—stooped; and he was shunning the wrath of Zeus,
text.note: θητεύων ὑπόεικε literally “yielded while serving (for hire)”; the subject is Paian (Apollo), who condescends to serve Admetos.

text.greek: οὕνεκά τοι Κύκλωπας ἀμαιμακέτοισιν ὀϊστοῖς
text.english: because indeed the Kyklopes with irresistible arrows
text.note: ἀμαιμακέτοισιν is a stereotyped epic epithet meaning “irresistible, unrelenting”; enclitic τοι adds emphasis (“indeed”).

text.greek: ἐν φθιτοῖσιν ἔτευξ' Ἀσκληπιοῦ εἵνεκα λώβης.
text.english: he smote among mortals, on account of the wrong done to Asklepios.
text.note: ἐν φθιτοῖσιν = “among mortals”; ἔτευξ’ (aor. of τεύχω) here has the sense “smote/struck.” The phrase Ἀσκληπιοῦ λώβης means “because of the outrage done to Asklepios” (i.e., Apollo avenged Zeus’ slaying of Asklepios by killing the Kyklopes).

text.greek: Ἤλυθε δ' Εὐρυτίων Ἴρου παῖς Ἀκτορίωνος
text.english: And there came Eurytion, son of Iros, son of Aktor,
text.note: Ἀκτορίωνος is a patronymic (“Aktorion”), here appositive to Ἴρου: Iros is the son of Aktor; thus Eurytion is Aktor’s grandson.

text.greek: τρηχείην Ὀπόεντα λιπὼν, σὺν δ' ἤλυθεν Ἴδας
text.english: leaving rugged Opoeis; and with him came Idas
text.note: Ὀπόεντα is the accusative of Opoeis (Opous), the Opuntian Locrian city; τρηχείην “rugged” is a conventional epithet of that terrain.

text.greek: Λυγκεύς θ', ὃς τήλιστα δι' αἰθέρος ἠδὲ θαλάσσης
text.english: and Lynkeus, who beyond all through the aether and the sea
text.note: τήλιστα means “to the greatest extent, surpassingly”; αἰθήρ is the upper air (“aether”).

text.greek: βένθεα, καὶ Πλουτῆος ὑποχθονίοιο ῥέεθρα
text.english: the depths, and the streams of chthonic Ploutes,
text.note: Πλουτῆος ὑποχθονίοιο = “of chthonic Ploutes (Pluto),” i.e., the Underworld; ῥέεθρα “streams” refers to the rivers of Hades.

text.greek: μοῦνος ἀπ' ἀνθρώπων δεινοῖσιν ὀπώπεεν ὄσσοις.
text.english: he alone among men with dread eyes could behold.
text.note: ὀπώπεεν (a perfect-form in epic usage) conveys Lynkeus’ extraordinary capacity: “he could behold.” δεινοῖσιν ὄσσοις “with dread (i.e., formidable, piercing) eyes.”

text.greek: Αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ Τελαμὼν συνεφέσπετο, τόν ῥ' ἐλόχευσεν
text.english: But when Telamon had joined the company, him she bore
text.note: συνεφέσπετο = “joined/followed in company” (epic of ἕπομαι); τόν refers to Telamon; ἐλόχευσεν = “bore in childbirth.”

text.greek: Αἰακῷ ἀτρύτῳ κούρη κλυτοῦ Ἀσωποῖο
text.english: to Aiakos the unwearied, the maiden of famed Asopos,
text.note: Aegina is the daughter of Asopos. Orphic genealogy here makes Aegina the mother of Telamon by Aiakos, differing from the more common tradition that Endeis was his mother; ἀτρύτος = “unwearied.”

text.greek: Αἴγιν' ἐν κροκάλῃσιν ἀλιστεφέος Σαλαμῖνος.
text.english: Aegina, amid the pebbles of sea‑wreathed Salamis.
text.note: κροκάλαι = rounded beach‑pebbles; ἀλιστέφεος = “sea‑wreathed/sea‑girt.” The phrase locates the birth on Salamis, fitting Telamon’s later kingship there. Αἴγιν’ shows elision of final -α before ἐν (nom. Αἴγινα).

text.greek: Δὴ τότ' Ἄβαντος παῖς νόθος ἤλυθε καρτερὸς Ἴδμων,
text.english: Then indeed came the stalwart Idmon, bastard son of Abas,
text.note: “nothos” (bastard) reconciles two traditions: Idmon is publicly reckoned son of Abas yet truly begotten by Apollon; “karteros” preserves the epic epithet. The scene is the heroes’ muster.

text.greek: τόν ῥ' ὑποκυσσαμένη τέκεν Ἀπόλλωνι ἄνακτι
text.english: whom, having conceived, she bore to lord Apollon
text.note: “hypokyssamenē” means “having conceived (by),” and the dative “Apolloni anakti” expresses paternity (“to/for lord Apollon”).

text.greek: Ἀμφρύσου παρὰ χεῦμα Φερητιὰς Ἀντιάνειρα.
text.english: beside the stream of Amphrysus—Pheretian Antianeira.
text.note: “para cheuma Amphrysou” = “beside the stream/flow of Amphrysus,” a Thessalian river associated with Apollon; “Pheretias” marks Antianeira as of Pherae. This line completes the syntax of the preceding.

text.greek: Τῷ καὶ μαντοσύνην ἔπορεν καὶ θέσφατον ὀμφήν
text.english: To him also Phoibos bestowed prophetic skill and a heaven‑ordained oracular voice,
text.note: θέσφατον ὀμφήν: literally “heaven‑ordained voice,” with ὀμφή denoting an oracular utterance; Φοῖβος = Apollo; μαντοσύνη = prophetic craft/skill.

text.greek: Φοῖβος, ἵν' ἀνθρώποισιν ἀρηρότα μυθίζοιτο.
text.english: so that he might speak to men words well‑fitted.
text.note: ἀρηρότα is the neuter plural perfect participle of ἀραρίσκω (“fit, join”), used substantively/adverbially = “(things) fitted, apt,” supplying an implied object such as “words”; μυθίζοιτο (deponent) “to utter/speak,” optative in a final clause after a secondary tense (ἔπορεν).

text.greek: Ἤλυθε δ' αὖ μετὰ τοῖσι Μενοίτιος ἐξ Ὀπόεντος,
text.english: And in turn there came among them Menoetius from Opus, a comrade of the Minyae;
text.note: μετὰ τοῖσι = “among them,” continuing the catalogue; Ὀπόεντος is the poetic genitive of Ὀπόεις, i.e., Opus (Opountian Locris); σύγχορτος lit. “pasturing together,” used metaphorically of comradeship (“comrade of the Minyae”).

text.greek: σύγχορτος Μινύαις· ἐπὶ δ' ἤλυθε δῖος Ὀϊλεύς.
text.english: and after him came godlike Oïleus.
text.note: δῖος is the standard Homeric epithet “godlike”; ἐπὶ δ’ ἤλυθε is a sequencing formula (“and then/after him came”). Oïleus is the Locrian hero, better known as the father of Aias the Lesser, but included among Argonauts in some traditions.

text.greek: Φλίας δ' ἐξίκανε περικλυτός ὅν ποτε Βάκχῳ
text.english: And far-famed Phlias came, whom once to Bakkhos
text.note: ἐξίκανε = “came, arrived.” The relative ὅν refers forward to the description of Phlias’ birth; Bakkhos is Dionysos.

text.greek: νύμφη ὑποκλινθεῖσα παρ' Ἀσωποῖο ῥοῇσι
text.english: a Nymph, yielding herself by the streams of Asopos, bore,
text.note: ὑποκλινθεῖσα is an erotic euphemism (“yielding herself”). Asopos is the river-god; other traditions name the mother (e.g., Chthonophyle), but here she is an unnamed Nymph by Asopos’ streams.

text.greek: τίκτεν, ἄμωμον ἔχοντα δέμας καὶ ἐπίφρονα μῆτιν.
text.english: possessing an unblemished frame and prudent counsel.
text.note: ἄμωμον δέμας = “unblemished body/form”; μῆτις with ἐπίφρων denotes sagacious, practical intelligence, pairing physical and mental excellence.

text.greek: Κηφεύς τ' Ἀρκαδίηθε μεθ' ἡρώεσσι πελάσθη.
text.english: And Cepheus too, from Arkadia, came among the heroes.
text.note: Ἀρκαδίηθε is an epic adverb meaning “from Arkadia” (suffix -θε ≈ -θεν). πελάσθη is an aorist passive used intransitively, “came near/approached.” Cepheus is the Arcadian hero (son of Aleus) known from Argonaut lists.

text.greek: Ἀλκαῖον δ' ἄν' ὅμιλον ἀπ' Ἀρκαδίης πολυμήλου
text.english: But Alcaeus, into the band, from sheep‑abounding Arcadia,
text.note: The reading Alcaeus (Alkaios) is likely corrupt; many emend to Ancaeus (Agkaios), the Arcadian Argonaut. πολυμήλου = “rich in flocks.”

text.greek: πέμψε πατὴρ γηραιὸς ἐπὶ πλόον Ἀξείνοιο·
text.english: his aged father sent him forth for the voyage to the Axenos;
text.note: Axenos = the “Inhospitable” Sea, i.e., the Black Sea (later Euxeinos Pontos).

text.greek: οὗτος δ' οὔποτε χλαῖναν ἐπὶ στιβαροῖς βάλεν ὤμοις,
text.english: he never cast a cloak upon his sturdy shoulders,

text.greek: ἀλλ' ἄρκτου λάσιον στέρνοις ἀμπίσχετο δέρμα.
text.english: but about his breast he wrapped the shaggy hide of a bear.

text.greek: Ναύπλιος αὖθ' ἵκανεν, Ἀμυμώνης φίλος υἱός,
text.english: Nauplius in turn came, the beloved son of Amymone,
text.note: philos huios can mean “beloved” or “one’s own” son; Amymone is the Danaid mother of Nauplius. ἵκανεν = “came, arrived.”

text.greek: ὃν τέκεν εὐνηθεῖσα περικλυτῷ Ἐννοσιγαίῳ
text.english: whom she bore after sharing the bed with far-famed Ennosigaios,
text.note: Ennosigaios is the epithet-name of Poseidon, here transliterated; periklutos = “far-famed.” εὐνηθεῖσα is literally “having been bedded (by),” with the dative Ἐννοσιγαίῳ marking the agent; rendered idiomatically.

text.greek: ἀγλαὸν ἠνορέην δέμας εἴκελον ἀθανάτοισι.
text.english: glorious in manly prowess, his form like unto the immortals.
text.note: ἀγλαὸν ἠνορέην is an accusative phrase; ἀγλαόν functions adverbially (“gloriously”) with ἠνορέην (“manly prowess”). δέμας εἴκελον ἀθανατοῖσι is formulaic: “in body like to the immortals,” with δέμας as accusative of respect and ἀθανατοῖσι as the dative after εἴκελος.

text.greek: Ταιναρίευς δ' Εὔφημος ἔβη Μαλεάτιδος ἄκρης
text.english: And Tainarian Euphemus went forth from the headland of Malea,
text.note: “Tainarian” (Tainarieus) = of Tainaron (Cape Matapan) in Laconia; “the headland of Malea” is Cape Malea. Epic ἔβη = “went/set out.”

text.greek: ἐκπρολιπὼν αὐλῶνας, ἁλικλύστους τε θεράπνας.
text.english: having left behind the glens and the sea‑surge‑washed precincts.
text.note: αὐλῶνες = “glens, hollows” (of the coastal landscape). θεράπνας = “abodes/precincts”; some take it as the toponym Therapnai in Laconia, but the epithet ἁλικλύστους (“sea‑washed”) better suits a generic sense of sea‑beaten districts than inland Therapne. ἐκπρολιπών = “having left behind.”

text.greek: Ἀγκαῖός τ' ἔμολε Πλευρώνιος, ὅς ῥα πορείας
text.english: Ankaios too came, the Pleuronian, who indeed had learned the heavenly courses of the stars,
text.note: Pleuronios = from Pleuron (Aetolia). ἔμολε is epic for “came,” and ἐδάη means “knew well/was versed in.” The line highlights Ankaios’ expertise in celestial navigation.

text.greek: οὐρανίας ἄστρων ἐδάη, κύκλους τε πλάνητας.
text.english: and the wandering circuits.
text.note: “Wandering circuits” (kykloi planētai) refers to the orbits of the planets, “wanderers” in contrast to the fixed stars.

text.greek: Δίζετο γὰρ τά τ' ἐόντα τά τ' ἐσσόμεν' ἀνθρώποισιν.
text.english: For he was inquiring into both the things that are and the things that shall be for mortals.
text.note: δίζετο is the middle of δίζημαι “seek, inquire”; τὰ τ᾽ ἐόντα τὰ τ᾽ ἐσσόμεν(α) is a Homeric formula (“what is and what will be”), here lacking the usual πρό τ᾽ ἐόντα (“what was before”; cf. Il. 1.70); ἐσσόμεν' = ἐσσόμενα by elision; ἀνθρώποισιν is the epic dative plural, “for mortals.”

text.greek: Ἐν δὲ Παλαιμόνιος Λέρνου νόθος ἤλυθεν υἱός·
text.english: And among them came Palaimonius, the illegitimate son of Lernos;
text.note: Παλαιμόνιος (Palaimonius) and Λέρνος (Lernos) are obscure; Λέρνου (genitive) is likely a personal name, not the toponym Lerna (which would be Λέρνης). Νόθος = “illegitimate.”

text.greek: σίνετο δὲ σφυρὰ δισσὰ πόδας δ' οὐκ ἦεν ἀρηρώς·
text.english: and his two ankle-bones were afflicted, and his feet were not well set;
text.note: σφυρά = “ankle(-bones), malleoli”; σίνετο = “was afflicted/maimed”; ἀρηρώς (perf. of ἀραρίσκω) = “well-fitted, sound,” here negated of the feet, indicating lameness.

text.greek: τοὔνεκεν Ἡφαίστοιο γόνον καλέεσκον ἅπαντες.
text.english: for this cause all were wont to call him the offspring of Hephaistos.
text.note: Hephaistos is proverbially lame; hence the nickname. καλέεσκον is an iterative/imperfective “they used/were wont to call.”

text.greek: Ἤλυθε δ' Ἀλφειοῖο λιπὼν Πισάτιδας ὄχθας
text.english: And Augeias came, leaving the Pisatid banks of Alpheios,
text.note: Pisatid: the district of Pisatis in Elis by the river Alpheios; Augeias is the subject (epic nominative in -ēs); λιπών is a circumstantial participle “having left.”

text.greek: Αὐγείης, υἱὸς πυριφεγγέος Ἠελίοιο.
text.english: the son of fire-bright Helios.
text.note: πυριφεγγέος means “fire-bright”; Ἠελίοιο is the epic genitive of Helios. Augeias is here explicitly the son of Helios (elsewhere sometimes Poseidon).

text.greek: Ναὶ μὴν καὶ δίσσοι ὅρπηκες ἀμύμονες ἧκον,
text.english: Aye, indeed, two blameless scions came as well,
text.note: horpēkes (‘young shoots; saplings’) used metaphorically of noble youths or scions; amymones is the conventional epic ‘blameless’.

text.greek: Ἀμφίων κλυτόφημος ἰδ' Ἀστέριος μενεχάρμης
text.english: Amphion, famed-of-report, and Asterios, staunch in battle,
text.note: klytophēmos = ‘renowned, of far-famed report’; menecharmēs = ‘steadfast/staunch in battle’.

text.greek: Πελλήνην προλιπόντ' ἠδ' ἤθεα πατρίδος αἴης.
text.english: after leaving Pellene and the haunts of their native land.
text.note: Pellene is the Achaean city; ēthea here means ‘haunts, accustomed abodes’ of the fatherland (not ‘customs’).

text.greek: Δισσὸν δ' αὖ Βορέου καλὸν στάχυν εἰσενόησα,
text.english: And again I espied the fair twin ear of Boreas,
text.note: στάχυς (“ear of grain”) is a poetic metaphor for offspring; the “twin ear” refers to Boreas’ pair of sons.

text.greek: οὓς τέκ' Ἐρεχθῆος θείου κλυτὴ Ὠρείθυια
text.english: whom renowned Oreithyia, daughter of divine Erechtheus, bore,
text.note: ἐκ + genitive is understood: Oreithyia is the daughter of Erechtheus; hence “of divine Erechtheus.”

text.greek: Ἰλισσοῦ παρὰ χεῦμα θεοῦ φιλότητι μιγεῖσα·
text.english: having mingled in love beside the flow of the god Ilissos;
text.note: θεοῦ is appositive to Ἰλισσοῦ: Ilissos is treated as a river-god; φιλότητι μιγεῖσα is the standard euphemism for sexual union (with Boreas, implied).

text.greek: οἳ δὴ καὶ ταρσοῖσιν ὑπουατίοις πεπότηντο,
text.english: who indeed had taken to flight with winglets at their ankles,
text.note: ταρσοῖσιν = “at the insteps/ankles.” The adjective ὑπουατίοις is obscure; most take it to mean something like “with ear-like appendages beneath,” i.e., small winglets at the ankles. Some have suspected emendation (e.g., to ὑποπτεροῖς, “under-winged”). πεπότηντο (perf. of πέτομαι) conveys a stative sense, “were winged/ready to fly.”

text.greek: Ζήτης καὶ Κάλαϊς δέμας εἴκελοι ἀθανάτοισιν.
text.english: Zetes and Kalais, in form like unto the immortals.

text.greek: Αὐτὰρ δὴ Πελίαο Φεραιόθεν ἤλυθ' ἄνακτος
text.english: But then there came from Pherae a kinsman of lord Pelias;
text.note: ἀγχιστεύς = “near-kin, kinsman.” Φεραιόθεν = “from Pherae” (Thessaly). The person implied is Admetus, nephew of Pelias.

text.greek: ἀγχιστεύς· νηὸς γὰρ ἐπ' Ἀργῴας γεγένητο
text.english: for he had come to be on board the ship Argo,
text.note: νηὸς is the Homeric genitive of ναῦς “ship” (not “temple”); ἐπ’ Ἀργῴας = “on [board] the Argo.” γεγένητο (perfect) indicates having been enrolled/appointed as part of the crew.

text.greek: ἄξεινον ποτὶ Φᾶσιν ἅμ' ἡρώεσσιν ἐλάσσαι.
text.english: to drive across the Axeinos toward Phasis together with the heroes.
text.note: ἄξεινον = the Axeinos (“Inhospitable” [Sea], i.e., the Black Sea), with understood πόντον; ἐλᾶσαι/ἐλάσσαι “to drive” is the epic verb for sailing; ποτὶ Φᾶσιν = “toward the Phasis” (the river in Colchis).

text.greek: Σὺν δέ οἱ ἦλθ' ἕταρος Ἡρακλέεος θείοιο
text.english: And with him there came a comrade of divine Herakles.
text.note: “theios” (divine/godlike) is a conventional epic epithet; “hetairos” = comrade, here identifying Hylas as the companion of Herakles.

text.greek: καλὸς Ὕλας· τὸν δ' οὔπω ὑπὲρ δροσεροῖο γενείου
text.english: the fair Hylas; over his dewy chin not yet
text.note: “droseros” (dewy) evokes the youthful bloom; “geneion” = chin.

text.greek: ἀργεννὰς ἐρύθηνε παρηίδας ἁβρὸς ἴουλος,
text.english: had the soft first-down reddened his bright cheeks,
text.note: “ioulos” is the first growth of beard (soft down); “argennas” means bright/silvery-white; the verb “eruthēne” (‘reddened’) takes the down as subject reddening the cheeks.

text.greek: ἀλλ' ἔτι κοῦρος ἔην, πολὺ δ' ἤνδανεν Ἡρακλῆϊ.
text.english: but he was still a boy, and he greatly pleased Herakles.
text.note: “kouros” denotes a youth/adolescent; “ēndanen” means ‘pleased, delighted.’

text.greek: - Οὗτοι μὲν ποτὶ νῆα καὶ ἐς λόχον ἠγερέθοντο.
text.english: These men, for their part, assembled at the ship and went into ambush.
text.note: λόχος here is the epic ‘ambush’/‘hiding-place’ (not ‘childbirth’); ἠγερέθοντο is an intransitive/middle aorist ‘gathered/assembled (themselves)’; ποτὶ = epic πρός ‘toward/at’. The single verb governs both prepositional phrases, indicating they mustered by the ship and took up a concealed position.

text.greek: Καί ῥά οἱ ἄλλοθεν ἄλλος ἐκέκλετο ἠδ' ἀγόρευε.
text.english: And then from every side one after another would call to him and speak.
text.note: ῥά marks transition (“and then”); ἄλλοθεν ἄλλος is a distributive idiom (“from one side and another,” hence “from every side”), with the singular implying successive speakers. ἐκέκλετο is the imperfect middle of κέλομαι (“call upon, bid, exhort”) used with the dative οἱ (“to him”); ἀγόρευε (impf. of ἀγορεύω) conveys formal public speaking. The imperfects suggest repeated or continued action: men addressed him in turn.

text.greek: Δεῖπνα δ' ἐπορσύνοντο πολυξείνοιο τραπέζης,
text.english: And they were preparing the feasts of the all‑hospitable board,
text.note: πολυξείνιος (“much-guesting, all-hospitable”) marks the epic tone of generous reception; τραπέζης in the genitive is descriptive (“of the board”). ἐπορσύνω (mid.) = “make ready, set out.”

text.greek: Αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ σίτοιο ποτοῦ θ' ἅλις ἔπλετο θυμός,
text.english: But when the heart had had its fill of food and of drink,
text.note: θυμός ἅλις ἔπλετο is a Homeric idiom for being satisfied; σῖτος = staple food, ποτός = drink (not necessarily specifically wine).

text.greek: ἥμενοι ἑξείης πόθεεν μέγα ἔργον ἕκαστος.
text.english: sitting in order, each man longed for the great enterprise.
text.note: ἑξείης = “in order, in a row.” πόθεεν (imperfect) conveys sustained yearning. μέγα ἔργον (“great work/deed”) refers to the Argonautic enterprise.

text.greek: Ἀνστάντες δ' ἅμα πάντες ἀπὸ ψαμάθοιο βαθείης
text.english: And rising up all together from the deep sand,
text.note: ἀνστάντες is an epic/orthographic variant of ἀναστάντες; ψαμάθοιο βαθείης = “deep beach-sand.”

text.greek: ἤϊον, ἔνθά τ' ἔμιμνεν ὑπὲρ ψαμάθου ἁλίη ναῦς,
text.english: they went to where the sea-faring ship was waiting upon the sand,
text.note: ἤϊον is the epic imperfect of εἶμι (“went”); ἁλίη ναῦς “sea-faring ship”; ὑπὲρ ψαμάθου indicates the ship is beached.

text.greek: τήν ῥά ποτ' εἰσορόωντες ἐθάμβεον· αὐτὰρ ἔπειτα
text.english: which, as they gazed upon it, they marveled at; but thereafter
text.note: τήν refers to the ship; ποτ’ can suggest “at times/once”; the imperfect ἐθάμβεον gives an iterative sense (“as they looked, they would marvel”).

text.greek: Ἄργος ἐφημοσύναισι νόου πόρσυνεν ὀχλίζειν,
text.english: Argos, with counsels of his mind, made ready the heaving,
text.note: Ἄργος is the builder of the ship; ἐφημοσύναις νόου = “by instructions/counsels of his mind”; ὀχλίζειν is a technical term for “heave” (set in motion with levers).

text.greek: δουρατέαισι φάλαγξι καὶ εὐστρέπτοισι κάλωσι
text.english: with wooden rollers and well-twisted cables,
text.note: δουρατέαισι φάλαγξι are wooden rollers; εὐστρέπτοις κάλωσι are well-twisted cables/ropes.

text.greek: πρυμνόθεν ἀρτήσας. Κάλεεν δ' ἐπὶ μόχθον ἱκάνειν
text.english: having made them fast from the stern. And he called on them to come to the toil,
text.note: πρυμνόθεν ἀρτήσας = “having made (the gear) fast from the stern,” i.e., attaching ropes/cables at the stern before the launch.

text.greek: πάντας κυδαίνων. Οἱ δ' ἐσσυμένως ὑπάκουσαν·
text.english: honoring them all. They eagerly obeyed;
text.note: κυδαίνων literally “honoring, exalting,” here “encouraging with praise.”

text.greek: τεύχεα δ' ἐκδύνοντο, περὶ στέρνοισι δ' ἀνῆπτον
text.english: they stripped off their armor and about their breasts they fastened

text.greek: σειραίην μήρινθον. Ἐπέβριθεν δ' ἄρ' ἕκαστος
text.english: a rope-thong harness. And each leaned his weight
text.note: σειραίην μήρινθον is a rare phrase for a rope-thong harness used for hauling; ἐπέβριθεν = “leaned/bore his weight (on it).”

text.greek: αἶψα θοὸν ποτὶ κῦμα κατειρύσαι εὔλαλον Ἀργώ.
text.english: straightway to haul the swift, well-voiced Argō toward the wave.
text.note: εὔλαλος (“well-voiced”) alludes to Argō’s speaking timber from Dodona; κατειρύσαι = “to draw/haul down” toward the sea.

text.greek: Ἣ δέ οἱ ἐγχριφθεῖσα ποτὶ ψαμάθῳ βεβάρητο,
text.english: But she, wedged into the sand, had grown heavy for him,
text.note: ἐγχριφθεῖσα is a rare/passive aorist participle (manuscripts vary: ἐγχριφθεῖσα/ἐγκριφθεῖσα) probably from ἐγκρῖπτω “to jam/wedge in”; hence “wedged.” The enclitic οἱ is a dative of interest (“for him”), likely referring to the leader (Jason). The subject “she” is the ship (Argo).

text.greek: αὐαλέοις φυκέεσσιν ἐρυκομένη ποτὶ χέρσῳ
text.english: being held fast toward the dry land by withered sea‑wrack,
text.note: αὐαλέοις = “dry, withered”; φυκέεσσιν = “seaweeds/sea‑wrack.” ποτὶ χέρσῳ is the epic preposition ποτί with χέρσος “dry land,” here “toward/against the shore.” ἐρυκομένη = “being held back/restrained.”

text.greek: ἡρώων παλάμῃσιν ὑπὸ στιβαρῇσιν ἀπειθής.
text.english: unyielding beneath the sturdy palms of the heroes.
text.note: ἀπειθής here means “unyielding, stubborn” rather than moral “disobedient.” ὑπό with the dative (παλάμῃσιν… στιβαρῇσιν) conveys resistance “beneath/under” their strong hands.

text.greek: Παχνώθη δ' αὖ θυμὸς Ἰάσονος· αὐτὰρ ἔμοιγε
text.english: And Jason’s spirit grew chill again; but to me, indeed,
text.note: Παχνώθη (“was frosted, grew chill”) is a vivid metaphor of fear or discouragement; ἔμοιγε is an emphatic dative (“to me indeed”).

text.greek: νεῦσεν ὀπιπτεύων ἵνα οἱ θάρσος τε βίην τε
text.english: he nodded, casting a glance at me, that for him courage and might
text.note: ὀπιπτεύων = “watching closely, glancing toward”; νεῦσεν “he nodded” as a signal; ἵνα introduces a purpose clause.

text.greek: μολπῇ ὑφ' ἡμετέρῃ κεκμηόσιν αἰὲν ὁρίνω.
text.english: I might ever rouse by my song in the wearied.
text.note: μολπῇ ὑφ’ ἡμετέρῃ = “by my song,” with ἡμετέρῃ the poetic plural for “my”; ὁρίνω governs accusatives (θάρσος, βίην) with a dative of the persons affected (κεκμηόσιν “the wearied [men]”); οἱ is an ethical dative “for him (Jason).”

text.greek: Αὐτὰρ ἐγὼ φόρμιγγα τιτηνάμενος μετὰ χερσί,
text.english: But I, shaking the phorminx in my hands,
text.note: phorminx: the epic lyre; τιτηνάμενος = “brandishing, vibrating.”

text.greek: μητρὸς ἐμῆς ἐκέρασσ' εὐτερπέα κόσμον ἀοιδῆς,
text.english: blended in my mother’s delightful adornment of song,
text.note: ἐκέρασσ’ (from κεράννυμι) “I mixed/tempered”; κόσμον ἀοιδῆς = the “order/adornment of song.” “My mother” is Kalliope, implying Orpheus’ Muse-taught craft.

text.greek: καί οἱ ἀπὸ στηθέων ὄπα λείριον ἐξελόχευσα·
text.english: and from my breast I brought forth for them a lily-like voice;
text.note: λείριον “lily-like” marks delicacy; ἐξελόχευσα (from λοχεύω) literally “I brought to birth,” i.e., “I delivered” a voice; οἱ = “for them,” the Argonauts.

text.greek: - "Ἔξοχον Ἡρώων Μινυήιον αἷμα γενέθλης,
text.english: “Illustrious Minyan blood of the Heroes’ lineage,
text.note: Μινυήιον “Minyan” (the Argonauts as Minyae); Ἡρώων “of Heroes”; αἷμα γενέθλης = “blood of birth/lineage”; ἔξοχον = “preeminent, illustrious.”

text.greek: εἰ δ' ἄγε νῦν στερροῖσιν ὑπὸ στέρνοισι κάλωας
text.english: come now, set the hawsers beneath your firm breasts
text.note: κάλωας = ship’s cables/hawsers; στερροῖσιν στέρνοισι “firm/stout breasts” reflects the hauling technique of passing the rope under the chest; εἶ δ’ ἄγε = idiomatic “come now.”

text.greek: βρίσαθ' ὁμορροθέοντες, ἐρείσατε δ' ἴχνια γαίῃ
text.english: bear down in unison, and brace your footprints in the earth,
text.note: βρίσαθ’ (aor. mid. imper.) = “bear/press down”; ὁμορροθέοντες = “moving/straining in concert”; ἐρείσατε = “brace, set firm.”

text.greek: ταρσοῖσιν ποδὸς ἄκρον ὑπερβλήδην τανύσαντες·
text.english: with your soles, stretching far out the extremity of the foot;
text.note: ταρσοῖσιν = “with the soles (of the feet)”; ποδὸς ἄκρον = “the extremity of the foot,” i.e., the toes; ὑπερβλήδην = “exceedingly, far out,” describing the hauling stance.

text.greek: καὶ χαροπὸν ποτὶ χεῦμα γεγηθότες ἕλξατε νῆα.
text.english: and, rejoicing, haul the ship toward the gleaming surge.”
text.note: χαροπὸν χεῦμα = “gleaming/bright surge (of the sea)”; ἕλξατε = “haul, drag”; γεγηθότες = “rejoicing.”

text.greek: - Ἀργὼ πεύκῃσιν τ' ἠδὲ δρυσὶ γομφωθεῖσα
text.english: Argo, pegged with pines and oaks,
text.note: “gomphōtheisa” = ‘pegged/dowelled together,’ i.e., mortise-and-tenon joinery; peukai/dryes are the ship’s pine and oak timbers.

text.greek: ἄι' ἐμῆς ἐνοπῆς καὶ γὰρ πάρος ἔκλυες ἤδη
text.english: hearken to my voice; for even before you hearkened,
text.note: “ἄι’” is the imperative of ἀίω, ‘hear!’; ἔκλυες can imply ‘heard and obeyed.’

text.greek: ἡνίκα δένδρε' ἔθελγον ἐν ὑλήεντι κολώνῃ
text.english: when I was bewitching the trees on a wooded knoll
text.note: “ἔθελγον” (θέλγω) ‘enchant/bewitch’; “κολώνη” = low wooded hill/knoll—Orphic topos of trees moved by song.

text.greek: πέτρας τ' ἠλιβάτους, καί μοι κατὰ πόντον ἔβαινες
text.english: and the pathless rocks, and for my sake you went over the sea,
text.note: “ἠλιβάτους” = ‘untraversable/steep, pathless’; “κατὰ πόντον ἔβαινες” ‘you went over/onto the sea.’

text.greek: οὔρε' ἀποπρολιποῦσα, ἐπέσπεο δ' αὖτε θαλάσσης
text.english: leaving the mountains far behind, and again you followed the
text.note: “ἀποπρολιποῦσα” intensifies ‘leaving far behind’; Argo is personified as responding to the singer.

text.greek: παρθενίης ἀτραπούς· σπέρχου δ' ἐπὶ Φᾶσιν ἀμείβειν,
text.english: virgin tracks of the sea; make haste to reach the Phasis,
text.note: “παρθενίης ἀτραπούς” ‘virgin paths,’ i.e., unsailed sea-routes; “Φᾶσιν” = the Colchian river Phasis.

text.greek: ἡμετέρῃ πίσυνος κιθάρῃ καὶ θεσκέλῳ ὀμφῇ."
text.english: trusting in my kithara and my god-wrought utterance.”
text.note: “πίσυνος” = ‘trusting, relying on’; “θεσκέλῳ ὀμφῇ” = ‘marvellous/divine (or oracular) voice/utterance’ (ὀμφή often has an oracular nuance).

text.greek: - Δὴ τότ' ἐπιβρομέουσα Τομαριὰς ἔκλυε φηγός
text.english: Then the Tomarian oak, booming aloft, obeyed the call,
text.note: “Τομαριὰς φηγός” = the oak of Tomaros, i.e., the Dodonaean oak; “ἐπιβρομέουσα” ‘booming/rumbling,’ echoing Zeus’ thunder; “ἤκλυε” = ‘hearkened/obeyed.’

text.greek: ἥν οἱ ὑποτροπίην Ἄργος θέτο νηῒ μελαίνῃ
text.english: the one which Argos set as the keelson for the black ship, at Pallas’ instigation;
text.note: “ὑποτροπίην” is a debated shipbuilding term; here taken as ‘keelson’ (an internal longitudinal timber), though some take it as an ‘under-keel’ fitting; Argos installs it by Pallas’ counsel.

text.greek: Παλλάδος ἐννεσίῃσιν· ἀνηέρθη δὲ μάλ' ὦκα
text.english: and she was very quickly lifted up, lightening her timbers, and swift she slid upon the sea;
text.note: “ἀνηέρθη” ‘was lifted (for launch)’; “δούρατ’ ἐλαφρίζουσα” ‘making her timbers light,’ i.e., buoyed as she takes the water.

text.greek: δούρατ' ἐλαφρίζουσα, θοὴ δ' ὠλίσθανε πόντῳ·
text.english: and as she pressed on she scattered the close-packed rollers
text.note: “φάλαγγες” here most plausibly ‘rollers’ (or ‘chocks’) used under the hull during launching; “ἐκέδασσε” ‘scattered, broke apart.’

text.greek: καί οἱ ἐπειγομένη θαμινὰς ἐκέδασσε φάλαγγας
text.english: which lay beneath her keel, held taut by a single rope.
text.note: “ὑπὸ τρόπι” = ‘beneath the keel’; “μιᾶς σχοίνιοιο ταθεῖσαι” ‘stretched/held taut by a single rope,’ i.e., lashings binding the rollers/chocks together.

text.greek: αἵ οἱ ὑπὸ τρόπι κεῖντο μιᾶς σχοίνοιο ταθεῖσαι.
text.english: [Translation missing]

text.greek: Ἐν δ' ἄρ' ἔβη, λιμένος χαροπὸν δ' ἀνεχάσσατο κῦμα·
text.english: And in she went, and the grim wave of the harbor recoiled.
text.note: “She” = the ship (neōs). “χαροπὸν” is rendered “grim,” a common epic epithet; the wave is personified as it “drew back” (ἀνεχάσσατο).

text.greek: Θῖνες δ' ἀμφέκλυσθεν· ἐγήθει δὲ φρέν' Ἰήσων,
text.english: And the sandbanks were washed all around; and Jason’s heart rejoiced.
text.note: Θῖνες are shore‑sands/sandbanks; ἀμφέκλυσθεν (“were washed all around”) evokes the surge on both sides as the ship enters.

text.greek: ἆλτο δ' ἔσω νεὸς Ἄργος, ἐφέσπετο δ' ἀγχόθι Τῖφυς
text.english: And he leapt inside the ship Argo, and Tiphys followed close at hand.
text.note: Subject of ἆλτο is Jason from the preceding hemistich; νεὸς Ἄργος = “the ship Argo” (not Argus the builder).

text.greek: καί οἱ ἐπάρτια θῆκαν ἀρηρότα πορσύνοντες,
