text.english: And for him they set the well‑fitted tackle, making all things ready,
text.note: ἐπάρτια = “tackle/rigging”; ἀρηρότα (from ἀραρίσκω) = “well‑fitted”; πορσύνειν = “to get things ready, equip.”

text.greek: ἱστόν τ' ἠδ' ὀθόνας· ἐπὶ δ' αὖτ' οἴηκας ἔδησαν,
text.english: the mast and the sail‑cloths; and thereon they bound the sheets,
text.note: ὀθόνες are the sail‑cloths. οἴηκες is best taken as “sheets/braces” (sail‑ropes); some manuscripts read οἴακες (“tiller‑handles”), but the context favors sheets.

text.greek: πρυμνόθεν ἀρτήσαντες, ἐπεσφίγξαντο δ' ἱμᾶσιν.
text.english: fastening them from the stern, and they tightened them with thongs.
text.note: πρυμνόθεν (“from the stern”) suits sheets led aft; ἐπεσφίγξαντο (“they tightened fast”) with ἱμᾶσιν (“thongs/straps”) describes the lashings.

text.greek: Αὐτὰρ ἔπειθ' ἑκάτερθεν ἐρετμοὺς ἡπλώσαντο,
text.english: But then they ran out the oars on either side,
text.note: ἡπλώσαντο (aor. mid. of ἁπλόω) has a nautical sense: “to run out/lay out” the oars into rowing position; ἑκάτερθεν = “on both sides (of the ship).”

text.greek: εἰσβαίνειν δ' ἐκέλευον ἐπειγομένους Μινύηας.
text.english: and they bade the Minyae to embark in eager haste.
text.note: Μινύηας (“Minyae”) is an epic designation for the Argonauts (descendants of Minyas); ἐπειγομένους is a circumstantial participle, “in haste/eagerly.”

text.greek: τοῖσιν δ' Αἰσονίδης ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα·
text.english: Then to them Aisonides spoke winged words:
text.note: “Aisonides” = Jason; “winged words” is the traditional epic formula for swift speech.

text.greek: - "Κέκλυτέ μευ, βασιλῆες ἀμύμονες, οὐ γὰρ ἔμοιγε
text.english: “Hear me, blameless kings; for to me indeed
text.note: Keklyte meu: meu (“of me”) is idiomatic for “hear me”; amymones (“blameless”) is a standard epic epithet of nobles/kings.

text.greek: ἁνδάνει ἐν πραπίδεσσιν ἀρειοτέροισιν ἀνάσσειν.
text.english: it does not please my heart to lord it over my betters.”
text.note: Prapides (“midriff, heart”) denotes the seat of thought; areioterosin is “better, nobler, stronger” (dative plural). Anassein usually governs the genitive “rule over,” but epic also shows a dative; sense: Jason declines to rule over those superior to him.

text.greek: Ὑμεῖς δ', ὅντιν' ἄρα κραδίη θυμὸς τε μενοινᾷ
text.english: But you, whomever your heart and spirit may desire,
text.note: κραδίη θυμὸς τε (“heart and spirit”) forms a paired subject treated as a unit; μενοινᾷ is the optative (“may desire”), expressing potentiality in this exhortation. The particle ἄρα is inferential and not translated.

text.greek: ἡγεμόνα στήσασθε· καὶ ᾧ περὶ πάντα μελήσει
text.english: appoint as leader; and it shall be his to care for all things,
text.note: ᾧ … μελήσει: dative with (impersonal) μέλει, “it will be a care to him,” hence “it shall be his to care for all things.”

text.greek: σημανέειν ὅ τι κεν ῥέξαι ἔπος ἠδὲ καὶ ἔργον
text.english: to indicate what is to be done, in word and in deed,
text.note: σημανέειν is the epic/Ionic infinitive of σημαίνω, “to indicate, give the signal.” ῥέξαι (“to do, perform”) with the formula ἔπος ἠδὲ καὶ ἔργον yields the idiom “in word and in deed.”

text.greek: πόντον ἐπιπλώσουσιν ἀφιξομένοις τ' ἐπὶ γαῖαν,
text.english: to those who will sail over the sea and to those who will come to the land,
text.note: πόντον ἐπιπλώσουσιν and ἀφιξομένοις are dative plural future participles dependent on σημανέειν, indicating the recipients: “to those who will sail … and to those who will come …,” not finite verbs.

text.greek: εἴτε καὶ ἐς Κόλχους καὶ ἐς ἀλλοδαποὺς ἀνθρώπους.
text.english: whether to the Colchians or to alien men.
text.note: εἴτε καὶ … καὶ here has the sense of “whether … or …”; ἀλλοδαπούς = “foreign, alien.” “Colchians” names the specific destination of the voyage.

text.greek: Καὶ γὰρ δὴ μοῦνοι σὺν ἐμοὶ πόλεες τε καὶ ἐσθλοί,
text.english: For indeed you alone, with me, both many and noble,
text.note: πόλεες is the Homeric form for “many”; the nominative can function vocatively in epic. μοῦνοι σὺν ἐμοί = “you alone together with me,” marking exclusivity; the finite verb is supplied by the following relative clause.

text.greek: οἵ ῥα καὶ ἀθανάτου ῥίζης γένος εὐχετάασθε,
text.english: who even boast yourselves a race from an immortal root,
text.note: εὐχετάασθε is a deponent “to boast/claim.” ῥίζης (“root”) is a genealogical metaphor; ἀθανάτου ῥίζης = divine/immortal descent.

text.greek: ξυνὸν ἀνηρείψασθε πόνον, κλέος ὄφρ' ἂν ἄροισθε.
text.english: take up the common toil, that you may win glory.
text.note: ξυνόν is the epic form of κοινόν (“common, shared”). ἀνηρείψασθε means “lift up/undertake.” ὄφρ’ ἄν with the aorist subjunctive ἄροισθε (of ἀρνύμαι, “win, gain for yourselves”) expresses purpose: “so that you may win.”

text.greek: Ἀλλ' οὐ δὴ κάρτιστον ἀρειότερόν τε γενέσθαι
text.english: But surely I do not suppose it possible to become mightier and more warlike—
text.note: κάρτιστον ἀρειότερον τε γενέσθαι: neuter adjectives used predicatively with the infinitive; understood subject ‘anyone.’ The comparison is completed by the genitive in the next line.

text.greek: Ἡρακλῆος ἄνακτος ὀΐομαι· ἴστε καὶ αὐτοί."
text.english: —than lord Herakles; you yourselves know it as well.
text.note: Ἡρακλῆος ἄνακτος: genitive of comparison with ἀρειότερον; ἄναξ ‘lord’ in epic style.

text.greek: - Ὣς ἔφαθ', οἱ δ' ἄρα πάντες ἐπῄνεον· ἐν δ' ἄρα φωνῇ
text.english: Thus he spoke, and they all approved; and with one voice
text.note: ἐν δ’ ἄρα φωνῇ is an idiom meaning ‘with one voice/in a single shout.’

text.greek: λαὸς ἐπερρόθεεν, Μινύαις ἐπικοίρανον εἶναι
text.english: the people roared aloud, that there be an overlord over the Minyai,
text.note: ἐπερρόθεεν ‘roared, thundered’ (onomatopoetic). ἐπίκοιρανος ‘one set in command, overlord’; here with infinitive εἶναι, the subject supplied in the next line.

text.greek: Ἀλκείδην, ὃς πᾶσι μέγ' ἔξοχος ἦεν ἑταίροις.
text.english: Alkeidēs, who was by far preeminent among all the comrades.
text.note: Ἀλκείδης is the patronymic of Herakles (‘descendant of Alkeus’). μέγ’ ἔξοχος = ‘by far preeminent’ (μέγα intensifies the adjective).

text.greek: Ἀλλ' οὐ πεῖθον ἄνακτα πεπνυμένον, ὅς ῥά οἱ ᾔδη
text.english: But they did not persuade the prudent lord, who indeed knew
text.note: “the prudent lord” is likely Herakles in context (the crew urge him to lead, but he refuses). The enclitic oi here functions as an ethical dative (“for his part”).

text.greek: Ἥρης ἐννεσίῃσι τετιμένον Αἴσονος υἱόν,
text.english: the son of Aison to be honored by Hera’s counsels,
text.note: ennesiēsi (“counsels, instigations, inspirations”) denotes divine prompting; “the son of Aison” is Jason.

text.greek: ὥς δή οἱ κλέος ἐσθλὸν ἐπεσσομένοισιν ὄπαζεν·
text.english: inasmuch as she was bestowing on him noble renown among those yet to come;
text.note: epessomenois (“those who will come after”) is a Homeric formula for posterity; “bestowing … noble renown” renders kleos esthlon … opazen (imperfect, ongoing).

text.greek: ὡς ῥά οἱ αὐτὸς ἔνισπεν, Ἰήσονα κοίρανον εἶναι
text.english: for he himself declared that Iason should be commander
text.note: enispen (“declared, told”); the subject remains the same “lord” (Herakles), who proclaims Jason leader. The dative oi may be merely ethical.

text.greek: πεντήκοντ' ἐρέταισιν, ἀνὰ τραφερήν τε καὶ ὑγρήν.
text.english: of the fifty oarsmen, over the dry and the wet.
text.note: “over the dry and the wet” is an epic periphrasis for “by land and by sea” (elliptic for “earth and sea”); pentēkont’ eretaisin = “fifty oarsmen,” i.e., the Argonauts.

text.greek: Καὶ τότε δὴ μάλα πάντες ἐπῄνεον, ὡς ἐκέλευεν
text.english: And then indeed all greatly approved, as Herakles bade,
text.note: ἐπῄνεον (“approved, endorsed”) is an imperfect used narratively; ὡς ἐκέλευεν Ἡρακλέης means “in accordance with the bidding of Herakles.”

text.greek: Ἡρακλέης, καὶ θῆκαν Ἰήσονα κοίρανον εἶναι.
text.english: and they appointed Iason to be commander.
text.note: θῆκαν … εἶναι is a formula for appointment (“they set X to be Y”); κοίρανος is Homeric for “chieftain/commander.” Ἰήσονα is an epic/Ionic form of Ἰάσονα (Iason).

text.greek: - Ἦμος δ' ἠέλιος τὸν ἀπείριτον αἰθέρα τέμνων
text.english: But when Helios, cleaving the boundless aether,

text.greek: ἵπποις ὠκυπόδεσσι κελαινὴν ἔντυε νύκτα,
text.english: with his swift-footed horses was bringing on black Night,
text.note: ἔντυε with νύκτα is rendered “was bringing on [Night]”; the dative ἵπποις marks the instrumental means (“with his swift‑footed horses”).

text.greek: τῆμος ἐνὶ πραπίδεσσιν ἐμήτιεν Αἴσονος υἱός
text.english: then in his breast the son of Aison was devising
text.note: πραπίδες = “breast, mind”; ἐμήτιεν conveys ongoing deliberation (“was devising”).

text.greek: πίστιν ἐφ' ἡρώεσσι καὶ ὅρκια συνθεσιάων
text.english: to establish a pledge among the heroes and oaths of compacts,
text.note: πίστιν here is a formal “pledge/assurance”; ἐπ’ ἡρώεσσι = “among/before the heroes.” συνθεσιάων (gen. pl.) = “of compacts/agreements.”

text.greek: θέσθαι ὄφρ' ἔμπεδα πάντα φυλασσόμενοι πεπίθοιντο·
text.english: so that, guarding them, they might trust that all would stand fast;
text.note: ἔμπεδα = “steadfast, secure.” ὄφρ’ with the optative (πεπίθοιντο) expresses purpose/result: “so that they might be assured.” The subject of πεπίθοιντο is the heroes; φυλασσόμενοι refers to keeping the pledge and oaths.

text.greek: καὶ τότε τοι, Μουσαῖε, φίλον τέκος Ἀντιοφήμου,
text.english: and then, Musaeus, dear child of Antiophemus,
text.note: Apostrophe to Musaeus situates the narration; Antiophemus supplies the traditional patronymic.

text.greek: πορσύναι μ' ἐκέλευε θοῶς ἱερήϊα καλά.
text.english: he bade me swiftly make ready goodly victims.
text.note: πορσύναι = “to get ready/provide.” ἱερήϊα are specifically sacrificial victims (not merely rites).

text.greek: - Αὐτὰρ ἐγὼ ψαφαραῖσιν ἐπ' ἠϊόνεσσιν ἐνεῖκα
text.english: But I brought to the pebbly strands
text.note: ψαφαραῖσιν ἐπ᾽ ἠϊόνεσσιν = “on pebbly shores/strands,” a conventional epic collocation for a beach of small stones.

text.greek: κᾶλα, τά τ' ἐκ δρυός ἐστι φερεσβίου· ἐν δ' ἄρ' ὕπερθε
text.english: the timbers, those from the life‑bearing oak; and on top
text.note: κᾶλα = “timbers” (pl. of κᾶλον, any piece of wood; can mean logs, spars, or oars); φερέσβιος is the traditional epithet “life‑bearing/life‑supporting” of the oak (notably of Zeus’ oak at Dodona). “On top” (ἐν δ᾽ ἄρ᾽ ὕπερθε) anticipates the action of the next line.

text.greek: πέπλῳ παρκατέθηκα θεοῖς ἐπινήχυτα δῶρα.
text.english: I set in place upon a peplos sea‑washed gifts for the gods.
text.note: παρκατέθηκα = “I set/laid down (beside/in addition),” a compound of παρά + κατατίθημι; ἐπινήχυτα = “sea‑washed,” likely indicating ritual lustration of offerings with seawater; πέπλος (peplos) is a cloth/robe used here as the offering cloth.

text.greek: Καὶ τότε δὴ κραντῆρα βοῶν περιμηκέα ταῦρον
text.english: And then indeed a very large krater for the cattle—
text.note: κραντῆρα is almost certainly a form of κρατῆρα “krater; mixing-bowl.” The syntax is compressed/anacoluthic: the vessel is introduced without an explicit verb (sc. “they set out/placed”), before the action of slaughter is narrated. Some editors emend the spelling to κρατῆρα. The placement of περιμηκέα most naturally modifies the krater here (“very large”).

text.greek: σφάζον, ἀνακλίνας κεφαλὴν εἰς αἰθέρα δῖαν,
text.english: they slaughtered the bull, having tilted back its head toward the bright aether,
text.note: σφάζον denotes ritual slaughter by cutting the throat; hence the detail “tilting back the head.”

text.greek: ζωόταμον· περὶ δ' αἷμα πυρῇ χέον ἔνθα καὶ ἔνθα.
text.english: while still alive; and around the fire they were pouring the blood, here and there.
text.note: ζωόταμον “cut while alive” emphasizes the immediacy of the sacrificial killing; ἔνθα καὶ ἔνθα = “hither and thither,” i.e., “on both sides/round about,” describing the distribution of blood around the fire.

text.greek: Αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ κραδίην θραύσας ποπάνοισιν ἔθηκα,
text.english: But when, having crushed the heart, I placed it with popanoi,
text.note: κραδίην θραύσας: literally “having broken/crushed the heart,” i.e., the victim’s heart prepared for the rite; θραύω can mean to break up into pieces. ποπάνοισιν: popanoi are small sacrificial cakes (instrumental dative), a technical ritual term.

text.greek: λείψας ὑγρὸν ἔλαιον, ἐπ' αὐτῷ δὲ γλάγος ἄμνης.
text.english: having poured liquid oil, and thereon the rennet of a lamb.
text.note: λείψας: aorist participle of λείβω “to pour (as a libation),” not of λείπω “to leave.” γλάγος ἄμνης: γλάγος is rare, ‘curdled milk/rennet’; with ἄμνης (‘of a lamb’) this denotes lamb’s rennet. ἐπ’ αὐτῷ refers back to the item just placed (sc. the offering/heart).

text.greek: Ἥρωας δ' ἐκέλευσα περισταδὸν ἀμφιχυθέντας
text.english: And I bade the heroes, thronging on every side,
text.note: περισταδὸν ἀμφιχυθέντας: a pleonastic combination; ἀμφιχύνω is used figuratively of ‘thronging’ or ‘swarming’ around.

text.greek: δούρατ' ἐπαμπήξασθαι ἰδ' ἄορα κωπήεντα,
text.english: to plant their spears and their hilted swords,
text.note: δούρατα here are ‘spears’ (not ‘timbers’); ἐπαμπήγνυσθαι = ‘to fix/plant (in the ground)’. ἄορα κωπήεντα is the standard epic phrase ‘hilted swords’. The line envisions the warriors planting their weapons as they prepare the rite.

text.greek: βύρσῃ τε σπλάγχνοισι τ' ἐρειδομέναις παλάμῃσι.
text.english: with the hide and the entrails braced in their hands.
text.note: βύρσῃ (‘hide’) and σπλάγχνοισι (‘entrails’) are instrumental/manner datives, referring to sacrificial handling; ἐρειδομέναις παλάμῃσι = ‘with hands braced/supporting’. The participle is fem. dat. pl., agreeing with implied παλάμαι; many take the phrase adverbially of manner (some emend to ἐρειδομένοις). The sense is ‘while handling the victim’s hide and entrails.’

text.greek: Θῆκα δ' ἄρ' ἐν μέσσῳ τεῦχος κυκεῶνος ἐρείσας
text.english: Then I set in the midst a vessel for kykeon, having set it firm,
text.note: Θῆκα is first-person aorist (“I set”); some read θῆκε (“he set”). τεῦχος = “vessel, implement”; ἐρείσας = “having set/propped it firmly.” Κυκεών (kykeon) is the ritual drink.

text.greek: ὀστράκεον, τῷ πάντα περιφραδέως ἐμέμικτο,
text.english: earthenware, wherein all things had been carefully mixed,
text.note: ὀστράκεον = “earthenware.” τῷ is a dative of respect/means (“in which”); περιφραδέως = “very carefully”; ἐμέμικτο (perf. mid.) implies prior thorough mixing.

text.greek: Δήμητρος μὲν πρῶτα φερέσβιος ἀλφίτου ἀκτή,
text.english: first, Demeter’s life-bringing barley-groats,
text.note: Δήμητρος (Demeter) in the genitive as metonym for grain; φερέσβιος = “life-bringing.” ἀκτή of ἀλφίτον denotes coarse meal/groats, not “shore.”

text.greek: αἷμα δ' ἐπὶ ταύροιο, θαλάσσης θ' ἁλμυρὸν ὕδωρ.
text.english: and, upon it, the blood of a bull, and the briny water of the sea.
text.note: ἐπὶ marks addition/overlay (“upon it”). The inclusion of bull’s blood and sea-water signals a ritual kykeon distinct from the Homeric culinary mixture; ἁλμυρόν = “briny.”

text.greek: Στέψασθαι δ' ἐκέλευσα κύκλους ἐρόεντας ἐλαίης·
text.english: And I bade them wreathe themselves with circles of sacred olive.
text.note: ἐρόεντας is likely for ἱερόεντας (“sacred”); κύκλους here means wreaths (circular garlands) of olive. The middle στεψάσθαι means “to wreathe oneself.”

text.greek: καὶ τότε χρυσείην φιάλην χείρεσσιν ἐμαῖσιν
text.english: Then, taking a golden bowl in my own hands,
text.note: φιάλη is a phiale, a shallow libation-bowl; translated here as “bowl.”

text.greek: ἀμπλήσας κυκεῶνος, ἐφεξείης ἐπένειμον
text.english: and filling it with kykeon, I apportioned it in succession,
text.note: κυκεών (kykeon) is a ritual drink (typically a barley-based mixture); ἐφεξείης means “in succession, one after another.”

text.greek: γεύειν ἄνδρα ἕκαστον ἐρισθενέων βασιλήων.
text.english: for each man among the very-mighty kings to taste.
text.note: ἐπένειμον with an infinitive (“to taste”) expresses the allotment/purpose; ἐρισθενέων is an epic intensive (“very-mighty”). “Kings” refers to the Argonaut leaders.

text.greek: Πυρκαϊῇ δ' ἐκέλευον Ἰήσονα λαμπάδα θέσθαι
text.english: And at the beacon-fire they bade Jason set a torch of dry pine.
text.note: πυρκαϊῇ (dat.) = “at/on the beacon/bonfire” (not necessarily a funerary pyre here). πεύκης ἀζαλέης is a genitive of material, “of dry/parched pine,” well-suited for kindling.

text.greek: πεύκης ἀζαλέης· ὑπὸ δ' ἔδραμε θεσπεσίη φλόξ.
text.english: And under it there ran a wondrous flame.
text.note: ὑπὸ … ἔδραμε is epic for a flame’s swift spread “from beneath.” θεσπεσίη = “wondrous, divinely-sent”; “wondrous” preserves the epic ambiguity.

text.greek: Δὴ τότ' ἐγὼ πρὸς χεῦμα πολυφλοίσβοιο θαλάσσης,
text.english: Then indeed I, toward the surge of the loud-roaring sea,
text.note: χεῦμα = “surge/outpouring”; πολυφλοίσβοιο θαλάσσης is the traditional epic epithet “loud-roaring sea.”

text.greek: χεῖρας ἐπαντείνας, τάδ' ἀπὸ γλώσσης ἀγόρευσα,
text.english: stretching out my hands, uttered these words from my tongue,
text.note: ἀγόρευσα has formal/solemn force (“declared, addressed”); ἀπὸ γλώσσης is a formulaic epic expression for speaking.

text.greek: - "Ὠκεανοῦ μεδέοντες ἁλικλύστοιό τε πόντου
text.english: “Guardians of Okeanos and of the brine-swollen sea, deep-dwelling blessed ones,
text.note: μεδέοντες = “guardians/holders of sway”; ἁλικλύστος literally “washed/beaten by brine” (hence “brine‑swollen”); ἐμβύθιοι = “in the depths, deep‑dwelling.” Okeanos is the world-encircling stream, distinct from the open sea (pontos).

text.greek: ἐμβύθιοι μάκαρες, καὶ ὅσοι ψαμμώδεας ἀκτάς
text.english: and all you who dwell along the sandy shores, sea-pebbled,
text.note: ἁλικροκάλους is a rare compound from ἅλς (sea, brine) + κρόκαλος (rounded pebble), meaning “sea‑pebbled” or “shingled by sea‑worn stones.”

text.greek: ναίεθ' ἁλικροκάλους, καὶ Τηθύος ἔσχατον ὕδωρ.
text.english: and upon Tethys’ utmost water.”
text.note: Τηθύος ἔσχατον ὕδωρ = “the outermost/farthest water of Tethys,” i.e., the world’s rim-waters; the object is governed elliptically by ναίεθ’ (“dwell”) from the previous line.

text.greek: Νηρέα μὲν πρώτιστα καλῶ πρέσβυστον ἁπάντων,
text.english: Nereus first of all I invoke, the eldest of them all,

text.greek: ἄμμιγα πεντήκοντα κόραις πάσαισιν ἐρανναῖς·
text.english: together with all his fifty lovely maidens;
text.note: ἄμμιγα = “together with,” an epic/ionic adverb; the fifty “maidens” are the Nereids.

text.greek: Γλαυκὴν δ' ἰχθυόεσσαν, ἀπείριτον Ἀμφιτρίτην,
text.english: and the glaucous, fish‑swarming sea, and boundless Amphitritê,
text.note: “Glaukên … ichthyoessan” functions substantively for “the sea” (Θάλασσα) without the noun expressed; “boundless” (ἀπείριτος) is a conventional maritime epithet of Amphitritê.

text.greek: Πρωτέα καὶ Φόρκυνα, καὶ εὐρυβίην Τρίτωνα,
text.english: Proteus and Phorkys, and Triton of broad might,
text.note: “εὐρυβίης” = “of broad might,” a set epithet of Triton.

text.greek: λαιψηρούς τ' ἀνέμους, αὔραις μίγα χρυσεοτάρσαις,
text.english: and the nimble winds, together with the golden‑ankled Aurai,
text.note: The Aurai are personified breezes; “golden‑ankled” (χρυσεοτάρσαις) is a nymph‑epithet.

text.greek: ἄστρα τε τηλεσίφαντα, καὶ ἀχλύα νυκτὸς ἐρεμνῆς
text.english: and the far‑shining stars, and the mist of murky Night,
text.note: “ τηλεσίφαντα” is a rare compound, here “far‑shining” of the stars; ἐρεμνός = “murky, dark.”

text.greek: αὐγήν τ' ἠελίοιο ποδῶν προποδηγέτιν ἵππων
text.english: and the beam of Hêlios, the guide that runs before the feet of his horses,
text.note: “προποδηγέτιν” literally “leading on before the feet,” i.e., the first light that precedes Helios’ chariot; hence the sun’s fore‑gleam.

text.greek: δαίμονας εἰναλίους τε μιγαζομένους ἥρωσιν,
text.english: and the sea‑daimones who mingle with heroes,
text.note: “δαίμονες εἰναλίοι” are marine spirits; “mingling with heroes” evokes their intercourse or companionship with heroic figures (e.g., Glaukos, Thetis, etc.).

text.greek: ἀκταίους τε θεοὺς, ποταμῶν θ' ἁλιμυρέα ῥεῖθρα·
text.english: and the shore‑dwelling gods, and the briny streams of the rivers;
text.note: “ἀκταῖοι θεοί” = deities of the shore/coast; “briny streams of the rivers” (ἁλιμυρέα ῥεῖθρα) points to river‑mouths mixing with the sea.

text.greek: αὐτόν τε Κρονίδην σεισίχθονα κυανοχαίτην,
text.english: and himself, the Kronidês, the Earth‑shaker, dark‑haired,
text.note: “Kronidês” (son of Kronos) here denotes Poseidon; “Earth‑shaker” (σεισίχθων) and “dark‑haired/blue‑haired” (κυανοχαίτης) are his fixed epithets.

text.greek: κύματος ἐκπροθορόντα μολεῖν ἐπιτάρροθον ὅρκων.
text.english: to come, leaping forth from the wave, as a helper of oaths.
text.note: “ἐπιτάρροθον ὅρκων” = “as ally/helper of oaths,” i.e., called as witness and enforcer of sworn pledges; “leaping forth from the wave” marks his sea‑epiphany.

text.greek: Τόφρα μὲν οὖν ἐπίκουροι Ἰάσονος ἔμπεδον αἰεί
text.english: So then, as helpers of Iason, ever steadfast,
text.note: Τόφρα is a transitional adverb (“so then,” “meanwhile”). ἔμπεδον is adverbial (“steadfast[ly]”). ἐπίκουροι governs the genitive (“helpers of Iason”).

text.greek: μίμνωμεν προφρόνως ξυνῶν ἐπαρηγόνες ἄθλων,
text.english: let us remain willingly, aid-bringers to our shared labors,
text.note: ξυνῶν is the epic form of κοινῶν (“shared, common”). ἐπαρηγόνες = “aid-bringing, succoring,” used predicatively of the subject; προφρόνως = “willingly, zealously.”

text.greek: ζῳοὶ νοστήσωμεν ἑὰ πρὸς δώμαθ' ἕκαστος·
text.english: and let each return alive to his own halls;
text.note: ζῳοί is emphatic, highlighting safe return; δώματα = “halls, house” in epic diction.

text.greek: ὃς δέ κε συνθεσίης δηλήσεται οὐκ ἀλεγίζων
text.english: but whoever shall harm the compact, recking not,
text.note: δηλέομαι takes the genitive (συνθεσίης) of the thing harmed; οὐκ ἀλεγίζων = “not caring, recking not.”

text.greek: ὅρκον ὑπερβάσιον, τούτου δ' ἐπιμάρτυροι ἔστων
text.english: by overstepping the oath—of this let witnesses be
text.note: ὑπερβάσιος (“overstepping, transgressive”) modifies ὅρκον; sense: “by transgressing the oath.” ἐπιμάρτυροι ἔστων is 3rd-pl imperative: “let X be witnesses.”

text.greek: ἰθύντειρα Δίκη καὶ Ἐριννύες αἰνοδότειραι."
text.english: straight-steering Dike and the dread-giving Erinyes.”
text.note: ἰθύντειρα (lit. “straight-guiding, straight-steering”) is an epithet of Dike; αἰνοδότειραι (“dread-giving”) of the Erinyes (spelled Ἐριννύες in some traditions).

text.greek: Ὣς ἐφάμην· οἱ δ' αὖτις ὁμοφροσύνῃ κατένευσαν
text.english: Thus I spoke; and they in turn nodded with one mind,
text.note: ὁμοφροσύνῃ = “with one mind, in unanimity”; κατένευσαν = “they nodded [assent],” a formulaic gesture of agreement.

text.greek: ὅρκια δειμαίνοντες, ἐσημήναντο δὲ χερσίν.
text.english: fearing the oaths, and signaled with their hands.
text.note: ἐσημήναντο χερσί(ν) = “they made a sign with their hands,” a gesture of assent/ratification; ὅρκια δειμαίνοντες = “fearing the (sanctity of the) oaths.”

text.greek: - Αὐτὰρ ἐπεί ῥ' ὄμοσάν τε τελεύτησαν τε τὸν ὅρκον,
text.english: But when indeed they had sworn and brought the oath to its fulfillment,
text.note: “To complete the oath” (τελεῦν τὸν ὅρκον) is a traditional formula, implying the full rite of swearing has been performed.

text.greek: δὴ τότε νηὸς ἑῆς κοῖλον κύτος εἰσεπέρησαν
text.english: then at that very time they passed into the hollow hull of their own ship,
text.note: κοῖλον κῦτος, literally “hollow belly,” is a conventional epic expression for the ship’s hull/hold.

text.greek: πάντες ἐφεξείης, ὑπὸ δὲ ζυγὰ τεύχε' ἔθεντο,
text.english: one after another, and beneath the benches they stowed their gear,
text.note: ζυγά are the thwarts or rowing-benches; τεύχεα here means ship’s gear/equipment (not martial arms).

text.greek: χεῖρας ἐρετμώσαντες· ἐκέκλετο δ' αὐτόθι Τῖφυς
text.english: setting their hands to the oars; and thereupon Tiphys called out
text.note: χεῖρας ἐρετμώσαντες is an idiom, “to set one’s hands to the oars”; ἐκέκλετο here conveys “gave the word/command.”

text.greek: ἐκταδίοις ὅπλοις δῆσαι παρὰ κλίμακα μακρήν
text.english: to make fast with the outspread tackle along the long ladder,
text.note: ἐκταδίοις ὅπλοις (“with outspread/spreading tackle”) is nautical; παρὰ κλίμακα μακρήν likely refers to the long shroud or rope-ladder used to ascend the mast/rigging; hence “make fast with the spread-out rigging along the long ladder.”

text.greek: ἱστία δ' ἁπλῶσαι, λιμένος δ' ἐκ πείσματα θέσθαι.
text.english: to unfurl the sails, and to cast off the moorings from the harbor.
text.note: λιμένος ἐκ πείσματα θέσθαι means “to cast off the harbor-moorings”; πείσματα are mooring cables/fastenings, with θέσθαι (middle) conveying removal/casting off.

text.greek: Καὶ τότε δὴ λίγυν οὖρον ἐπιπροέηκε νέεσθαι
text.english: And then indeed she sent forth a fair, whistling breeze for sailing.
text.note: λιγύν οὖρον: literally “clear-/shrill-sounding wind,” an epic epithet applied to a favorable breeze; hence “fair, whistling.” νέεσθαι here = “to sail,” not “to return.” ἐπιπροέηκε = “sent forth to speed onward,” aorist sense in context.

text.greek: Ἥρη, Ζηνὸς ἄκοιτις, ἐπείγετο δ' ἐς πλόον Ἀργώ.
text.english: Hera, consort of Zeus; and Argo hastened to the voyage.
text.note: Ἥρη, Ζηνὸς ἄκοιτις appositionally identifies the subject of the previous line. ἐπείγετο (mid.) ἐς πλόον = “pressed on/hastened to the voyage.” Ἀργώ is the ship personified as the grammatical subject.

text.greek: Οἱ δ' ἄρ' ἐπ' εἰρεσίην ἔπεχον χεῖράς τε νόον τε
text.english: Then they kept both hands and mind upon the rowing,
text.note: εἰρεσίη = “rowing, oarage”; the collocation “hands and mind” marks full concentration on the task.

text.greek: ἄκμητοι βασιλῆες, ἐτέτμετο δ' ἄσπετος ἅλμη,
text.english: the unwearied kings, and the measureless brine was being cloven,
text.note: ἄκμητοι = “unwearied” (also “in their prime”); ἐτέτμετο is an epic (plu)perfect used with imperfect force, hence “was being cloven”; ἄσπετος = “immeasurable, boundless.”

text.greek: ἀφροῦ ἅμ' οἰδαίνοντος ὑπὸ τρόπιν ἔνθα καὶ ἔνθα.
text.english: as the foam swelled beneath the keel, on this side and on that.
text.note: Genitive absolute: ἀφροῦ ἅμ’ οἰδαίνοντος = “as the foam swelled”; τρόπις = “keel”; ἔνθα καὶ ἔνθα = “on this side and on that.”

text.greek: Τῆμος δ' ἱερὸς ὄρθρος ἀπ' Ὠκεανοῖο ῥοάων
text.english: Then holy dawn from the streams of Okeanos
text.note: Τῆμος = “then, at that time,” an epic-temporal adverb; ἱερὸς ὄρθρος (“holy dawn”) is a formulaic epithet; Ὠκεανός is the world-encircling river.

text.greek: ἀντολίας ἤνοιγεν, ἐπέσπετο δ' Ἠριγένεια
text.english: was opening the East, and Erigeneia attended,
text.note: ἀντολίαι (pl.) = “the East, the risings (of the sun)”; ἐπέσπετο = “attended, followed hard upon.” Ἠριγένεια is the Dawn-goddess (Eos), “Early-born,” here transliterated.

text.greek: ἡδὺ φάος θνητοῖσι καὶ ἀθανάτοισι φέρουσα·
text.english: bringing sweet light to mortals and immortals;
text.note: φάος is a poetic synonym for φῶς (“light”); ἡδύ = “sweet, pleasant,” suited to epic diction.

text.greek: καὶ τότε δὴ σκοπιαί τε καὶ ἠνεμόεσσα κολώνη
text.english: and then indeed the lookout-heights and the wind‑swept hill
text.note: σκοπιαί = “lookout-places, watch-heights”; κολώνη = “mound, hill,” here with the Homeric epithet ἠνεμόεσσα (“wind-swept”).

text.greek: Πηλίου ὑλήεντος ἀπ' ἠϊόνος κατέφαινε.
text.english: from the strand of woody Pelion came into view.
text.note: ἀπ’ ἠϊόνος = “from the strand/shore.” κατέφαινε can be taken intransitively (“came into view,” as translated) though the singular verb with two subjects is epic; alternatively, it may be construed transitively with Dawn as the subject (“she made visible the lookout-heights and the wind-swept hill from the shore of woody Pelion”).

text.greek: Τῖφυς δ' ἀμπαύσας δισσῆς οἰήια χειρός
text.english: But Tiphys, taking his two hands off the steering-ropes,
text.note: οἰήια = the steering-ropes (from οἴαξ, tiller/helm); δισσῆς χειρός is genitive “of both hands.” ἀμπαύσας is effectively “ceasing/letting go” (either transitive of the ropes or with genitive of separation).

text.greek: τυτθὸν ὑπειρεσίῃσιν ἐκέκλετο κῦμα χαράσσειν·
text.english: called for them to furrow the wave a little with under-strokes;
text.note: κέκλετο is the Homeric middle “he called/urged.” ὑπειρεσίῃσιν (dat. pl.) = “with under-strokes” (of the oars), i.e., gentle or checking strokes; κῦμα χαράσσειν = “to furrow/score the wave.”

text.greek: καί ῥα θοῶς ἀκτῇσιν ὑπέδραμον· ἐκ δ' ἄρα νηός
text.english: and swiftly they ran in under the shores;
text.note: ὑπέδραμον ἀκτῇσιν is a nautical idiom: “they ran in under the shores,” i.e., made landfall quickly; subject = the crew/ship collectively.

text.greek: κλίμακα δαυρατέην λιμένων ἔντοσθε χάλασσαν.
text.english: and from the ship they lowered a wooden ladder within the haven.
text.note: δαυρατέην = “wooden, timbered” (from δαῦρα, timbers). κλίμαξ here is the boarding ladder/gangway; λιμένων (pl.) is generic for the harbor-basin; hence “within the haven.”

text.greek: Ἐκ δ' ἔβαν ἥρωες Μινύαι, παύσαντο δὲ μόχθου·
text.english: Forth went the Minyan heroes, and they ceased from toil.

text.greek: τοῖσι δὲ μύθων ἦρχεν ὁμιλαδὸν ἱππότα Πηλεύς·
text.english: And among them, in assembly, Peleus the horseman began to speak words:
text.note: ὁμιλαδόν: adverb “in company, in assembly.”

text.greek: - "Ὦ φίλοι, ἀθρεῖτε σκοπιῆς προὔχοντα κολωνόν,
text.english: “Friends, look upon the projecting hill of the lookout,
text.note: σκοπιῆς προὔχοντα κολωνόν: literally “the hill projecting from/of the lookout”; κολωνός is a knoll or mound used here of a promontory feature.

text.greek: μέσσῳ ἐνὶ πρηῶνι κατάσκιον, ἐνθάδε Χείρων
text.english: shaded in the midst of the headland; here Cheiron
text.note: πρηών: a slope or headland/promontory; κατάσκιον “shaded.”

text.greek: ναίει ἐνὶ σπήλυγγι, δικαιότατος Κενταύρων
text.english: dwells in a cave, the most righteous of the Centaurs

text.greek: οἳ τράφεν ἐν Φολόῃ, Πίνδου τ' αἰπεινὰ κάρηνα,
text.english: who were reared on Pholoē and the lofty crests of Pindos,
text.note: Pholoē (in Arcadia/Elis) and Pindos (the mountain range in Thessaly/Epirus) are traditional haunts of Centaurs.

text.greek: ὅς ῥα δικασπολίῃ μέλεται καὶ ἀκεύμασι νούσων·
text.english: who indeed is devoted to civic justice and to remedies for diseases;
text.note: δικασπολίη: rare compound, “city-justice, civic jurisprudence”; ἀκεύματα “remedies, cures.”

text.greek: ἄλλοτε δ' αὖ Φοίβου κιθάρην μετὰ χερσὶν ἀράσσων,
text.english: and at other times again, striking in his hands the kithara of Phoibos,

text.greek: ἢ λιγυρὴν φόρμιγγα χελυκλόνον Ἑρμάωνος,
text.english: or the clear‑toned tortoise‑shell phorminx of Hermes,
text.note: Ἑρμάωνος is an epic genitive for Hermes; χελυκλόνον “tortoise‑sounding,” i.e., of a tortoise‑shell lyre (phorminx).

text.greek: πᾶσι περικτιόνεσσι δικασπολίας ἀναφαίνει.
text.english: he makes manifest to all the dwellers round about the ordinances of civic justice.”
text.note: περικτίονες: “neighbors, dwellers round about”; ἀναφαίνει “makes manifest, proclaims.”

text.greek: Τόφρα καὶ ἡμέτερον κοῦρον Θέτις ἀργυρόπεζα
text.english: Meanwhile too, silver-footed Thetis our boy,
text.note: Argyropedza (“silver-footed”) is the fixed Homeric epithet of Thetis. Hēmeteron (“our”) is a parental plural, referring to the child of Thetis and Peleus—Achilles.

text.greek: νήπιον, ἀρτιγένεθλον, ἐν ἀγκαλίδεσσι λαβοῦσα,
text.english: an infant, newly born, took in her arms,
text.note: Nēpion means “infant” (literally “uncomprehending”); artigenethlon “newly born.” En agkalidesi is “in [her] arms,” an epic plural. The participle labousa supplies the sense “having taken [him].”

text.greek: Πήλιον εἰνοσίφυλλον ἔβη, Χείρωνί τ' ἔδωκεν
text.english: went to leaf-shaking Pelion and gave him to Cheiron,
text.note: Einosiphyllon (“leaf-shaking”) is an epic compound applied to wind-tossed wooded mountains; Pelion is the Thessalian mountain of Cheiron, the wise Centaur.

text.greek: εὖ καὶ ἐπισταμένως ἀγαπαζέμεν ἠδ' ἀτιτάλλειν.
text.english: to cherish well and skilfully and to rear.
text.note: Agapazemen “to cherish, treat with affection”; epistamenōs “knowingly, skilfully”; atitallein “to rear, nurse.” The paired infinitives express purpose: Thetis entrusts the child to Cheiron to be lovingly and expertly reared.

text.greek: Ὃν δή μοι πόθος ἐστὶ περὶ φρένα θηήσασθαι.
text.english: Whom indeed a longing is upon my heart to behold in wonder.
text.note: περὶ φρένα: literally “around/about the heart,” an epic idiom meaning “at/in my heart, in my mind.”

text.greek: Ἀλλὰ, φίλοι, πελάσωμεν ἐπὶ σπέος, ὄφρα ἴδωμαι
text.english: But, friends, let us draw near to the cave, that I may behold
text.note: σπέος = “cave,” here the grotto of Cheiron; the speaker in context is Peleus addressing his comrades.

text.greek: ἕξιν παιδὸς ἐμοῖο, καὶ ἤθεσιν οἷσι κέκασται."
text.english: the condition of my own child, and the dispositions wherein he excels.”
text.note: ἕξις can mean “state, condition,” also “training”; ἤθεα = “habits, dispositions”; κέκασται = “is preeminent/excels.”

text.greek: - Ὣς εἰπὼν ἐξῖκεν ἀταρπιτόν· οἷ δ' ἑπόμεσθα·
text.english: So speaking he reached the pathless track; and we followed him;
text.note: ἀταρπιτόν = “pathless/untrodden (way).” Formulaic epic diction.

text.greek: Αὐτὰρ ἐπ' εἰς αὐλὴν εἰσήλθομεν ἠεροειδῆ
text.english: and then we entered into the misty courtyard,
text.note: αὐλή here denotes the forecourt/yard before a dwelling; ἠεροειδής = “misty.” The sequence ἐπ’ εἰς is metrically driven and effectively means “then/thereupon into.”

text.greek: καὶ προσκεκλιμένος μὲν ἐπ' οὐδαίοιο χαμεύνης
text.english: and there, reclining upon an earthen couch,
text.note: οὐδαῖος = “of the ground, earthen”; χαμευνή = “couch on the ground”; προσκεκλιμένος = “reclining, leaning upon.”

text.greek: κεῖτο μέγας Κένταυρος, ἀπηρήρειστο δὲ πέτρῃ
text.english: lay the great Kentauros, propped against a rock,
text.note: ἀπηρήρειστο (perf. mid./pass.) = “was propped/leaning against,” conveying a settled posture.

text.greek: ἱππείαισιν ὁπλαῖσι τανυσσάμενος θοὰ κῶλα.
text.english: having stretched out his swift horse-limbs.
text.note: ἱππείαισιν ὁπλαῖσι is poetic for the centaur’s equine limbs (ὅπλα can denote an animal’s ‘equipment’ for motion, as wings for birds); hence “horse-limbs.”

text.greek: Ἀγχοῦ δ' ἱστάμενος Θέτιδος καὶ Πηλέος υἱός
text.english: And close at hand stood the son of Thetis and Peleus,
text.note: “The son of Thetis and Peleus” identifies Achilles; ἄγχοῦ = ‘near, close by’; the participle ἱστάμενος is rendered idiomatically as a finite verb for smoothness.

text.greek: χειρὶ λύραν ἤρασσε, φρένας δ' ἐπετέρπετο Χείρων.
text.english: with his hand he kept striking the lyre, and Cheiron rejoiced in his heart.
text.note: ἤρασσε (iterative/imperfect of ἀράσσω) = ‘kept striking’; φρένας ἐπετέρπετο is a Homeric idiom ‘he took delight in his heart/mind,’ with middle voice marking personal pleasure; subject shifts from Achilles (striking) to Cheiron (delighting).

text.greek: Ἀλλ' ὅτε δή ῥ' ἄθρησεν ἀγακλειτοὺς βασιλῆας
text.english: But when indeed he beheld the illustrious kings,
text.note: ἄθρησεν = “beheld, gazed upon” (from ἀθρέω), not “gathered” (cf. ἀθροίζω).

text.greek: ἀσπασίως ἀνόρουσε, κύσεν δ' ἄρα φῶτα ἕκαστον·
text.english: gladly he sprang up, and he kissed each man;
text.note: φῶτα = “man, mortal” in epic diction.

text.greek: δαῖτά τ' ἐπόρσυνεν· μέθυ δ' ἀμφιφορεῦσι κόμισσεν,
text.english: he made ready a feast, and brought wine in amphorae,
text.note: μέθυ here denotes wine (not mead); the amphorae and the explicit οἶνος in 405 confirm the sense.

text.greek: ῥωγαλέαις τ' ἔστρωσεν ὑπὸ στιβάδεσσι πέτηλα·
text.english: and he strewed leaves beneath the rough pallets;
text.note: ῥωγαλέαις = “coarse, rough”; στιβάδες are leaf-beds; πέτηλα = “leaves” (poetic form of πέταλα).

text.greek: κλινθῆναι δ' ἐκέλευσεν, ἀδαιδάλτοις δ' ὑπὸ πλακταῖς
text.english: and he bade them recline beneath unadorned planks,
text.note: ἀδαιδάλτοις … πλακταῖς = “unadorned planks,” i.e., the plain roof/ceiling; ὑπό with the dative means “beneath.” Some have taken πλακταί as platters, but ὑπό would then be awkward.

text.greek: κρεῖα χύδην προὔθηκε συῶν ἐλάφων τε ταχειῶν·
text.english: and he set forth in heaps the meats of swine and of swift deer;
text.note: χύδην = “in heaps, en masse”; κρέα = “cuts/meats.”

text.greek: αὐτὰρ ἔπειτ' ἐπένειμε ποτὸν μελιηδέος οἴνου.
text.english: and thereafter he apportioned the draught of honey-sweet wine.
text.note: ἐπένειμε = “dealt out, apportioned,” commonly of distributing portions or drink.

text.greek: - Ἀλλ' ὅτε δὴ δόρποιο ποτοῦ θ' ἅλις ἔπλετο θυμός
text.english: But when at last their spirit was sated with supper and with drink,

text.greek: χερσὶν ἐπικροτέοντες ὁμόκλεον, ὄφρ' ἂν ἔγωγε
text.english: clapping with their hands they shouted in unison, until I myself
text.note: ὁμόκλεον usually means “to rebuke/threaten” in early epic, but here it denotes a collective shout or outcry; ἐπικροτέοντες is “clapping” to mark time or encourage the performer.

text.greek: δηρίσω Χείρωνι διωλύγιον κιθαρίζων.
text.english: should vie with Cheiron, playing the kithara in a most clamorous strain.
text.note: δηρίσω is aorist subjunctive with ὄφρ’ ἄν (“until I should contend”). διωλύγιον is obscure (a rare/hapax formation), probably related to ὀλολυγή (“ritual ululation”); taken adverbially with κιθαρίζων, it conveys “very loudly/clamorously.” The “contest with Cheiron” is a friendly musical rivalry with the Centaur.

text.greek: Ἀλλ' ἐγὼ οὐ πιθόμην· περὶ γάρ με ἐπήλυθεν αἰδώς,
text.english: But I did not obey; for a reverent shame came over me,
text.note: αἰδώς conveys reverential modesty or shame; περὶ μὲ ἐπήλυθεν is an epic idiom “came over me.”

text.greek: ὁπλότερον γεγαῶτα γεραιτέρῳ ἰσοφαρίζειν·
text.english: at, being the younger, matching myself as an equal with an elder;
text.note: ὁπλότερον γεγαῶτα = “being born the younger”; γεραιτέρῳ = “to an elder.” ἰσοφαρίζειν “to match as an equal, rival” explains the cause of the αἰδώς.

text.greek: μέσφ' αὐτὸς Χείρων ἐλιλαίετο καί μ' ἀέκοντα
text.english: even Cheiron himself kept earnestly entreating me, and, though I was unwilling,
text.note: μέσφ’ is a contracted form (likely μέν σφ’), giving concessive/emphatic force (“even indeed”); ἐλιλαίετο (from λιλαιόμαι) “kept beseeching/longing for.” ἀέκοντα is the accusative with ἠνώγει (“bade [me], though unwilling”).

text.greek: ἠνώγει ᾄδων ἐριδαινέμεν εἵνεκα μολπῆς.
text.english: he bade me, as he sang, to engage in rivalry for the sake of song.
text.note: ᾄδων (nominative participle) most naturally modifies Cheiron: “as he sang.” ἐριδαινέμεν is the epic infinitive of ἐριδαίνω “to contend,” and εἵνεκα μολπῆς indicates a singing-contest.

text.greek: Πρῶτος δ' αὖ Κένταυρος ἀείρατο πηκτίδα καλήν
text.english: First then the Centaur took up the fair pektis,
text.note: πηκτίς (pektis) is a Lydian/Anatolian stringed instrument (harp- or lyre-like). “The Centaur” is almost certainly Cheiron, Achilles’ tutor; αείρατο (middle) suggests “took up” or “raised for himself.” Some have proposed πληκτίδα (“plectrum”), but πήκτιδα is generally preferred as the instrument itself.

text.greek: ἥν ῥα τότ' ἐν χείρεσσι φέρων ὤρεξεν Ἀχιλλεύς.
text.english: which Achilles then, bearing it in his hands, held forth.
text.note: ὤρεξεν (from ὀρέγω) means “stretched/held out,” not “played”; the line depicts Achilles presenting or extending the instrument he carries in his hands.

text.greek: Ὅς δ' ἄρ' ἄειδε μάχην Κενταύρων ὀμβριμοθύμων,
text.english: Who then sang of the battle of the storm‑spirited Centaurs,
text.note: Ὅς δ’ ἄρ’ ἄειδε is a relative to prior context (“who then sang”); ὀμβριμοθύμων = “storm‑spirited/impetuous,” an epic epithet of violent temper.

text.greek: οὓς Λαπίθαι κατέπεφνον ἀτασθαλίης ἕνεκα σφῶν
text.english: whom the Lapiths slew on account of their own recklessness,
text.note: σφῶν (“their own”) is ambiguous in reference; context favors the Centaurs’ recklessness (ἀτασθαλία) as the cause, matching the traditional myth.

text.greek: ἠδ' ὥς Ἡρακλῆϊ καταντία μαιμώοντες
text.english: and how, raging against Herakles, they fought in Pholoë,
text.note: καταντίa with the dative = “against, facing”; μαιμώοντες = “raging, frenzied.” Φολόη (Pholoë) is the mountain connected with the Centaur Pholos and Herakles’ encounter.

text.greek: ἐν Φολόῃ δήρισαν· ἐπεὶ μένος οἴνου ἔγειρεν.
text.english: since the might of wine had roused them.
text.note: μένος οἴνου (“the might/fury of wine”) personifies wine’s inciting power; ἐπεί is causal (“since”).

text.greek: - Αὐτὰρ ἔγωγε μετ' αὐτὸν ἑλὼν φόρμιγγα λιγεῖαν,
text.english: But I myself, after him, taking up the clear-toned phorminx,
text.note: met’ auton can mean “after him” (temporal succession) or “in turn”; the context favors temporal succession in performance.

text.greek: ἐκ στόματος μελίγηρυν ἱεὶς ἀνέπεμπον ἀοιδήν·
text.english: launching from my mouth honey-sweet song, I sent it up,
text.note: The verb pair ἱεὶς … ἀνέπεμπον (“launching/sending up”) suits hymnic diction, implying an upward-directed song/prayer.

text.greek: Πρῶτα μὲν ἀρχαίου χάεος μελανήφατον ὕμνον,
text.english: First, a dark-voiced hymn of primordial Chaos,
text.note: μελανήφατος (“dark-voiced/dark-uttered”) modifies ὕμνον, not Χάος; hence “a dark-voiced hymn of primordial Chaos.”

text.greek: ὡς ἐπάμειψε φύσεις, ὥς τ' οὐρανὸς ἐς πέρας ἦλθε·
text.english: how it transmuted the natures, and how heaven came to its bound;
text.note: ἐπάμειψε φύσεις is cosmogonic: “changed/transmuted the natures” (i.e., primordial elements or states). οὐρανὸς ἐς πέρας ἦλθε = the delimitation of heaven; Ouranos may be cosmic “heaven,” not necessarily the theonym here.

text.greek: γῆς τ' εὐρυστέρνου γένεσιν, πυθμένας τε θαλάσσης·
text.english: and the birth of broad‑bosomed Earth, and the sea’s foundations;
text.note: εὐρυστέρνος is the traditional epithet “broad‑bosomed” for Earth; πυθμένες θαλάσσης are the sea’s “foundations/bases,” i.e., its deeps or structural roots.

text.greek: πρεσβύτατόν τε καὶ αὐτοτελῆ πολύμητιν Ἔρωτα,
text.english: and Eros, eldest and self‑complete, of much counsel,
text.note: αὐτοτελής (“self‑complete, self-sufficient”) is a technical Orphic attribute of Eros; πολύμητις (“of much counsel”) is striking for Eros, marking creative intelligence.

text.greek: ὅσσα τ' ἔφυσεν ἅπαντα, διέκρινε δ' ἄλλον ἀπ' ἄλλου·
text.english: all that he brought to be, and how he set one apart from another;
text.note: Subject understood as Eros: ἔφυσεν “brought forth/generated”; διέκρινε “separated, distinguished” the elements—an Orphic theme of cosmogonic differentiation.

text.greek: καὶ Κρόνον αἰνολέτην, ὥς τ' ἐς Δία τερπικέραυνον
text.english: and Kronos the dread‑destroyer, and how unto Zeus the Thunder‑delighter
text.note: αἰνολέτης is rare/uncertain; rendered “dread‑destroyer” (alternatively “grim‑slayer”), apt for Kronos’ violent myth. τερπικέραυνος is the set epithet “Thunder‑delighter” of Zeus.

text.greek: ἤλυθεν ἀθανάτων μακάρων βασιλήϊος ἀρχή.
text.english: came the kingly rule of the blessed immortals.
text.note: ἤλυθεν … βασιλήϊος ἀρχή = “the kingly rule came.” μακάρων ἀθανάτων = “of the blessed immortals,” a standard epic periphrasis for the gods.

text.greek: Μέλπον θ' ὁπλοτέρων μακάρων γένεσίν τε κρίσιν τε·
text.english: Celebrating the birth and the judgment of the younger Blessed Ones;
text.note: ὁπλοτέρων μακάρων = the younger generation of gods (as opposed to the elder/Titans). κρίσις may mean “judgment/decision” or the “apportionment” of honors after the succession conflict; translation keeps the ambiguity.

text.greek: καὶ Βριμοῦς, Βάκχοιο, Γιγάντων τ' ἔργ' ἀΐδηλα,
text.english: and the baleful deeds of Brimo, of Bakchos, and of the Giants,
text.note: Brimo is a dread epithet (often of Persephone or Hekate); Bakchos = Dionysos. ἀΐδηλα here means “baleful, ruinous,” not “invisible.”

text.greek: ἀνθρώπων τ' ὀλιγοδρανέων πολυεθνέα φύτλην
text.english: and the many‑nationed stock of men of feeble might,
text.note: ὀλιγοδρανής = “feeble in might.” πολυεθνής = “of many peoples/tribes.” φύτλη is a poetic form for “stock, race” (cf. φύτλον/φῦλον).

text.greek: ἤειδον· στεινὸν δὲ διὰ σπέος ἤλυθεν αὐδή,
text.english: they sang; and through the strait cave the voice went forth,
text.note: σπέος = “cave, grotto.” στεινόν = “narrow, strait.” ἤλυθεν is an epic form of “came (forth).”

text.greek: ἡμετέρης χέλυος μελιχρὴν ὄπα γηρυούσης.
text.english: as our shell was uttering a honey‑sweet voice.
text.note: χελύς is the tortoise‑shell lyre; the genitive absolute (“of our shell uttering…”) indicates accompaniment. The first‑person ἡμετέρης points to the narrator’s own lyre (Orpheus).

text.greek: Ἔστατο δ' ἄκρα κάρηνα καὶ ἄγκεα δενδρήεντα
text.english: And the uttermost summits and the tree-clad glens stood still
text.note: Neuter plural subjects (ἄκρα κάρηνα, ἄγκεα) take a singular verb (ἔστατο). Πηλίου, though enjambed, governs “the tree-clad glens” and the whole landscape phrase.

text.greek: Πηλίου, ὑψηλάς τε μετὰ δρύας ἤλυθε γῆρυς.
text.english: of Pelion, and amid the lofty oaks went the sound.
text.note: γῆρυς can mean “voice,” “cry,” or more generally “sound”; I render it neutrally as “the sound.” μετά with the accusative (μετὰ ὑψηλὰς δρῦας) = “amid/among the tall oaks.”

text.greek: Καί ῥ' αἱ μὲν πρόρριζοι ἐπ' αὔλιον ἐθρώσκοντο
text.english: And then the trees, root and all, were leaping toward the fold,
text.note: πρόρριζοι (“root-and-all”) implies trees as the subject (supplied from context); ἐθρώσκοντο (“were leaping”) evokes the topos of trees moving to song.

text.greek: πέτραι τ' ἐσμαράγουν· Θῆρες δ' ἀΐοντες ἀοιδῆς,
text.english: and the rocks were ringing; and the beasts, hearing the song,
text.note: ἐσμαράγουν = “were resounding, crashing”; Θῆρες = wild beasts.

text.greek: σπήλυγγος προπάροιθεν ἀλυσκάζοντες ἔμιμνον·
text.english: remained before the cavern, shying away;
text.note: ἀλυσκάζοντες = “shying, shrinking back”; σπήλυγξ = “cavern,” here Cheiron’s cave.

text.greek: οἰωνοί τ' ἐκυκλοῦντο βοαύλια Κενταύροιο
text.english: and the birds were circling the Centaur’s cattle-stalls,
text.note: βοαύλια = “cattle-stalls, byres” (rare); οἰωνοί = “birds (of omen)”; Κενταύροιο refers to Cheiron.

text.greek: ταρσοῖς κεκμηῶσιν, ἑῆς δ' ἐλάθοντο καλιῆς.
text.english: with their feet worn out, and they forgot their own nest.
text.note: ταρσοῖς = “tarsi, feet” (of birds); καλιά = “hut,” by extension “nest”; ἐλάθοντο + gen. = “forgot” (lit. “failed to remember”) their own nest.

text.greek: Αὐτὰρ ὁρῶν Κένταυρος ἐθάμβεε, χεῖρ' ἐπὶ καρπῷ
text.english: But when he saw it, the Centaur was astonished, brandishing hand upon wrist thick and fast,
text.note: “χειρ’ ἐπὶ καρπῷ πυκνὸν ἐπισσείων”: the phrase depicts an emphatic, repeated hand-gesture—literally “shaking/brandishing the hand upon the wrist.” πυκνόν functions adverbially (“in rapid succession”); ἐπισσείων (from ἐπισείω) conveys vigorous, repeated motion.

text.greek: πυκνὸν ἐπισσείων, οὖδας δ' ἤρασσεν ὁπλῇσι.
text.english: and with his hooves he smote the earth.
text.note: οὖδας is a poetic term for “ground/earth.” ἤρασσεν (impf.) suggests iterative action (“kept striking”). ὁπλῇσι is “with his hooves” (dative plural of ὁπλή), not “with arms” (ὅπλα).

text.greek: Τῖφυς δ' εἰσεπέρησε νεὼς ἄπο, καί ῥ' ἐκέλευσεν
text.english: But Tiphys came in from the ship and straightway gave the word,
text.note: νεὼς is the Homeric genitive of ναῦς (“ship”). The combination εἰσεπέρησε … ἄπο (“came in … from”) is idiomatic; sense: “came ashore/into the company from the ship.” Tiphys is the helmsman.

text.greek: ὦκα περᾶν Μινύαισιν· ἐγὼ δ' ἄμπαυον ἀοιδῆς,
text.english: to cross swiftly, for the Minyans; and I broke off my song,
text.note: περᾶν here means “to cross (the sea), make the passage.” Μινύαισιν is a dative of the persons commanded (“bade the Minyans”).

text.greek: οἳ δὲ θοῶς ἤγερθεν, ἔδυνε δὲ τεύχε' ἕκαστος.
text.english: and they quickly sprang up, and each donned his gear.
text.note: ἤγερθεν is intransitive (“they roused themselves”). τεύχεα denotes “gear,” typically “arms/armor”; δύειν τεύχεα is the epic idiom “to don armor.”

text.greek: Παῖδα δ' ἐν ἀγκαλίδεσσιν ἀνίσχανεν ἱππότα Πηλεύς,
text.english: And the horseman Peleus raised the child in his arms,

text.greek: καί ῥ' ἔκυσεν κεφαλήν τε καὶ ἄμφω φώεα καλά,
text.english: and he kissed his head and both fair eyes,
text.note: φώεα (often printed φάεα, “lights”) is epic for the eyes; with ἄμφω it means “both eyes.”

text.greek: δακρυόεν γελόων· κηλήθη δὲ φρέν' Ἀχιλλεύς.
text.english: laughing with tears; and Achilleus’ heart was enchanted.
text.note: δακρυόεν γελόων conveys simultaneous weeping and laughter. κηλήθη (aorist passive of κηλέω) means “was charmed/enchanted”; the subject is the infant Achilleus (φρέν’ = φρήν, ‘heart/mind’).

text.greek: Αὐτὰρ ἐμοὶ Κένταυρος ἑῇ γέρας ὤπασε χειρί,
text.english: But to me the Centaur, with his own hand, bestowed an honor‑gift,
text.note: Κένταυρος here almost certainly refers to Cheiron; γέρας is the epic “honor‑gift,” emphasizing the prestige of the bestowal, and ἑῇ χειρί underscores the personal act of giving.

text.greek: νεβρὴν παραλέην ξεινήιον ὄφρα φέροιμι.
text.english: a shaggy‑edged fawnskin, a guest‑gift, that I might bear it.
text.note: νεβρίς is the Bacchic fawnskin; παραλέην is difficult, commonly taken as “rough/shaggy (at the edges), untrimmed.” ξεινήιον is a “guest‑gift,” and φέροιμι (“bear”) can imply “wear” in epic diction.

text.greek: Ἀλλ' ὅτε δὴ σπήλυγγος ἄπο προθορόντες ἔβημεν
text.english: But when at length, leaping forth from the cavern, we set out,

text.greek: ἄκρης ἐκ σκοπιῆς ὁ γέρων ἀνὰ χεῖρας ἀείρων
text.english: from the top of the watch-peak the old man, upraising his hands,
text.note: σκοπιή = “watch-peak, lookout”; ἀνὰ χεῖρας ἀείρων describes the conventional Homeric prayer-gesture (“raising his hands upward”).

text.greek: Φιλλυρίδης ἠρᾶτο, θεοὺς δ' ἐπεκέκλετο πάντας
text.english: Philyridēs prayed, and he called upon all the gods,
text.note: Φιλλυρίδης (“son of Philyra”) is the patronymic of Cheiron, used as his name.

text.greek: νόστον μὲν Μινύαισιν, ἰδὲ κλέος ἐσθλὸν ἀρέσθαι
text.english: for a homecoming for the Minyae, and that they might win noble renown
text.note: ἀρέσθαι (middle) = “to win/obtain for oneself,” taking the accusative of the thing (renown) and, as here, the dative of advantage (continued in the next line). “Minyae” designates the Argonauts.

text.greek: ὁπλοτέροις βασιλεῦσι καὶ ἐσσομένοις μερόπεσσιν.
text.english: for the younger kings and for mortals yet to come.
text.note: The datives (“for the younger kings … for mortals yet to come”) express advantage; “younger kings” refers to the youthful leaders of the expedition. μερόπες is an epic term for “mortals” (lit. “articulate-speaking men”).

text.greek: - Αὐτὰρ ἐπεί τ' ἐπὶ θῖνα καὶ ἐς νέα πάντες ἔβησαν,
text.english: But when they had come to the strand and all had gone aboard the ship,

text.greek: ἐν προτέροις θώκοισι καθίζανον· ἐν δ' ἄρ' ἐρετμοῖς
text.english: they took their seats upon the forward thwarts; and then upon the oars
text.note: θῶκοι are the rowers’ benches or “thwarts”; προτέροις marks the forward benches. The imperfect καθίζανον conveys the settling of the crew into their places.

text.greek: χεῖρας ἐφαπλώσαντες, ἐπί ῥ' ἅλα τύπτον ἕκαστος,
text.english: stretching out their hands, each smote the brine,

text.greek: Πήλιον ἐκνεύσαντες· ὑπὲρ μέγα λαῖτμά τε πόντου
text.english: having stood off from Pelion; over the great trough of the sea
text.note: ἐκνεύσαντες is nautical: “to stand off/clear from” (the shore or landmark); Pelion locates the Pagasaean launch. λαῖτμα denotes the open “trough/deep” of the sea.

text.greek: ἀφρὸς ἐπιζείων χαροπὴν λεύκαινε θάλασσαν.
text.english: the foam, seething up, whitened the gleaming sea.
text.note: χαροπὴν is an epic epithet meaning “gleaming/bright”; ἐπιζείων (“seething up”) modifies ἀφρός (“foam”). λεύκαινε (imperfect) = “was whitening/whitened.”

text.greek: Πισσαίη δ' ἀπέκρυφθεν ἄκρη καὶ Σηπιὰς ἀκτή,
text.english: And the Pissaean headland was hidden from view, and the Sepias shore,
text.note: Πισσαίη ἄκρη: a promontory on the Magnesian/Thessalian coast; exact identification is debated. Σηπιὰς ἀκτή is Cape Sepias, famed in later tradition for shipwrecks (e.g., Xerxes’ fleet).

text.greek: φάνθη δὲ Σκίαθος, Δολοπός τ' ἀνεφαίνετο σῆμα,
text.english: and Skiathos showed itself, and the tomb of Dolops rose into sight,
text.note: Δολοπός σῆμα: sēma usually “tomb” but also “seamark”; in Apollonius (Arg. 1.587) it is a well-known tumulus used by sailors near Skiathos. The eponym “Dolops” is uncertain; the line likely refers to a local hero’s mound rather than the Dolopian ethnos.

text.greek: ἀγχίαλός θ' Ὁμόλη, ῥεῖθρόν θ' ἁλιμυρὲς ἐναύλου
text.english: and Homole hard by the sea, and the briny current of Enavlos,
text.note: ἀγχίαλός (“close to the sea”) modifies Homole; though Homole is a Thessalian mountain, the name can denote the coastal region at its foothills. ῥεῖθρον ἁλιμυρές ἐναύλου: taken as “the briny stream of Enavlos,” Enavlos being a hydronym; some have suspected a reference to the torrent Anauros and propose emendation to Ἀναύρου.

text.greek: ὃς διὰ πολλὴν γαῖαν ἱεῖ μεγαλόβρομον ὕδωρ.
text.english: which through a great stretch of land sends forth loud-roaring water.
text.note: ὃς refers to the stream just mentioned; μεγαλόβρομον (“loud-roaring”) is a traditional epic compound.

text.greek: Οὐλύμπου δὲ βαθυσκοπέλου πρηῶνας ἐρυμνούς
text.english: and the rugged forelands of deep-gazing Olympus,
text.note: βαθυσκοπέλου is an elevated epithet; here taken as “deep-gazing” (i.e., far-seen or looking out over the deep). πρηῶνας (“forelands, brows”) can denote jutting spurs or headlands; ἐρυμνούς = “rugged/steep.”

text.greek: εἰσέδρακον Μινύαι, καὶ Ἄθω δενδρώδεα κάμψαν,
text.english: the Minyae beheld, and they rounded woody Athos,
text.note: εἰσέδρακον is an aorist of εἰσοράω, “beheld.” κάμψαν is nautical, “rounded (a headland/cape).”

text.greek: Πελλήνην τ' εὐρεῖαν· ἰδὲ ζαθέην Σαμοθρῄκην,
text.english: and broad Pellene; and most holy Samothrace,
text.note: The transmitted Πελλήνη (Pellene, in Achaea) is likely a corruption for Παλήνη (Pallene, the Chalcidic peninsula), which fits the northern Aegean itinerary with Athos and Samothrace; many editors emend accordingly. ζαθέην = “most holy.”

text.greek: ἔνθα καὶ ὅρκια φρικτὰ θεῶν ἄρρηκτα βροτοῖσιν,
text.english: where too the dread oaths of the gods, unbreakable for mortals,
text.note: Refers to the Samothracian Mysteries; “dread oaths of the gods” suggests solemn, inviolable oaths connected with the cult. ἄρρηκτα = “unbreakable” (not to be confused with ἄρρητα, “unspeakable”).

text.greek: ἄσμενοι εἰσεπέρησαν ἐμῇς ὑποθημοσύνῃσιν
text.english: the heroes, at my counsels, gladly passed within,
text.note: εἰσεπέρασαν literally “passed within/entered,” here understood of entering/undergoing the Samothracian rites, done “at my counsels” (Orpheus as narrator-guide).

text.greek: ἥρωες· μέγα γάρ σφιν ὀφέλσιμον ἀνθρώποισι
text.english: for great to them—aye, to mortal men—is the benefit
text.note: σφιν ἀνθρώποισι is a double dative: “for them—indeed, for mortal men (generally).” ὀφέλσιμον = “beneficial, of great avail.”

text.greek: τῆσδε θυηπολίης, ἄμοτον πλωτῆρσιν ἑκάστοις.
text.english: of this sacrificial rite, unfailing for each seafarer.
text.note: θυηπολίη denotes sacrificial service/rite (here the Samothracian cult); ἄμοτον means “without stint, unfailing,” i.e., a benefit continually available to each mariner (πλωτῆρσιν ἑκάστοις).

text.greek: Σιντιακαῖς δ' ὀφρῦσιν ἐκέλσαμεν ὠκύαλον ναῦν
text.english: To the Sintian headlands we urged the sea-swift ship,
text.note: “Sintian brows” (Σιντιακαῖς ὀφρῦσιν): ὀφρῦς (‘brow’) is used metaphorically of cliffs/headlands; the Sintians are the early inhabitants of Lemnos. ἐκέλσαμεν = ‘we urged/impelled’; ὠκύαλος = ‘sea‑swift’.

text.greek: Λήμνῳ ἐν ἠγαθέῃ· τόθι περ κακὰ ἔργα μεμήλει
text.english: in goodly Lemnos; there indeed evil deeds preoccupied the women,
text.note: ἠγαθέῃ = ‘goodly, noble’ (epic). μεμήλει with dative (‘is a care to’) yields ‘preoccupied’.

text.greek: θηλυτέραις· αἳ γάρ κεν ἀϊστώσαντο συνεύνους
text.english: for they had annihilated their bed-mates by their own recklessness,
text.note: ἀϊστόω = ‘make unseen,’ hence ‘annihilate/kill’; συνεύνους = ‘bed‑mates.’ κεν + optative has potential/gnomic force; in context it reports the notorious Lemnian massacre as effectively realized. ἀτασθαλίαι = ‘reckless wickedness.’

text.greek: σφῇσιν ἀτασθαλίῃσι, καὶ ἡ κλυτὴ Ὑψιπύλεια
text.english: and she, famed Hypsipyle,
text.note: κλυτὴ Ὑψιπύλεια = ‘famed Hypsipyle’ (queen of Lemnos). The form Ὑψιπύλεια is an epic variant of Hypsipyle.

text.greek: ἐλδομέναις κραίνεσκε, γυναικῶν εἶδος ἀρίστη.
text.english: would satisfy the longing of the women, best in form among women.
text.note: ἐλδομέναις (dat. fem. pl.) = ‘for the longing women’; κραίνεσκε (iterative imperf.) = ‘used to fulfill/bring to pass,’ with the implicit object ‘their desire (for union with the Argonauts).’ γυναικῶν εἶδος ἀρίστη = ‘best in form among women’ (epic formula for outstanding beauty).

text.greek: Ἀλλὰ τί σοι περὶ τῶνδε πόλυν λόγον ἀμφαδὸν εἰπεῖν,
text.english: But why should I speak to you at length, and plainly, of these things,
text.note: Line 476: ἀμφαδόν = “openly, plainly.” The line is a rhetorical aporia (“why recount at length...”).

text.greek: ὅσσον ἐφ' ἵμερον ὦρσεν ἀγαυαῖς Λημνιάδεσσι
text.english: how great a longing Kypris, nurse of love, stirred in the proud Lemnian women
text.note: Lines 477–478: Kypris (Aphrodite) is called ἐρωτοτρόφος, “nurse/rearer of love.” ἀγαυαῖς conveys epic “proud/illustrious.” Μινύαι are the Minyae (Argonauts). μιγῆναι is sexual “to mingle” in beds.

text.greek: Κύπρις ἐρωτοτρόφος, Μινύαις εἰς λέκτρα μιγῆναι;
text.english: to mingle in bed with the Minyae?
text.note: Line 479: φίλτροις = “love-philtres/charms,” not necessarily a literal potion; ἐδάμασσεν (“tamed, subdued”) is a conventional erotic metaphor. Hypsipyle is the Lemnian queen.

text.greek: φίλτροις Ὑψιπύλην ἐρατοῖς ἐδάμασσεν Ἰήσων·
text.english: With lovely philtres Jason subdued Hypsipyle;
text.note: Line 480: ἄλλῃ δ’ ἄλλος ἔμικτο is elliptical: “one [man] with one [woman], another with another.” ἐκλελάθοντο (perf.) emphasizes utter forgetfulness of the journey/expedition (πορεία).

text.greek: ἄλλῃ δ' ἄλλος ἔμικτο· καὶ ἐκλελάθοντο πορείης,
text.english: one man mingled with one woman, another with another; and they quite forgot the voyage,
text.note: Lines 481–482: ἀποτροπίοις ἐνοπαῖς = “apotropaic cries/strains,” i.e., song that turns away (here, eros or delay). θελξίφρονι θυμῷ ἡμετέρῳ (“with our mind-bewitching heart”) presents Orpheus’ own inspired, enchanting intent as the instrument of the song; θελχθέντες (“enchanted”) picks up the effect on the crew. The εἰ μή clause gives a contrary-to-fact sense: they would have remained, had they not been charmed back to the ship.

text.greek: εἰ μὴ ἀποτροπίοις ἐνοπαῖς θελξίφρονι θυμῷ
text.english: had it not been that, with apotropaic strains, with our mind-bewitching heart,
text.note: Line 483: εἰρεσίη = “oarage/rowing”; μὀχθος = the toil of seafaring. ἐπεμνήσαντο = “they called to mind, bethought them of.”

text.greek: ἡμετέρῳ θελχθέντες ἔβαν ποτὶ νῆα μέλαιναν,
text.english: enchanted, they went toward the black ship,

text.greek: εἰρεσίην ποθέοντες ἐπεμνήσαντο δὲ μόχθου.
text.english: yearning for the oar, and they called the toil to mind.

text.greek: - Ἔνθεν ἐς Ἑλλήσποντον ἅμ' ἠῴους φέρεν οὖρος
text.english: Thence into the Hellespont, along with early Dawn, a fair wind bore them,
text.note: οὖρος is a technical term for a “fair” or favorable sailing wind; ἠῴους (“with early Dawn”) marks the time of departure in elevated diction.

text.greek: ἀκραὴς Ζέφυρος, στεινῆς ἀπάτερθεν Ἀβύδου,
text.english: the steady Zephyros, past narrow Abydos,
text.note: ἀκραὴς with Zephyros is rendered “steady”; the adjective can mean “untempered, sheer, keen,” of a wind blowing full. στεινῆς Ἀβύδου (“narrow Abydos”) evokes the strait at Sestos–Abydos; ἀπάτερθεν is taken idiomatically as “past/from beyond.”

text.greek: Ἴλιον Δαρδανίην, Πιτύην τ' ἐπὶ δέξι' ἔχοντας,
text.english: having Dardanian Ilion and Pitye upon the right,
text.note: ἐπὶ δέξι’ = “on the right (hand),” i.e., to starboard as they sail; Πιτύη is Pitye/Pityeia on the Troad coast.

text.greek: οὗ καὶ Ἀβαρνιάδος Περκώτης τ' εὔσταχυν αἶαν
text.english: where too the land of Abarnias and Percote, rich in ears of corn,
text.note: Ἀβαρνιάδος likely refers to the district of Abarnis (a promontory/region near Lampsacus); Περκώτη (Percote) is a Troad town. εὔσταχυν = “rich in ears (of grain),” i.e., very fertile.

text.greek: ἀργυρέαις Αἴσηπος ἐπικλύζει προχοῇσιν.
text.english: Aisepos floods with its silver outpourings.
text.note: Αἴσηπος (Aisepos) is the Troad river (cf. Il. 2.825); ἀργυρέαις προχοῇσιν = “with silver outpourings/streams,” a conventional epithet for bright, shining waters. ἐπικλύζει = “floods/overflows,” here of irrigating the fertile plain.

text.greek: Αἶψα δ' ἐπιθρώσκουσα θέεν πολυηγόρος Ἀργώ.
text.english: And straightway, leaping forward, the much-speaking Argo sped.
text.note: πολυηγόρος (‘much-speaking’) likely alludes to Argo’s oracular Dodonaean beam; some take it as ‘much-spoken-of’. θέεν is augmentless imperfect 3 sg of θέω, used of ships ‘to speed’; ἐπιθρώσκουσα = ‘leaping forward.’

text.greek: Αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ ψαμάθοισιν ἐκέλσαμεν, ἐν δ' ἄρα Τῖφυς
text.english: But when we had beached her upon the sands, then Tiphys
text.note: ἐκέλσαμεν (from the verb κελλάω/κελλ-) means “to run a ship aground, beach”; ψαμάθοισιν = “on the sands.”

text.greek: ἰθύντωρ ἀκάτοιο, καὶ ἀγλαὸς Αἴσονος υἱός,
text.english: the steersman of the barque, and the illustrious son of Aison,
text.note: ἰθύντωρ is a technical term for “helmsman/steersman”; ἀκάτη (“barque”) is a common epic term for the Argo.

text.greek: σύν τ' ἄλλοι Μινύαι γλαυκώπιδι Τριτογενείῃ
text.english: together with the other Minyae, to gray-eyed Tritogeneia
text.note: γλαυκώπιδι Τριτογενείῃ is Athena (dative of recipient) with her epithet “gray‑eyed Tritogeneia.”

text.greek: θῆκαν ἀείραντες βριθὺν λίθον, ἔνθα δὲ νύμφαι
text.english: set up, having lifted, a heavy stone; and there the Nymphs
text.note: βριθὺν λίθον (“a heavy stone”) is best taken as a votive/dedicatory stone set up for Athena.

text.greek: κρήνῃ ὑπ' Ἀρτακίῃ καλὰ νάματα πλημμύρουσιν·
text.english: by the Artacian spring make fair waters overflow;
text.note: The Artacian spring (Artacia) is a famous fountain near Kyzikos on the Propontis; ὑπ’ with the dative here = “at/by.”

text.greek: οὕνεκά οἱ πλώουσιν ἀνὰ πλατὺν Ἑλλήσποντον
text.english: because, thanks to her, as they voyaged over the broad Hellespont,
text.note: οἱ is dative singular referring to Athena: “thanks to her/for her sake,” explaining the dedication.

text.greek: εὔδιος ἀντεβόλησε μυχοῦ ἔντοσθε γαλήνη,
text.english: a fair-weather calm met them within the inner recess,
text.note: μυχὸυ ἔντοσθε = “within the inmost recess,” i.e., of the harbor; εὔδιος γαλήνη (“fair‑weather calm”) is personified as “meeting” them (ἀντεβόλησε).

text.greek: οὐδ' εἰς γαῖαν ἔριψαν ἐϋγνάμπτους ἀγκύρας,
text.english: nor did they cast to earth their well-curved anchors,
text.note: “Cast to earth” is Homeric/epic idiom for lowering anchors to the seabed; ἐϋγνάμπτους = “well‑curved.”

text.greek: κύμασι θεινόμενοι ὑπὸ χειμερίαισιν ἀήταις.
text.english: being smitten by waves beneath wintry blasts.
text.note: The participle “being smitten” indicates the usual condition requiring anchors—battering waves under wintry blasts—which in this case they avoided thanks to the calm.

text.greek: Ἐνθάδε προσύνοντες ἐπὶ κροκάλαις προυχούσαις
text.english: Here, assembling upon the jutting shingle,
text.note: κροκάλαις προυχούσαις: κροκάλη = rounded pebble, hence “shingle”; προυχούσαις = “projecting, jutting,” describing a pebbly spit or out-jutting beach. προσύνοντες = “assembling, coming together.”

text.greek: δεῖπνά τε καὶ κλισίην, δόρπου μεμνήμεθ' ἕκαστοι.
text.english: we prepared meals and a lodging, each of us mindful of supper.
text.note: δεῖπνα = “meals” (general), δόρπος = specifically the evening meal “supper”; κλισίη is Homeric for “hut/tent,” here “lodging/camp.” The syntax is slightly elliptical: μεμνήμεθ’ governs the genitive δόρπου, while “δεῖπνα τε καὶ κλισίην” are understood as what they set about/prepared.

text.greek: Δὴ τότε κεκλιμένοισιν ἐπήλυθε Κύζικος ἥρως,
text.english: Then indeed the hero Kyzikos came up to them as they reclined,
text.note: κεκλιμένοισιν is a dative plural “to the reclining [men],” likely of the Argonauts at banquet; ἐπήλυθε carries the nuance “came upon/approached.”

text.greek: ὃς Δολόπων ἤνασσε περικτιόνων ἀνθρώπων.
text.english: who held sway over the Doliones, men dwelling round about.
text.note: The transmitted Δολόπων (“Dolopes”) is likely corrupt; most emend to Δολιόνων (“Doliones”), the people over whom Kyzikos is king in the tradition (cf. Apollonius Rhodius 1.936–960). περικτιόνων ἀνθρώπων is a Homeric-style formula meaning “of the surrounding/neighbouring men.”

text.greek: Αἰνῆος φίλος υἱὸς ὅν οἱ τέκε δῖα γυναικῶν
text.english: the beloved son of Aineus, whom a divine among women bore to him,
text.note: This refers to King Cyzicus, son of Aineus; dia gynaikōn (“divine among women”) is a standard epic epithet for a noble lady.

text.greek: Εὐσώρου θυγάτηρ Αἰνίππη καλλιπάρῃος·
text.english: Eusoros’ daughter Ainippē, fair-cheeked;
text.note: The mother’s name appears here as Ainippē; Apollonius Rhodius gives Aenētē as the daughter of Eusoros—likely a variant tradition. “Fair‑cheeked” (kalliparēios) is a conventional epithet.

text.greek: ὅς ῥα φιλοξενίῃ Μινύας ἐγέρηρεν ἅπαντας,
text.english: who by his hospitality roused all the Minyans,
text.note: “Minyans” is an epic designation for the Argonauts. The verb egerēren (“roused”) conveys ‘cheered/animated’ them through acts of xenia (guest‑friendship).

text.greek: σφάζων πῖά τε μῆλα καὶ εἱλίποδας ἕλικας βοῦς,
text.english: slaughtering fat sheep and shambling, curving-horned bulls,
text.note: eilipodes (“shambling, rolling‑gaited”) and helikas (“curving[-horned]”) are Homeric stock epithets for cattle; “bulls” renders bous in this sacrificial context.

text.greek: ἀγροτέρους τε σύας· δῶκεν δ' ἔπι οἶνον ἐρυθρόν,
text.english: and wild swine; and he gave moreover red wine,
text.note: agroterous syas most naturally means “wild swine” (as opposed to domesticated pigs).

text.greek: σῖτον δ' ἄφθονον ἧκεν ἀποπλώουσι φέρεσθαι,
text.english: and sent abundant grain for those setting sail to carry,
text.note: sitos can mean ‘grain’ or, more generally, ‘provisions’; hēken … pheresthai = ‘sent [it] to be carried’ by those setting sail.

text.greek: χλαίνας τ' ἠδὲ τάπητας, ἐϋννήτους τε χιτῶνας.
text.english: and cloaks and rugs, and well-spun tunics.
text.note: chlaina = cloak; tapētēs = rug/coverlet; eunnētos = ‘well‑spun/well‑woven,’ marking quality textiles.

text.greek: Φίλετο δ' αὖ παρεόντας ὁμηλικίης ἕνεκα σφῆς·
text.english: In turn, he cherished those present because they were of like age.
text.note: φίλετο is the epic middle (‘was fond of, showed affection to’). ὁμηλικίης ἕνεκα σφῆς = ‘on account of their being age-mates’; σφῆς (3rd-pl. reflexive) may refer to the group collectively. δ’ αὖ conveys resumption/‘in turn’.

text.greek: καί ῥα πανημερίῃσιν ἐν εἰλαπίναισιν ὅμαρτεν.
text.english: And indeed he took part in all-day banquets.
text.note: ὅμαρτεν is the epic aorist of ὁμαρτέω, ‘to accompany, join in’; used intransitively here with ἐν + dat. πανημερίῃσι(ν) is an adverbial dative plural, ‘throughout the whole day’. εἰλαπίναι are festive banquets.

text.greek: - Ἀλλ' ὅτε γ' Ὠκεανοῖο ῥόον βαπτίζετο Τιτάν,
text.english: But when the Titan was dipped in the stream of Okeanos,
text.note: “Titan” here denotes the Sun (Helios); βαπτίζετο (“was dipped/immersed”) evokes sunset into the encircling stream of Okeanos.

text.greek: μήνη δ' ἀστροχίτων ἔπαγεν μελαναυγέα ὄρφνην,
text.english: and the star-robed Moon brought on the black-gleaming gloom,
text.note: μήνη is ‘Moon’ (not ‘month’) in Orphic diction; ἀστροχίτων = ‘star-robed’; μελαναυγέα ὄρφνη is an oxymoronic ‘black-gleaming gloom’; ἔπαγεν = ‘brought on.’

text.greek: τῆμος ἀρηίφατοι κίον ἀνέρες, οἵ ῥα νέμοντο
text.english: then went forth men renowned in war, who indeed were dwelling
text.note: ἀρηίφατοι = ‘spoken-of for Ares,’ hence ‘war-famed’; κίον is epic aorist ‘they went’; οἵ ῥα marks the relative with a slight emphatic/confirmatory nuance.

text.greek: ἀρκτῴοις ἐν ὄρεσσι, τεθηπότες εἴκελα θηρσί
text.english: among the northern mountains, awestruck, like unto wild beasts,
text.note: ἀρκτῴοις = ‘northern’ (lit. ‘of the Bear’); τεθηπότες = ‘awestruck, astonied’; εἴκελα θηρσί = ‘like unto wild beasts.’

text.greek: Τιτᾶσι, βριαροῖς τ' ἐναλίγκιοι ἠδὲ Γίγασιν·
text.english: like to the Titans, and akin to stalwart men, and to the Giants;
text.note: βριαροῖς is the adjective ‘stout/strong,’ not the proper name Briareus; ἐναλίγκιοι = ‘akin to, like unto’; the triad Titans/‘stalwart’/Giants heightens their monstrous might.

text.greek: ἓξ γὰρ χεῖρες ἑκάστῳ ἀπ' ὤμων ἀΐσσοντο.
text.english: for from the shoulders of each six hands shot forth.
text.note: ἀΐσσοντο = ‘shot/darted forth,’ vividly of limbs; the six-armed men recall Hundred-Handers typology but with six hands per man.

text.greek: Οὓς τότ' ἐσαθρήσαντες ἀμαιμάκετοι βασιλῆες,
text.english: Then, when they had caught sight of them, the unconquerable kings
text.note: ἐσαθρήσαντες: aorist ptc. of (εἰ)σαθρέω, “on seeing, after catching sight”; ἀμαιμάκετοι = “unconquerable, irresistible,” a conventional epic epithet. Some editions read εἰσαθρήσαντες.

text.greek: ἐς μόθον ὁρμαίνοντες ἀρήϊα τεύχε' ἔδυνον.
text.english: intent on the fray, donned their warlike gear.
text.note: ἐς μόθον = “into the fray, battle-throng”; ὁρμαίνοντες here “being minded/intent,” not “rushing”; ἀρήϊα (Areian) means “warlike, of Ares,” hence “warlike gear.”

text.greek: Καὶ ῥ' οἳ μὲν πευκῇσιν ἀμύνονθ' οἳ δ' ἐλάτῃσιν·
text.english: And then some defended themselves with pines, and others with firs;
text.note: Peurkēisin / elatēisin are instrumental datives: “with pines/firs,” i.e., using weapons or cudgels of those woods (fir/pine shafts or boughs). The middle ἀμύνονθ’ means “were defending themselves/warding off [the foe].”

text.greek: ἐν δ' ἔπεσαν Μινύαισι κατὰ σκοτόεσσαν ὁμίχλην.
text.english: and they fell among the Minyae through the shadow-dark mist.
text.note: ἐν ἔπεσαν + dative (“fell among”) is an epic idiom for closing in combat. Minyae = the Argonauts. κατά with the accusative marks motion “through/down through” the σκοτόεσσαν ὁμίχλην (“shadow-dark mist”), a Homeric-style formula.

text.greek: Οὕς τοι ἐπειγομένους κτεῖνεν Διὸς ἄλκιμος υἱός,
text.english: Those indeed, as they were rushing on, the valiant son of Zeus slew,
text.note: τοι is an enclitic intensifier (“indeed”); “the son of Zeus” designates Herakles.

text.greek: τόξῳ ὀϊστεύων· σὺν δ' Αἰνέος ὤλεσε παῖδα
text.english: shooting with the bow; and along with them he destroyed Kyzikos, the son of Aineus,
text.note: σύν here is adverbial (“along with, in addition”); Αἰνέος is the genitive of Aineus, father of Kyzikos. The Orphic Argonautica has Herakles as Kyzikos’ slayer, differing from the more familiar Apollonian version where Jason kills him.

text.greek: Κύζικον, οὔτι ἑκὼν, ἀλλ' ἀφραδίῃσι πεδηθείς·
text.english: not at all willingly, but fettered by heedlessness;
text.note: ἀφραδίῃσι is a poetic plural (“acts of folly/heedlessness”); πεδηθείς (“fettered”) is metaphorical for being constrained by error.

text.greek: τῷ δ' ἄρα μόρσιμον ἧεν ὑφ' Ἡρακλῆι δαμῆναι.
text.english: for it was his doom to be subdued by Herakles.
text.note: μόρσιμον ἧεν is an epic idiom for “it was fated/doom had it”; δαμῆναι (aorist passive of δαμάζω) = “to be overpowered/slain,” with ὑφ’ Ἡρακλῆι marking the agent.

text.greek: Αἶψα δέ οἱ Μινύαι κοίλης ἔντοσθεν ἔβησαν
text.english: Straightway the Minyae stepped within the hollow ship.
text.note: οἱ is an ethical dative (“for him”), likely referring to Iason; νηός completes the enjambed phrase κοίλης [νηὸς] ἔντοσθεν ἔβησαν = “went within the hollow ship.”

text.greek: νηὸς τευχήρεις, ποτὶ δὲ ζυγὸν ἷζον ἕκαστος.
text.english: Well-equipped, each took his seat at the thwart.
text.note: τευχήρεις = “accoutred, in full gear,” modifying the Minyae; ζυγόν is the rower’s bench (thwart). The plural ἷζον with ἕκαστος is epic usage (“they sat, each [man] ...”).

text.greek: Τῖφυς δὲ πρύμνηθεν ἐπήπυεν ἠδ' ἐκέλευε
text.english: Then Tiphys from the stern raised a shout and gave the order
text.note: πρύμνηθεν = “from the stern”; ἐπῆπυεν is Homeric “raised a shout”; ἐκέλευε governs the aorist infinitives that follow.

text.greek: κλίμακα νηὸς ἔσω ἐρύσαι, καὶ πείσματα λῦσαι.
text.english: to haul the ladder aboard the ship, and to loose the hawsers.
text.note: κλῖμαξ is the boarding-ladder/gangway; νηὸς ἔσω literally “into the ship”; πεῖσματα are mooring cables (“hawsers”); λῦσαι = “loose, cast off.”

text.greek: Ἀλλ' οὔ οἱ λύοντο κάλοι, δεσμοῖσι δ' ἀφύκτοις
text.english: But his hawsers would not be loosed; rather, with inescapable bonds
text.note: κάλοι = mooring-ropes/hawsers; οἱ is a dative of interest (“for him”), i.e., for Tiphys.

text.greek: ὠκείης στροφάλιγγος ἀρηρότες ἐσφίγγοντο,
text.english: fitted to the swift capstan they were gripped tight,
text.note: στροφάλιγξ, literally a ‘whirler’ or ‘humming-top’, here denotes a rotating ship’s device (capstan/windlass); ἀρηρότες = ‘fitted to’; ἐσφίγγοντο = ‘were being tightened’.

text.greek: νῆα κατείργοντες· θάμβησε δὲ Τῖφυς ἀμύμων,
text.english: holding the ship in check; and Tiphys the blameless was amazed,
text.note: Tiphys ἀμύμων preserves the epic epithet “blameless/noble.”

text.greek: ἄφθογγος δέ οἱ ἧκε χερῶν οἰήϊα νηός
text.english: and speechless, the tiller-ropes of the ship Argo slipped from his hands,
text.note: οἰήϊα are the tiller-ropes (steering-gear) controlling the rudder; ἧκε = ‘let go, fell from’; Ἀργῴης is the epic genitive “of Argo.”

text.greek: Ἀργῴης· οὐ γάρ οἱ ἐέλπετο κῦμα περῆσαι.
text.english: for he did not expect to pass over the wave.
text.note: κῦμα περῆσαι = “to pass over/through the wave,” an idiom for clearing a dangerous swell or breaker.

text.greek: Ῥείη γὰρ κοτέεσκε δεδουπότος εἵνεκα λαοῦ·
text.english: For Rheia was wont to be wroth on account of the people’s din.
text.note: Line 535: kotéeske is the iterative imperfect (“used to be angry”). Dedoupotos (gen. sg.) is the perfect participle of doupéō (“to thud, make a crashing noise”), here “the people’s din/uproar.”

text.greek: Ἀλλ' ὅτε πρὸς μέσατον νυκτὸς προὔβαινεν ἀταρπός,
text.english: But when the path of night advanced toward its midmost point,
text.note: Line 536: “Path of night” (atarpos) is a poetic periphrasis for the progress of the hours; mésaton = “midpoint.”

text.greek: ἄστρα τε τηλεφανῆ δῦνεν ῥόον Ὠκεανοῖο,
text.english: and the far-shining stars were sinking beneath the stream of Oceanos,
text.note: Line 537: “Far-shining” (telephanē) is a conventional epic epithet of stars; “stream of Oceanos” (rhoos Ōkeanoio) is the cosmic river into which the stars set.

text.greek: ὄσσε κυβερνήτῃ προσεπέστιχε νήδυμος ὕπνος.
text.english: sweet sleep stole upon the helmsman’s eyes.
text.note: Line 538: Osse is the epic dual “eyes.” Nēdymos = “sweet, balmy.” Prosepéstiche is an epic form meaning “came/stole upon,” with the dative of person (kybernētēi) and the accusative “eyes.”

text.greek: Τῷ δὲ βαθὺ κνώσσοντι θεὰ μενέδουπος Ἀθήνη
text.english: But to him, as he slumbered deep, the goddess Athene, steadfast-resounding,
text.note: Line 539: μενέδουπος is a rare/Orphic epithet; likely from μένω + δοῦπος (“enduring-din”), hence “steadfast-resounding,” suiting Athene’s warlike aspect. Some take it as ‘steadfast in counsel’ by association with μῆτις.

text.greek: ἄγχι παρισταμένη παρ' ἐτήτυμα σήματ' ἔφαινεν·
text.english: standing close at hand, displayed true tokens beside him;
text.note: Line 540: The phrase ἄγχι παρισταμένη marks a divine epiphany; σήματα are “true tokens,” here dream-signs.

text.greek: ὧδε δ' ὁμοκλήσασα θεηγόρον ἔννεπε μῦθον·
text.english: and thus, calling out, she spoke a god-declaring word:
text.note: Line 541: θεηγόρος (“god-declaring”) is rare, indicating a speech carrying divine authority/revelation.

text.greek: - "Εὕδεις Ἀγνιάδη, γλυκερῷ βεβολημένος ὕπνῳ,
text.english: “You sleep, Agniades, smitten by sweet sleep,
text.note: Line 542: Ἀγνιάδη = “Agniades,” the patronymic of Tiphys (son of Hagnias/Hagnis).

text.greek: κῶμα περὶ βλεφάροισι βαλών· ἀλλ' ἔγρεο Τῖφυ,
text.english: having cast a stupor upon your eyelids; but awake, Tiphys,

text.greek: κέκλεο δ' ἡρώεσσι μολεῖν ἐπὶ νήνεμον ἀκτήν,
text.english: and summon the heroes to go to a windless shore,

text.greek: νηὸς ἄπο προθορόντας, ὅθι ξένος ἐν ψαμάθοισι
text.english: springing forth from the ship, where a stranger upon the sands
text.note: Line 545: ξένος can mean both “stranger” and “guest-friend,” anticipating the theme of ξενία in 549.

text.greek: κεῖται ἀποφθίμενος· τῷ οἱ κτέρεα κτερεΐξαι
text.english: lies bereft of life; for him perform the burial-gifts,
text.note: Line 546: τῷ οἱ is an idiomatic dative construction (“for him … to him”); κτερεΐζειν = “to pay funeral honors/offer burial-gifts.”

text.greek: παμμήτειρα Ῥέη κέλεται γέρα, ἠδέ τε λοιβάς
text.english: for All-counselling Rheia enjoins these honors, and libations,
text.note: Line 547: παμμήτειρα (“All-counselling”) is an Orphic epithet of Rheia; γέρα here = “rites/honors” due to the dead.

text.greek: δοῦναι ὑποχθονίοις καὶ δάκρυα λειβέμεν ὄσσων,
text.english: to be given to those beneath the earth, and to let tears fall from your eyes,
text.note: Line 548: ὑποχθόνιοι = the chthonic powers/spirits of the dead; the libations are directed to them.

text.greek: αἰδομένους Θέμιν ἀγνοτελῆ ξενίην τε τράπεζαν·
text.english: in reverence for Themis of pure rites and the table of guest-friendship;
text.note: Line 549: ἀγνοτελής (“of pure rites”) is a rare epithet of Themis; ξενίη τράπεζα = “the table of guest-friendship,” emblematic of sacred hospitality (ξενία).

text.greek: ὅν ῥ' ἀέκων ἔκτεινε βαλὼν διὰ νύκτερον ὄρφνην
text.english: whom, though unwilling, Heracles slew by a cast through the nightly gloom,
text.note: Line 550: ἀέκων modifies Heracles (“though unwilling”); βαλών implies a hurled weapon (ellipsis of the object) cast in the night’s darkness.

text.greek: Ἡρακλέης, θυμὸν δὲ θεᾶς ἐχολώσατε Ῥείης.
text.english: and you have angered the spirit of the goddess Rheia.”
text.note: Line 551: ἐχολώσατε is 2nd pl., addressing the Argonauts collectively as having provoked Rheia’s wrath.

text.greek: Ἀλλ' ὁπόταν θεσμοῖς ξεῖνον σεβάσησθε θανόντα
text.english: But whenever by the rites you honor the guest‑friend who has died,
text.note: thesmois = ‘rites, established customs’; xeinon = ‘guest‑friend,’ not merely ‘stranger,’ referring to King Cyzicus in context.

text.greek: Δίνδυμον αὐτίκ' ἔπειτα Ῥέης ἕδος εἰσαναβάντες
text.english: then straightway, having ascended Dindymon, the seat of Rhea,
text.note: Dindymon: the Phrygian mountain near Cyzicus; ‘seat of Rhea’ identifies her as the Mother (Meter Dindymene).

text.greek: ἱλασμοῖς ἱεροῖς Γαίης ἀρέσασθε θύγατρα,
text.english: with holy propitiations appease the daughter of Gaia,
text.note: ‘daughter of Gaia’ = Rhea (daughter of Uranus and Gaia); hilasmoi = propitiatory rites.
