text.greek: πείσματα δ' ἀράμενοι, τότε δὴ μνώεσθε πλοοῖο."
text.english: and when you have taken up your moorings, then indeed bethink you of the voyage.”
text.note: peismata = ship’s cables/moorings; aramenoi = ‘having taken up’ (i.e., weighing the moorings).

text.greek: - Ὣς εἰποῦσα θεὰ πάλιν ἐτράπετ', ἶσον ὀϊστῷ
text.english: Thus having spoken, the goddess turned back again, like an arrow,
text.note: Epic simile ‘like an arrow’ marks the goddess’s sudden departure.

text.greek: οὐρανὸν ἐσσυμένη. Τοῦ δ' αὐτίκα κῶμ' ἐκεδάσθη,
text.english: hastening to heaven. And straightway his trance was scattered,
text.note: kōma = deep sleep/trance; ‘was scattered’ renders ekedasthe (‘was dispelled’).

text.greek: πρύμνης δ' ἆλτο θοῶς· ἀνέγειρε δὲ λαὸν ἀϋτῇ
text.english: and from the stern he sprang swiftly;
text.note: prymnēs: he had been at the stern; alto = ‘he sprang.’

text.greek: τοίχων ἔνθα καὶ ἔνθα παρακλιδὸν ὑπνώοντας,
text.english: and with a shout he roused the host, who were sleeping along the walls here and there, leaning sidelong,
text.note: toichōn may be city/building walls or, loosely, bulwarks; paraklidon = ‘leaning sideways, slantwise.’

text.greek: ψυχῇ ὑποτρομέων· ἄφαρ ἡρώεσσι δ' ὀνείρου
text.english: trembling in spirit;
text.note: psychēi hypotromeōn = ‘quivering at heart,’ i.e., emotionally shaken by the vision.

text.greek: φάσματα πᾶσιν ἔειπεν, ἐπιδρομάδην ἀγορεύων.
text.english: and at once he told to all the heroes the phantoms of the dream, speaking in a rush.
text.note: phasmata oneirou = ‘dream‑phantoms/apparitions’; epidromadēn = ‘in swift succession, hurriedly.’

text.greek: Οἱ δὲ θοῶς ἤγερθεν, ἐπ' ᾐόνα δ' ἆλτο ἕκαστος.
text.english: Then they swiftly were roused, and each leapt upon the strand.
text.note: ἤγερθεν is the Homeric aorist passive of ἐγείρω used intransitively (“were roused, got up”); ᾐόνα is the epic form of ἠϊών (“shore, strand,” often written ἠϊόνα); ἆλτο is 3rd singular aorist middle of ἅλλομαι, agreeing with the singular ἕκαστος (“each”).

text.greek: Ἡ δὲ κατ' ὀρφναίοιο πόλου χρυσήνιος ἠὼς
text.english: And along the murky vault of the sky moved golden Eos,
text.note: χρυσήνιος is an elevated epithet (“golden”) applied to Eos; κατ’ ὀρφναίοιο πόλου suggests motion “along/across” the darkling sky.

text.greek: ἀντολίας ἤνοιγεν, ἐδέχνυτο δ' οὐρανὸς ὄρθρον·
text.english: opening the risings of the East, and heaven was revealing daybreak;
text.note: ἀντολίαι (plural) literally “risings,” i.e., the East/sunrise; ἐδείχνυτο (middle) gives “was revealing/was showing itself.”

text.greek: καὶ τότ' ἀριστῆες Μινύαι νέκυν εἰσενόησαν
text.english: then the Minyan champions perceived a corpse,
text.note: ἀριστῆες Μινύαι = “the Minyan champions,” a traditional designation for the Argonauts; νέκυν = “a corpse.”

text.greek: αἵματι καὶ κονίῃ πεπαλαγμένον· ἀμφὶ γὰρ ἄλλοι
text.english: bespattered with blood and dust; for all about, others
text.note: πεπαλαγμένον is the perfect participle of παλάσσω, “to besmear/sprinkle,” hence “bespattered” with blood and dust.

text.greek: δήϊοι ἀμφὶς ἔκειντο, πελώρια σώματα θηρῶν.
text.english: war-slain were lying on every side—the huge bodies of beasts.
text.note: δήϊοι used substantively = “the war-slain”; θηρῶν is appositional, clarifying that the fallen were beasts (“the huge bodies of beasts”).

text.greek: - Ἀλλ' οἳ μὲν βασιλῆα περισταδὸν ἀμφιχυθέντες
text.english: But they, standing in a ring and thronging about the king,
text.note: περισταδόν … ἀμφιχυθέντες: the adverb “in a ring/on all sides” with the participle of ἀμφιχέω (“to pour around”) is a figurative hendiadys for “to throng/press about” the corpse before burial.

text.greek: Κύζικον εὐξέστοισιν ὑπὸ πλακέεσσιν ἔθηκαν,
text.english: laid Kyzikos beneath well‑smoothed slabs,
text.note: εὐξέστοισιν πλακέεσσιν: “well‑smoothed slabs,” i.e., flat stone cover; ἔθηκαν = “laid/placed” in the sense of interment; Κύζικον is the slain king Kyzikos.

text.greek: ἂν δ' ἄρα τύμβον ἔχευαν, ἐδωμήσαντο δὲ σῆμα.
text.english: and then they heaped up a tumulus and built a marker.
text.note: ἂν δ’ ἄρα is an epic connective (“and then”); τύμβον ἔχευαν = “they heaped a barrow”; ἐδωμήσαντο (middle) = “they built,” and σῆμα denotes the grave‑marker/monument distinct from the earthen mound.

text.greek: Φιτροὺς δ' αἶψα κόμιζον, ἰδ' ἔντομα πορσύνοντες
text.english: And straightway they brought the pots, and, preparing the cut victims,
text.note: The reading Φιτροὺς is likely a corruption; most editors take χύτρους (“pots/jars”), supported by χύτλων/χύτρων in 573. πορσύνω = “busy with, prepare.”

text.greek: παμμέλαν' ἐν βόθροις μετεκίαθον· αὐτὰρ ἔγωγε
text.english: they sent the all‑black offerings down into the pits; but I myself
text.note: ἔντομα here = “cut/slain victims” (not “insects”): a technical term of chthonic sacrifice. παμμέλαν’ = “all‑black,” the proper color for chthonic victims; βόθροι are ritual pits for under‑earth deities; μετεκίαθον = “sent down (to the dead).”

text.greek: ψυχὴν ἱλασάμην, σπένδων μειλίγματα χύτλων
text.english: propitiated the soul, pouring as libations the pots’ soothing offerings,
text.note: μειλίγματα = “soothing/mollifying offerings,” standard for appeasing the dead; χύτλων is a form of χύτρων (“of pots/jars”).

text.greek: ὕδατί τ' ἠδὲ γάλακτι, μελισσορύτων ἀπὸ νασμῶν
text.english: with water and with milk, adding libations from honey‑flowing streams,
text.note: μελισσορύτων ἀπὸ νασμῶν is a periphrasis for honey (“honey‑flowing streams”); συμπροχέων = “pouring along with,” i.e., in addition to the water and milk.

text.greek: λοιβαῖς συμπροχέων, καὶ ἐμοῖς ὕμνοισι γεραίρων.
text.english: and honoring it with my own hymns.
text.note: γεραίρω = “honor,” here with hymns as part of the chthonic rite.

text.greek: - Αὐτὸς δ' Αἰσονίδης προυθήκατο πᾶσιν ἄεθλον,
text.english: But Aisonides himself proclaimed a contest for all,
text.note: προυθήκατο (middle) = “set forth/announced/proposed.” ἄεθλον (sg.) here is best taken as “contest,” contrasting with ἄεθλα (pl.) “prizes” in the next line.

text.greek: τυμβιδίου ἐπ' ἀγῶνος ἑταίροις ἔμμεν' ἄεθλα,
text.english: prizes to be for his comrades at the funeral games,
text.note: τυμβιδίου ἐπ’ ἀγῶνος = “at the funeral contest/games” (lit. “on the tomb’s contest”). ἔμμεν’ = ἔμμεναι “to be.” ἑταίροις = “for the comrades (the Argonauts).”

text.greek: δῶρα τά οἱ πόρεν Ὑψιπύλη Λήμνοιο φέρεσθαι.
text.english: the gifts that Hypsipyle of Lemnos had given him to carry away.
text.note: δῶρα … φέρεσθαι = “gifts to bear away.” οἱ = “to him.” The line explains that the prizes were the parting gifts bestowed by Hypsipyle of Lemnos on Aisonides (Iason).

text.greek: Ἀγκαίῳ μὲν δῶκε πάλης γέρας ἀμφικύπελλον
text.english: To Ankaios he gave, as the prize of wrestling, a two‑handled cup,
text.note: ἀμφικύπελλον: the noun “cup” (δέπας/κύπελλον) is understood; the adjective denotes a two‑handled goblet and is a conventional epic epithet for prize‑cups.

text.greek: χρύσειον πολυχανδὲς ἔχειν· Πηλῆι δ' ἔδωκε
text.english: golden and wide‑mouthed, to keep; and to Peleus he gave,
text.note: πολυχανδές is rare and likely from χαίνω (“to gape”), hence “wide‑mouthed, capacious”; less plausibly from ἁνδάνω (“to please”). ἔχειν here = “to keep (as one’s own),” a formulaic prize expression.

text.greek: θάσσοντι σταδίοισι, ποδωκείης ἕνεκα σφῆς
text.english: as being the swifter in the footraces, by reason of his own fleetness of foot,
text.note: θάσσοντι σταδίοισι: literally “to him being swifter in the stadium‑races.” σφῆς is the archaic reflexive “his own,” stressing Peleus’ inherent speed (ποδωκείη = ‘fleetness of foot’).

text.greek: χλαῖναν φοινικέην, πολυδαίδαλον ἔργον Ἀθήνης.
text.english: a purple cloak, a many‑wrought work of Athena.
text.note: φοινικέην denotes costly purple/crimson dye; πολυδαίδαλον “much‑wrought, elaborate.” “Work of Athena” alludes to the goddess’s patronage of weaving.

text.greek: Αὐτὰρ παγκρατίοιο δόκεν γέρας Ἡρακλῆϊ
text.english: But as the prize of the pankration he gave to Herakles
text.note: “παγκρατίοιο” (of the pankration): the all-in contest combining wrestling and boxing; “γέρας” is an honorific prize.

text.greek: ἀργύρεον κρητῆρα παναίολον· ἱππασίης δέ
text.english: a silver krater, all-gleaming; and for horsemanship
text.note: “παναίολον” from αἰόλος with pan-: ‘all-variegated, shimmering’; κρητήρ (krater) is a large mixing-bowl.

text.greek: Κάστορι, χρυσείων φαλάρων πολυτεχνέα κόσμον·
text.english: to Kastor, a skillfully wrought adornment of golden phalerae;
text.note: “φαλάρων” (phalerae): decorative metal discs for horse-harness; “πολυτεχνέα” = ‘much-/skillfully wrought.’

text.greek: πυγμαχίης δὲ τάπητα λιανθέα δῶκε φέρεσθαι
text.english: and for boxing he gave a very delicate tapestry to be borne away
text.note: “λιανθέα” is a rare epithet; probably ‘very delicate/soft’ (possibly ‘richly patterned’). “δῶκε φέρεσθαι” = ‘gave to be carried off (as a prize).’

text.greek: ἀθλοφόρῳ Πολυδεύκει· ὃ γὰρ κλυτὸν ᾔρατο νῖκος.
text.english: by prize-winning Polydeukes; for he had taken the glorious victory.
text.note: “ἀθλοφόρῳ” = ‘bearing off the prize’; “ᾔρατο” (‘he took up’) is idiomatic for ‘won’ a victory.

text.greek: Αὐτὸς δ' εὐκαμπὲς τόξον λάβεν ἠδ' ἄρ' ὀϊστούς,
text.english: But he himself took up the well‑curved bow and the arrows,
text.note: eukampes (“well‑curved/pliant”) is a conventional bow‑epithet; autos (“he himself”) marks emphatic subject.

text.greek: τεινάμενος δέ οἱ ἧκε βέλος, τὸ δ' ἀπέπτατο τηλοῦ·
text.english: and, drawing it, he let fly a shaft, and it sped afar;
text.note: teinamenos (“drawing [the bowstring]”); hoi is a dative of goal/advantage (“at him/at his mark”); héke belos is a Homeric formula “let fly a shaft”; têlou (“afar”) keeps the epic adverbial tone.

text.greek: Δῶκε δ' ἄρ' Αἰσονίδῃ Μινύης λόχος εἵνεκα τιμῆς
text.english: then the Minyan band gave to Aisonides, for the sake of honor,
text.note: Aisonidēs (“son of Aison,” i.e., Jason) is preserved as an epic patronymic; Minyēs lochos (“the Minyan band”) refers to the Argonauts; heineka timēs = “for the sake of honor/as an honor.”

text.greek: πλέξας εὐανθῆ στέφανον τανυφύλλου ἐλαίης.
text.english: weaving a rich‑blossomed wreath of the long‑leaved olive.
text.note: euanthēs (“rich‑blossomed”) and tanyphyllos (“long‑leaved”) are traditional epithets applied to the olive; plexas (“weaving”) agrees with singular lochos as a collective subject.

text.greek: Αὐτὰρ ἐμοὶ μολπῆς γέρας ὤπασε δῖος Ἰήσων
text.english: But to me godlike Iason bestowed the meed of song,
text.note: γέρας (“meed, honorific portion”) is the technical term for a prize or share; μολπῆς is “of song.” ὤπασε (from ὀπάζω) = “bestowed/granted.” Αὐτὰρ is the epic adversative “but/then.”

text.greek: ἐμβάδα χρυσείην γε τιταινομένην πτερύγεσσι.
text.english: a golden sandal, indeed, with pinions outspread.
text.note: ἐμβάς = “sandal” (acc. sg. ἐμβάδα); the singular can function collectively in epic. τιταινομένην (from τιταίνω) means “stretched/extended,” here idiomatically “with [its] wings outspread.” πτέρυγες are “wings/winglets,” perhaps decorative flaps; the image evokes winged footwear (cf. Hermes). γε is an enclitic intensifier (“indeed”).

text.greek: - Λῦτο δ' ἀγὼν, φήμη δὲ διέπτατο δώματος εἴσω
text.english: The combat ceased, and tidings flew within the palace.

text.greek: Κυζίκου οἰχομένου· τοῦ δ' ὡς κλύε σύγγαμος αἰνή
text.english: that Kyzikos was no more; and when his ill‑fated wedded consort heard it,
text.note: οἰχομένου literally “gone,” a common euphemism for “dead.” σύγγαμος = “wedded consort.” αἰνή literally “dreadful,” here conveying the wife’s pitiable, grievous state.

text.greek: στήθεα δρυπτομένη λίγ' ἐκώκυεν· ἀμφὶ δὲ δειρῆς
text.english: tearing at her breasts she wailed shrilly; and about her neck

text.greek: ἀψαμένη μήρινθα, βρόχῳ ἀπὸ θυμὸν ὄλεσσε.
text.english: having set a headband, she destroyed her life with a noose.
text.note: μήρινθα is a rare word, probably a woman’s headband or hair‑net, here used as an improvised ligature; cf. βρόχῳ “with a noose.” Some manuscripts vary the form (μήρινθα/μείρινθα).

text.greek: Γῆ δ' ὑποδεξαμένη πλακὶ δάκρυα, πίδακος ἧκε
text.english: And Ge, having received the tears upon her level expanse, sent forth a spring,
text.note: Ge is the personified Earth. plaki (dat. of plax) means “flat surface/plain.” pidax (“spring, fountain”) is archaic; the genitive with heke (“sent forth”) is epic/poetic usage for producing or emitting something.

text.greek: βλύζουσ' ἀργυροειδὲς ὕδωρ κρήνης ἀπὸ μέσσης
text.english: gushing silver‑bright water, ever‑flowing, from the midst of the fountain,
text.note: blyzein means “to bubble/gush.” argyroeides = “silver‑like/bright.” “from the midst of the fountain” (krēnēs apo messēs) stresses the emergence at the very center; aenaon (“ever‑flowing”) qualifies the water/spring.

text.greek: ἀέναον· Κλείτην δὲ περικτίονες καλέουσι.
text.english: and the dwellers round about call it Kleite.
text.note: Kleite is the eponym of the spring (cf. Kleite, wife of Kyzikos, in the Argonautic myth). periktiones is Homeric for “those dwelling round about, neighbors.”

text.greek: - Καὶ τότε δὴ βασιλῆες ὀνειροπόλον διὰ πύστιν,
text.english: And then indeed the kings, for a dream-oracular inquiry,
text.note: ὀνειροπόλον διὰ πύστιν = “inquiry by means of a dream,” i.e., a dream-oracle/oneiromancy; πύστις is ‘consultation, inquiry’.

text.greek: κνημὸν ἐπὶ ζάθεον καὶ Δίνδυμον ἀκρώρειαν,
text.english: went to the holy foothill and the summit-ridge of Dindymon,
text.note: κνημός = ‘foothill, lower slope’; ἀκρώρεια = ‘crest/summit-ridge’. Δίνδυμον is Mount Dindymon (Dindymus), sacred to the Mother (Rheia/Cybele). ἐπὶ + acc. indicates motion onto.

text.greek: ὄφρα κε μειλίξαιντ' εὐοινίστοις ἐπὶ λοιβαῖς
text.english: so that they might appease with wine-rich libations
text.note: εὐοινίστος = ‘rich in wine’; λοιβαί = ‘libations’. μειλίσσω = ‘soothe/propitiate’.

text.greek: Ῥείην πρεσβυγενῆ, θυμὸν δ' ἀλέαιντο ἀνάσσης.
text.english: Rheia the elder-born, and avert the queen’s wrath.
text.note: πρεσβυγενής = ‘born earlier, elder-born,’ an epithet of Rheia. θυμὸν ἀλέαιντο = idiomatically ‘to avert/avoid the (angry) spirit,’ i.e., her wrath; ἀνάσση = ‘queen/mistress’ as a divine title.

text.greek: Αὐτὰρ ἐγὼν ἑπόμην, φόρμιγγα δὲ χερσὶν ἄειρον,
text.english: But I for my part followed, and I raised the phorminx in my hands,
text.note: phorminx: the epic lyre associated with Orpheus; ἄειρον is imperfect (“was lifting/held aloft”).

text.greek: Ἄργος δ' αὖθ' ἵκανε, λιπὼν εὐεργέα νῆα,
text.english: and Argos came once more, leaving the well-wrought ship,
text.note: Argos here is the craftsman, builder of the Argo; εὐεργέα means “well-wrought,” a standard epic epithet for crafted objects.

text.greek: ὅσγε τανυφλοίου ἐλάτης ἀμφιπλεκὲς ἔρνος
text.english: who cut off the shoot of the long-barked fir, entwined by a withered vine,
text.note: τανυφλοίος = “long-barked” (of fir); ἔρνος = “shoot/branch.” ἀμφιπλεκές governs a genitive: the shoot is “entwined by” the vine.

text.greek: ἀμπέλου αὐαλέης ὀξεῖ ἀπέκερσε σιδήρῳ·
text.english: with sharp iron;
text.note: “sharp iron” is the conventional periphrasis for a blade or tool; ἀπέκερσε = “cut off.”

text.greek: Ξέσσε δ' ἐπισταμένως βρέτας ἱερὸν ἰδμοσύνῃσι,
text.english: and he expertly carved, by his skill, a holy cult-image,
text.note: βρέτας denotes a wooden cult statue (xoanon); ἰδμοσύνῃσι = “by/with (his) skill(s), know-how.”

text.greek: μίμνειν ἔμπεδον αἰὲν ἐπεσσομένοις ἀνθρώποις·
text.english: to remain steadfast forever for men yet to come;
text.note: ἐπεσσομένοις = “those who will come later” (Homeric future participle); ἔμπεδον = “firm, steadfast.”

text.greek: λάασι δ' εὐτύκτοις δωμήσατο οἶκον ἀνάσσῃ.
text.english: and with well-fitted stones he built a house for the Lady.
text.note: οἶκον ἀνάσσῃ = “a house for the Lady,” i.e., a temple for a goddess; εὐτύκτοις λάασι = “with well-dressed stones.”

text.greek: Ἐν δ' ἄρ' ἐπειγόμενοι Μινύαι (μέγα δ' ἔξοχα πάντων
text.english: Then in their haste the Minyans (and Aisonides, far surpassing them all)
text.note: Aisonides is the patronymic for Iason (Jason), emphasizing his preeminence: “greatly beyond all the rest.”

text.greek: Αἰσονίδης) λιθάκεσσιν ἀρηρότα βωμὸν ἔτευξαν
text.english: fashioned an altar well-fitted with stones,
text.note: lithakessin arerota literally “well-joined with stones”; the phrase underscores careful stonework in the altar’s construction.

text.greek: ᾧ ἔπι ταυροθύτους λοιβὰς ἠδ' ἱερὰ καλά
text.english: upon which bull‑sacrificial libations and fair holy offerings
text.note: taurothytoi loibai = “libations attendant on a bull-sacrifice,” an unusual but intelligible collocation indicating libations as part of a tauric rite.

text.greek: ῥέξαν ἀριστῆες· σπονδαῖσι δ' ἐτέρπετο Ῥείη.
text.english: the chieftains performed; and Rheia took delight in the libations.
text.note: Rheia is transliterated (Rhea), the Mother of the Gods; note the variation between loibai and spondai, both terms for libations.

text.greek: Αὐτὰρ ἔμ' ἤνωγον κλῇσαι θεὸν ἠδὲ γερῆραι,
text.english: But they enjoined me to celebrate the god and to honor him,
text.note: κλῇσαι is the aorist infinitive of κλείω/κλείζω “to celebrate, make famous,” not κλείω/κλῄω “to shut.” γερῆραι (from γεραίρω) means “to honor (with rites/gifts).” ἤνωγον = “they were urging/enjoining.”

text.greek: ὄφρα κεν ἀντομένοις νόστον μελιηδέ' ὀπάσσοι.
text.english: so that, upon meeting him, he might bestow a honey-sweet homecoming.
text.note: ὄφρα κεν + optative expresses purpose/contingency. ἀντομένοις (dat. pl.) = “to those who meet (him),” with the object (the god) understood from the previous line. ὀπάσσοι (from ὀπάζω) = “might grant/bestow.” μελιηδέ’ is the epic form of μελιηδέα (“honey-sweet”), with apocope before a vowel. νόστον = “homecoming/return.”

text.greek: - Ἀλλ' ὅτε δὴ θυέεσσι λιταῖσί τε γουνασάμεσθα,
text.english: But when at last with sacrifices and with prayers we had supplicated,
text.note: γουνάσασθαι here = “to supplicate,” literally “to bend the knee”; θυέεσσι λιταῖσί τε is an instrumental dative, “with sacrifices and with prayers.”

text.greek: Ἀργῴην ποτὶ νῆα κατήλθομεν· ἐν δ' ἄρα Τῖφυς
text.english: we descended to the Argo; and then Tiphys
text.note: Ἀργῴην νῆα is taken as “the Argo,” i.e., the ship’s proper name; κατῆλθομεν “we went/descended (to).”

text.greek: ἥρωας πρύμνηθεν ἐκέκλετο· σὺν δ' ἄρα πάντες
text.english: was calling the heroes from the stern; and together all
text.note: Τῖφυς is the helmsman; πρύμνηθεν “from the stern”; ἐκέκλετο imperfect “was calling/summoning.”

text.greek: ἐσσύμενοι θώκοισιν ἐπὶ προτέροισι κάθιζον,
text.english: in haste sat down upon the foremost benches,
text.note: ἐσσύμενοι “hastening, in haste”; θώκοι are the rowers’ benches; προτέροισι “forward/foremost.”

text.greek: βάντες ὑπὲρ θώκοιο, καὶ εἰρεσίης μνώοντο.
text.english: stepping over the bench, and made ready the oar.
text.note: βάντες ὑπὲρ θώκοιο “stepping over the bench” (singular generic); εἰρεσίη is the epic word for “oar”; μνώοντο “were mindful of,” here “made ready/turned attention to.”

text.greek: Ἀπροφάτως δ' ἀπὸ γῆς λεπτοὶ λύοντο κάλωες
text.english: Without a word the slender hawsers were loosed from the land,
text.note: ἀπροφάτως can mean “silently, without announcement”; κάλωες are mooring‑cables/hawsers; λύοντο in nautical context = “cast off.”

text.greek: πείσματα δ' ἡπλώθη· κραιπνὸν δ' ἀπὸ Δινδύμου ἄκρης
text.english: and the sheets were spread,
text.note: πείσματα are the sail‑sheets (ropes controlling a sail); neuter plural with singular verb ἡπλώθη is standard Greek syntax.

text.greek: ἴκμενον οὖρον ἐφῆκε Ῥέη λιπαροκρήδεμνος.
text.english: and swiftly from the peak of Dindymos bright‑veiled Rhea sent a favoring breeze.
text.note: κραιπνόν functions adverbially (“swiftly”); Δίνδυμος is Rhea’s mountain; ἴκμενον οὖρον is a set phrase for a fair wind; λιπαροκρήδεμνος = “bright‑/shining‑veiled.”

text.greek: Ἡμεῖς δ' αὖτ' ἐπὶ νηῒ γεράσμια πέμπομεν ἱρά,
text.english: And we in turn offered upon the ship the honor-offerings, holy things,
text.note: γεράσμια ἱρά = “honor-offerings, sacred gifts”; ἐπὶ νηῒ can mean “upon/for the ship,” implying cultic honors paid to the ship itself.

text.greek: Βωμὸν ἐπιστέψαντες ἐπεσσομένοισι πυθέσθαι
text.english: having wreathed an altar, for those who would come thereafter to learn,
text.note: ἐπιστέψαντες = “having wreathed (with garlands)”; ἐπεσσομένοισι dat. “for those who will come later”; πυθέσθαι “to learn by inquiry,” with the content supplied in the next line.

text.greek: Πεισματίην τόθι πείσματ' ἐεργομένης λύθεν Ἀργοῦς.
text.english: that there at Peismatie the mooring-ropes of Argo, though she was shut in, were loosed.
text.note: Πεισματίην is best taken as a toponym (“Peismatie,” ‘the Mooring[-place]’) from πείσμα “mooring-rope,” giving an aetiology; ἐεργομένης = “shut in/held fast.” Some take πεισματίην adverbially (“as a mooring”), but the toponymic sense suits the context.

text.greek: - Αὐτὰρ ἐπεί γ' ὀθόνας ἀκάτου πλήρωσεν ἀήτης,
text.english: But when the blast had filled the vessel’s sails,
text.note: “akatos” is a light seagoing vessel; “aētēs” here = a driving gust/blast of wind.

text.greek: θῦνε διαπρήσσουσ' ἁλιμυρέα κύματα πόντου,
text.english: she sped, cleaving through the briny waves of the sea,

text.greek: Μύσια δὲ σχεδόθεν παραμείβετο πείρατα γαίης·
text.english: and she passed close by the borders of the land of Mysia;
text.note: “schedothen” = “at close range, hard by,” emphasizing proximity to Mysia’s borders.

text.greek: αἶψα δὲ Ῥυνδακίους προχοὰς ἤμειψε θέουσα,
text.english: and straightway, racing on, she passed the outflows of Ryndakos,
text.note: “prochoai” are a river’s mouths/outflows; “Ryndakos” (Ryndacus) is the Mysian river flowing to the Propontis.

text.greek: καλούς τ' ἐς λιμένας ψαμαθώδεας εἰσεπέρησε,
text.english: and made her way into fair, sandy havens,
text.note: “eiseperēse” = “forced/pressed her way into”; “psamathōdeis limenes” = sandy-bottomed/sandy havens.

text.greek: κέλσε δ' ἐπ' αἰγιαλῷ· προτόνοις δ' ἐπὶ χεῖρα βαλόντες,
text.english: and grounded upon the beach; and, laying hand upon the forestays,
text.note: “kellō” = to beach/run aground (of ships); “protonoi” are the forestays of the mast.

text.greek: ἱστία μηρύσαντο καὶ ἀμφ' ἱμᾶσιν ἔδησαν,
text.english: they furled the sails and bound them about with thongs,
text.note: “mērysanto” = reefed/furled; “himas” are lashings/thongs used to tie the sails.

text.greek: κλίμακα δ' ἐξώκειλαν ἐπὶ χθονὸς, ἐκ δ' ἔβαν αὐτοί,
text.english: and ran out a ladder onto the ground, and they themselves went ashore,
text.note: “exōkeilan” lit. “drove out onto land” is applied to the “klimax” (ladder), i.e., they ran out the gangplank for disembarkation.

text.greek: σίτου καὶ πόσιος λελιημένοι· ἀμφὶ δὲ κναμός
text.english: eager for food and drink; and round about the wooded slope
text.note: “leliēmenoi” (perf. mid.) = “being in eager desire, longing.” “knamos” denotes a wooded mountain-side/slope.

text.greek: Ἀργάνθου κατέφαινε, βαθυσκόπελοί τε κολῶναι.
text.english: of Arganthos was visible, and the steep-cragged hillocks.
text.note: “Arganthos” is a local Mysian height near Cyzicus; “bathyskopeloi kolōnai” = steep/crag-deep hillocks or mounded crags.

text.greek: - Ἡρακλέης δ' ἠπείγετ' ἀν' ὑλήεντας ἐναύλους,
text.english: But Herakles hastened up through the wooded glens,
text.note: ἐναύλους is best taken as “glens/ravines,” i.e., wooded hollows (often of stream-beds); ἀνὰ with the accusative conveys “up through.” ἠπείγετο = “made haste, pressed on.”

text.greek: τόξον ἔχων παλάμαις ἰδὲ τριγλώχινας ὀϊστούς
text.english: holding his bow in his hands, and three‑barbed arrows,
text.note: τριγλώχινας means “three‑barbed,” of arrowheads; παλάμαις (“with his hands”) is an epic pleonasm reinforcing the vividness of the arming detail.

text.greek: ὄφρα κε θηρήσαιτο, πόροι δ' ἐπὶ δόρπον ἑταίροις,
text.english: so that he might take game and provide supper for his comrades,
text.note: ὄφρα κε + optative expresses purpose (“so that he might”); πόροι is potential/optative of provision (“provide”); δόρπον is the evening meal, “supper.”

text.greek: ἢ σύας, ἢ πόρτιν κεραὴν, ἢ ἄγριον αἶγα.
text.english: either swine, or a horned heifer, or a wild goat.
text.note: σύας is generic “swine,” not necessarily boars; πόρτις is a “heifer” (young cow); κεραὴν = “horned”; ἄγριον αἶγα = “wild goat.”

text.greek: Τοῦ δ' ἀφομαρτήσαντος Ὕλας ἐξίκετο νηός
text.english: But once he had escaped his notice, Hylas made for the ship,
text.note: Τοῦ … ἀφομαρτήσαντος is a genitive absolute, with τοῦ most plausibly referring to Herakles (“after he had slipped from his notice”); ἐξίκετο νηός takes the genitive of goal (“reached/made for the ship”); rendering as “made for” eases the narrative sequence with the next line.

text.greek: λάθρα ἐπισπόμενος· σκολιῆς δ' ἀλίτησεν ἀταρποῦ
text.english: following in secret; yet he wandered from a crooked bypath,
text.note: Σκολιῆς ἀταρποῦ: ἀταρπός is a “side-track/bypath”; ἀλίτησεν here = “went astray, missed,” not “sinned.”

text.greek: ὕλῃ ἔνι πλαγχθεὶς, ἐν δὲ σπέος ἥλυθε Νυμφῶν
text.english: driven astray in the forest, and he came into the cave of the Nymphai
text.note: Πλαγχθείς (aor. pass. of πλάζομαι) = “driven/wandering astray”; ὕλη = “forest/wood”; σπέος is the epic word for “cave.” “Nymphai” is retained as a theonym.

text.greek: Λιμνακίδων· αἱ δέ σφιν ἐσαθρήσασαι ἰόντα
text.english: the Limnakides; and they, when they spied him coming,
text.note: Λιμνακίδες = “Lake-Nymphs” (of pools/marshes); ἐσαθρήσασαι = “having marked/spied”; σφιν is an ethical dative (“to them/on their part”).

text.greek: κοῦρον ἔτ' ἀντίθεον κατερύκανον, ὄφρα σὺν αὐταῖς
text.english: a youth still godlike, restrained him, so that with them
text.note: Κοῦρον ἔτ’ ἀντίθεον = “a youth still godlike”; κατερύκανον (aor.) = “restrained/detained.”

text.greek: ἀθάνατός τε πέλῃ καὶ ἀγήραος ἤματα πάντα.
text.english: he might be immortal and ageless all his days.
text.note: ὄφρα + subjunctive expresses purpose (“so that”); πέλῃ (subj. of πέλω) = “might be”; ἀγήραος = “ageless”; ἤματα πάντα is the epic idiom for “for all his days, forever.”

text.greek: - Ἀλλ' ὅτε πρὸς μεσάτην ἠῶ φέρεν ὠκέας ἵππους
text.english: But when Helios was bearing his swift horses toward mid-morning,
text.note: πρὸς μεσάτην ἠῶ: “toward mid‑morning”; epic diction marking the time of day. Helios’ “swift horses” are the Sun’s team.

text.greek: Ἠέλιος, κραιπνὸς δ' ἐξ οὔρεος ἔπνεεν οὖρος,
text.english: and a swift fair wind was blowing from the mountain,
text.note: οὖρος is a “fair/favouring wind”; κραιπνός (“rapid, nimble”) qualifies the wind. ἐξ οὔρεος suggests a land-breeze descending from high ground.

text.greek: ἐν δ' ἔπεσ' ἀργενναῖς ὀθόναις, Τῖφυς δ' ἐγεγώνει
text.english: and it fell upon the white sails, and Tiphys was calling out
text.note: ὀθόναι are “linen cloths,” i.e., sails; ἀργενναῖς = “white, gleaming.” The subject of ἔπεσ’ (“fell upon”) is the wind.

text.greek: νηὸς ἔσω περάαν, θινὸς δ' ἐκ πείσματα λύειν·
text.english: to drive the ship inward and to loose the moorings from the beach;
text.note: νηὸς ἔσω περάαν: “to drive the ship inward,” i.e., out from shore into the open sea; θινός = “beach, strand”; πείσματα = “mooring-ropes, cables.” The infinitives depend on ἐγεγώνει (“was calling out [to]”).

text.greek: οἳ δὲ κυβερνητῆρος ἐφημοσύναις ἐπίθοντο.
text.english: and they obeyed the helmsman’s injunctions.
text.note: ἐφημοσύναις (“injunctions, directions”) is a rarer word; Tiphys is the κυβερνήτης (helmsman). ἐπίθοντο = “they obeyed, hearkened.”

text.greek: Εἰλατίδης δ' ἀνὰ πρῶνα θοῶς Πολύφημος ἔβαινεν,
text.english: And Eilatides Polyphemus was going swiftly up along the headland,
text.note: Eilatides = “son of Eilatus/Elatus,” the Lapith Polyphemus (not the Cyclops). ἀνὰ πρῶνα (“up along the headland/slope”): πρών can mean headland or prow; here the topographical sense suits the context.

text.greek: ὄφρα κεν Ἡρακλῆα θοῶς ἐπὶ νῆα καλέσσοι·
text.english: so that he might swiftly summon Herakles to the ship;
text.note: No special difficulty; repetition of “swiftly” (thoōs) echoes epic diction.

text.greek: ἀλλ' οὔ οἱ ξύμβλητο· μολεῖν γάρ οἱ οὔτι πέπρωτο
text.english: but he did not encounter him;
text.note: ξύμβλητο is epic for “met/encountered” (aorist middle); the dative οἱ refers to Herakles as the one not encountered.

text.greek: Φᾶσιν καλλίροον μένος ὄβριμον Ἡρακλῆος.
text.english: for the overmastering might of Herakles was by no means fated to come to the fair‑flowing Phasis.
text.note: μολεῖν … πέπρωτο + dat. (“it was fated for him to come”): the dat. οἱ = Herakles. Φᾶσις is the river of Colchis; καλλίροος = “fair‑flowing.” μένος ὄβριμον (“overmastering might”) is a formulaic epithet of Herakles.

text.greek: - Αὐτὰρ ἐπηῶοι λυγρὴν ἐπεράσσαμεν αἶαν,
text.english: But on the next day we crossed to the baleful land,
text.note: ἐπηῶοι is an adverbial form meaning “on the next day”; λυγρὴν αἶαν (“baleful land”) foreshadows the grim encounter with Amycus.

text.greek: ἔνθ' Ἄμυκος Βεβρύκεσσιν ὑπερφιάλοισιν ἄνασσεν·
text.english: where Amycus ruled the over-proud Bebryces;
text.note: Bebryces: a tribe located in northwestern Asia Minor (Bithynia).

text.greek: ὅστε Πανομφαίου Ζηνὸς θέμιν οὐκ ἀλεγίζων
text.english: who, not heeding the ordinance of Panomphaios Zeus,
text.note: Panomphaios (“of all oracles/voices,” from pan- + omphē) is an epithet of Zeus; “ordinance” renders θέμις as divine/customary right, especially relevant to xenia (guest-right).

text.greek: ἆθλον ἐπὶ ξείνοισι περικτιόνων ἀνθρώπων,
text.english: set a challenge against strangers from the peoples dwelling round about,
text.note: ἆθλον ἐπὶ + dat. conveys “to impose/set a challenge upon”; ξείνοι are “strangers/guests,” περικτιόνων ἀνθρώπων “men dwelling round about, neighbors.”

text.greek: ὅστις ἐπὶ σταθμοὺς ἠδ' ἀστεμφῆ δόμον ἵξῃ,
text.english: whosoever should come to his steads and unshaken house,
text.note: σταθμοί are “steads, quarters, lodgings”; ἀστεμφής means “unshaken, firm,” a formulaic epithet for a solid house.

text.greek: θήκατο, πυγμαχίης ὑπερόπλου πειρηθῆναι.
text.english: ordaining that they be put to the test in overweening boxing.
text.note: θῆκατο … πειρηθῆναι = “he set/established (as rule) that they be tried”; πυγμαχίης ὑπερόπλου = “overweening/overmighty boxing,” marking the arrogant brutality of the bout (and by implication of Amycus).

text.greek: Τὸν μὲν ἄρ' ἠΐστωσε βίῃ κρατερὸς Πολυδεύκης,
text.english: Then mighty Polydeukes slew him by force,
text.note: ἠΐστωσε is the aorist of ἀϊστόω “make unseen,” a poetic euphemism for “destroy/kill”; hence “slew him.” The ‘him’ is Amykos, felled by Polydeukes.

text.greek: τύψας ἀπροφάτως κεφαλὴν σκληροῖσιν ἱμᾶσι·
text.english: striking his head unawares with hard thongs;
text.note: ἱμᾶσι are the leather thongs used by boxers; ἀπροφάτως means “without warning, unawares.”

text.greek: λαοὺς δ' αὖ Βεβρύκων Μινύαι χαλκῷ κατένηραν·
text.english: and the Minyans laid low the Bebrycians’ people with bronze.
text.note: χαλκῷ (“with bronze”) = with bronze weapons; Μινύαι (Minyans) are the Argonauts. λαοὺς Βεβρύκων = “the people/hosts of the Bebrycians.”

text.greek: - Ἔνθα δ' ἀφορμηθέντες, ὑπ' εἰρεσίῃ δὲ καμόντες,
text.english: From there we set out, and, wearied beneath the oar,
text.note: εἰρεσίη = “rowing, oarage”; thus “wearied beneath the oar” (i.e., by hard rowing).

text.greek: Βιθυνῶν μέγα ἄστυ βαθείῃ κέλσαμεν ἀκτῇ
text.english: we ran her aground on the deep shore by the great city of the Bithynians,
text.note: κέλσαμεν is the aorist of κέλλω “run (a ship) aground, beach.” βαθεῖα ἀκτή is “deep(-water) shore,” i.e., with deep water close in.

text.greek: σπεύδοντες προχοαῖς ἠδ' ἐν νιφαργέσιν ὕλαις,
text.english: hastening to the river outflows and the snow-bright woods,
text.note: προχοαί are “outflows, river-mouths/streams”; νιφαργής = “snow-bright, snow-gleaming,” a poetic epithet of the woods.

text.greek: ἕσπεροι αὐλισθέντες ἐφωπλισσάμεθα δόρπον.
text.english: and, having bivouacked at eventide, we made our supper ready.
text.note: ἐφωπλισσάμεθα (middle) = “we made ready (for ourselves).” ἕσπεροι is adverbial “at evening, toward dusk.”

text.greek: Ἔνθα ποτ' αἰνόγαμος Φινεὺς ὑπερήνορι θυμῷ
text.english: There once the ill-wedded Phineus, in his overweening heart,
text.note: αἰνόγαμος = “ill-wedded,” alluding to Phineus’ disastrous marriage; ὑπερήνορι θυμῷ conveys overbearing/overweening spirit rather than laudable “manliness.”

text.greek: δοιοὺς ἐξαλάωσε γόνους, προβλῆσί τε πέτραις
text.english: blinded his two sons, and by casting them forth upon jutting rocks
text.note: δοιοὺς = epic for “two”; ἐξαλάωσε “blinded utterly.” προβλῆσι πέτραις is an instrumental/manner dative, “by exposure on jutting rocks,” i.e., infanticidal abandonment.

text.greek: θηρσὶν ἕλωρ προὔθηκε γυναίων εἵνεκα φίλτρων·
text.english: he set them as prey for beasts, because of women’s love-charms;
text.note: γυναιῶν φίλτρων = “women’s love-charms/philters,” generic plural, likely referring to the manipulations of his wife; ἕλωρ θηρσί = “prey for beasts.”

text.greek: τοὺς δὲ καὶ ἀσκηθεῖς καὶ ὀπωπότας αὖθις ἔτευξαν
text.english: but them the sons of renowned Boreas made again both unscathed and seeing,
text.note: ἀσκηθεῖς = “unharmed, unscathed”; ὀπωπότας is the perfect participle of ὁράω (“having seen,” i.e., “seeing”), with αὖθις indicating restoration (“again”); ἔτευξαν (from τεύχω) with double predicate accusative = “made them [to be] ….”

text.greek: παῖδε κλυτοῦ Βορέου· Φινεῖ δέ οἱ ὤπασαν ἄτην
text.english: and upon Phineus they sent the ruin of grievous rancor,
text.note: παῖδε κλυτοῦ Βορέου = the Boreads (Zetes and Calais). ὤπασαν ἄτην ἀργαλέοιο κότου: ὀπάζω “to grant/inflict,” ἄτη “ruin/baneful delusion,” κότος a long-nursed rancor. Orphic tradition here makes the Boreads the agents of Phineus’ blinding.

text.greek: ἀργαλέοιο κότου, φωτὸς δ' ἀπενόσφισαν αὐγάς.
text.english: and they deprived him of the light of day.
text.note: φωτὸς αὐγὰς = “the light/rays of day” (idiom); ἀπενόσφισαν = “they deprived/robbed [him of].” This passage preserves a variant in which the Boreads punish Phineus by blinding him.

text.greek: Αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ ζαμενὴς Βορέης στροφάδεσσιν ἀέλλαις
text.english: But when vehement Boreas, with whirling squalls,
text.note: ζαμενής = “vehement, raging.” στροφάδεσσιν ἀέλλαις = “with whirling squalls” (dative of manner); στροφάδες here are not the Στροφάδες islands but ‘eddies/whirls.’

text.greek: ἁρπάξας ἐκύλινδε διὰ δρυμὰ πυκνὰ καὶ ὕλας
text.english: having snatched [them] up, rolled along through the dense thickets and woods
text.note: The object of ἁρπάξας and ἐκύλινδε is implicit (what the wind seizes and rolls—leaves, debris, all before him). δρυμὰ … καὶ ὕλας forms a near-synonymous pair, “thickets and woods.”

text.greek: Βιστονίης, ἵνα κῆρ ὀλοὴν καὶ πότμον ἐπίσπῃ.
text.english: of Bistonia, so that he might bring on baleful death and doom.
text.note: Βιστονίη = Bistonia, a Thracian land (of the Bistones). ἵνα introduces a purpose clause. κῆρ ὀλοήν καὶ πότμον is an intensifying hendiadys (“baleful death and doom”). ἐπίσπῃ (subj.) = “bring upon, draw on.”

text.greek: - Αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ Φινῆος Ἀγηνορίδαο λιπόντες
text.english: But when we had left the lodging of the Agenorid Phineus,
text.note: “Agenorid” renders Ἀγηνορίδαο (descendant/son of Agenor); αὖλιν is “lodging/encampment,” not necessarily a palace.

text.greek: αὖλιν, ὑπὲρ μέγα λαῖτμα θαλάσσης ἐξικόμεσθα
text.english: we came across the great gulf of the sea, near to the Kyaneai Rocks,
text.note: λαῖτμα is a poetic term for a yawning gulf or deep; ὑπέρ here conveys movement “across/over.”

text.greek: ἀγχοῦ Κυανέαις πέτραις, ἅς μοι ποτὲ μήτηρ
text.english: which once my mother
text.note: Κυανέαι πέτραι are the “Kyaneai (Dark-Bluish) Rocks,” i.e., the Symplegades/Clashing Rocks of the Bosporus; ἀγχοῦ = “near, hard by.”

text.greek: ἡμετέρη κατέλεξε περίφρων Καλλιόπεια.
text.english: our own, very wise Kalliopeia, recounted to me.
text.note: The narrator is Orpheus; hence “our mother” (ἡμετέρη) refers to his own mother, the Muse Kalliopeia. περίφρων is an epithet “very wise/prudent”; κατέλεξε means “recounted (in full), related.”

text.greek: Οὐ γάρ οἱ ἐξυπάλυξις ὀϊζυροῖο πόνοιο,
text.english: For there is for him no escape from woeful toil,
text.note: ἐξυπάλυξις is a rare noun, literally “a slipping-out,” hence “escape”; ὀϊζυρός = “woeful, pitiable.”

text.greek: ἀλλὰ κατειρύμεναι ἀνέμων ἀργῇσιν ἀέλλαις
text.english: but, hemmed in by the bright squalls of the winds,
text.note: κατειρύμεναι (from κατειρύω) = “shut in, hemmed in”; ἀργῇσιν ἀέλλαις = “bright/white squalls.” The feminine morphology anticipates a feminine subject (sc. πέτραι).

text.greek: ξυμβλῆτες πίπτουσιν ἐπ' ἀλλήλαισιν ἰοῦσαι·
text.english: clashing they fall upon one another as they rush;
text.note: ξυμβλῆτες = “clashing/meeting (ones),” used substantively; with fem. dat. ἀλλήλαισιν it points to the Clashing Rocks (Symplegades) as the implied subject; ἰοῦσαι = “rushing, going.”

text.greek: δοῦπός τ' ἂμ πέλαγός τε καὶ οὐρανὸν εὐρὺν ἵκανεν
text.english: and the boom reached over the sea and the broad heaven
text.note: δοῦπος = “boom, thud.” ἂμ here functions adverbially (“over/throughout”), so “reached over the sea and broad heaven.”

text.greek: ῥηγνυμένοιο κλύδωνος, ὀρινομένης τε θαλάσσης·
text.english: from the rending of the billow and the heaving of the sea;
text.note: Genitives are causal: “from/of the rending of the billow” (ῥηγνυμένοιο κλύδωνος) and “of the heaving sea” (ὀρινομένης θαλάσσης).

text.greek: κύματι παφλάζοντι περιβρέμει ἄσπετος ἅλμη.
text.english: with the seething wave an immeasurable brine roared around.
text.note: ἄσπετος = “unspeakable, immense”; παφλάζοντι = “seething, splashing”; περιβρέμει = “roars all around.”

text.greek: Ἀλλ' ἐγὼ Ἀγνιάδῃ τάδ' ἀπὸ γλώσσης ἀγόρευσα,
text.english: But I spoke these words forth from my tongue to the Hagniades,
text.note: “Hagniades” is the patronymic “son of Hagnias,” i.e., Tiphys the helmsman; ἀπὸ γλώσσης ἀγόρευσα is formulaic epic diction (“spoke forth from my tongue”).

text.greek: πρύμναν ἔπειθ' ὁρόειν ὄφρ' ἂν πεφυλαγμένος εἴη.
text.english: then to look to the stern, that he might be on his guard.
text.note: πρύμναν ὁρόειν is a nautical idiom, “look to/mind the stern,” i.e., attend to the helm; ἔπειθ’ = ἔπειτα (“then”); ὄφρ’ ἂν … εἴη expresses purpose (“so that he might be on his guard”).

text.greek: Τοῦ δὲ καὶ εἰσαΐοντος ἐπαχνώθη φίλον ἦτορ,
text.english: And as he listened, his dear heart grew numb,
text.note: ἐπαχνώθη literally “grew thick, congealed,” used metaphorically of the heart becoming numb or benumbed (with fear).

text.greek: ἐν στέρνοισι δὲ κεῦθεν, ἅ οἱ τελέεσθαι ἔμελλεν,
text.english: and in his breast he hid what was destined to be fulfilled for him,
text.note: The transmitted κεῦθεν is best taken as Homeric imperfect κεύθεεν “he hid/kept hidden.” ἅ οἱ τελέεσθαι ἔμελλεν = “the things that were about to be accomplished for him.”

text.greek: μοῦνος ἀφ' ἡρώων· ἀλλὰ γλαυκῶπις Ἀθήνη
text.english: alone apart from the heroes; but glaukōpis Athēnē
text.note: μοῦνος ἀφ’ ἡρώων = “alone, apart from the other heroes,” marking his secrecy.

text.greek: Ἥρης ἐννεσίῃσιν ἐρωδιὸν ἧκε φέρεσθαι
text.english: at Hērē’s promptings sent a heron to be borne
text.note: ἐννεσίῃσιν = “promptings, instigations.” ἧκε φέρεσθαι is Homeric for “sent to be borne (to fly).” ἐρωδιόν = “heron,” here an omen-bird (contrast Apollonius’ dove).

text.greek: ἄκρην ἱστοκεραῖαν· ὃ δ' ἀσχαλόων πεπότητο,
text.english: to the tip of the mast’s yard‑arm; but it, in distress, kept flying,
text.note: ἱστοκεραῖαν = “the mast’s yard‑arm” (κέρας of the ἱστός); ἀσχαλόων = “troubled, vexed, flustered.”

text.greek: πέτραις δ' ἐν μυχάταισιν ὑπὸ πτερύγεσσιν ἀερθείς
text.english: and, borne aloft beneath its wings in the inmost clefts of the rocks,
text.note: μυχάταισιν = “inmost recesses, clefts.” ἀερθείς = “borne aloft”; “beneath its wings” suggests the lifting air under the wings.

text.greek: δινεῖται· ταὶ δ' αἶψα κραδαινόμεναι ἑκάτερθεν
text.english: it was whirled about; and they, quickly shaking on either side,
text.note: ταί refers to the Clashing Rocks (Symplegades); κραδαινόμεναι = “quivering, shaking”; ἑκάτερθεν = “on either side.”

text.greek: σύμπεσον ἀλλήλαισι, καὶ οὐρῆς ἄκρον ἔκερσαν
text.english: crashed together and sheared off the tip of the bird’s tail,
text.note: ἔκερσαν (from κείρω) = “sheared off.” οὐρῆς ἄκρον = “the tip of the tail,” a favorable omen indicating near‑miss and thus possible safe passage.

text.greek: ὄρνιθος· περὶ δέ σφιν ἐτώσιον ἠρείσαντο.
text.english: and among them there arose a futile wrangling.
text.note: ἐτώσιον = “to no purpose, futile(ly).” ἠρείσαντο (mid. of ἐρίζω) = “they wrangled/contended”; σφιν = “among them,” i.e., among the heroes.

text.greek: Τῖφυς δ' ἐκπρολιπόντος ἐρωδιοῦ αἰπὺν ὄλεθρον
text.english: But Tiphys, when the heron had escaped grim destruction,
text.note: Genitive absolute: “ἐκπρολιπόντος ἐρωδιοῦ” = “when the heron had left behind (i.e., escaped) death.” Orphic Argonautica uses a heron, not the Apollonian dove, to test the Symplegades; “αἰπὺν ὄλεθρον” = “grim doom.”

text.greek: σῖγα μὲν ἡρώεσσιν ἐκέκλετο· τοὶ δ' ἀΐοντες,
text.english: quietly called to the heroes; and they, hearing,
text.note: “σῖγα” adverb “quietly, softly.” “ἐκέκλετο” middle ‘called to, summoned.’

text.greek: ἱέμενοι θοὰ κύμαθ' ὑπειρεσίῃσι χάρασσον·
text.english: eagerly were furrowing the swift waves with their oars;
text.note: “ὑπειρεσίῃσι” is epic for ‘oars’ (cf. εἴρεσις/ἐρετμός); “χαράσσειν κύματ’” = ‘to score/furrow the waves.’

text.greek: αὐτὰρ ἐγὼ μολπῇσι παρήπαφον ἡμετέρῃσι
text.english: but I with my own songs enchanted
text.note: “παρήπαφον” (from παραπαφέω) ‘soothe/charm by song,’ marking Orpheus’ magical effect; “ἡμετέρῃσι μολπῇσι” = ‘with my/our songs.’

text.greek: πέτρας ἠλιβάτους· αἱ δ' ἀλλήλων ἀπόρουσαν.
text.english: the sheer rocks; and they sprang apart from one another.
text.note: “πέτρας ἠλιβάτους” = ‘sheer/precipitous rocks’ (epic epithet; often of cliffs); “ἀπόρουσαν” from ὀρούω with ἀπό-, ‘leapt/sprang apart,’ describing the Symplegades parting.

text.greek: Κῦμα δ' ἀνερρόχθησε· βυθὸς δ' ὑποείκαθε νηΐ,
text.english: And the billow roared back; and the deep yielded beneath the ship,
text.note: ἀνερρόχθησε (from the root of ῥόχθος, “roar”) conveys a wave surging/recoiling with a roar; ὑποείκαθε = “gave way/yielded,” with νηί as dative of advantage (“to/for the ship”).

text.greek: ἡμετέρῃ πίσυνος κιθάρῃ, διὰ θέσκελον αὐδήν.
text.english: relying on our kithara, through the wondrous voice.
text.note: πίσυνος (“trusting in, relying on”) governs the dative κιθάρῃ; syntactically it most naturally modifies βυθός (“the deep”), personifying the sea as yielding in trust of Orpheus’ music. διὰ θέσκελον αὐδήν = “by means of the wondrous (divinely wrought) voice.” ἡμετέρῃ (“our”) reflects Orpheus’ self-reference.

text.greek: Ἀλλ' ὅτε δὴ πορθμοῖο κατὰ στόμα καὶ διὰ πέτρας
text.english: But when indeed the noisy keel had passed by the mouth of the strait and through the Cyanean Rocks,
text.note: πορθμοῖο κατὰ στόμα = “by/at the mouth of the strait,” i.e., the Bosporus; Κυανέας = the Cyanean (Symplegades) Rocks. λάλος τρόπις literally “talkative keel,” a conventional metaphor for the keel resounding in the water; ἤμειψε = “passed, traversed” (of crossing a stretch).

text.greek: Κυανέας ἤμειψε λάλος τρόπις, αὐτίκ' ἄρ' αἵ γε
text.english: straightway those rocks were rooted from the depths,
text.note: αἵ γε refers back to the Cyanean Rocks. βυσσόθεν = “from the abyss/deep.” ἐρριζοῦντο (impf.) = “were rooted, took root,” describing their becoming fixed after the Argo’s passage (a standard motif).

text.greek: βυσσόθεν ἐρριζοῦντο, καὶ ἔμπεδον αἰὲν ἔμιμνον.
text.english: and thereafter they remained forever steadfast.
text.note: ἔμπεδον (“firm, steadfast”) is used adverbially; αἰὲν = “ever, forever”; ἔμιμνον = “remained.” No textual difficulty is apparent.

text.greek: Οὕτω γὰρ Μοῖραι τάδ' ἐπεκλώσαντο βαρεῖαι.
text.english: For thus the Moirai, heavy, spun out these things.
text.note: ἐπεκλῶσαντο (aor. mid. of ἐπικλώθω) uses the fate‑spinning metaphor, hence “spun out” = “ordained”; βαρεῖαι literally “heavy,” an epic epithet of the Moirai meaning grievous/stern.

text.greek: - Καὶ τότε δὴ προφυγόντες ἀδευκέα πήματ' ὀλέθρου,
text.english: And then indeed, having beforehand escaped the hard-to-avoid woes of destruction,
text.note: ἀδευκέα = “hard to avoid, ineluctable”; προφυγόντες conveys an anticipatory escape (“forestalling” disaster).

text.greek: Ῥηβανοῦ προχοαῖσι μέλαιν' ἐξικόμεθ' ἀκτήν,
text.english: we reached the black shore at the outflows of the Rhebanos,
text.note: Ῥηβανοῦ: likely the river Rhebas on the Bithynian Euxeinos coast; προχοαί = “outflows, mouths.”

text.greek: νῆσον ὑπὲρ δολιχὴν Θυνηίδα, τῆς ἀπάτερθεν
text.english: beyond the long island Thynias, on the far side of which
text.note: ὑπέρ here means “beyond/over against”; Θυνηίς = Thynias Island off the Bithynian coast; ἀπάτερθεν = “on the far side (of it).”

text.greek: Τέμβριος ἰχθυόεις θαλεραῖς πλημμύρεται ὄχθαις,
text.english: the fish-rich Tembrios floods its luxuriant banks,
text.note: Τέμβριος = the Tembris, a tributary of the Sangarios; θαλερός = “luxuriant, flourishing”; πλημμύρεται = “floods/overflows.”

text.greek: Σαγγάριός θ' ὃς κύματ' ἐπιτρέχει Εὐξείνοιο.
text.english: and Sangarios too, which runs its waves upon the Euxeinos.
text.note: Σαγγάριος = the Sangarios (Sangarius) River; Εὔξεινος = the Euxeinos (the Black Sea). The idiom κύματα ἐπιτρέχει means the river “runs/empties its waves upon” the sea.

text.greek: Ἀλλ' ὅτ' ἐπ' αἰγιαλὸν ἐπενεισάμεθ' εἰρεσίῃσιν,
text.english: But when we had driven her up upon the beach with our oars,
text.note: ἐπενεισάμεθα εἰρεσίῃσι(ν): epic idiom “to drive a ship up (to land) with the oars.”

text.greek: ἀμφὶ Λύκοιο ῥέεθρον ἐκέλσαμεν, ᾧ ἔπι λαοῖς
text.english: we beached her beside the stream of Lykos, by which Lykos ruled the peoples,
text.note: ἐκέλσαμεν (from κέλλω) = “we beached [the ship].” ᾧ ἔπι λαοῖς κραῖνε: epic construction with ἐπί + dat. “over/among,” and κραίνω “to rule”; thus “where Lykos ruled the peoples.” Lykos here is the Mariandynian king by the river Lykos (cf. Apollonius Rhod. 2).

text.greek: κραῖνε Λύκος ποταμοῖο φερώνυμος, ὅς ῥ' ὑπέδεκτο
text.english: Lykos, eponym of the river, who took in
text.note: ποταμοῖο φερώνυμος = “eponym of the river,” i.e., the river was named after Lykos (epic unaugmented imperfect κραῖνε = “was ruling”).

text.greek: ἥρωας Μινύας, ξενίῃ δ' ὑπέδεκτο τραπέζη,
text.english: the Minyan heroes, and made them welcome at the guest-table,
text.note: ξενίῃ … τραπέζῃ, dat. of instrument/attendant circumstance: “with a guest-table,” i.e., hospitality at table; ὑπέδεκτο repeated for emphasis (“received,” “welcomed”).

text.greek: φίλετο δ' αὖ νύκτας τε καὶ ἤματα συνεχὲς αἰεί.
text.english: and in turn he showed them friendship, by night and by day, unceasingly.
text.note: φίλετο (middle) with understood object = “he showed [them] affection/kindness.” νύκτας τε καὶ ἤματα is a formula “by night and by day”; συνεχὲς αἰεί emphasizes unceasing, constant hospitality.

text.greek: Ἔνθα καὶ αἶσα παρέσχε καταφθίσθαι δύο φῶτας,
text.english: There too did Aisa grant that two men should perish,
text.note: Aisa is the personified Fate; φῶτες is epic for “men/warriors,” and καταφθίσθαι carries the force “to perish utterly.”

text.greek: Ἀμπυκίδην Ἴδμωνα, κυβερνητῆρά τε Τῖφυν.
text.english: Idmon, Ampycides, and Tiphys the helmsman.
text.note: Ampycides is the patronymic “son of Ampycus,” identifying Idmon (the seer); κυβερνήτης denotes the ship’s helmsman, here Tiphys.

text.greek: Τοῦ μὲν δὴ κατὰ σῶμα λυγρὴ ἠρείσατο νοῦσος,
text.english: Of the one indeed a baneful disease settled upon his body,
text.note: “The one … the other” refers to Tiphys (dead of disease) and Idmon (slain by a boar). ἠρείσατο (“pressed/settled upon”) with κατὰ σῶμα gives the sense “weighed down his body.”

text.greek: τὸν δ' ἔκτεινεν θὴρ, σῦς ἄγριος· ἂν δ' ἄρα τοῖς γε
text.english: but the other a beast slew, a savage boar; and then for those men
text.note: θὴρ, σῦς ἄγριος is appositional (“a beast, a wild boar”). The particle cluster ἂν δ’ ἄρα is epic and here merely marks narrative progression (“then indeed”), not modality.

text.greek: τύμβους χευάμενοι πολιὴν ἐπενεισάμεθ' ἅλμην,
text.english: having heaped their tombs we poured the hoary brine,
text.note: ἐπενεισάμεθ’ ἅλμην likely means “we poured brine upon [the tombs]” (a sailors’ libation); some take it as “we put to sea again,” but the funerary context favors libation. πολιός (“hoary, gray”) is a conventional epithet of sea-brine.

text.greek: Ἀγκαίῳ πίσυνοι· τὸν γὰρ φάσαν ἴδριν ἅπαντες
text.english: trusting in Ancaeus; for all declared him an adept
text.note: πίσυνοι with the dative = “trusting in, relying on.” Ἀγκαίῳ is Ancaeus, who succeeds Tiphys as helmsman.

text.greek: ναυτιλίης σφετέρῃσι δαημοσύνῃσι κεκάσθαι.
text.english: in seamanship, pre‑eminent by his own expertise.
text.note: ἴδρις = “adept, expert.” κεκάσθαι is the perfect infinitive of καίνυμαι (“to excel, be pre‑eminent”). σφετέρῃσι δαημοσύνῃσι (“by his own skills/know‑how”) is poetical plural.

text.greek: Αὐτὰρ πηδαλίων οἰήια λάζετο χειρί
text.english: But he grasped in his hand the rudders’ tiller‑ropes,
text.note: οἰήια are the helm- or tiller-ropes used to control the πηδάλια (steering oars/rudders). The middle λάζετο conveys deliberate seizing/grasping.

text.greek: νῆα κατιθύνων ἐπὶ Παρθενίοιο ῥέεθρα,
text.english: steering the ship upon the streams of Parthenios,
text.note: κατιθύνων = κατ‑ἰθύνων, “directing/steering (down/straight).” ἐπὶ with the accusative ῥέεθρα expresses motion “onto/into” the river’s currents.

text.greek: ὃν δὴ Καλλίχορόν μιν ἐπώνυμόν οἱ καλέουσιν,
text.english: whom indeed they call, as his by‑name, Kallichoros,
text.note: Καλλίχορον (“Fair‑Dancing”) is treated as an ἐπώνυμον (by‑name/epithet) of the river Parthenios; μιν and οἱ reflect the customary personification of a river as masculine. The exact local reference of “Kallichoros” is likely cultic/toponymic.

text.greek: ὅν τοι ἐγὼ μύθοισιν ἐπὶ προτέροισιν ἔλεξα.
text.english: whom, you know, I mentioned in earlier words.
text.note: τοι is an enclitic adding assurance (“you know”); the poet refers to prior mention “in earlier words.”

text.greek: - Ἔνθεν ἄκραν προβλῆτα παραπλώσαντες ἔβημεν
text.english: Thence, having coasted past a projecting headland, we came
text.note: ἄκραν προβλῆτα = “projecting/jutting headland”; παραπλώσαντες “coasting past.” Epic ἔβημεν used idiomatically for “we came (to).”

text.greek: γῆν ἐπὶ Παφλαγόνων, τὴν δὴ παράμειψε θέουσα
text.english: to the land of the Paphlagonians, which indeed, as she raced,
text.note: θέουσα (“running, speeding”) is a conventional epithet of swift motion, used of the ship; τὴν refers back to γῆν (the Paphlagonian land); παραμείψε “passed by.”

text.greek: Ἀργὼ ὑπὲρ μέγα λαῖτμα· Καραμβιακὴν δ' ἵκετ' ἄκρην,
text.english: Argo passed by over a great yawning deep; she reached the Karambian headland,
text.note: μέγα λαῖτμα = “great yawning deep/gulf,” a Homeric term for the open sea; Καραμβιακὴ ἄκρη = the promontory of Carambis (modern Kerempe Burnu).

text.greek: ᾗ ἐνὶ Θερμώδων κεῖται Ἅλυος τε ῥέεθρον,
text.english: where lie the Thermodon and the stream of Halys,
text.note: κεῖται used of rivers’ situation/outlet; ῥέεθρον = “flow/stream” (poetic). The line compresses coastal geography, associating Carambis with the Thermodon and the Halys.

text.greek: βάλλον ἐπ' αἰγιαλὸν, δίνας ἁλιμυρέας ἕλκον.
text.english: striking upon the shore and drawing briny eddies.
text.note: βάλλον and ἕλκον are epic (unaugmented) imperfects with the rivers (Thermodon and Halys) as subject: “they strike upon the shingle and draw/drag briny eddies” where they meet the sea.

text.greek: Νέρθε δ' ὑποθρώσκουσι βορειάδος ἀντίον ἄρκτου
text.english: Down below, over against the Northern Bear, the waters surge up from beneath.
text.note: ὑποθρώσκουσι (“leap/spring up from beneath”) is used of the sea’s swell; the subject is implicit. βορειάδος ἀρ́κτου (“the Northern Bear”) is the constellation (Ursa Major), so “opposite the Northern Bear” means north-facing (the south shore of the Euxine faces north).

text.greek: μακρὰ Θεμισκύρης Δοιαντίδος ἅψεα κεῖται·
text.english: There lie the long reaches of Themiscyra of Doiantis.
text.note: ἅψεα is a rare neuter plural (“edges, fringes, reaches”), here of coastline; neuter plural takes singular κεῖται. Θεμισκύρη (Themiscyra) is the Amazon land on the Thermodon. Δοιαντίδος is obscure: likely “of Doiantis,” an eponymic designation tied to the Amazons; the exact referent is uncertain in our text.

text.greek: ἄγχι δ' Ἀμαζονίδων δαμνίππων ἄστεα κεῖται,
text.english: Hard by lie the cities of the Amazons, breakers of horses.
text.note: δαμνίππων = “horse-breaking/horse-taming,” a traditional epic epithet.

text.greek: καὶ Χάλυβες, Τιβαρηνά τ' ἔθνη, λαοί τε Βέχειρες
text.english: And the Chalybes, and the Tibarenian tribes, and the peoples of the Becheires,
text.note: Βέχειρες: obscure ethnonym; the reading is uncertain and has been variously identified (e.g., with the Byzeres). I retain the transmitted form.

text.greek: μίγδην ἐν Μοσύνοισι πέδον περιναιετάουσι·
text.english: mingled together they inhabit the plain round about among the Mosynoi;
text.note: Μοσύνοισι may denote the Mosynoeci (a Pontic people) or literally “in the mossynes,” their timber towers (cf. Herodotus). μίγδην = “mingled together”; περιναιετάω = “dwell around (the plain).”

text.greek: λαιὰ δ' ἐπιπλώσαντες ἐκέλσαμεν αἰγιαλοῖσι
text.english: and, coasting with the land to port, we ran the ship up on the beaches,
text.note: λαιὰ = “to port/with the land on the left” (nautical). ἐκέλσαμεν is the aorist of κέλλω, “run a ship ashore”; ἐπιπλώσαντες = “coasting along.”

text.greek: ἧχι τε Μάκροι ἔσαν Μαριανδύνοισιν ὅμουροι.
text.english: where the Makroi were neighbors to the Mariandynoi.

text.greek: Νέρθε δέ τοι Ἑλίκης δολιχὸς παρακέκλιται αὐχὴν
text.english: Down below, for you, the long neck of Helike lies bent aside.
text.note: Helike is most likely the Great Bear (Ursa Major), commonly used as a northern marker (“under Helike” = in the north). The phrase “long neck” (dolichos auchen) is unusual for the Bear; some take Helike here as a landform (a peninsula/isthmus) with a “neck.”

text.greek: ἔνθα δ' ὑπωρείῃσιν ἐπὶ προβλῆσι κυκλοῦνται
text.english: There, along the foothills, upon the projecting promontories,
text.note: hyporeiesin = “at/along the lower slopes,” i.e., foothills; problēsis = “projections,” here the jutting spurs or headlands.

text.greek: τηλεφανεῖς αὐλῶνες ὑπὲρ μυχὸν εὐρέα κόλπου·
text.english: far-seen ravines encircle the inmost recess of a broad gulf;
text.note: aulōnes are “hollows/valleys, ravines” (not “pipes”); telephaneis = “visible from afar.” hyper muchon = “over/above the innermost recess” of the gulf; kyklountai suggests they gird or ring it.

text.greek: οὗ Σύμης ὄρος ἐστὶ πολύς τ' εὐθαλὴς λειμών,
text.english: where stands the mountain of Syme and a luxuriant meadow in abundance,
text.note: Syme here is uncertain; it is unlikely to be the Aegean island Syme. Many take it as a local mountain/toponym in the eastern Euxine/Caucasian region.

text.greek: ἐνθάδ' Ἀράξου ῥεῦμα μεγαβρεμέτου ποταμοῖο,
text.english: here is the stream of the loud‑thundering river Araxes,
text.note: megabremetos = “loud‑thundering/roaring,” an epic epithet for a powerful river. Araxes is the great Armenian/Caucasian river, treated here as proximate to the Euxine’s eastern recess.

text.greek: ἐξ οὗ Θερμώδων Φᾶσις Τάναΐς τε ῥέουσιν,
text.english: from which Thermodon, Phasis, and Tanais flow,
text.note: The hydrology is mythic: Thermodon, Phasis, and Tanais are poetically derived from Araxes as a common source.

text.greek: οὗ Κόλχων κλυτὰ φῦλα καὶ Ἡνιόχων καὶ Ἀραξῶν.
text.english: where dwell the famed tribes of the Colchians, the Heniocheans, and the Araxians.
text.note: Klyta phyla = “famed tribes.” The Heniocheans (Heniokhoi) are a people of the eastern Black Sea coast (Strabo mentions them). “Araxians” renders Araxōn as an ethnicon (people of the Araxes).

text.greek: Ὃν παραμειβόμενοι, μυχάτοις ἐπεπλείομεν ὅρμοις
text.english: Having passed it by, we sailed along the innermost havens,
text.note: μυχάτοις ὅρμοις literally “innermost moorings/anchorages,” suggesting coast‑hugging among deep inlets; ὅν (“it”) picks up a landmark named in the preceding context.

text.greek: Οὔρων, Χιδναίων τε, Χαρανδαίων, Σολύμων τε
text.english: of the Ourians, and of the Chidnaians, the Charandaians, and the Solymi,
text.note: A string of ethnics in the genitive dependent on ὅρμοις (“havens of …”). Οὔρων is uncertain: likely a tribal name (“Ourians”), though formally identical with the gen. pl. of οὖρος (“favorable wind”); Χιδναῖοι (from Chidna) and Χαρανδαῖοι (from Caranda) are obscure Anatolian groups; Σόλυμοι are the Solymi of Lycia.

text.greek: Ἀσσυρίων τε λεὼν, τρηχὺν δ' ἀγκῶνα Σινώπης,
text.english: and the folk of the Assyrians, and the rugged elbow of Sinope,
text.note: λεὼν is epic for λαός (“people”). “Assyrians” here is a broad, poetic label for eastern peoples. ἀγκών (“elbow”) is a standard term for a jutting headland; Sinope’s promontory fits the image.

text.greek: καὶ Φίλυρας Ναπάτας τε καὶ ἄστεα πυκνὰ Σαπείρων
text.english: and those of the Philyres and the Napatae, and the close‑packed cities of the Sapeires,
text.note: Φίλυρες and Σάπειρες (Sapeires/Sasperi) are peoples of the southern Euxine/Trans‑Colchian regions. Ναπάται likely “Glen‑dwellers” (from νάπη, “wooded vale”). The cases are compressed in epic style; many editors print different case‑forms (e.g., Φιλυρέων).

text.greek: Βύζηράς τ' ἐπὶ τοῖσιν, ἰδ' ἄξενα φῦλα Σιγύμνων.
text.english: and, besides these, we saw the Byzeres and the inhospitable tribes of the Sigymni.
text.note: Βύζηρες (Byzeres) and Σιγύμνοι (Sigymni) are rare ethnics; the latter recalls Herodotus’ Sigynnae. ἐπὶ τοῖσιν means “in addition to these.” ἰδ’ = εἴδομεν (“we saw”), governing the accusatives that follow; ἄξενα (“inhospitable”) echoes the epithet of the Euxine (Axenos).

text.greek: - Ἷκτο δ' ὑπὸ πνοιῇς ἀνέμου πλησίστιος Ἀργὼ
text.english: And under the breaths of the wind Argo drew in close,
text.note: πλησίστιος is used adverbially (“very near, close at hand”); some take it with a nautical nuance (“close to the wind”). Ἷκτο is the epic aorist of ἱκνέομαι (“came, reached”).

text.greek: ὄρθριον, ἐρχομένης ἠοῦς ἐπ' ἀπείρονα κόσμον,
text.english: at dawn, as Eos was coming over the boundless world,
text.note: ἠώς is the personified Dawn (here transliterated as Eos). ὄρθριον is an adverbial “at daybreak.” ἐπ’ ἀπείρονα κόσμον = “over the boundless world.”

text.greek: ἐσχατ' ἔπ' Ἀξείνου Φᾶσιν κατὰ καλλιρέεθρον.
text.english: to the uttermost bounds of the Axenos, along the fair‑flowing Phasis.
text.note: ἐσχάτ’ = ἐσχάτα, “the farthest bounds.” Ἀξείνου is the older form of the name for the Black Sea (“Inhospitable,” later Εὔξεινος). κατὰ with a river often means motion “along/down” the stream; καλλιρέεθρον is the stock epithet “fair‑flowing.”

text.greek: Αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ ποταμοῖο διὰ στόμα πρηῢ ῥέοντος
text.english: But when through the mouth of the gently‑flowing river
text.note: The clause runs on to the next line; the gently‑flowing river is the Phasis implied by context.

text.greek: ἱκόμεθ' αὐτίκ' ἄρα στέφανον καὶ τεῖχος ἐρυμνόν
text.english: we came, straightway then the crown and the strong wall
text.note: “Crown” (stephanos) is the city’s encircling circuit; “strong wall” renders teichos erumnos (“well‑defended wall”).

text.greek: Αἰήτου κατέφαινε καὶ ἄλσεα τοῖς ἔπι κῶας
text.english: of Aietes came into view, and the groves whereon the fleece
text.note: “Came into view” renders impersonal/ intransitive katephaine; “groves” (alsēa) likely alludes to the sacred groves (sc. of Ares).

text.greek: χρύσεον ᾐώρητο χαλαζαίῃ ἐπὶ φηγῷ.
text.english: golden, was hanging upon a hail‑beaten oak.
text.note: “Hail‑beaten” renders chalazaiē, an epic epithet; some take it as “hail‑smitten,” others propose different nuances or emendations; phēgos is the oak on which the Golden Fleece hangs.

text.greek: Ἀγκαῖος δ' ἤνωγε παραιφάμενος ἐπέεσσι
text.english: But Ankaios bade them, counseling with words,
text.note: ἤνωγε is the epic verb “he bade/urged.” The phrase παραιφάμενος ἐπέεσσι is formulaic, “advising/counseling with words.”

text.greek: λαίφεά τε στέλλειν, καὶ ἐπίκριον αὖθι χαλάσσαι
text.english: to furl the canvas, and on the spot to slacken the stay‑rope,
text.note: λαίφεα (“canvas”) = sails; στέλλειν in nautical context means “to furl/take in.” ἐπίκριον is a technical term for the stay‑rope attached high on the mast; αὖθι means “on the spot.”

text.greek: ἱστὸν ἀνακλίναντας, ὑπ' εἰρεσίῃ δὲ νέεσθαι.
text.english: the mast inclined, and to make way under oars.
text.note: ἱστὸν ἀνακλίναντας = “tilting/inclining the mast,” preparatory to rowing; ὑπ’ εἰρεσίῃ = “under oarage,” i.e., under oars.

text.greek: Ὣς οἳ μὲν τὰ ἕκαστα πονήατο· αὐτὰρ Ἰήσων
text.english: Thus they busied themselves with each task; but Jason

text.greek: αὐτίκα μερμήριζε κατὰ φρένα καὶ κατὰ θυμόν,
text.english: straightway pondered in mind and in spirit,

text.greek: ξυνὴν μὲν Μινύαισιν ἄδην ἀνενείκατο φωνήν,
text.english: whether to raise a common voice among the Minyans in full,
text.note: ξυνὴν φωνήν: “a common/shared voice,” i.e., a collective consultation or declaration. ἀνενείκατο (epic) = “raised/brought up” (sc. the matter/voice) to the group; ἄδην = “to the full, fully.” ξυνήν is the epic form for κοινήν.

text.greek: ἠέ γ' ἐπ' Αἰήταο μόλῃ δόμον οἶος ἀπ' ἄλλων,
text.english: or indeed to go to the house of Aiētes alone, apart from the others,
text.note: μόλοι (deliberative aor. subj.) “should he go”; οἶος ἀπ᾽ ἄλλων = “alone, apart from the others.”

text.greek: μειλιχίοις στέρξῃ τε παραιφάμενος ἐπέεσσιν·
text.english: and win him over, coaxing with gentle words;
text.note: στέρξῃ = “win (his) favor”; παραιφάμενος = “coaxing, gently persuading.” μειλιχίοις ἐπέεσσιν = “with gentle (honeyed) words.”

text.greek: ἠὲ μεθ' ἡρώεσσι καὶ ἐς μόθον αὐτίκα λεύσσοι.
text.english: or with the heroes to face the fray forthwith.
text.note: μόθος = “fray, din of battle.” λεύσσοι (deliberative optative) “look toward” is idiomatic for “face”; note the epic alternation of moods alongside μόλοι/στέρξῃ.

text.greek: - Ἀλλ' οὐ γὰρ Μινύαισιν ἐπήνδανε πᾶσι νέεσθαι·
text.english: Yet not to all the Minyai was it pleasing to return.
text.note: ἐπήνδανε + dative = “was pleasing to”; νέεσθαι is the epic verb “to return (homeward).” “Minyai” = the Minyae/Argonauts.

text.greek: δεῖμα δ' ἐνὶ φρεσὶ θῆκε θεὰ λευκώλενος Ἥρη,
text.english: And the white-armed goddess Hērē set fear within their hearts,
text.note: λευκώλενος (“white-armed”) is a fixed Homeric epithet of Hērē; ἐνὶ φρεσί = “in their hearts/minds.”

text.greek: ἀμβολίην θ' ἵνα δὴ τελέσῃ, τάπερ αἶσα γενέσθαι.
text.english: so that she might indeed accomplish a postponement—the very thing that Aisa had ordained to come to pass.
text.note: ἀμβολίην = “delay, postponement” (rare epic noun); ἵνα + subjunctive expresses purpose; τά περ is emphatic (“precisely that”); αἶσα (Aisa) personified = Fate; γενέσθαι = “to come to pass.”

text.greek: Ὦκα δ' ἄρ' οὖλον ὄνειρον ἀπ' οὐρανοῦ ἧκε φέρεσθαι
text.english: Swiftly then a baneful dream came wafted from heaven
text.note: ἧκε φέρεσθαι can be taken as “was sent to be borne” (with an implied divine sender, cf. Il. 2.6–8) or more neutrally “came wafted”; the translation keeps the epic allusion to the oûlos oneiros.

text.greek: εἰς δόμον Αἰήταο· συθεὶς δ' ὅγε δεῖμα πέλωρον
text.english: into the house of Aiētēs; and, rousing a monstrous dread,
text.note: συθείς is a rare participle; most take it as “having stirred/roused,” governing δεῖμα (“dread”). δεῖμα πέλωρον = “monstrous dread.”

text.greek: Ἔσκηψεν βασιλῆα περὶ φρένας, ὅς νιν ἔδοξε
text.english: it fell upon the king about his wits; and he thought that it
text.note: ἔσκηψεν (“swooped/fell suddenly”) is used of thunderbolts and sudden calamities; περὶ φρένας = “upon/around his mind.” ὅς refers to Aiētēs; νιν (“it”) refers to the dream.

text.greek: παρθένου ἣν ἀτίταλλεν ἐνὶ μεγάροισιν ἑοῖσι
text.english: —of the maiden whom he reared in his own halls—
text.note: ἀτίταλλεν is epic for “reared/brought up,” stressing Aiētēs’ paternal role toward the maiden (Medeia).

text.greek: Μηδείας κόλποισιν ἐν ἱμερτοῖσι συθῆναι
text.english: had sunk into Medeia’s lovely bosoms,
text.note: συθῆναι is another rare form from the same root as συθείς; here “to sink/settle (into).” κόλποι are “bosoms/lap,” and ἱμερτοῖσι = “lovely, desirable.”

text.greek: ἀστέρα παμφανόωντα δι' ἠερίοιο πορείης.
text.english: a star all-shining along the airy course.
text.note: δι’ ἠερίοιο πορείας (“along/through the airy course”) is a Homeric-sounding periphrasis for the star’s path; the dream’s image of a star falling into Medeia’s bosom portends the hero’s arrival and union.

text.greek: Ἣ δ' ἐπεὶ ἐν πέπλοισι λάβεν κεχαρηότι θυμῷ,
text.english: But she, when she had taken it within her robes, with rejoicing heart,
text.note: “in her robes” renders en peploisi (peplos = woman’s garment); kechareōti thymōi is a perfect participle used adverbially, “with a heart gladdened.”

text.greek: ἧκε φέρουσ' εἰς χεύματ' ἐυρρείτου ποταμοῖο
text.english: went bearing it to the outflows of the well‑flowing river Phasis;
text.note: cheumata (“pourings, outflows”) denotes the river’s discharging waters; eurreitou is an epic compound epithet, “well‑flowing.”

text.greek: Φάσιδος· ἀστέρα δ' αἰὲν ἀναρπάξαντα ῥέεθρον
text.english: and a star, ever having caught the current,
text.note: astera (“a star”) is striking; many take it as a proleptic allusion to the ship Argo’s later stellar form (the constellation), poetically called a “star” as it “catches the current.” The phrase anarpaxanta rheeθron (“having snatched/caught the current”) suits a vessel taking the stream. Some editors emend aien (“ever”) to aipsa (“quickly”), which improves the sense but is not in the given text.

text.greek: οἴχεσθαι πόντοιο δι' Ἀξείνοιο φέροντα.
text.english: went off, carrying it through the sea of the Axeinos.
text.note: Axeinos is the archaic name of the Black Sea (later Euxeinos). Oichesthai pheronta is a Homeric idiom, “to go off carrying [it],” the object being the (Golden) Fleece from the preceding context.

text.greek: - Ταῦτα δ' ἐσαθρῆσας δολίου ἐξέσσυτο ὕπνου,
text.english: And having clearly discerned these things, he sprang out of guileful sleep,
text.note: ἐσαθρῆσας = “having seen clearly, distinctly.” δολίου ὕπνου (“guileful sleep”) points to deceptive dreams.

text.greek: ἀπροφανῆ, στυγερὸν δὲ περὶ φρένας εἵλκετο δεῖμα·
text.english: while it was not yet light, and he drew a loathsome dread about his wits;
text.note: ἀπροφανῆ is best taken as an adverbial accusative “before it was light/not yet manifest.” Some take it as “without divulging [the dream],” i.e., not making it known.

text.greek: ἆλτο δ' ἄρ' ἐξ εὐνῆς· δμωσὶ δὲ οἱ ὦκ' ἐπέτελλεν
text.english: he leapt from the couch, and straightway he bade the slaves

text.greek: ἵππους ἐντύνειν, ὑπὸ δὲ ζεύξασθαι ἀπήνην,
text.english: to gear the horses and to yoke the wagon beneath,
text.note: ἀπήνη is a wagon (not a war‑chariot). ὑπὸ ζεύξασθαι “to yoke beneath” refers to fastening under the yoke/pole.

text.greek: ὄφρα κε μειλίξαιτο κιὼν ἐπὶ ῥεῖθρον ἐραννόν
text.english: so that, going to the lovely stream, he might propitiate
text.note: μειλίξαιτο (aor. opt.) = “might appease/propitiate,” used of rites to placate deities/spirits; ὄφρα κε with optative marks purpose in narrative past.

text.greek: Φᾶσι δινήεντα, σὺν ἐνδαπίῃς μίγα νύμφαις,
text.english: eddy‑whirling Phasis, together with the native nymphs,
text.note: Φᾶσι δινήεντα is the object of μειλίξαιτο; μίγα is an adverb “mingled/together,” and ἐνδαπίαι “native, local,” hence “together with the local nymphs.”

text.greek: ψυχάς θ' Ἡρώων, ὅσσαι τ' ἐπὶ ῥεῖθρον ἄμειβον.
text.english: and the souls of Heroes, as many as were passing along the stream.
text.note: ψυχὰς Ἡρώων are also objects of propitiation; ὅσσαι τ’ ἐπὶ ῥεῖθρον ἄμειβον uses the imperfect for habitual action, “as many as were wont to pass along the stream,” reflecting an Orphic-ritual milieu.

text.greek: Θυγατέρας δ' ἔκλῃζε θυώδεος ἐκ θαλάμοιο,
text.english: And he summoned his daughters out from the incense-reeking chamber,
text.note: “ἔκλῃζε” here means “summoned/called forth”; “θυώδεος” modifies the inner chamber as “incense-scented/incense-reeking,” an epic epithet of sacred fragrance.

text.greek: Χαλκιόπην σὺν παισὶν ἀποφθιμένου Φρίξοιο,
text.english: Chalciope with the sons of Phrixus, now deceased,
text.note: “ἀποφθιμένου” is a genitive of the deceased; Chalciope is accompanied by the sons she had by Phrixus.

text.greek: ἠδ' ἁπαλὴν Μήδειαν ἀριπρεπὲς εἶδος ἔχουσαν
text.english: and tender Medea, bearing a most conspicuous beauty,
text.note: “ἁπαλή” conveys youthful softness; “ἀριπρεπὲς εἶδος ἔχουσαν” = “of strikingly manifest appearance,” i.e., conspicuous beauty.

text.greek: παρθένον αἰδοίην, ὄφρ' ἂν συνέποιτο κίοντι.
text.english: a modest maiden, that she might accompany him as he went.
text.note: “ὄφρ’ ἂν … συνέποιτο” is an epic purpose clause with optative; “κιόντι” (dative) means “to him as he went,” likely Aeetes, whom the maiden is to accompany.

text.greek: Ἄψυρτος δ' ἀπάνευθε δόμους ναίεσκε πόληος·
text.english: But Apsyrtos dwelt apart from the city’s houses.
text.note: ναίεσκε is an iterative/durative imperfect (“used to dwell”); ἀπάνευθε emphasizes separation (“apart, away from”).

text.greek: ἅρμα δ' ἐπὶ χρύσειον ἔβη μίγα θυγατέρεσσιν
text.english: and onto the golden chariot he stepped, together with his daughters,
text.note: μίγα = “together (with),” here governing the dative θυγατέρεσσιν; ἔβη ἐπὶ ἅρμα is the epic idiom “mounted the chariot.”

text.greek: Αἰήτης· τὸν δ' αἶψα δι' ἐκ πεδίου φέρον ἵπποι
text.english: Aiētes; and straightway the horses bore him out through the plain
text.note: δι’ ἐκ πεδίου is a marked combination of prepositions; rendered as “out through the plain” to convey the intensifying effect.

text.greek: χεῖλος ὑπὲρ ποταμοῦ δονακώδεος, ἔνθα περ αἰεί
text.english: over the reed-grown bank of the river,
text.note: χεῖλος = “lip, bank” of a river; δονακώδεος = “reed-grown” (from δόναξ, “reed”).

text.greek: εὐχωλὰς ῥείθροισι καὶ ἱερὰ κάλ' ἐκόμιζεν.
text.english: where indeed he was ever bringing vows to the streams and fair sacrifices.
text.note: εὐχωλάς is taken as “vows”/“votive offerings” (not “boasts”); ἐκόμιζεν is habitual (“was ever bringing”). The streams (ῥείθρα) receive cultic offerings.

text.greek: - Κείναισιν δ' ὄχθαισιν ὑπόδρομος ἤλυθεν Ἀργώ.
text.english: And to those banks the Argo came, gliding stealthily along.
text.note: ὑπόδρομος (lit. “running under”) is rare; here it is best taken adverbially of the ship’s motion, suggesting a low, covert glide (possibly ‘under the banks’ or ‘under oars’). The dative κείναισιν ὄχθαισιν functions as a Homeric/epic locative of goal: ‘to/at those banks.’

text.greek: Καί ῥα τότ' Αἰήτης εἰσέδρακεν, ἐν δ' ἄρα πολλούς,
text.english: And then Aietes gazed within, and therein were many
text.note: εἰσέδρακεν: epic aorist of εἰσδέρκομαι (“to look/gaze into”); ἐν δ’ ἄρα = “and therein, indeed.” The verb of perception is carried into the next line.

text.greek: ἑξείης ἥρωας ὁμιλαδὸν ἑδριόωντας,
text.english: heroes, in due order, sitting together in a throng,
text.note: ἑξείης = “in order, in a row”; ὁμιλαδόν = “in a throng, all together”; ἑδριόωντας (from ἑδριόω) = “sitting, seated.” Accusative participle depends on the implied ‘seeing.’

text.greek: ἀθανάτοις ἰκέλους· περὶ γάρ ῥά ἑ τεύχεα λάμπε.
text.english: like unto the Immortals; for all around them their gear was gleaming.
text.note: ἀθανατοῖς ἰκέλους = formulaic “like unto the Immortals.” ἑ = enclitic 3rd-person possessive “their.” τεύχεα = “arms, gear, armor”; neuter plural subject with singular verb λάμπε (epic usage).

text.greek: Τοῖσι δ' ἄρ' ἐν πάντεσσι μετέπρεπε δῖος Ἰήσων.
text.english: And among them all godlike Iason shone preeminent.
text.note: μετέπρεπε is a Homeric formula meaning ‘stood out among, was conspicuous’; δῖος is the conventional epic epithet ‘godlike.’

text.greek: Ἥρη γὰρ περὶ πάμπαν ἐτίετο, καί οἱ ἔδωκε
text.english: For Hēra held him in the utmost honor, and to him she gave

text.greek: κάλλος τε μέγεθός τε καὶ ἠνορέην ὑπέροπλον.
text.english: both beauty and stature and manly prowess beyond measure.
text.note: ὑπέροπλον (neut. sg.) is used adverbially; though elsewhere it can carry a pejorative sense (“overweening”), here it intensifies ἠνορέην (“manly prowess/valor”) and is best taken as “beyond measure,” not implying arrogance.

text.greek: Ἀλλ' ὅτε δὴ σχεδὸν ὄντες ἐπ' ἀλλήλοις βάλον ὄσσε,
text.english: But when, being close at hand, they cast their eyes upon one another,
text.note: βαλεῖν ὄσσε (“cast the eyes”) is a Homeric idiom for fixing one’s gaze; σχεδόν ὄντες = “at close quarters.”

text.greek: Αἰήτης Μινύαι τε, περὶ φρένα παχνώθησαν.
text.english: Aeëtes and the Minyai were frost-numbed about the heart.
text.note: παχνώθησαν (“were frosted/chilled”) metaphorically = “were benumbed with fear”; περὶ φρένα (“about the heart/mind,” seat of emotion). Μινύαι here denotes the Argonauts.

text.greek: Πρόσθε γὰρ Αἰήτης μὲν ἐφ' ἅρματος ἠέλιος ὣς
text.english: For at the front Aeëtes upon his chariot, like Helios,
text.note: Πρόσθε = “in front, at the head (of the procession)”; ἠέλιος ὣς = “like Helios,” apt since Aeëtes is Helios’ son.

text.greek: λάμπετο μαρμαρυγαῖσι πέριξ χρυσέων ἀπὸ πέπλων·
text.english: was shining with gleams all around from his golden robes;
text.note: μαρμαρυγαῖσι = “flashes, coruscations”; περίξ … ἀπό expresses radiance spreading “all around” from the garments.

text.greek: ἀμφὶ δέ οἱ στεφάνην κεφαλὴ ἔχε θυσσανόεσσαν
text.english: and around his head there was a tassel‑fringed crown
text.note: θυσσανόεσσαν = “tassel‑fringed”; στεφάνην is a “crown/wreath.” The construction κεφαλὴ ἔχε ≈ “his head bore/wore.”

text.greek: ἀκτῖσιν φλογέαις· σκῆπτρον δ' ἐν χερσὶν ἐνώμα
text.english: with flaming rays; and in his hands he was wielding a scepter,
text.note: ἀκτῖσιν φλογέαις = “with flaming rays,” evoking a radiate solar crown; ἐνώμα is imperf. of νωμάω, “he was wielding/brandishing.”

text.greek: ἀστεροπαῖς ἴκελον· δοιὼ δ' ἑκάτερθεν ἕηστον
text.english: like lightning‑flashes; and on either side his two daughters sat,
text.note: ἀστεροπαῖς likely = dat. pl. of ἀστεροπή (“lightning‑flash”) in epic form (for ἀστεροπαῖσι), “like lightning‑flashes.” ἕηστον is dual, emphasizing “the two” daughters seated on either side.

text.greek: θυγατέρες· ταῖς γάρ κεν ἀγαλλόμενος πεφόρητο.
text.english: for, exulting in them, he would be borne along.
text.note: πεφόρητο is pluperfect mid./pass. of φορέω (“be carried”), with iterative nuance: “he would be borne.” ἀγαλλόμενος with dat. (ταῖς) = “exulting in/over them.”

text.greek: Σμερδνὸν ὑπ' ὀφθαλμοῖσιν ἐσέδρακε νηῒ πελασθείς,
text.english: Dreadfully he glared from beneath his brows, having drawn near the ship,
text.note: “glared from beneath his brows”: ὑπ’ ὀφθαλμοῖσιν with (ἐ)δέρκεσθαι conveys the epic idiom of a dread glare from under the brows; ἐσέδρακε here is best taken from δέρκομαι (“glared”).

text.greek: καί οἱ ἀπὸ στηθέων βριαρὴν ἀνενείκατο φωνήν
text.english: and from his chest he lifted up a mighty voice,

text.greek: δεινὸν ὁμοκλήσας· μέγα δ' ἀντιάχων ἐγεγώνει·
text.english: terribly threatening; and, with great reverberation, he boomed:
text.note: ἀντιάχων (“reverberating, echoing back”) and ἐγεγώνει (“he boomed/pealed”) emphasize the resounding threat.

text.greek: - "Φράζετον οἵτινες ἐστὲ, τί δὲ χρέος ὗμας ἱκάνει,
text.english: “Declare who you are, and what need has come upon you,
text.note: Φράζετον is dual imperative (“you two, tell”), an epic convention likely addressing a pair of spokesmen or leaders.

text.greek: ἔκ ποθεν ἐλδομένοισι Κυτηΐδα γαῖαν ἀμεῖψαι,
text.english: from where you come, in your desire to cross the Cytaean land,
text.note: Κυτηΐδα γαῖαν (“Cytaean land”) refers to Colchis; Cytaea was a Colchian locality, whence Hekatē’s epithet “Cytaean.”

text.greek: οὐδ' ἄρ' ἐμὴν ἀλέγοντες ἀνακτορίην πεφόβησθε,
text.english: nor, it seems, have you feared my sovereignty, paying it no heed,
text.note: ἀλέγοντες = “taking heed, regarding”; the sense is that they have shown no fear precisely by not regarding his lordship.

text.greek: οὐδὲ λεὼν σκήπτροισιν ἐπήρανον ἡμετέροισι
text.english: nor the people beneath our scepters,
text.note: λεὼν … σκήπτροισιν ἐπήρανον ἡμετέροισι is difficult; I render the sense as “the people beneath our scepters,” i.e., under royal authority. The verb ἐπήρανον is obscure here (perhaps “established/confirmed”).

text.greek: Κόλχων, οἵ κεν Ἄρηϊ δορυσσόῳ εἰσὶν ἀτειρεῖς,
text.english: the Kolchians, who are unyielding in spear‑wielding Arēs,
text.note: δορυσσόος is an epic epithet, “spear‑wielding,” of Arēs (divine name transliterated).

text.greek: ἐς μόθον ἱεμένοις εὖ εἰδότες ἶφι μάχεσθαι."
text.english: eager for the fray, well knowing to fight by might.”
text.note: μόθος = “the fray, the din of battle”; ἶφι = “by might, by force.”

text.greek: Ὣς ἔφαθ'· οἱ δ' ἄρα πάντες ἀκὴν ἐγένοντο σιωπῇ.
text.english: So he spoke; and they all fell still in silence.

text.greek: Αἰσονίδῃ δ' ἄρα θάρσος ἐνὶ πραπίδεσσιν ὄπασσεν,
text.english: Then to Aisonides she put courage within his heart,
text.note: Aisonides = Jason; πραπίδεσσιν (‘in his midriff/wits’) is rendered idiomatically as “heart” in epic style.

text.greek: Ἥρη πρέσβα θεά· μέγα δ' ἀντιάχων ἐγεγώνει·
text.english: Hera, the venerable goddess; and, going to meet them, he spoke out in a great voice:
text.note: πρέσβα = “venerable/august,” not “ambassador.” ἀντιάχων (“going to meet”) is the epic participle of ἀντιάζω; ἐγεγώνει (from γεγωνέω) means “spoke out loud/clear-voiced.”

text.greek: - "Οὔτέ νυ ληϊστῆρες ἱκάνομεν, οὔτέ τιν' ἄλλην
text.english: “Neither now have we come as pirates, nor

text.greek: γαῖαν ἐπιστρωφῶντες, ἐγείρομεν ὕβριος αἴσῃ
text.english: as we range over some other land do we rouse, in wanton fashion,
text.note: ἐπιστρωφῶντες = “ranging (to and fro).” ὕβριος αἴσῃ is idiomatic: literally “by the portion/measure of outrage (hybris),” taken adverbially here as “in wanton fashion/in the spirit of outrage.”

text.greek: ἔργ' ἄδικ' ἀνθρώποισιν, ἃ δὴ πολέες μεμάασι
text.english: unjust deeds against men, which indeed many
text.note: μεμάασι + infinitive = “are eager to (do).” ἔργ’ ἄδικ’ ἀνθρώποισιν = “unjust deeds against men/people.”

text.greek: τετλάμεν ἐν βιοτῇ κέρδους ἕνεκεν σφετέροιο.
text.english: are eager to dare in life for the sake of their own profit.”
text.note: τετλάμεν is an epic infinitival form of τλᾶν/τλῆναι (“to dare/endure”); here “to dare.” σφετέροιο = “their own (private).”

text.greek: Ἀλλά μοι ἆθλον ἔταξε Ποσειδῶνος φίλος υἱός
text.english: But the beloved son of Poseidōn laid upon me a labor,
text.note: ἆθλον here is “labor/ordeal,” not “prize”; φίλος as an epithet = “beloved.”

text.greek: πατροκασίγνητος Πελίας, χρύσεον ποτὶ κῶας
text.english: Pelias, my father’s brother, after the golden fleece,
text.note: πατροκασίγνητος = “father’s brother” (paternal uncle). The compound can also mean “sharing the same father.” Traditions differ on Jason’s kinship with Pelias; the Orphic poet presents him as a paternal uncle. χρύσεον κῶας = “golden fleece.”

text.greek: λαζομένους ἀφικέσθαι ἐϋκτιμένην ἐς Ἰωλκόν.
text.english: to come to well-built Iolkos after seizing it.
