text.note: λαζομένους (from λάζομαι) = “seizing, taking hold of”; with ποτὶ (πρός) + acc indicating aim/purpose. κῶας is singular (“fleece”) despite the -ας ending. ἐϋκτιμένην is the epic epithet “well-built.”

text.greek: Οὐδέ τι δὴ νώνυμνοι ἐμοὶ ἐρίηρες ἑταῖροι·
text.english: Nor indeed are my trusty comrades at all nameless to me;
text.note: νώνυμνοι = “nameless,” i.e., not obscure or of unknown name; ἐρίηρες is a Homeric epithet meaning “trusty/faithful.”

text.greek: οἳ μὲν γὰρ μακάρων, οἳ δ' ἡρώων γένος ἐσμέν.
text.english: for some are of the stock of the Blessed Ones, and some are of the race of heroes.
text.note: μακάρων = “the Blessed [Ones],” a periphrasis for the gods; γένος ἐσμέν = “we are of the stock/race.” The partition οἳ μέν … οἳ δέ divides the company into those of divine parentage and those of heroic lineage.

text.greek: Οὐδέ τι μὴν πολέμου ἀδαήμονες οὐδὲ μόθοιο,
text.english: Nor, indeed, are we unacquainted with war or with the tumult of battle,
text.note: μῶθος (here μόθοιο) is the Homeric ‘din’ or ‘melee’ of battle; I render “tumult of battle.”

text.greek: ξεῖνοι δ' εὐχόμεθ' εἶναι ἐφέστιοι, ὣς γὰρ ἄμεινον."
text.english: but we profess to be hearth‑guests; for thus is it better.”
text.note: ἐφέστιοι “at the hearth” evokes the status of protected guests/suppliants under xenia and the sanctity of Hestia’s hearth.

text.greek: - Ὣς φάτο· τοῦ δ' ἄρα θυμὸς ὀρίνετο ἶσος ἀέλλῃ
text.english: So he spoke; and the spirit of Aietes was stirred like a whirlwind,
text.note: ἀέλλη “whirlwind, squall” underlies the simile of sudden, violent agitation.

text.greek: Αἰήτεω, καὶ σμερδνὸν ἐσέδρακεν ὀφθαλμοῖσιν,
text.english: and he glared dreadly with his eyes,
text.note: ἐσέδρακεν is an intensive aorist “he gazed/stared upon”; σμερδνόν “dreadly, terribly.”

text.greek: φρικτὸν ἐφ' ἡρώεσσι δόλον καὶ μῆτιν ὑφαίνων·
text.english: weaving a shudderous stratagem and counsel against the heroes;
text.note: Formulaic “weaving” (ὑφαίνων) of δόλος and μῆτις expresses plotting against the heroes.

text.greek: ὀψὲ δὲ δὴ Μινύαισι τοίην ἀνενείκατο φωνήν·
text.english: and at length to the Minyae he uttered this voice:
text.note: ὀψὲ δὴ marks delayed response; ἀνενείκατο φωνήν is epic “lifted up/uttered a voice.”

text.greek: - "Εἰ μὲν δὴ Κόλχοισιν ἀρηιφάτοισιν ἐσάντα
text.english: “If indeed ye would, face to face, set upon the war‑famed Colchians
text.note: ἐς ἄντα (“face to face, against”) is the likely reading for ἐσάντα; ἀρηίφατοι = “renowned in war.” Note also ἐπιθεῖσθον: a dual form in -σθον used here for the plural addressees (epic/archaizing usage).

text.greek: μαρναμένοις ἐπιθεῖσθον, ἀποφθίσειν μένος ἀνδρῶν
text.english: as they fight, and deem to bring to naught the might of men,
text.note: ἀποφθίσσειν μένος ἀνδρῶν = “to bring to naught the battle-might of men,” an idiomatic Homeric collocation.

text.greek: ἔλπεσθ' ὥς κεν ἀδήριτον γέρας ἔσσετ' ἐν ὑμῖν,
text.english: hoping that the prize will be yours without a fight,
text.note: ἀδήριτον γέρας “an unfought/uncontested prize.”

text.greek: κῶας ἀειρομένους ἰέναι πρὸς πατρίδα γαῖαν;
text.english: and to go bearing the fleece to your fatherland;
text.note: ἀείρω “to lift/bear”; the participle marks the fleece borne as a trophy en route home.

text.greek: εἰ δέ γε παῦροι ἐόντες ὑποκλίνοιτε φάλαγγι
text.english: but if, being few, ye would bow beneath our phalanx,
text.note: παῦροι ἐόντες “being few, understrength”; φάλαγξ “phalanx/battle‑line.”

text.greek: ἡμετέρῃ, τότε νῆα καταφθιμένοισι κεάξαι·
text.english: then shall we splinter your ship over you when ye are undone;
text.note: κεάξαι (“to split, shiver”) with νῆα: syntax is elliptical; I render the sense as a direct threat (“we shall splinter …”).

text.greek: εἰ δέ κέ μοι πείθοισθε, τὸ καὶ πολὺ κέρδιόν ἐστιν,
text.english: but if ye would hearken to me—and that were far more profitable—
text.note: κέρδιον “more profitable/advantageous,” with modal κέ marking potentiality.

text.greek: κρίναντες τιν' ἄριστον, ἢ ὃς βασιλεύτερός ἐστιν,
text.english: choosing someone who is best, or who is of more kingly rank,
text.note: βασιλεύτερος “more kingly,” i.e., of higher royal standing or more fit to rule; contrasted with ἄριστος in merit.

text.greek: ὄφρά κε πειρηθεὶς ἀέθλων οὓς αὐτὸς ἐνίσπω,
text.english: so that, when he has been tried by the trials which I myself proclaim,
text.note: ἀέθλοι here are set “ordeals/tasks”; ἐνίσπω “I declare/prescribe.”

text.greek: κῶας ἕλῃ χρύσειον, ὃ καὶ γέρας ἔσσεται ὑμῖν."
text.english: he may seize the Golden Fleece, which shall also be your prize.”
text.note: γέρας “prize/guerdon” for the whole company, though won by one champion.

text.greek: - Ὣς εἰπὼν ἵπποισιν ἐκέκλετο· τοὶ δ' ἄρ' ὀπίσσω
text.english: So speaking he called to his horses; and they, turning back,
text.note: ἵπποισιν ἐκέκλετο shows Aietes in his chariot; ἀμειβόμενοι “wheeling, changing direction.”

text.greek: βῆσαν ἀμειβόμενοι, Μινύαις δ' ἄχος ἔπλετο θυμῷ,
text.english: went, wheeling; and grief came upon the Minyae in their heart,
text.note: θυμῷ “in spirit/heart” is the inner seat of emotion; ἄχος “grief.”

text.greek: καί ῥα τόθ' Ἡρακλῆος ἔχον πόθον, οὐ γὰρ ἔμιμνον
text.english: and then they felt longing for Herakles; for they did not await
text.note: πόθος “longing/yearning”; μένω with accusative (ἔμιμνον ἔθνος) = “to await/withstand (an enemy).”

text.greek: ἔθνος ἀμαιμάκετον Κόλχων καὶ θούριον Ἄρην.
text.english: the invincible host of the Colchians and impetuous Ares.
text.note: ἀμαιμάκετον “unconquerable, irresistible”; θούριος Ἄρης is the fixed epithet “impetuous/battle‑fierce Ares.”

text.greek: - Νῦν δέ σοι, ὦ Μουσαῖε, παραδρομάδην ἀγορεύσω
text.english: But now, O Musaeus, I shall speak to you in passing.
text.note: παραδρομάδην literally “in running-past fashion,” i.e., “cursorily, in passing.” The vocative Μουσαῖε marks a direct address to Musaeus; δέ signals a transition (“but now”).

text.greek: οἷά περ αἰνόμοροι Μινύαι πάθον, ἠδ' ὅσ' ἔρεξαν·
text.english: such as the grim‑fated Minyae endured, and all that they wrought;
text.note: ainomoroi (grim‑fated): an epic epithet meaning dread‑doomed; “Minyae” is a traditional designation for the Argonauts.

text.greek: ὥς τ' ἄψορρος ὄρουσ' ἐκ δώματος Αἰήταο
text.english: how they sprang back again from the palace of Aietes,
text.note: apsorros: adverb “back, back again”; dōma rendered as “palace” in epic register; Aietes (Aietes) is the Colchian king.

text.greek: Ἄργος ἐϋμμελίης Φρίξου παῖς ὅν ῥα ἔτικτε
text.english: Argos, good‑at‑the‑ashen‑spear, the son of Phrixus, whom she indeed bore—
text.note: eummelies: literally “of the good ashen spear,” a conventional martial epithet; ὅν ῥα ἔτικτε (“whom she indeed bore”) has an implied subject from context, namely Chalciope, daughter of Aietes, mother of Phrixus’ sons.

text.greek: Χαλκιόπη (τῷ γὰρ παρελέξατο πατρὸς ἐνιπῇ
text.english: Chalciopē (for at her father’s rebuke she took him to her bed
text.note: παρελέξατο (middle) is the epic idiom for sexual union/being wed; τῷ (“to him”) refers to Phrixus. πατρὸς ἐνιπῇ literally “at her father’s rebuke,” here effectively “at her father’s behest/command.” The whole clause is parenthetical.

text.greek: ἡνίχ' ὑπὲρ νώτῳ κριοῦ Κόλχοισι πελάσθη)
text.english: when he came near to the Colchians upon a ram’s back),
text.note: ὑπὲρ νώτῳ κριοῦ = “on a ram’s back,” alluding to Phrixus’ arrival in Kolchis on the Golden Ram; πελάσθη is the aorist “came near/approached.”

text.greek: ἀγγέλλων Μινύαισιν, ἃ δὴ τελέεσθαι ἔμελλε
text.english: announcing to the Minyae the things that indeed were destined to be accomplished.
text.note: ἀγγέλλων is a nominative masc. participle, its subject understood as Phrixus from the parenthetical; Μινύαισι(ν) = the Minyae, i.e., the Argonauts. ἃ δὴ τελέεσθαι ἔμελλε expresses destined futurity (“what was fated to be fulfilled”).

text.greek: σφῇσιν ἀτασθαλίησι πολυφθόρου Αἰήταο·
text.english: by the reckless follies of ruin-bringing Aeëtes;
text.note: σφῇσιν ἀτασθαλίησι is a Homeric turn (“by his own reckless follies”); πολυφθόρος (“ruin-bringing,” “much-destroying”) is an epithet applied here to Aeëtes.

text.greek: ἠδ' ὡς παρθενίοις αὐτοῦ φίλτροις ἐδαμάσθη
text.english: and how by maidenly love-charms for him she was subdued,
text.note: φίλτρα are “love-charms” or “love-spells”; παρθενίοις (“maidenly”) stresses Medea’s virgin state. αὐτοῦ (“of him”) is an objective genitive referring to Jason. ἐδαμάσθη (“was tamed/subdued”) is conventional of being overcome by love.

text.greek: αἰνόγαμος Μήδεια, θεᾶς Ἥρης διὰ βουλάς,
text.english: dread-wedded Medea, through the counsels of the goddess Hērē,
text.note: αἰνόγαμος (“dread-wedded”) is a proleptic epithet of Medea, foreshadowing her baleful marriage; θεᾶς Ἥρης (“of the goddess Hērē”) underscores divine causation.

text.greek: ἐν γάρ οἱ ἵμερον ὦρσεν ἐρωτοτρόφος Κυθέρεια,
text.english: For within her Cythereia, nurse of love, stirred desire,
text.note: "en gar hoi": the enclitic dative hoi marks the person affected (“in her”); the referent in context is likely Medea. "Eroto‑trophos" is an epithet of Cythereia (Aphrodite), “nurse/rearer of love.”

text.greek: ἧκε δ' ἄρ' ἰὸν ὑπὸ σπλάγχνοις δασπλῆτις Ἐριννύς·
text.english: and the fierce‑smiter Erinys sent a dart beneath her entrails;
text.note: Dasplêtis (δασπλῆτις) is a rare epithet, probably from plêssô (“smite”): “harsh-/fierce‑smiter.” The phrase “sent a dart beneath the vitals” (hupo splanchnois) uses ios (“arrow/poison”) for love’s wound. Erinys is left as theonym per instruction.

text.greek: ὥς τε βόας ζεύγλαισι δαμάσσατο πυριπνέοντας
text.english: as when with yoke‑bands one subdues the fire‑breathing bulls.
text.note: Zeuglai are the yoke‑straps/harness. The simile (hôs te) leaves the apodosis implicit: desire binds her as if yoking even the fire‑breathing bulls, an allusion to Aeêtes’ team overcome in the Argonautic saga.

text.greek: τετράγυον θέμενος σπόρον αὔλακι, τόν ῥ' ἐκόμισσε
text.english: Having set the seed for four acres in the furrow, which he brought,
text.note: τετράγυον: literally “of four gyai,” a land‑measure (≈ ‘acres’); hence “seed for four acres.” αὔλαξ is the plough‑furrow. τόν ρ’ ἐκόμισσε is enjambed; the subject is supplied in the next line.

text.greek: Φρίξος ἐϋμμελίης, ὅτ' ἔβη δόμον Αἰήταο,
text.english: Phrixus, ashen‑speared, when he went to the house of Aeëtes,
text.note: ἐϋμμελίης: “ashen‑speared,” a martial epithet (lit. ‘with good ash‑spear’). Applied unexpectedly to Phrixus; some have suspected an emendation to εὐμήλης (“rich in flocks”), which would suit Phrixus’ pastoral associations, but the transmitted reading can stand as a poetic epithet.

text.greek: ἕδνον ἐνυάλιόν τε δρακοντείων ἀπ' ὀδόντων·
text.english: a bride‑gift of Enyalios too, from the dragon’s teeth.
text.note: ἕδνον: ‘bride‑gift.’ ἐνυάλιόν: ‘of Enyalios’ (Enyalios = Ares), i.e., warlike; the teeth are those of the dragon sacred to Ares. The poet presents the dragon’s teeth as the bridal gift Phrixus brought to Aeëtes upon marrying his daughter.

text.greek: ἠδ' ὡς δυσμενέων σπαρτῶν στάχυν ἐξενάριξεν
text.english: and how he despoiled the harvest of the hostile Sown-men,
text.note: σπαρτῶν = the “Sown-men” (Spartoi) sprung from the dragon’s teeth; στάχυν (“ear of grain”) casts them as a crop; ἐξενάριξεν is the martial “strip/despoil (the slain),” hence “slaughter/despoil the harvest.”

text.greek: αὐτοφόνῳ παλάμῃ, πῶς δ' ἀγλαὸν ᾔρατο κῦδος
text.english: with his murderous hand, and how Aisonides won bright glory,
text.note: αὐτοφόνῳ παλάμῃ literally “with a self-slaughtering hand”: either “murderous hand” of Jason or alluding to the Spartoi’s mutual slaughter prompted by his stratagem; ᾔρατο (mid.) = “took up/won.”

text.greek: Αἰσονίδης· ὥς δ' ἦλθε δι' ἐκ μεγάρων λελαθοῦσα
text.english: and how she came forth unseen out through the halls,
text.note: The subject of ἦλθε…λελαθοῦσα is Medea; δι’ ἐκ is epic pleonasm (“through, out of”); λελαθοῦσα = “unseen, having escaped notice.”

text.greek: λῖτι καλυψαμένη ἑανῷ, διὰ νύκτερον ὄρφνην,
text.english: veiling herself in a linen robe, through the nocturnal gloom,
text.note: λῖτι ἑανῷ: λῖτι is an epic dative-locative of λῖτον (“linen”), used adverbially; ἑανός denotes a fine garment or robe. νύκτερον ὄρφνην = “nightly darkness/gloom.”

text.greek: παρθένος αἰνολεχής· περὶ γάρ ῥά ἑ τεῖρον ἔρωτες
text.english: a grim-voiced maiden; for on every side loves were wearing her down,
text.note: αἰνολεχής is a rare compound, likely “dread-/grim-voiced” (cf. epic use of αἰνός + speech), fitting Medea’s incantatory character; alternative derivations from λέχος (“bed”) are less apt here. ἔρωτες (plural) may denote either multiple passions or personified Erotes; τεῖρον (from τείρω) “wear down, distress”; περὶ ἑ suggests “on every side, all around her.”

text.greek: νηὸς ἐπ' Ἄργῴας πελάσαι, καὶ πότνι' Ἀνάγκη
text.english: to draw near to the ship Argo, and Lady Ananke—
text.note: νηὸς ἐπ᾽ Ἄργῴας is best taken as “to the ship Argo” (genitival/adjectival formation for the named ship). πελᾶσαι is the aorist infinitive of πελάζω, expressing the impulse/aim (“to approach”). πότνι᾽ Ἀνάγκη = “Lady Ananke,” the personification of Necessity; the syntax anticipates a verb of compulsion in the following line.

text.greek: οὔτιν' ὀπιζομένη, πατρὸς χόλον οὐκ ἀλέγουσα·
text.english: dreading no one, not caring for her father’s wrath;
text.note: ὀπίζομαι = “to fear, have regard for”; οὔ τινα = “no one.” ἀλεγέω + gen. = “to care for.” “Her father” is supplied from context (Aeëtes).

text.greek: ἠδ' ὡς ἀμφιπλακεῖσα περιπτύξασά τε μορφάς,
text.english: and when, having twined about him and clasped his form,
text.note: ἀμφιπλακεῖσα and περιπτύξασα are aorist participles denoting close embrace; μορφάς (pl.) is a poetic plural for “form/body.” ὡς here is temporal (“when/as”).

text.greek: στέρνα τε μαιμώωσα κύσεν χαρίεν τε πρόσωπον,
text.english: and, with heaving breasts, she kissed his lovely face,
text.note: στέρνα is an accusative of respect with the intransitive μαιμώωσα (“panting as to the breast”), rendered idiomatically as “with heaving breasts.” χαρίεν = “lovely, graceful.” κύσεν = “kissed.”

text.greek: δάκρυσι πλημμύρουσα γενειάδας· οὐδέ τιν' αἰδῶ
text.english: She flooded her cheeks with tears; nor did any sense of shame
text.note: γενειάδες, literally “beards/chins,” in epic can denote the cheeks, especially of women; αἰδώς here is “modesty, sense of shame,” the understood object of ἔσχε being her impulse.

text.greek: ἔσχε πόθων ἥρωος, ἐλαυνομένη δ' ὑπὸ φίλτρων,
text.english: restrain her yearning for the hero, but, driven by love‑charms,
text.note: πόθων ἥρωος is an objective genitive, “yearning for the hero (Jason).” φίλτρα may mean love‑spells or love‑potions; the phrase conveys compulsion by erotic magic/charms.

text.greek: παρθενίην ἔρριψε, γάμων τ' εὐήνορα θυμόν,
text.english: she cast off her maidenhood and set her heart upon wedlock,
text.note: παρθενίην ἔρριψε is an idiom, “she cast off maidenhood.” εὐήνορα (from εὐήνωρ, “well‑disposed toward a man/men”) with γάμων (objective gen.) yields “a heart well‑inclined to marriage.” The construction effectively means “she cast off maidenhood and set her heart on marriage,” rather than literally throwing away a marriage‑friendly heart.

text.greek: ἄλλα τ' αὖ πολλὰ καὶ ἐσύστερον αὖθις ἀκούσῃ,
text.english: and many other things again you shall hear later on,
text.note: ἐσύστερον = ἐς ὕστερον (“later on”); ἀκούσῃ (2nd sg aor. subj.) functions with future sense in the narrator’s address (“you shall hear”).

text.greek: - Ἀλλ' ὅτε δὴ Μήδεια λίπεν δόμον Αἰήταο
text.english: But when indeed Medea left the house of Aeëtes,
text.note: Αἰήταο is the Homeric genitive of Aiëtēs; the leading dash is editorial, marking transition.

text.greek: λαθριδίῃ καὶ νηὸς ἐφ' ἡμετέρης ἐπελάσθη,
text.english: in secret, and drew near to our ship,
text.note: λαθριδίῃ is a dative of manner (“in secret, stealthily”); νηὸς (gen. sg. of epic νηῦς, “ship”) with ἐπὶ + gen. expresses motion “toward/onto”; ἐπελάσθη is aorist middle of (ἐπ)πελάζω, “came/drew near.”

text.greek: δὴ τότ' ἄρα κατὰ θυμὸν ἐμηδόμεθ', ὄφρα μολόντες
text.english: Then indeed we took counsel in our hearts, so that, when we had come,
text.note: δὴ τότ' ἄρα intensifies the narrative; ἐμηδόμεθ' is the imperfect middle of μήδομαι, “devise, take counsel.” ὄφρα introduces purpose; μολόντες is the aorist participle of βλώσκω, “come.”

text.greek: ἀμφ' ἱερῆς φηγοῖο δέρας χρύσειον ἕλωμεν
text.english: we might seize the Golden Fleece from about the sacred oak,
text.note: ἱερῆς φηγοῖο is the epic genitive of φηγός, “oak.” In the Argonautic tradition the Fleece hangs on a sacred oak (elsewhere specified as Ares’). ἕλωμεν (subjunctive of αἱρέω) marks purpose, “that we might seize.”

text.greek: ῥᾷστα· περὶ φρεσὶ δ' ᾗσι δοκεύομεν, οὐδέ τις ἡμέων
text.english: most easily; and in our minds we kept watch, nor did any one of us—
text.note: ῥᾷστα is the superlative adverb “most easily,” qualifying ἕλωμεν. περὶ φρεσὶ … δοκεύομεν literally “we were keeping watch with/over our minds,” transferring the usual physical vigilance of δοκεύω to mental alertness. οὐδέ τις ἡμέων is enjambed; its governing verb follows in the next line.

text.greek: ἔγνω μόχθον ἄελπτον· ἐφέσπετο γὰρ μέγα ἔργον
text.english: He recognized an unforeseen toil; for a great enterprise was pressing on
text.note: ἐφέσπετο (often printed ἐπέσπετο) means “was following upon/pressing on.” The subject is singular (“he recognized”), contextually the leader, but the task bears upon all the heroes in the next line.

text.greek: πᾶσιν ἐφ' ἡρώεσσι, κακῶν δ' ἀνεφαίνετο πυθμήν·
text.english: upon all the heroes, and the very foundation of evils was being revealed.
text.note: πυθμήν literally “bottom/foundation,” here “root/source” of evils; ἀνεφαίνετο (imperfect) conveys a process of becoming manifest.

text.greek: Πρόσθε γὰρ Αἰήταο δόμων ποταμοῖό τ' ἐρυμνοῦ,
text.english: For before the halls of Aiētēs and the mighty river,
text.note: πρόσθε with the genitive = “before, in front of.” ποταμοῖο ἐρυμνοῦ (“the mighty/strong river”) likely alludes to the Phasis; ἐρυμνός is an epic epithet more usual of walls/cities, here transferred to a river. The sentence continues beyond this line.

text.greek: ἐννέ' ἐπ' ὀργυιῶν ἕρκος περιμήκετον ἄντην
text.english: In front a very long rampart, nine fathoms in measure,
text.note: ὀργυιά = a “fathom” (arm‑span); the phrase indicates the wall’s measure (likely height). ἄντην means “in front, opposite.” Περιμήκετον = “very long/lofty,” here of a fortification.

text.greek: φρουρεῖται πύργοισι καὶ εὐξέστοισι μύδροισιν,
text.english: is guarded by towers and by well-wrought ironwork,
text.note: μύδροις (lit. “red‑hot lumps/iron masses”) here probably denotes iron clamps or ironwork binding/finishing the masonry; εὐξέστοις = “well-wrought, well-smoothed.” Some take the word broadly as “well-dressed blocks,” but an iron sense suits the term.

text.greek: ἑπτὰ περὶ στεφάνοισι κυκλούμενον· ἐν δ' ἄρα τρισσαί
text.english: ringed about with seven crowns; and within there are three—
text.note: στεφάνοισι (“crowns”) in an architectural/urban sense = “rings/circuits” of walls; hence “seven rings.” The clause ἐν δ’ ἄρα τρισσαί is incomplete here; the following verse supplies the noun (e.g., ‘gates’ or another structural element).

text.greek: χαλκήρεις πύλαι εἰσὶ πελώριοι· ἐν δ' ἄρα ταῖσι
text.english: Brazen gates there are, colossal; and upon them
text.note: χαλκήρεις = “brazen, bronze-fitted”; πελώριοι = “monstrous, colossal.” The phrase ἐν δ’ ἄρα ταῖσι here has locative force, “upon them,” anticipating the next line.

text.greek: τεῖχος ἐπιθρώσκει, περὶ δ' αὖ χρύσειαι ἐπάλξεις.
text.english: a wall towers up, and all around are golden battlements.
text.note: ἐπιθρώσκει (from ἐπιθρῴσκω) literally “leaps up,” here “towers up” of a wall. ἐπάλξεις = “battlements, parapets”; περὶ δ’ αὖ = “and round about, in turn.”

text.greek: Αὐτὰρ ἐπὶ σταθμοῖο πυλῶν τηλῶπις ἄνασσα
text.english: But at the steading’s gates the far-seen queen
text.note: σταθμός here means “homestead/steading; court,” and πύλων “gates”; τηλῶπις (“far‑seen”) suits a torch‑bearing threshold goddess (Hekate conflated with Artemis).

text.greek: ἵστανεν αἰθύουσα πυρὸς σέλας, ἥν κέ νυ Κόλχοι
text.english: took her stand, flashing the blaze of fire, whom the Colchians
text.note: αἰθύουσα is “darting/flashing,” of the fire’s blaze; ἵστανεν = “she took her stand.” The scene evokes a torch‑epiphany at the gate.

text.greek: Ἄρτεμιν ἐμπυλίην κελαδοδρόμον ἱλάσκονται,
text.english: propitiate as Artemis Empylia, loud‑rushing,
text.note: ἐμπυλίη (“at‑the‑gate”) is a cult epithet; κελαδοδρόμος = “loud‑rushing,” perhaps of the goddess’s noisy nocturnal progress and hounds. The Colchians propitiate her under Artemis’s name (syncretism with Hekate).

text.greek: δεινήν τ' ἀνθρώποισιν ἰδεῖν δεινήν τ' ἐσακοῦσαι,
text.english: dread for mortals to behold and dread to hear,
text.note: Formulaic doubling “dread to see and hear” underscores the awe of the epiphany.

text.greek: εἰ μή τις τελεταῖς πελάσει καὶ θύσθλα καθαρμῶν,
text.english: unless one draw near with initiatory rites and the thystla of purifications,
text.note: τελεταί = “initiatory rites”; θύσθλα (thystla) are Bacchic ritual implements; καθαρμῶν “of purifications.”

text.greek: ὅσσα περ ἀρήτειρα καθάρματα μύστις ἔκευθε,
text.english: as many bane‑averting purifications as the initiate kept concealed,
text.note: ἀρήτειρα modifies καθάρματα: “bane‑averting purifications.” μύστις = “female initiate” (here Medea); ἔκευθε “kept hidden,” stressing mystery secrecy.

text.greek: δεινολεχὴς Μήδεια Κυτηιάσιν μίγα κούραις.
text.english: Medea of dread speech, having mingled with the Cytaean maidens.
text.note: δεινολεχής = “terrible in speech,” hinting at potent incantations; Κυτηιάσιν “of Cytaea,” a Colchian locale linked with Hekate/Medea; μίγα = “mingled/joined with,” i.e., among the local maidens.

text.greek: Οὐδέ τις ἐνδοτέρω κείνην ὁδὸν εἰσεπέρησεν
text.english: Nor did any man pass farther within along that way,
text.note: εἰσεπέρησεν (aorist of εἰσ‑περάω) = “to pass through into”; ἐνδοτέρω = “further inward.”

text.greek: ἐνδάπιος, ξεῖνός τε βροτῶν ὑπὲρ οὐδὸν ἀμείψας·
text.english: whether a man of the household or a stranger after crossing the threshold of mortals;
text.note: ἐνδάπιος = “of the household, native”; contrasted with ξεῖνος (“stranger/guest”). The idiom ὑπὲρ οὐδὸν ἀμείψας = “having crossed over the threshold.” βροτῶν is a generic “of mortals.” The participle modifies τις implicitly (“no one … whether native or stranger, who has crossed…”).

text.greek: εἴργει γὰρ πάντη δεινὴ θεὸς ἡγεμόνεια,
text.english: for a dread goddess, Hegemonia, bars it on every side,
text.note: ἡγεμόνεια is taken as a personified goddess (“Hegemonia”); some understand it as an epithet or aspect of Hekate as guide/leader. εἴργει = “keeps off, bars.”

text.greek: λύσσαν ἐπιπνείουσα πυριγλήνοις σκυλάκεσσιν.
text.english: breathing madness upon fire‑eyed whelps.
text.note: πυριγλήνοις from πῦρ + γλήνη (“pupil of the eye”) = “fiery‑eyed.” σκυλάκες = “whelps, hounds.” ἐπιπνείουσα = “breathing upon, inspiring,” hence “breathing madness.”

text.greek: Ἐν δέ σφιν πυμάτῳ μυχῷ ἕρκεος ἄλσος ἀμείβει,
text.english: And there, in the furthest inner recess of the enclosure, a grove stretches,
text.note: ἕρκος = an enclosing wall or fence; ἀμείβει here ‘extends, runs along’.

text.greek: δένδρεσιν εὐθαλέεσσι κατάσκιον, ᾧ ἔνι πολλαί
text.english: shaded with luxuriant trees, wherein are many
text.note: No special difficulty.

text.greek: δάφναι τ' ἠδὲ κράνειαι ἰδ' εὐμήκεις πλατάνιστοι·
text.english: laurels and cornels and tall plane-trees;
text.note: κράνεια = cornel(-cherry); πλατάνιστος = plane-tree; εὐμήκεις ‘tall/long-limbed’.

text.greek: ἐν δὲ πόαι ῥίζῃσι κατηρεφέες χθαμαλῇσιν,
text.english: and there the grasses, overhung with shade down at their lowly roots,
text.note: κατηρεφές ‘overhung, overshadowed’; χθαμαλαῖ ῥίζαι ‘low-lying roots’.

text.greek: ἀσφόδελος, κλύμενός τε καὶ εὐειδὴς ἀδίαντος,
text.english: asphodel, and the renowned and fair Adiantum,
text.note: ἀδίαντος = maidenhair fern; κλούμενος/κλύμενος ‘renowned’, εὐειδής ‘fair to see’.

text.greek: καὶ θρύον ἠδὲ κύπειρον, ἀριστερεών τ' ἀμενηνά,
text.english: and rush and galingale, and the feeble aristereon,
text.note: θρύον is likely ‘rush’; κύπειρον is cyperus/galingale. ἀριστερεών is an obscure plant-name; ἀμενηνά ‘sapless/feeble’ (sense uncertain).

text.greek: ὅρμινόν τε καὶ εἰρύσιμον κύκλαμίς τε θεουδής,
text.english: horminon and erusimon, and the god-fearing cyclamen,
text.note: ὅρμινον (horminon) is probably clary/sage; εἰρύσιμον (erusimon) = hedge-mustard/rocket (Erysimum). θεουδής ‘god-fearing’ is a rare, reverential epithet applied to the plant.

text.greek: στοιχὰς, παιονίη τε πολύκνημόν τε κάτερνες·
text.english: stoechas, and peony, and polyknemon, and katernes;
text.note: στοιχάς = stoechas (a type of lavender); πολύκνημον and κάτερνες are obscure ancient plant-names of uncertain identification.

text.greek: μανδραγόρης, πόλιόν τ', ἐπὶ δὲ ψαφαρὸν δίκταμνον
text.english: mandrake, and pennyroyal, and moreover the dappled dittany,
text.note: πόλιον = pennyroyal (Mentha pulegium); ψαφαρός ‘dappled, grey-mottled’; δίκταμνον = Cretan dittany.

text.greek: εὔοδμός τε κρόκος, ἰδὲ κάρδαμον· ἐν δ' ἄρα κῆμος,
text.english: and fragrant crocus, and cress; and there too kēmos,
text.note: κρόκος = saffron; κάρδαμον in classical Greek is ‘cress’ (not cardamom). κῆμος is an obscure plant-name.

text.greek: σμίλαξ, ἠδὲ χαμαίμηλον, μήκων τε μέλαινα,
text.english: smilax, and chamomile, and the black poppy,
text.note: σμίλαξ is a climbing plant (smilax/sarsaparilla-type); χαμαίμηλον = chamomile; μέλαινα applied to poppy denotes a dark/black variety.

text.greek: ἄλκυα καὶ πάνακες, καὶ κάρπασον, ἠδ' ἀκόνιτον,
text.english: alkya and all-heal, and karpasos, and aconite,
text.note: ἄλκυα is uncertain; some take a related form to be ἄλθεα (marsh-mallow). πανάκες = ‘all-heal’ (a name for various medicinals). κάρπασος may be safflower or cotton (the term is ambiguous). ἀκόνιτον = aconite/wolfsbane.

text.greek: ἀλλά τε δηλήεντα κατὰ χθόνα πολλὰ πεφύκει.
text.english: and many other baneful growths have sprung up over the earth.
text.note: δηλήεντα ‘baneful, hurtful’ underscores the toxic/medicinal character of many listed herbs.

text.greek: Μέσσον δ' ἠερόμηκες ἐπὶ στύπος ἄλσεϊ πολλῷ
text.english: And in the midst, sky‑reaching, a trunk in the thick grove,
text.note: ἠερόμηκες = “sky-/air-reaching,” an epic compound. στύπος = “trunk, stump.” The finite verb follows in the next line (ἥπλωται).

text.greek: ἥπλωται φηγοῖο πέριξ κλαδεῶσιν ἐρυμνόν,
text.english: is spread out, stout all around with the boughs of a phegos‑oak;
text.note: φηγός (phegos) can denote “oak” (epic usage; sometimes rendered “beech”); “oak” is adopted here. ἥπλωται = “has been spread out.” ἐρυμνόν = “stout, strong, well-fortified,” used metaphorically of the dense branching.

text.greek: ἐν δ' ἄρα οἱ χρύσειον ἐπεκρέματ' ἔνθα καὶ ἔνθα
text.english: and upon it the Golden Fleece hung down, on this side and that,
text.note: ἐν δ’ ἄρα οἱ = “and upon it” (enclitic dative). ἔνθα καὶ ἔνθα = “on this side and that.” χρύσειον δέρας = the Golden Fleece.

text.greek: ὅρπηκος ταναοῖο δέρας, τό κεν αἶψα δοκεύει
text.english: from a tall sapling, which a dread serpent straightway keeps watch over,
text.note: ὅρπηξ = “sapling, young shoot” (also a supporting pole); hence “from a tall sapling.” δοκεύει = “keeps watch, lies in wait.” αἶψα intensifies the immediacy (“straightway, ever alert”).

text.greek: δεινὸς ὄφις, θνητοῖς ὀλοὸν τέρας, οὐ φατὸν εἰπεῖν.
text.english: a baleful portent to mortals, not to be spoken of in speech.
text.note: τέρας = “portent, prodigy.” οὐ φατὸν εἰπεῖν = formulaic “unspeakable to tell,” stressing ineffability. θνητοῖς is dative of reference (“to mortals”).

text.greek: Χρυσαῖς γὰρ φολίδεσσιν ἐθείρεται, ἐν δ' ἄρα πρέμνον
text.english: For he bristles with golden scales, and there at the trunk
text.note: ἐθείρεται (from ἔθειρα, “mane”) is used metaphorically: “bristles” or “is fringed.” χρυσαῖς φολίδεσσιν = “with golden scales,” of the dragon guarding the Fleece.

text.greek: ἀπλάτοις ὁλκοῖσι φορεύμενος ἀμφιπολεύει
text.english: being borne along in unapproachable drag‑tracks he keeps watch around
text.note: ὁλκοῖς are the “drag‑marks/furrows” a serpent leaves; ἀπλάτοις = “unapproachable, formidable.” ἀμφιπολεύει = “keeps watch/goes round.”

text.greek: σῆμα χαμαζήλοιο Διὸς, ποτὶ κῶας ἀμείβων·
text.english: the low‑lying token of Zeus, as he makes for the Fleece;
text.note: σῆμα here is best “token/sign,” likely the sacred oak‑stock (πρέμνον) as a sign of Zeus (oak sacred to Zeus). χαμαζήλοιο = “low to the ground.” ποτὶ κῶας ἀμείβων = “as he passes/makes for the Fleece.”

text.greek: φρουραῖς δ' ἀδμήτοις ἐπιμαίεται ἄμμορος ὕπνου
text.english: and he is bent on unbroken watches, having no share in sleep,
text.note: ἐπιμαίεται = “is eager for/presses upon,” here “is bent on.” ἀδμήτοις φρουραῖς metaphorically “unbroken/untamed watches,” i.e., ceaseless vigil. ἄμμορος ὕπνου = “having no share of sleep.”

text.greek: γλαυκοῖς ἀμφ' ὄσσοισιν ἀναιδέα κανθὸν ἑλίσσων.
text.english: rolling a pitiless canthus about his gleaming‑grey eyes.
text.note: κανθός = the canthus (corner/white) of the eye; ἀναιδής “shameless, pitiless” of the fierce gaze. γλαυκός denotes gleaming grey/greenish eyes.

text.greek: - Αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ κλύομεν τόδ' ἐτήτυμον ὡς ἐτέτυκτο,
text.english: But when we heard this sure truth, how it had been brought to pass,
text.note: etētumon … etetukto: “true” and “had been wrought/brought to pass,” preserving the epic flavor of teukhomai in the pluperfect.

text.greek: ἀμφί γε Μουνυχίης Ἑκάτης φρουρῆς τε δράκοντος,
text.english: concerning Hekate of Munychia and the sentinel serpent,
text.note: Munychia: the Athenian harbor-hill with a famous cult of Artemis Munychia; the poet speaks of “Hekate of Munychia,” reflecting conflation/overlap of Artemis and Hekate. “Sentinel serpent” = the guardian dragon of the Fleece.

text.greek: πάνθ' ὅσα οἱ κατέλεξεν ἀριφραδέως Μήδεια,
text.english: all that Medeia recounted to him full plainly,
text.note: hoi = “to him,” i.e., to Iason; ariphradeōs “very plainly/clearly,” stressing Medeia’s precise instructions.

text.greek: διζόμεθ' ἠμὲν ἄελπτον ὀϊζυροῖο πόνοιο
text.english: we deliberated both upon the unlooked-for burden of woeful toil,
text.note: dizometha “we were weighing two courses”; aelpton oizyroio ponoio = “the unlooked-for [prospect] of woeful toil,” an idiomatic, compressed epic expression.

text.greek: ὥς κέ νιν Ἀγροτέρην μειλιξάμενοι πεπίθοιμεν,
text.english: how we might, having soothed her—Agroterē—persuade her,
text.note: Agroterē is an epithet of Artemis (“the Huntress”); nin is the feminine pronoun “her,” with Agroterē in apposition. meilixamenoi implies ritual appeasement/propitiation.

text.greek: ἠδ' ὡς θῆρα πέλωρον ἱκοίμεθα, τόφρ' ἀνελόντες
text.english: and how we might reach the monstrous quarry, until, when we had slain it,
text.note: thēr pelōros = “monstrous beast/quarry,” the Colchian dragon; to phr’ = “until then/so long as,” here leading to the outcome clause with the aorist participle anelontes (“having slain”).

text.greek: δέρμ' ἀπονοστήσαιμεν ἑὴν ἐς πατρίδα γαῖαν.
text.english: we might bear the hide back to our own fatherland.
text.note: derm’ = “the hide,” i.e., the Golden Fleece; aponostēsaimen is used transitively, “bear/bring back [home].”

text.greek: Καὶ τότε δὴ μετὰ πᾶσιν ὁμόκλεεν ἡρώεσσι
text.english: And then indeed he called out in warning among all the heroes,

text.greek: Μόψος (ὁ γάρ τ' ἐδάη σφῇσιν τάδε μαντοσύνῃσιν)
text.english: Mopsus (for by his own mantic arts he had learned these things),

text.greek: ὄφρ' ἐμὲ γουνάσωνται, ἐπιστίβωσι δὲ ἔργον,
text.english: that they should supplicate me, and press on with the task,
text.note: Here the first person “me” is the deity speaking through the oracle; i.e., Artemis. ὄφρα with the subjunctive marks purpose. ἐπιστίβω ἔργον means “press on with the task” or “set to the work.”

text.greek: Ἄρτεμιν ἵλασθαι, θέλξαι δ' ὑπερήνορα θῆρα.
text.english: to propitiate Artemis and charm the overweening beast.
text.note: ὑπερήνορα (“overmighty, overweening”) is an epithet usually of men, transferred here to the θήρ (“beast”); the specific animal is not specified in the line. θέλξαι = “to charm/soothe.”

text.greek: Ὣς οἳ μὲν λίσσοντο περισταδόν· αὐτὰρ ἔγωγε
text.english: Thus they kept beseeching on every side; but I, for my part,

text.greek: Αἰσονίδην ἐκέλευσα δύω δὴ φῶτε κραταιώ
text.english: bade Aisonides that two mighty men indeed—
text.note: Aisonides = Jason. The particle dē adds emphasis (“indeed”); phōte krataiō is dual, “two mighty men.”

text.greek: Κάστορά θ' ἱππόδαμον καὶ πὺξ ἀγαθὸν Πολυδεύκεα,
text.english: Castor the horse-tamer and Polydeukes, good at boxing,—
text.note: Formulaic epithets: hippodamon = “horse‑taming”; pyx agathon = “good at boxing.”

text.greek: Μόψον τ' Ἀμπυκίδην ἰέναι πρὸς τέρματα μόχθου·
text.english: and Mopsus, the son of Ampyx—should go toward the bounds of the toil;
text.note: The infinitive ienai (“to go”) governs all the accusatives named (the two heroes and Mopsus). Pros tέρματα μόχθου = “toward the bounds/end of the toil,” an idiom for the goal or limit of the ordeal.

text.greek: Αὐτὰρ ἐμοὶ Μήδεια συνέσπετο μούνη ἀπ' ἄλλων.
text.english: but Medeia alone accompanied me, apart from the others.

text.greek: - Ἡνίκα δ' εἰς σηκοὺς ἱκόμην ζάθεόν τε θεράπνην,
text.english: But when I came into the precincts and the most holy sanctuary,
text.note: σηκοί are sacred enclosures; θεράπνη denotes a shrine/cult‑seat; ζάθεος means “most holy.”

text.greek: χώρῳ ἐπὶ πλακόεντι βόθρον τρίστοιχον ὄρυξα,
text.english: upon a level stretch of ground I dug a triple‑ordered pit,
text.note: πλακόεντι = “level, flat.” βόθρος is a sacrificial pit for chthonic rites; τρίστοιχον “triple‑ordered/threefold,” i.e., arranged in three rows or sections.

text.greek: φιτρούς τ' ἀρκεύθοιο καὶ ἀζαλέης ἀπὸ κέδρου,
text.english: and kindling‑twigs of juniper and of dry cedar,
text.note: φιτρούς is a rare word for small sticks/kindling (cf. Hesychius: φίτρα = φρύγανα). ἀζαλέος = “parched, dry,” not related to the modern “azalea.”

text.greek: ῥάμνον τ' ὀξυτέροιο, πολυκλαύτων τ' αἰγείρων,
text.english: buckthorn of the sharper sort, and the much‑weeping poplars,
text.note: ῥάμνος = buckthorn; ὀξυτέροιο “of the sharper (more thorny) kind.” πολυκλαύτων “much‑weeping” is a traditional funerary epithet of the black poplar (aigeiros).

text.greek: ὦκα φέρων νήησα πυρὴν ἔμπροσθε βόθροιο.
text.english: swiftly bearing them I piled a pyre before the pit.
text.note: νήησα = “I heaped/piled,” aorist of νέω (II). ἔμπροσθε βόθροιο “before the pit” underscores the chthonic sacrificial setting.

text.greek: Πολλὰ δέ μοι φέρε πάμπαν ἐπισταμένη Μήδεια,
text.english: And Mēdeia, wholly skilled, brought me many things,
text.note: φέρε is the unaugmented imperfect (“she brought”); πάμπαν ἐπισταμένη = “wholly skilled” (sc. in her arts); the object is indefinite (“many things”), supplied by context.

text.greek: φωριαμῶν ἀνελοῦσα θυώδεος ἐξ ἀδύτοιο.
text.english: having taken them up from the coffers of the incense‑scented adyton.
text.note: φωριαμῶν = “coffers, chests” (rare/late word); ἀνελοῦσα = aorist ptc. “having taken up,” with genitive of separation; ἐξ ἀδύτοιο θυώδεος = “from the incense-scented inner shrine (adyton),” with epic genitives (-εος, -οιο).

text.greek: Αὐτίκα δ' οὐλαοπλάσμαθ' ὑπὸ πέπλους ἐπονεύμην
text.english: Straightway I busied myself beneath the veils with cicatrizing plasters,
text.note: οὐλαοπλάσματα (acc. pl.) is a technical pharmaco-medical term, ‘cicatrizing plasters’ (from οὐλή ‘scar’ + πλάσσω ‘mould’), aptly used of Medea’s ointments; ἐπονεύμην (middle) = ‘I busied myself (with)’, from πονεύω ‘to toil, be active’; ὑπὸ πέπλους suggests ritual head-veiling during chthonic rites.

text.greek: ἂν δὲ πυρὴν ἐπέβαλλον, ἰδ' ἔντομα θύματ' ἔρεζον,
text.english: and I would pile upon the pyre, and I performed cut-up offerings,
text.note: ἄν with the imperfect ἐπέβαλλον marks iterative/habitual past (‘I would pile’). ἔντομα θύματα are ‘cut’ or ‘gashed’ offerings, a technical term in Hecatean/underworld ritual (cf. Apollonius Rhodius 3.1030–1036).

text.greek: σκύμνους παμμέλανας σκυλάκων τρισσοὺς ἱερεύσας.
text.english: having sacrificed three all-black whelps of dogs.
text.note: σκύμνους σκυλάκων is pleonastic (‘whelps of dogs’) to stress youthful victims; παμμέλανας ‘all-black’ is the standard color for chthonic sacrifices; τρισσούς ‘three’ suits Hekate’s triple aspect.

text.greek: Αἵματι δ' αὖ χάλκανθον ἰδὲ στρούθειον ἔμιξα,
text.english: And with blood again I mixed chalkanthon and stroutheion,
text.note: chalkanthon = copper sulphate/blue vitriol; stroutheion (στρουθεῖον) is an obscure pharmakon (probably a plant; cf. Dioscorides), left transliterated.

text.greek: κνῆκόν τε σχιστὴν, ἐπί τε ψύλλιον ἀηδὲς,
text.english: and split knekon, and in addition the loathsome psyllion,
text.note: knēkon = safflower (Carthamus), a dye-plant; schistē (“split”) likely refers to a processed/flaked form. psyllion = fleawort (Plantago), noted here as “loathsome” (ἀηδές).

text.greek: ἄγχουσάν τ' ἐρυθρὴν, ἰδὲ χάλκιμον· αὐτὰρ ἔπειτα
text.english: and red anchousa, and chalkimos; but then,
text.note: anchousa (ἄγχουσα) = alkanet/alkanin-bearing root used as a red dye; chalkimos (χάλκιμον) = verdigris (copper rust).

text.greek: νηδύας ἐμπλήσας σκυλάκων, φιτροῖσιν ἔθηκα·
text.english: filling the bellies of puppies, I set them in jars;
text.note: “Bellies of puppies” (νηδύας σκυλάκων) are used as ritual containers in chthonic magic. φιτροῖσιν is probably a corruption of πίθροισιν (“large jars”); hence “I set them in jars.”

text.greek: ὕδατι δ' αὖ μίξας χολάδας χεόμην περὶ βόθρον,
text.english: and mixing galls with water, I poured [it] round about the pit,
text.note: χολάδες may mean “galls” (oak-galls) or “gall(-bladders)/bile”; either suits a harsh, chthonic libation. Translation keeps the ambiguity with “galls.”

text.greek: ὄρφνινα θ' ἑσσάμενος φάρη καὶ ἀπεχθέα χαλκόν
text.english: and, donning dusk-black garments and hateful bronze,
text.note: ὄρφνινα φάρη = “dusk-black garments.” ἀπεχθέα χαλκόν = “hateful bronze,” the clanging bronze used in underworld rites.

text.greek: κρούων ἐλλισάμην· αἱ δ' ὁτραλέως ἐπάκουσαν,
text.english: striking it I summoned them; and they swiftly hearkened,
text.note: ἐλλισάμην (“I summoned by incantation/rite”); combined with κρούων (“striking”) indicates summoning by clashing bronze.

text.greek: ῥήξασαι κενεῶνας ἀμειδήτοιο βερέθρου,
text.english: bursting the wombs of the unsmiling abyss,
text.note: κενεῶνας = “bellies/wombs”; βέρεθρον = “abyss, pit.” Vivid metaphor for the Furies forcing up from the underworld.

text.greek: Τισιφόνη τε καὶ Ἀληκτὼ καὶ δῖα Μέγαιρα,
text.english: Tisiphonē and Allecto and divine Megaera,
text.note: The three Erinyes are named; δῖα (“divine”) is conventional epic epithet, not contradicting their dread.

text.greek: πεύκαις ἀζαλέαις φόνιον σέλας ἀΐσσουσαι.
text.english: brandishing dry-pine torches and hurling a murderous blaze.
text.note: πεύκαις ἀζαλέαις = “dry/pared pines,” i.e., pine-wood torches; φόνιον σέλας = “murderous blaze.”

text.greek: Καίετο δ' αὐτίκα βόθρος, ἐσμαράγει δ' ὀλοὸν πῦρ·
text.english: And straightway the pit burned, and the baneful fire crackled.
text.note: βόθρος is a ritual “pit” for chthonic offerings; ἐσμαράγει (onomatopoetic, often of clashing or roaring) here of the fire’s crackling/roar. Some witnesses have forms like ἐσμάραγε; the sense is auditory tumult.

text.greek: λιγνὺς δ' αἰθαλόεσσα χύθη περιμήκετα καπνόν.
text.english: And sooty reek was poured out, a far‑stretching smoke.
text.note: λιγνύς αἰθαλόεσσα is a formula for thick, sooty reek; χύθη is “was poured out.” περιμήκετα modifies καπνόν (“far‑stretching/long‑drawn smoke”).

text.greek: Αὐτίκα δ' ἐξ Ἀΐδαο διὰ φλογὸς ἠγέρθησαν
text.english: And straightway out of Aidēs, through the flame, they were roused.
text.note: Aidēs is transliterated. The passive ἠγέρθησαν (“were roused”) commonly describes the summoning of the dead; διὰ φλογὸς (“through the flame”) may allude to a ritual or pyric medium. The subject is feminine plural, supplied by the epithets in the next line.

text.greek: δειναὶ, θαμβήτειραι, ἀπηνέες, ἀπροσόρατοι.
text.english: dread, wonder‑striking, ruthless, not to be looked upon.
text.note: θαμβήτειραι is a rare epithet, literally “astonishment-/wonder‑causing.” ἀπροσόρατοι, from ὁράω with πρός-, means “impossible to look upon (face to face).” The cluster of feminine plurals marks unnamed dread female beings.

text.greek: Ἣ μὲν γὰρ δέμας ἔσχε σιδήρεον, ἣν καλέουσι
text.english: For she had a body of iron, her whom the Chthonians call Pandora;
text.note: “Pandora” here is a chthonic epithet/title, not necessarily the Hesiodic figure; “chthonians” means the underworld powers or denizens.

text.greek: Πανδώρην χθόνιοι· σὺν δ' αἰολόμορφος ἵκανε
text.english: and in her company there came, of shifting form,
text.note: aiolomorphos = “changeful/variegated in form,” highlighting Hekate’s polymorphy; “with her” likely refers back to the figure just named, Pandora.

text.greek: τρισσοκέφαλος, ἰδεῖν ὀλοὸν τέρας οὔτι δαϊκτὸν,
text.english: triple‑headed—a baleful prodigy to behold, not to be withstood in battle—Hekate, child of Tartaros;
text.note: oûti daiktón = “not to be fought/withstood in battle”; Tartaropais (“child of Tartaros”) is a rare Orphic epithet of Hekate, stressing her underworld origin; trissokephalos = “triple‑headed.”

text.greek: Ταρταρόπαις Ἑκάτη· λαιοῦ δ' ἄρ' ἐπεσσύθη ὤμου
text.english: and from her left shoulder there sprang a horse with flowing mane;
text.note: “From the left shoulder” suggests a bestial head or form projecting; epessythê conveys a sudden rush/leap forth; the horse head aligns with Hekate’s monstrous, composite aspect.

text.greek: ἵππος χαιτήεις· κατὰ δεξιὰ δ' ἦεν ἀθρῆσαι
text.english: and on the right there was to be seen a rabid‑eyed bitch;
text.note: skylakê is a diminutive of “dog,” but in epic may be merely stylistic; lyssôpis = “rabid‑eyed, raging‑eyed.”

text.greek: λυσσῶπις σκυλάκη· μέσση δ' ἔφυ ἀγριόμορφος
text.english: and in the middle she was savage in shape;
text.note: “In the middle she was savage in form” most naturally refers to the central head/form of the triple figure, left unspecified but characterized as wild/feral.

text.greek: χερσὶν δ' ἀμφοτέραις ἔχεν ἄορα κωπήεντα.
text.english: and in both hands she held swords with hilts.
text.note: aora kôpêenta = “swords with hilts/hafted blades” (kôpê = handle); not “oars,” despite the cognate form for “oar.”

text.greek: Ἐγκύκλιαι δινεῦντο περὶ βόθρον ἔνθα καὶ ἔνθα
text.english: Encircling, Pandora and Hekate were whirling round the pit, hither and thither.
text.note: “Enkykliai” (fem. pl.) is taken predicatively with the two goddesses, meaning “encircling/revolving”; βόθρος is the chthonic “pit” of necromantic rites; ἔνθα καὶ ἔνθα = “hither and thither.”

text.greek: Πανδώρη Ἑκάτη τε· συνεσσεύοντο δὲ Ποιναί.
text.english: And the Poinae were rushing together.
text.note: Πανδώρη is an epic/Doric form of Pandora; some take it as an epithet (“All-giver”) potentially applied to Hekate/Earth. Ποίναι are the personified Retributions (akin to Erinyes), here as Hekate’s attendants. συνεσσεύοντο (from συν- + σεύω) = “were rushing together.”

text.greek: Ἐκ δ' ἄφαρ Ἀρτέμιδος φρουρὸν δέμας ἧκε χαμάζε
text.english: And straightway, out from Artemis, the warder in person let fall to the ground the pine‑brands from his hands,
text.note: ἐκ Ἀρτέμιδος is best taken metonymically as “out from [the temple/shrine of] Artemis.” φρουρὸν δέμας, literally “a guardian body/form,” is compressed epic diction; here it denotes the temple‑guard “in person.” πεύκας likely means pine‑wood torches/brands. The syntax is abrupt but coherent in epic style.

text.greek: πεύκας ἐκ χειρῶν, ἐς δ' οὐρανὸν ἤραρεν ὄσσε.
text.english: and he fastened his eyes upon the sky.
text.note: ἤραρεν ὄσσε (from ἀραρίσκω) is a Homeric idiom meaning “fixed/fastened his eyes.”

text.greek: Σαῖνον δὲ σκύλακες πρόπολοι, λύοντο δ' ὀχῆες
text.english: And the attendant hounds were fawning, and the clasps of the silver bolts were being loosed;
text.note: σαίνειν of dogs “fawning, wagging (the tail)”; ὀχῆες are the fastenings/holders of bolts—hence “clasps of the silver bolts.”

text.greek: κλείθρων ἀργυρέων, ἀνὰ δ' ἔπτατο καλὰ θύρετρα
text.english: and the fair doors of the wide‑built wall flew open;
text.note: ἔπτατο (“flew up”) is idiomatic of doors opening; θύρετρα can denote folding doors/gates; εὐρυμενής = “wide‑built, widely‑spread,” of city walls.

text.greek: τείχεος εὐρυμενοῦς, ὑπεφαίνετο δ' ἄλσος ἐρυμνόν.
text.english: and a secure grove came into view.
text.note: ἐρυμνός = “strong, secure, well‑defended”; for a grove it suggests an enclosed or inviolate sacred precinct rather than mere physical strength.

text.greek: - Αὐτὰρ ἐγὼν ὑπὲρ οὐδὸν ἔβην· τῆμος δέ τε κούρη
text.english: But I crossed the threshold; thereupon the maiden
text.note: Autar egōn is the epic connective “but I”; huper oudon ebin is a set phrase for “I crossed the threshold.” Tēmos means “then/thereupon.”

text.greek: Αἰήτεω Μήδεια καὶ Αἴσονος ἀγλαὸς υἱός,
text.english: Medea, daughter of Aietes, and the glorious son of Aison,
text.note: Aiëteō is the epic genitive “of Aietes,” functioning as a patronymic; “the glorious son of Aison” is Jason.

text.greek: Τυνδαρίδαι τ' ἤπειγον ὁμοῦ, σὺν δ' ἕσπετο Μόψος.
text.english: the Tyndarids too pressed on together, and Mopsus followed in company.
text.note: Ēpeigon can be transitive (“urged [someone] on”) or intransitive (“pressed on, made haste”); here rendered intransitively to fit the group subject. The Tyndarids are the Dioscuri (Castor and Polydeuces). Syn d’ hespeto (“and [he] followed in company”) uses syn adverbially with hépomai.

text.greek: Ἀλλ' ὅτε δὴ σχεδόθεν κατεφαίνετο φηγὸς ἐραννή,
text.english: But when at last the lovely oak was seen from close at hand,
text.note: phēgos in epic generally = “oak” (not “beech”); eranē = “lovely, gracious,” a stock epithet for trees/groves.

text.greek: κρηπίς τε ξενίοιο Διὸς καὶ βώμιος ἕδρη,
text.english: and the platform of Zeus Xenios and the altar’s seat,
text.note: Krēpis and hedra both denote a foundation/platform; Zeus Xenios is Zeus as protector of strangers and hospitality.

text.greek: ἔνθα δράκων ὁλκοῖσιν ὑπὸ πλατέεσσιν ἑλιχθείς
text.english: there the dragon, coiled in his broad convolutions beneath it,
text.note: The phrase holkoisin hypo plateessin helichtheis is compressed and much discussed: holkoi literally “drag-tracks/furrows,” here likely metaphorical of serpentine folds; platees “broad.” The translation renders the sense (“broad convolutions beneath [the oak]”).

text.greek: δινεύων ἀνάειρε κάρη βλοσυρόν τε γένειον,
text.english: whirling, lifted on high his head and his grim beard,
text.note: Geneion (“beard/chin”): dragons in Greek poetic diction can be ‘bearded’; thus “grim beard” preserves the epic coloring.

text.greek: ἂν δ' ὀλοὸν σύριγξ' ἐπὶ δ' ἔβραχεν ἄσπετος αἰθήρ·
text.english: and aloft he sent a baneful hiss, and the boundless Aither bellowed over it;
text.note: Syrinx here = “hiss” by metonymy (cf. syrygmos); some emend to syrygmon. Aspe tos = “boundless, unspeakable.” Aither is capitalized as a personified upper sky.

text.greek: Δένδρεα δ' ἐσμαράγησε, κραδαινόμεν' ἔνθα καὶ ἔνθα
text.english: and the trees crashed, shaken this way and that
text.note: Prym nothen ek rhizēs is an emphatic hendiadys, “from the very root,” underscoring the force of the shaking.

text.greek: πρυμνόθεν ἐκ ῥίζης· ἰάχησε δὲ σύσκιον ἄλσος.
text.english: from the base, from the root; and the shadowy grove rang out.
text.note: Suskion = “deep/shadowy” (densely shaded), standard of sacred groves.

text.greek: Αὐτὰρ ἔμ' ἠδ' ἑτάρους τρόμος ἔλλαβε· νόσφι δὲ μούνη
text.english: But a tremor seized me and my comrades; apart, alone,
text.note: νόσφι δὲ μούνη is enjambed: “apart, alone” prepares the exception—namely Medeia—in the next line; ἔλλαβε (‘seized’) is a common epic formula for sudden emotion.

text.greek: Μήδει' ἐνὶ στέρνοισιν ἀκαμπέα θυμὸν ἐνώμα·
text.english: Medeia within her breast wielded an unbending spirit;
text.note: ἐνώμα is the aorist of νωμάω, “to wield, handle, direct”; θυμός here is the seat of resolve/courage, hence “unbending spirit.” The form Μήδει’ is elided for metrical reasons (for Μήδεια).

text.greek: δρέψατο γὰρ παλάμῃσι λυγρῶν ἀποθρίσματα ῥιζῶν.
text.english: for with her palms she gathered the scrapings of baneful roots.
text.note: ἀποθρίσματα ῥιζῶν are ‘scrapings/shavings of roots,’ a technical phrasing for pharmaka; λυγρός means ‘baneful, baleful.’ δρέψατο (middle) suggests deliberate, personal action—‘she plucked for herself.’

text.greek: Καὶ τότ' ἐγὼ φόρμιγγος ἐφήρμοσα θέσκελον ὀμφήν,
text.english: And then I fitted to the phorminx a wondrous strain,
text.note: phorminx: the epic lyre; ἐφήρμοσα “fitted/attuned.” θέσκελος ὀμφή, literally “wondrous/divine voice,” here a lofty term for a musical strain (ὀμφή often means oracular ‘voice’).

text.greek: κλάγξα δ' ἄρ' ἐξ ὑπάτης χέλυος βαρυηχέα φωνήν
text.english: and from the hypatê of the shell I rang out a deep-resounding voice,
text.note: ὑπάτη is the technical name for the lowest (gravest) string in the ancient Greek system; χέλυς is the tortoise-shell lyre. κλάγξα conveys a ringing/pealing sound; βαρυηχέα “deep-sounding.”

text.greek: σιγαλέως ἄφθεγκτον ἐμοῖς ὑπὸ χείλεσι πέμπων.
text.english: sending it unuttered beneath my lips, in silence.
text.note: σιγαλέως likely = “silently” (cf. σιγηλῶς). ἄφθεγκτον “unuttered/wordless,” indicating instrumental sound without vocalization; ὑπὸ χείλεσι, “beneath my lips,” idiomatically, with the lips not speaking.

text.greek: Κλῇξα γὰρ ὕπνον ἄνακτα θεῶν πάντων τ' ἀνθρώπων,
text.english: For I called upon Hypnos, lord of the gods and of all men,
text.note: κλῇξα (“I called upon”) from κλῄζω; Ὕπνος (Hypnos) is personified Sleep, here strikingly styled “lord of gods and men,” echoing and inverting the usual title of Zeus.

text.greek: ὄφρα μολὼν θέλξειε μένος βριαροῖο δράκοντος.
text.english: so that, when he came, he might lull the might of the sturdy dragon.
text.note: θέλξειε (“might charm/lull”) suits Hypnos’ power; μολών is the aorist participle of βλώσκω (“to come”); βριαροῖο = “sturdy, strong,” not the proper name Briareus; δράκων = “dragon/serpent.”

text.greek: Ῥίμφα δέ μοι ὑπάκουσε, Κυτηΐδα δ' ἧκ' ἐπὶ γαῖαν.
text.english: And swiftly he hearkened to me, and he sent the Kyteïan upon the land.
text.note: ῥίμφα = ‘swiftly, lightly’ (epic adverb). ἧκ’ = ἧκε ‘he sent.’ Κυτηΐδα is the accusative of Κυτηΐς, a gentilic ‘the Kyteïan (woman),’ i.e., Medea, so called from Cyt(a)ea in Colchis; cf. the more familiar ‘Cytaean’ epithet in other poets. The subject of the verbs is the deity previously invoked in context.

text.greek: Κοιμίσσας δ' ὅγε φῦλα πανημερίων ἀνθρώπων,
text.english: But when he had lulled to sleep the tribes of day‑long mortals,
text.note: πανημερίων (“of all-day”) suggests mortals active or toiling by day; the implied subject is Hypnos (Sleep), picked up by the winged imagery in line 1011.

text.greek: καὶ ζαμενεῖς ἀνέμων πνοιὰς, καὶ κύματα πόντου,
text.english: and the vehement blasts of the winds, and the billows of the sea,
text.note: ζαμενεῖς is an epic adjective meaning “vehement, violent,” modifying the wind’s “blasts” (πνοιὰς).

text.greek: πηγάς τ' ἀενάων ὑδάτων, ποταμῶν τε ῥέεθρα,
text.english: and the springs of ever‑flowing waters, and the streams of rivers,
text.note: ἀενάων ὑδάτων is a formulaic “ever-flowing”; the pairing πηγαί/ῥέεθρα distinguishes springs from river-currents.

text.greek: θῆράς τ' οἰωνούς τε, τά τε ζώει τε καὶ ἕρπει,
text.english: both wild beasts and birds, and whatever lives and crawls,
text.note: τὰ τε ζώει τε καὶ ἕρπει is a totalizing formula (“all that lives and crawls”); note the epic neuter plural with singular verb (ζώει).

text.greek: εὐνάζων ἤμειψεν ὑπὸ χρυσέαις πτερύγεσσιν.
text.english: lulling them to rest, he withdrew beneath his golden wings.
text.note: εὐνάζων … ἤμειψεν ὑπὸ χρυσέαις πτερύγεσσιν: “withdrew beneath his golden wings,” the wings identifying Hypnos; χρυσέαις marks divine radiance.

text.greek: Ἷξε δ' ὑπὸ στυφελῶν Κόλχων εὐανθέα χῶρον·
text.english: He reached the bloom‑laden land of the harsh Kolchians;
text.note: ὑπὸ + gen. here conveys dominion/locale (“in the land of”); εὐανθής = “bloom‑laden”; στυφελός = “harsh, unyielding.”

text.greek: κῶμα δ' ἄφαρ κατέμαρψε πελωρίου ὄσσε δράκοντος,
text.english: and straightway deep slumber seized the eyes of the monstrous serpent,
text.note: κῶμα = deep, deathlike sleep; ὄσσε is dual (“both eyes”).

text.greek: ἰσοπαλὲς θανάτῳ· δολιχὴν δ' ἀμφ' αὐχένι δειρήν
text.english: equal to death; and it laid its long neck about its throat,
text.note: ἰσοπαλὲς θανάτῳ is a traditional formula for sleep’s potency; ἀμφ’ αὐχένι δειρήν (neck about the neck) vividly describes the serpent coiling upon itself.

text.greek: θῆκε καρηβαρέων φολίσιν· θάμβησε δ' ἰδοῦσα
text.english: with head‑heavy scales. And dread‑fated Medeia, on seeing, was amazed,
text.note: καρηβαρέων φολίσιν is instrumental (“with head‑heavy scales”), suggesting the droop of the scaly, heavy head; αἰνόποτμος is Medeia’s tragic epithet.

text.greek: αἰνόποτμος Μήδεια· καὶ Αἴσονος ἀγλαὸν υἷα
text.english: and she came, emboldening Aison’s illustrious son
text.note: ἧκ’ = ἦκε; “Aison’s illustrious son” is the epic periphrasis for Jason; ἐπιθαρσύνω = “to embolden, cheer on.”

text.greek: ἧκ' ἐπιθαρσύνουσα θοῶς πρέμνοιο λαβέσθαι
text.english: to grasp quickly the stump, for the golden‑woolled fleece;
text.note: πρέμνον = base/stump (of Ares’ oak); κῶας χρυσεόμαλλον = “golden‑woolled fleece,” with κῶας a synonym of δέρας used in the next line.

text.greek: κῶας χρυσεόμαλλον· ὁ δ' οὐκ ἀπίθησεν ἀκούσας·
text.english: and, hearing, he did not disobey;
text.note: οὐκ ἀπίθησεν = “did not disobey,” the epic litotes for “obeyed.”

text.greek: αὐτὰρ ἀειράμενος δέρας ἄπλετον ἷκτ' ἐπὶ νῆα.
text.english: but, lifting the immense hide, he made his way to the ship.
text.note: δέρας ἄπλετον = “immense hide/fleece”; ἷκτ’ ἐπὶ νῆα = “he reached the ship.”

text.greek: - Ἥρωες Μινύαι μέγ' ἐγήθεον, ἂν δ' ἄρα χεῖρας
text.english: The Minyan heroes rejoiced greatly; then indeed their hands
text.note: “Minyan heroes” (Minyae) identifies the Argonauts as descendants of Minyas; ἂν δ’ ἄρα is a Homeric particle cluster meaning “then indeed”; the mention of hands anticipates the prayer gesture completed in the next line.

text.greek: ἀθανάτοις ἤειραν, οἳ οὐρανὸν εὐρὺν ἔχουσιν.
text.english: they raised to the Immortals, who hold the broad heaven.
text.note: “The Immortals” = the gods; οἳ οὐρανὸν εὐρὺν ἔχουσιν is a Homeric formula, “who hold the broad heaven,” characterizing the Olympians; ἤειραν (epic aorist of αἴρω) refers to the ritual raising of hands in prayer.

text.greek: Ὣς οἳ μὲν περὶ κῶας ὀπώπεον· αἶψα δ' Αἰήτης
text.english: Thus they for their part were gazing upon the fleece;
text.note: ὀπώπεον is an epic form meaning “were gazing/beholding.” κῶας (“fleece”) here denotes the Golden Fleece; περὶ with the accusative conveys “around/about,” rendered idiomatically as “upon.”

text.greek: ἀμφιπόλων ἤκουσεν ἀποιχομένην Μήδειαν.
text.english: but straightway Aeëtes heard from the handmaids that Medea was gone.
text.note: ἀκούω takes the genitive of the person from whom one hears (ἀμφιπόλων, “handmaids/attendants”) and an accusative + participle for the content (Μήδειαν ἀποιχομένην, “that Medea was gone/absent”).

text.greek: Ὦκα δ' ἄρ' Ἀψύρτῳ ἐπετέλλετο λαὸν ἀγεῖραι
text.english: Quickly then he bade Apsyrtos to muster the host.
text.note: Subject of ἐπετέλλετο is implicit (Aeētes in context); dative Ἀψύρτῳ marks the person commanded; λαόν rendered “host.”

text.greek: μαστεύειν δ' ἄρα παῖδα κασιγνήτην καὶ ὅπατρον·
text.english: and to track down the maiden, his sister by the same father.
text.note: μαστεύειν = “to track down, search out.” ὅπατρον = “of the same father” (homopatric), specifying Medea as Apsyrtos’ sister; παῖδα κασιγνήτην refers to Medea as “the maiden sister.”

text.greek: ἀλλά οἱ ὠκὺς ἔπειγε παρὰ προχοὰς ποταμοῖο
text.english: but swiftly he pressed on beside the river’s mouths
text.note: οἱ is an ethical/indirect dative (“for him”); ὠκὺς ἔπειγε is rendered intransitively as “he pressed on swiftly.” προχοαί = “outflows, mouths” of a river.

text.greek: εἰς λόχον ἡρώων, ἔκιχεν δ' ἄρα παρθένον αἰνήν.
text.english: into an ambush of heroes, and he came upon the dread maiden.
text.note: παρθένον αἰνήν = “dread/terrible maiden,” an elevated epithet of Medea; λόχος ἡρώων = the Argonauts’ ambush.

text.greek: Νὺξ δὲ τότ' ἀστροχίτων μέσσην παράμειβε πορείαν,
text.english: And Night, star-cloaked, was then passing the mid-course of her journey,
text.note: “astrochitōn” = “star-cloaked,” a conventional epic epithet for Night; “mid-course” signals midnight.

text.greek: Ἐκ δ' ἐτελεῖτο δόλος στυγερὸς καὶ κῆρες ἀϊδναί
text.english: and the baleful stratagem was fulfilled, and the unseen Keres
text.note: “Keres aïdnai” are the “unseen” death-spirits; the singular verb with plural subject is a common poetic license. “stygeros” = “baleful.”

text.greek: Μηδείης ὑπ' ἔρωτος, ἐρικλυτοῦ Ἀψύρτοιο,
text.english: of very-renowned Apsyrtos, under the compulsion of Medeia’s love;
text.note: “hyp’ erōtos” expresses causation (“under the compulsion of love”), here Medeia’s love for Iason; “eriklytos” = “very-renowned.” The genitive “Apsyrtoio” depends on “Keres.”

text.greek: ὅν ῥα κατακτείναντες, ἐπὶ προχοὰς μεθέηκαν
text.english: whom, when they had slain him, they released at the mouths of the river as it surged;
text.note: “prochoai” are river-mouths/outfalls; “ornymenou potamoio” = “of the surging/rising river.” The river is unnamed; the context points to the region of the Apsyrtides.

text.greek: ὀρνυμένου ποταμοῖο· φέρεν δ' ὅγε πνεύματι κραιπνῷ·
text.english: and it bore him along with a swift blast;
text.note: “pneuma” (“breath, blast”) metaphorically for the driving force of the current (possibly wind-aided). The pronoun “hoge” refers back to the river.

text.greek: θεινόμενος δὲ δίναις εἰς κῦμ' ἁλὸς ἀτρυγέτοιο,
text.english: buffeted by eddies into the wave of the unharvested sea,
text.note: “halos atrugetoio” = “unharvested sea,” a Homeric formula; “theinomenos” = “smitten/buffeted,” of a body tossed by eddies (dīnai).

text.greek: κέλσεν ὑπὲρ νήσων, Ἀψυρτίδας ἃς καλέουσιν,
text.english: he was swept past the islands which they call the Apsyrtides,
text.note: “Apsyrtides” are the Apsyrtian Isles (traditionally in the northern Adriatic). The verb “kelsen” conveys being driven/swept along; the exact nuance is debated.

text.greek: ἀλλά οἱ οὔτι λάθον Δι' ἐπόψιον οὐδὲ θέμιστας.
text.english: but in no wise did they escape Zeus the Overseer nor the ordinances.
text.note: “Di’ epopsion” = “Zeus the Overseer/Watchful,” emphasizing divine surveillance; “themistas” = the (divine) ordinances/laws (of Themis). The line foreshadows retribution for the murderers.

text.greek: Αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ νηὸς μὲν ἔσω κίον, ἐκ δ' ἑκάτερθεν
text.english: But when they had gone within the ship, and from either side,
text.note: ἔσω νηός = “aboard, within the ship”; ἑκάτερθεν ὄχθης = “from either bank,” implying river-mooring on both sides.

text.greek: ὄχθης πείσματ' ἔκοψαν, ὑπ' εἰρεσίῃς δὲ θοῇσι
text.english: of the bank they cut the mooring-ropes, and beneath the swift oarage,
text.note: πεῖσματα = mooring-cables; ὑπ’ εἰρεσίῃς θοῇσι is an epic idiom, “under the impulse of swift oars.”

text.greek: πλεῖον ἐπειγόμενοι ποταμοῦ τάμον οὔτι κατευθύ
text.english: pressing on to sail, they clove the river not on a straight course,
text.note: τάμον (“clove, cut”) is a conventional verb for cutting a course through water; οὔτι κατευθὺ (“not straight”) indicates a slanting/irregular course, likely from current or steering error.

text.greek: πόντον ἐπ' ἰχθυόεντα διὰ στόμα Φάσιδος εὐρύ
text.english: toward the fish-rich sea, through the wide mouth of the Phasis,
text.note: Phasis = the Colchian river (modern Rioni); ἰχθυόεις πόντος is a traditional epithet, “fish-rich sea.”

text.greek: ἰέμεθ' ἀμπλακίῃ δ' ἐφορεύμεθα πολλὸν ὀπίσσω
text.english: we made for it; yet through a misstep we were borne far backward,
text.note: ἰέμεθ’ = “we made/hastened (toward it)”; ἀμπλακίῃ = “by an error, misjudgment”; ἐφορεύμεθα (iterative nuance) = “we kept being carried,” here “driven back,” probably by current/swell.

text.greek: αἰὲν ἀναπλείοντες· ἐλείπετο δ' ἄστεα Κόλχων
text.english: ever putting back; and the cities of the Colchians were being left behind by the heedless Minyae,
text.note: ἀναπλεῖν can mean “sail back” or “sail upstream”; ἀφραδέσιν Μινύαις is a dative of agent/instrument, “by/through the heedlessness of the Minyae” (the Argonauts).

text.greek: ἀφραδέσιν Μινύαις, σκοτερὴ δέ τε ἄμφεχεν ὄρφνη.
text.english: and murky dusk encompassed us all around.
text.note: ἐλείπετο (singular with neuter plural ἄστεα) is idiomatic in epic; ὄρφνη = “dusk, murk,” σκοτερὴ stressing density; ἄμφεχεν = “encompassed on all sides.”

text.greek: - Αὐτὰρ ἐπειγόμενοι θέομεν ῥόον ἀφραδίῃσι,
text.english: But pressing on, we rushed along the current in heedlessness,
text.note: θέομεν (“we run”) is used of swift movement, often of ships; ἀφραδίῃσι is an adverbial dative, “in/through rashness, heedlessness.”

text.greek: μεσσάτιοι πεδίοιο· βροτοὶ δέ μιν ἀμφινέμονται
text.english: midmost of the plain; and mortals dwell around it,
text.note: μεσσάτιοι πεδίοιο modifies the action (“midmost of the plain”); μιν (“it”) most naturally refers back to ῥόον (“the stream”).

text.greek: Γυμνοὶ Βουονόμαι τε καὶ Ἄρκυες ἀγροιῶται,
text.english: the Gymnoi, the Bouonomai, and the Arkyes, field‑dwellers,
text.note: The ethnics are problematic: Γυμνοί may be a descriptive “the naked [people]” or an ethnonym; Βουονόμαι likely an ethnonym, perhaps related to “cow‑herders” (cf. βους + νέμω); Ἄρκυες is obscure. ἀγροιῶται = “field‑dwellers, rustics.”

text.greek: Κερκετικῶν τ' ἀνδρῶν φῦλον, Σινδῶν τ' ἀγερώχων·
text.english: the tribe of Kerketic men, and of the lordly Sindoi,
text.note: Κερκετικοί = the Kerketai (Cercetae) of the Euxine’s eastern shores; Σίνδοι = the Sindoi of the Maeotic region. ἀγερώχων is an epic epithet, “lordly, proud.”

text.greek: οἳ κείσαντο μεσηγὺ Χαρανδαίων τ' αὐλώνων,
text.english: who settled themselves between the Charandai and the Aulones,
text.note: Χαρανδαῖοι and Αὐλῶνες are usually taken as tribal names; αὐλώνων could also mean “of the ravines,” but the parallel with Χαρανδαίων favors ethnics. κείσαντο (mid.) = “they settled (themselves).”

text.greek: Καυκάσιον παρὰ πρῶνα, διὰ στεινῆς Ἐρυθείας.
text.english: beside the Caucasian slope, through narrow Erytheia.
text.note: Καυκάσιον πρῶνα = the slope/brow of the Caucasus. Ἐρυθεία is elsewhere the far‑western isle of Geryon; here “narrow Erytheia” likely denotes a local strait or narrow region; the toponymy is debated.

text.greek: Ἀλλ' ὅτ' ἀπ' ἀντολίης ἐφάνη τερψίμβροτος ἠώς,
text.english: But when from the East appeared Eos, mortals-delighting Dawn,
text.note: ἀντολίη = “the East, the Orient”; τερψίμβροτος is a traditional epithet (“delighting mortals”) of Eos (Dawn).

text.greek: ποιανθεῖ νήσῳ προσεκέλσαμεν· ἔνθα δὲ δισσοί
text.english: we put in at a meadow-blooming island; and there two
text.note: ποιανθεῖ (“meadow-blooming”), a poetic compound from πόα (“grass”) + ἄνθος (“flower”); προσεκέλσαμεν is a nautical “put in/made landfall.”

text.greek: χεύμασιν ἀπλώτοισι περισχίζουσι ῥέεθρα
text.english: currents with outspread floodwaters split it all around,
text.note: χεῦμα (“outpouring, flood”) + ἀπλώτος (“spread out, outspread”); the object of περισχίζουσι (“split round about”) is the island, understood from the previous line.

text.greek: Φᾶσις τ' εὐρυμενὴς ἀκαλαρρείτης τε Σαράγγης·
text.english: Phasis, broad-flowing, and Saranges, ill-flowing;
text.note: εὐρυμενής here rendered “broad-flowing” (lit. “widely spread”); ἀκαλαρρείτης is rare, literally “not fair-flowing,” hence “ill-flowing,” perhaps hinting at turbid or unruly flow.

text.greek: τόν ῥα πλημμύρουσα διὰ χθονὸς εἰς ἅλα πέμπει
text.english: this one indeed flood-swollen Maiotis sends through the land to the sea,
text.note: Μαιῶτις is the Maeotis (Sea of Azov) personified; τόν likely refers to the nearer river (Saranges). The poet’s geography imagines Maeotis sending its waters “through the land” toward the sea.

text.greek: Μαιῶτις καναχηδὸν, ἑλειονόμου διὰ ποίης.
text.english: with a clanging roar, through the grass of the marsh-meadow.
text.note: καναχηδόν = “with a clanging/roaring din”; ἑλειονόμου (“marsh-pastured/marsh-meadow”), a rare compound; hence “through the grass of the marsh-meadow.”

text.greek: Καὶ τόθ' ὑπ' εἰρεσίῃ πλέομεν διὰ νύκτα καὶ ἦμαρ·
text.english: And then beneath the oar-stroke we sailed through night and day.
text.note: ὑπ’ εἰρεσίῃ = “under the oarage,” a conventional epic idiom for rowing; διὰ νύκτα καὶ ἦμαρ = “through night and day,” i.e., continuously.

text.greek: δισσαῖς δ' ἐν τριμόροισι Βοὸς πόρον ἐξικόμεσθα
text.english: And by its two mouths, in the three‑part sea, we reached the Bosporus,
text.note: δισσαῖς ἐν τριμόροισι: the dative is elliptical, most naturally supplying “mouths” (στόμασιν). The “three‑part sea” is the connected basins of Pontus–Propontis–Aegean; λίμνη (“lake”) is epic for “sea.”

text.greek: λίμνης ὄντα μεσηγὺ, βοοκλόπος οὗποτε Τιτάν
text.english: lying midmost of the sea, where once the cattle‑rustling Titan
text.note: βοοκλόπος Τιτάν: “Titan” is a divine title (often of Helios), but the scene evokes bovine crossing lore at the Bosporus (etymologically “Cow’s Ford,” linked to Io). The epithet “cattle‑rustling” is striking and has prompted varying identifications (Zeus in bovine myth, Helios, etc.); the line likely conflates such traditions.

text.greek: ταύρῳ ἐφεζόμενος βριαρῷ πόρον ἔσχισε λίμνης.
text.english: sitting astride a mighty bull, cleft the strait of the sea.
text.note: πόρος (“ford, passage”) here = “strait.” ἐφεζόμενος with the dative = “sitting upon, astride.”

text.greek: Καί ῥα πανημερίῃσι πονεύμενοι εἰρεσίῃσι,
text.english: And then, toiling all day long with the oars,
text.note: εἰρεσίαι (“oars”) is a poetic term; πανημερίῃσι is an instrumental dative, “throughout whole days.”

text.greek: Μαιώτας πρώτους ἀφικάνομεν ἁβροχίτωνας·
text.english: we first reached the soft‑robed Maeotae;
text.note: The Maeotae dwell by Lake Maeotis (the Sea of Azov). ἁβροχίτωνες “soft‑/luxury‑robed” is an epic epithet.

text.greek: ἠδὲ Γελωνὸν ἔθνος, Βαθυχαίτων τ' ἄπλετα φῦλα,
text.english: and the nation of the Geloni, and the boundless tribes of the Deep‑robed,
text.note: Βαθυχαίτων may be an ethnicon (“Bathychaitones”) or an epithet meaning “deep-/long‑robed” applied to the tribes; the reference is uncertain.

text.greek: Σαυρομάτας τε, Γέτας καὶ Γυμναίους Κέκρυφάς τε
text.english: and the Sauromatae, the Getae, the Gymnaei, and the Kekryphae,
text.note: Κεκρυφάς is an obscure ethnicon; the form recalls κέκρυφα(λη), a woman’s hair‑net, and many consider the reading uncertain.

text.greek: ἀρσωπάς τ' Ἀρίμασπας, ἔθνη πολυπήμονα λαῶν
text.english: and the grim‑eyed Arimaspians—much‑afflicted peoples of men—
text.note: ἀρσωπάς is likely corrupt; many emend to ἀγριωπάς “grim‑eyed,” fitting the Arimaspians (mythic one‑eyed Scythian people). ἔθνη πολυπήμονα λαῶν = “much‑afflicted peoples of men.”

text.greek: ὧν περιναιετάει ἐν γῇ Μαιώτιδα λίμνην.
text.english: in whose land folk dwell around the Maeotic lake.
text.note: Syntax: περιναιετάει with accusative Μαιώτιδα λίμνην conveys “is inhabited around the Maeotic lake” in their land; Lake Maeotis = the Sea of Azov.

text.greek: - Αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ μὲν τοῖσι δύην ἀμέγαρτον ἔθηκαν
text.english: But when indeed the Immortals granted them an ungrudged passage,
text.note: δύην ἀμέγαρτον is difficult. δύη usually means “distress,” but here most take it (by context and from δύω ‘enter, pass through’) as “a passage/way,” with ἀμέγαρτος (‘ungrudged, freely granted’) describing divine favor—thus “an ungrudged passage.” Some have suspected corruption, but the sense “the gods granted them an unhindered way” suits the context.

text.greek: ἀθάνατοι, πύματον δὲ βυθοῦ διαμείψαμεν ὕδωρ,
text.english: and at the last we traversed the water of the deep,
text.note: πύματον (‘last, final’) suggests the final reach of waters before the transition to the stream leading to Okeanos. Note the narrator’s first-person plural, consistent with Orpheus’ voice in this poem.

text.greek: (ὄχθῃσι χθαμαλῇσιν ἀποβλύει αἰπὺν ὄλεθρον,
text.english: (along low banks it belches sheer destruction,
text.note: The subject is the powerful stream just below; ἀποβλύει (‘spouts, belches forth’) and αἰπὺν ὄλεθρον (“sheer ruin”) depict a destructive outflow along low banks.

text.greek: ῥοίζῳ ἐλαυνομένη· καναχεῖ δέ τοι ἄσπετος ὕλη
text.english: driven with a roar; and a boundless woodland clatters
text.note: ῥοίζος is the rushing roar of water; καναχεῖ (“clatters, rings”) is onomatopoetic. ἄσπετος (“boundless, unspeakable”) is epic hyperbole for an immense forest swept along.

text.greek: ἀρκτῴοις περάτεσσιν ἐπέρχεται Ὠκεανόνδε)·
text.english: and at the Arctic boundaries it goes toward Okeanos);
text.note: ἀρκτῴοις περάτεσσιν (“at the northern boundaries,” i.e., under the Bear/Arctos) reflects mythic northern geography; Ὠκεανό(ν)δε (with -δε) means “toward Okeanos.” The river is often identified by commentators with a northern world-river (e.g., Eridanus or Tanais) in mythic cartography.

text.greek: τῷ ῥα τόθ' ἁρπαχθεῖσα διὰ στόματος κίεν Ἀργώ.
text.english: by it then, snatched along, through the mouth went Argo.
text.note: τῷ refers to the stream just described; διὰ στόματος is “through the (river’s) mouth.” ἁρπαχθεῖσα conveys being seized/swept by the current.

text.greek: Ἐννέα μὲν νύκτας τε καὶ ἤματα μοχθίζοντες
text.english: Nine nights and days, toiling,
text.note: μὲν is lightly contrastive; the syntax continues into the following lines with the main verb at 1072.

text.greek: λείπομεν ἔνθα καὶ ἔνθα βροτῶν ἀγνώσια φῦλα,
text.english: we left behind, here and there, the unknown tribes of mortals,
text.note: ἀγνώσια φῦλα: “unknown tribes,” i.e., peoples unfamiliar to Greeks; ἔνθα καὶ ἔνθα = “here and there, hither and thither.”

text.greek: Πακτῶν Αρκτείων τε γένος, Λελίων τ' ἀγερώχων,
text.english: the race of the Paktoi and the Arkteioi, and the lordly Lelioi,
text.note: Paktoi likely the Pactyans (Indo-Iranian region); Arkteioi are obscure/uncertain; Lelioi likewise uncertain. ἀγερώχων = “lordly, high-handed.”

text.greek: τοξοφόρους τε Σκύθας, Ἄρεος πιστοὺς θεράποντας·
text.english: and the bow-bearing Scythians, faithful attendants of Ares;
text.note: Scythians stereotyped in Greek ethnography as archers and devotees of war; hence “bow-bearing … attendants of Ares.”

text.greek: Ταύρους τ' ἀνδροφάγους, οἳ ἀμειδέα θύσθλα φέρουσι
text.english: and the man-eating Taurians, who carry unsmiling sacrificial implements
text.note: The Taurians (of the Crimea) were famed in myth for grim rites. θύσθλα are “sacrificial implements” (often a Bacchic term); ἀμειδέα = “unsmiling, grim.”

text.greek: Μουνυχίῃ, βροτέῳ δ' ἐπιδεύεται αἵματι κρητήρ·
text.english: at Mounychia, and the krater is in want of mortal blood;
text.note: Μουνυχίῃ may mean “at Mounychia” (the Attic sanctuary/festival of Artemis Mounychia) or “for Mounychia (Artemis).” The krater “in want of mortal blood” evokes the (reported) Taurian custom of human sacrifice to Artemis.

text.greek: ἂν δ' ἄρ' Ὑπερβορέους, Νομάδας καὶ Κάσπιον ἔθνος.
text.english: and then the Hyperboreans, the Nomads, and the Caspian nation.
text.note: ἂν δ’ ἄρ’ is problematic; many emend to ἔνθα/ἔπειτα δ’ ἄρ’. The line continues the ethnographic catalogue: Hyperboreans, generic “Nomads,” and a Caspian people.

text.greek: - Αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ δεκάτη ἐφάνη φαεσίμβροτος ἠώς,
text.english: But when the tenth, man-illumining Dawn appeared,

text.greek: Ῥιπαίους αὐλῶνας ἐκέλσαμεν, ἐκ δ' ἄφαρ Ἄργώ
text.english: we cleared the Rhipaean glens, and straightway Argo
text.note: Ῥιπαίους αὐλῶνας: the ‘Rhipaean’ glens/vales, i.e., mythical northern mountains; ἐκέλσαμεν is a nautical aorist (probably from κέλλω), here ‘we cleared/sailed out of.’

text.greek: ἆγεν ἐπιπροθέουσα διὰ στεινοῖο ῥεέθρου·
text.english: led on, rushing forward, through the narrow current;

text.greek: ἔμπεσε δ' Ὠκεανῷ, Κρόνιον δέ ἑ κικλήσκουσι,
text.english: and it fell into Okeanos; they call it the Kronian,
text.note: ἔμπεσε (‘fell into’) is used of a stream debouching; ἑ (‘it’) refers to the sea understood; Κρόνιον (‘Kronian’) denotes the sea associated with Kronos (the far northern ocean).

text.greek: πόντον Ὑπερβόρεοι μέροπες, νεκρήν τε θάλασσαν·
text.english: sea, the Hyperborean mortal men, and the Dead Sea.
text.note: Μέροπες (‘meropes’) is the Homeric epithet ‘articulate-speaking’ for men; ‘Dead Sea’ here means the motionless northern ocean, not the Levantine lake.

text.greek: Οὐκέτι δὲ προφυγεῖν ἐδοκεῦμεν λυγρὸν ὄλεθρον
text.english: No longer did we deem we should elude woeful destruction,

text.greek: εἰ μὴ ἄρ' ὁρμαίνουσαν ὑπὸ κρατερῇφι βίηφι
text.english: unless, as she was being driven under mighty force,
text.note: ὁρμαίνουσαν (‘pondering/hesitating’) is used by personification of the ship; ὑπὸ κρατερῇφι βίηφι likely refers to the force of the stream/current driving her.

text.greek: νῆα μολεῖν ἴθυν' ἐπὶ δεξιὸν αἰγιαλοῖο
text.english: the ship were made to go straight for the right-hand shore,

text.greek: Ἀγκαῖος, ξεστοῖσι πιθήσας πηδαλίοισιν.
text.english: by Ankaios, who made her obey the well-planed steering-oars.
text.note: πηδάλια are steering-oars (not a fixed sternpost rudder); ξεστοῖσι = ‘well-planed/polished,’ marking fine craftsmanship.

text.greek: Ἣ δ' ἔθορεν δισσαῖσι βιησαμένη παλάμῃσιν.
text.english: She leapt up, exerting her strength with both hands.
text.note: βιησαμένη is the middle participle of βιάζομαι (“to use force, strain”), here expressing manner; δισσαῖσι παλάμῃσιν is an instrumental dative, “with both hands.” ἔθορεν is the aorist of θρῴσκω (“to spring, leap”).

text.greek: Ἀλλ' ὅτε δὴ μογερῇσιν ἐδαμνάμεθ' εἰρεσίῃσι,
text.english: But when at last we were overcome by the toilsome oars,
text.note: μογερῇσιν (dat. pl. of μογερός, “toilsome, wretched”) modifies εἰρεσίῃσι (“oars”) in an instrumental dative; ἐδαμνάμεθ’ (“we were overcome/worn down”) conveys exhaustion from rowing.

text.greek: χεῖρες δ' οὐκέτ' ἔμιμνον, ἀκηχέμενοι δὲ φίλον κῆρ
text.english: our hands could hold out no longer, and, grieving in our dear heart,

text.greek: πήχεας ἀμπλέξαντες, ἐνηρείσαντο μέτωπα,
text.english: having twined our forearms, we propped our brows upon them,
text.note: πήχεας = “forearms”; ἐνηρείσαντο is the aorist middle of (ἐν-)ἐρείδω, “to press/lean,” with an understood object of support (“upon them,” i.e., the folded arms).

text.greek: ἱδρῶ ἀποψύχοντε· κέαρ δ' ἐπετείρετο λιμῷ.
text.english: letting the sweat cool; and our heart was sorely pressed by hunger.
text.note: ἱδρῶ ἀποψύχοντε = “cooling (off) the sweat,” a compressed expression; ἐπετείρετο (from ἐπιτείρω) “was pressed/oppressed” takes the dative λιμῷ (“by hunger”).

text.greek: Ἀγκαῖος δ' ἐξᾶλτο, καὶ ἄλλους πάντας ὄτρυνεν
text.english: But Ankaios leapt forth and roused all the others,

text.greek: ἥρωας, μαλακοῖσι παραιφάμενος ἐπέεσσιν·
text.english: the heroes, coaxing them with gentle words.
text.note: “παραιφάμενος” conveys soothing/coaxing persuasion; hence “coaxing … with gentle words.”

text.greek: Οἳ δ' ἐπεὶ οὖν τέναγός τε πολυστρέπτοισι κάλωσι
text.english: And when then, with many-twisted cables, toward the shoal
text.note: τέναγος is a rare term for “shoal/lagoon” and the syntax is enjambed; it is taken adverbially with the following participle (“going toward/into the shoal”).

text.greek: βάντες ὑπὲρ τοίχων ἅλαδε σφυρὰ κοῦφα βάλοντο,
text.english: they went, over the bulwarks seaward they lightly cast their nimble ankles,
text.note: σφυρά “ankles”: σφυρά κοῦφα βάλONTO is idiomatic for leaping lightly down; hence “lightly cast their nimble ankles.”

text.greek: ὦκα δ' ἄρ' ἀρτήσαντο πολυστρέπτοισι κάλωσι,
text.english: and quickly they made fast with the many-twisted cables,

text.greek: πρύμνης ἐξ ὑπάτης, δολιχὴν μήρινθα βαλόντες
text.english: from the lofty stern, casting a long mooring-rope,
text.note: μήρινθα is a nautical term for a mooring-rope/cable; ἐξ ὑπάτης “from the lofty [part]” refers to the raised stern.

text.greek: Ἄργος τ' Ἀγκαῖός τε καὶ ἀρχὰς δῶκαν ἑλέσθαι·
text.english: and Argos and Ankaios too gave the word to take the lead;
text.note: Ἀρχὰς δῶκαν ἑλέσθαι is an idiom, “gave the word to begin/to take the lead,” here the signal to start the haul.

text.greek: ἡρώων τοὶ δ' αἶψα δι' αἰγιαλοῖο θέοντες
text.english: and the heroes straightway, running along the strand,

text.greek: σῦρον ἐπειγόμενοι· σὺν δ' ἕσπετο ποντοπόρος νηῦς,
text.english: were dragging her in haste; and the sea-faring ship followed with them,

text.greek: τέμνουσ' ὑγρὰ κέλευθα παρὰ ξεστοῖς κροκάλοισιν.
text.english: cleaving wet ways beside the polished pebbles.
text.note: “ὑγρὰ κέλευθα” (lit. “wet ways”) is an epic expression for the paths cut through water; “ξεστοῖς κροκάλοισιν” are smoothed/polished beach-pebbles.

text.greek: Οὐ γάρ οἱ λιγὺς οὖρος ὑπὸ πνοιῇσιν ὄρινε
text.english: For no shrilling fair wind beneath the blasts
text.note: λιγὺς οὖρος = “shrilling/shrill fair wind”; οἱ is a dative of reference (“for them,” i.e., the Argonauts). ὑπὸ πνοιῇσιν βυκτάων ἀνέμων is instrumental (“beneath/by the blasts of close‑packed winds”), emphasizing that no breeze at all stirred the water.

text.greek: βυκτάων ἀνέμων κείνην ἅλα· κωφὰ δὲ πόντος
text.english: of close‑packed winds stirred that sea for them; the sea was mute,
text.note: κωφὰ (“deaf”) is a conventional metaphor for a dead calm, hence “mute.” Note that κείνην ἅλα (“that sea”) is the object carried over from the previous line’s ὄρινε (“stirred”).

text.greek: κεῖθ' οὗπέρ θ' Ἑλίκης καὶ Τηθύος ἔσχατον ὕδωρ.
text.english: there where lies the uttermost water of Helike and Tethys.
text.note: Helike = the Great Bear (Ursa Major); Tethys = the personified Ocean. ἔσχατον ὕδωρ (“uttermost water”) evokes the world-encircling Ocean at the limits of the sea, a Homeric-style cosmographic periphrasis.

text.greek: - Αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ ἕκτη φαεσίμβροτος ἤλυθεν ἠώς,
text.english: But when the sixth dawn, light-bringing to mortals, had come,
text.note: φαεσίμβροτος (“light-bringing to mortals”) is a traditional epic epithet of Dawn (ἠώς).

text.greek: ἔθνος ἐς ἀφνειὸν καὶ πλούσιον ἐξικόμεσθα
text.english: we reached a nation opulent and wealthy,

text.greek: Μακροβίων, οἳ δὴ πολέας ζώουσ' ἐνιαυτούς,
text.english: of the Makrobioi, who indeed live many years,
text.note: Μακροβίων is the ethnonym “Long-lived,” known from Greek ethnographic lore (cf. Herodotus).

text.greek: δώδεκα χιλιάδας μηνῶν ἑκατονταετήρων
text.english: twelve thousand months of centuries’ span,
text.note: The phrase δώδεκα χιλιάδας μηνῶν ἑκατονταετήρων is notoriously compact: either “twelve thousand months” (≈ 1000 years), with ἑκατονταετήρων (“of centuries”) underscoring the centuried span, or hyperbolically “hundred-year months.” The translation takes it as months amounting to centuries.

text.greek: πληθούσης μήνης χαλεπῶν ἔκτοσθεν ἁπάντων·
text.english: while the moon is waxing, outside all hardships;
