text.note: μήνη here is best taken as “moon” (not merely “month”): πληθούσης μήνης = “as the moon waxes,” a lunar measure of their painless life.

text.greek: αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ μηνὸς τὸ πεπρωμένον ἐξανύσωσιν,
text.english: but when they fulfil the fated portion of the month,
text.note: τὸ πεπρωμένον (“the fated/allotted [portion]”) continues the temporal imagery; μηνός keeps the lunar/monthly register.

text.greek: ὕπνῳ ὑπὸ γλυκερῷ θανάτου μάρπτουσι τελευτήν·
text.english: in the sweet sleep of death they meet their end;
text.note: μάρπτουσι τελευτήν (“they seize/meet their end”) renders an idiom; “sweet sleep of death” is an epic euphemism for dying gently.

text.greek: Οὐ δ' ἄρα τοῖσι μέλει βίοτος καὶ ἔργ' ἀνθρώπων,
text.english: nor are livelihood and the works of mortals a care to them,

text.greek: ποίαις δ' ἐν μεσάταις μελιηδέα φορβὰ νέμονται
text.english: but amid grassy meadows they graze honey-sweet pasture,
text.note: νέμονται with φορβή (“graze pasture”) is literal but applied to these blissful mortals; ποίαις μεσάταις = “meadows in the midst,” i.e., lush central meads.

text.greek: ἕρσῃ ὑπ' ἀμβροσίῃ θεῖον ποτὸν ἐξαρύοντες,
text.english: beneath ambrosial dew, drawing forth divine drink,
text.note: ἕρση ἀμβροσία (“ambrosial dew”) evokes paradisal sustenance; θεῖον ποτόν (“divine drink”) recalls, without naming, the fare of the blessed.

text.greek: πάντες ὁμῶς στίλβοντες ὁμηλικίην ἐρατεινήν·
text.english: all alike resplendent in lovely coeval youth;
text.note: ὁμηλικίη (“coeval age”) suggests ageless, equal prime for all; στἰλβοντες (“shining”) marks ideal beauty.

text.greek: Μειλιχίη δέ τοι αἰὲν ἐπ' ὀφρύσι νεῦσε γαλήνη
text.english: and a gentle calm ever nods upon their brows
text.note: Μειλιχίη γαλήνη is a personified “gentle calm”; νεῦσε ἐπ’ ὀφρύσι (“nods upon the brows”) = “rests/abides upon their faces,” an epic turn.

text.greek: παίδεσιν ἠδὲ τοκεῦσιν, ἐπὶ φρεσὶν ἠδὲ νόοιο,
text.english: for children and for parents alike, upon heart and upon mind,
text.note: The double expression ἐπὶ φρεσὶν ἠδὲ νόοιο (mixed dative/genitive) jointly denotes the inner faculties (heart/mind).

text.greek: αἴσιμά τε ῥέζειν πεπνυμένα τ' ἐξαγορεύειν.
text.english: to do what is due and to utter prudent words.
text.note: αἴσιμα = “what is fitting/right (according to due order/fate)”; πεπνυμένα = “prudent, sage”; ἐξαγορεύειν = “to speak out plainly/declare.”

text.greek: - Καὶ τοὺς μέν ῥ' ἀθρόους παραμείβομεν, αἰγιαλόνδε
text.english: And those we passed by in a body, to the strand, treading with our feet.
text.note: ἀθρόους can be taken adverbially (“altogether”) or as qualifying τούς (“those [standing] in a mass”); the antecedent is from the prior context. αἰγιαλόνδε is the Homeric allative “to the strand.” ποσσὶν ἐπιστείβοντες literally “pressing with the feet,” likely of towing/hauling the ship along the shore.

text.greek: ποσσὶν ἐπιστείβοντες· ἔπειτα δὲ Κιμμερίοισι
text.english: then to the Cimmerians,
text.note: Κιμμερίοισι (dat. pl.) “to the Cimmerians,” the sunless people of Od. 11; the dative of goal is completed by ἱκάνομεν in the next line.

text.greek: νῆα θοὴν ἐπάγοντες ἱκάνομεν, οἵ ῥά τε μοῦνοι
text.english: bringing the swift ship, we came,
text.note: ἐπάγοντες (“bringing along/toward”) is a technical verb for towing or beaching a ship; nuance retained in the translation.

text.greek: αἴγλης ἄμμοροί εἰσι πυριβρόμου ἠελίοιο.
text.english: who alone are without a share in the radiance of fire-roaring Helios.
text.note: αἴγλης ἄμμοροι = “without a share of radiance” (genitive with ἄμμορος). πυριβρόμου ἠελίοιο is an Orphic-style epithet, “fire-roaring Helios,” preserving the theonym Helios.

text.greek: Ἐν μὲν γὰρ Ῥίπαιον ὄρος καὶ Κάλπιος αὐχήν
text.english: For indeed the Rhipaean mountain and the Calpian neck
text.note: Ῥίπαιον ὄρος (Rhipaean mountain) is the mythic northern range; Κάλπιος αὐχήν (“Calpian neck”) refers to Calpe (the Rock of Gibraltar), here imagined as a ridge/neck. The juxtaposition is part of a poetic, non‑literal world‑geography.

text.greek: ἀντολίας εἴργουσιν ἐπικέκλιται δὲ πελώρη
text.english: shut out the dawns; and huge Phlegra leans over,
text.note: ἀντολίας (plural) = “sunrises/dawns.” πελώρη (“huge, monstrous”) modifies Φλέγρη (Phlegra), a toponym with mythic resonance; ἐπικέκλιται “leans over/overhangs.”

text.greek: ἆσσον ἐπισκιάουσα μεσημβρινὸν ἠέρα Φλέγρη·
text.english: casting a nearer shadow on the noonday air.
text.note: ἆσσον “nearer, more closely”; ἐπισκιάουσα “overshadowing.” μεσημβρινὸν ἠέρα “the noonday/southern air,” a poetic way to mark the south.

text.greek: δείελον αὖ κρύπτουσι φάος ταναηκέες Ἄλπεις
text.english: In turn the sky‑pointing Alps hide the clear light
text.note: ταναηκέες “sky‑pointing, long‑peaked.” δείελον φάος “clear/bright daylight.”

text.greek: κείνοισιν μερόπεσσιν, ἀχλὺς δ' ἐπικέκλιται αἰεί,
text.english: from those mortal men, and a mist ever lies upon them.
text.note: κείνοισιν μερόπεσσιν “for those mortal men” (meropes = humans). The antecedent of “them” (regions/inhabitants) is deliberately broad; ἀχλὺς ἐπικέκλιται “a mist lies/hangs over.”

text.greek: Ἔνθα δ' ἀφορμηθέντες ἐπειγομένοισι πόδεσσιν
text.english: Thence, setting out with hurrying feet,
text.note: ἀφορμηθέντες “setting out, taking departure”; ἐπειγομένοισι πόδεσσιν “with hurrying/pressed feet,” a Homeric‑style instrumental dative.

text.greek: ἵξομεν ἀγκῶνα στυφελὸν καὶ νήνεμον ἀκτήν,
text.english: we reached a rugged elbow and a windless shore,
text.note: ἀγκών “elbow,” a common metaphor for a projecting headland; στυφελός “harsh, rugged”; νήνεμος ἀκτή “windless shore.”

text.greek: ἔνθα περ ἀμβλύζων ποταμὸς δίναισι βαθείαις
text.english: where indeed a river, murmuring with deep eddies,
text.note: ἀμβλύζων is onomatopoetic, often of a dull/muffled plashing or murmuring; “with deep eddies” (δίναισι βαθείαις) explains the sound.

text.greek: θείει χρυσορόας Ἀχέρων κρυεροῦ διὰ χώρου,
text.english: runs, the gold‑flowing Acheron, through a chill land,
text.note: θείει “runs, speeds.” χρυσορόας Ἀχέρων “gold‑flowing Acheron” is striking and unusual for Acheron (more typical of Pactolus); likely an ornamental color‑epithet or a transferred trait. κρυεροῦ διὰ χώρου “through a chill land.”

text.greek: ἀργυροειδὲς ὕδος προρέων, λίμνη τε κελαινή
text.english: pouring forth silver‑bright water; and a dusky lake
text.note: ἀργυροειδὲς ὕδος “silver‑like water,” i.e., silvery in appearance; λίμνη κελαινὴ “dusky/dark lake,” plausibly the Acherousian lake.

text.greek: ἀνδέχεται· παταγεῖ δὲ παρ' ὄχθαισιν ποταμοῖο
text.english: receives it; and by the river‑banks the luxuriant trees resound,
text.note: παταγεῖ (from παταγέω) “clatters, resounds,” here of trees along the bank, taking plural δένδρεα as subject with singular verb (epic convention).

text.greek: δένδρεα τηλεθάοντα ποτὶ σχεδὸν οἷσιν καρπός
text.english: close upon which the fruit lies heavy,
text.note: τηλεθάοντα “luxuriant, flourishing.” ποτὶ σχεδόν “close upon/near at hand.” οἷσιν dative of relation: “close upon which (trees) the fruit….” βέβριθε (perf.) “has weighed [them] down/is heavy.”

text.greek: βέβριθε νύκτας τε καὶ ἤματα συννεχὲς αἰεί.
text.english: by nights and by days, unceasingly, forever.
text.note: νύκτας τε καὶ ἤματα συννεχές αἰεί piles adverbs for epic emphasis: “by night and by day, continuously, always.”

text.greek: Ἀμφὶ δέ οἱ χθαμαλή τε καὶ εὔβοτος Ἑρμιονεία
text.english: And around it low-lying and well-pastured Hermione
text.note: Ἀμφὶ δέ οἱ = “around it,” with the dative pronoun referring to a previously mentioned locale; χθαμαλή “low-lying,” εὔβοτος “rich in pasture.” Ἑρμιονεία = Hermione (city/territory in Argolis); epic form varies (cf. Ἑρμιονείη).

text.greek: τείχεσιν ἠρήρεισται ἐϋκτιμέναις ἐπ' ἀγυιαῖς.
text.english: is girt with walls along her well-built streets.
text.note: ἠρήρεισται (perf. pass. 3 sg. of ἀραρίσκω) “has been fitted/fastened,” hence “is girt” with τείχεσιν “walls.” ἐπ’ ἀγυιαῖς ἐϋκτιμέναις = “along the well-built streets” (the adjective agrees with ἀγυιαῖς, not with τείχεσιν).

text.greek: Ἐν δὲ γένη ζώουσι δικαιοτάτων ἀνθρώπων
text.english: And there dwell the races of the most righteous men,
text.note: “There” (En de) points back to the locale just described in context; gēnē = “races/tribes,” retaining epic diction.

text.greek: οἷσιν ἀποφθιμένοισιν ἅλις ναῦς ἴα τέτυκται,
text.english: for whom, once they have perished, a single ship has been made ready in sufficiency,
text.note: ἅλις is transmitted here; it can be taken adverbially “enough, in sufficiency,” yielding the sense that “one ship suffices” (sc. the ferry). Many take ἅλις as ἁλί (“at sea”), but the context of Acheron and the ferry favors the adverbial reading. ναῦς ἴα emphasizes “a single ship,” and τέτυκται (perf. mid.) = “has been fashioned/is ready.”

text.greek: καὶ δ' αὖ αἱ ψυχαὶ μετεκίαθον εἰς Ἀχέροντα
text.english: and again their souls passed across to Acheron
text.note: μετεκίαθον (aor.) = “went across/went after,” of souls moving toward/over Acheron (the underworld river).

text.greek: πορθμίδος ἐκ γλαφυρῆς· σχεδόθεν δέ οἱ εἰσὶ πόληες
text.english: from the hollow ferry-boat; and near to it are cities,
text.note: πορθμίδος is the ferry-boat (not the ferryman; cf. πορθμεύς). γλαφυρῆς = “hollow,” standard epic epithet for boats. οἱ is dative referring to Acheron: “near to it.” πόληες is epic for πόλεις.

text.greek: ἄρρηκτοί τ' Ἀίδαο πύλαι καὶ δῆμος ὀνείρων.
text.english: and the unbreakable gates of Aidēs and the district of Dreams.
text.note: ἄρρηκτοι “unbreakable” (of the gates of Aidēs). δῆμος ὀνείρων = the “district/domain of Dreams,” with δῆμος used in a topographical sense rather than “people.”

text.greek: Ἀλλ' ὅτε δὴ καὶ τῶνδε πόλιν καὶ ἤθεα λαῶν
text.english: But when indeed even the city of these men and the ways of the people
text.note: ἤθεα (“ways, customs, habits”) of a people; τῶνδε refers deictically to the group just encountered.

text.greek: σφῇ ἄτῃ βαρὺν οἶτον ἀναπλήσαντες ἔβημεν,
text.english: we had brought to the full measure of heavy doom by their own infatuation, we went our way,
text.note: σφῇ ἄτῃ is an instrumental dative (“by their own infatuation/delusion”). βαρὺν οἶτον ἀναπλήσαντες is a compressed epic idiom, “bringing heavy doom to fulfillment”; the translation expands the sense to avoid the double accusative with πόλιν καὶ ἤθεα.

text.greek: δή ῥα τότ' Ἀγκαῖος νηὸς κίεν· αἶψα δὲ πάντας
text.english: then indeed Ankaios made for the ship; and straightway
text.note: νηὸς κίεν is Homeric for “went to the ship,” with the genitive after a verb of motion indicating goal.

text.greek: εἰσβαίνειν ἐκέλευσε κεκμηότας ἄμμιγ' ἑταίρους.
text.english: he bade all the comrades, wearied, to embark together.
text.note: ἄμμιγ’ (for ἅμμιγα) is an adverb “together”; κεκμηότας (perf. part.) has present force, “wearied, spent.”

text.greek: Τοὺς ὅγε καὶ μύθοισι προσηύδα μειλιχίοισι·
text.english: And to them he indeed addressed gentle words:
text.note: ὅγε (“he indeed”) gives emphatic focus to the subject; μειλιχίοις μύθοισι is a traditional epic formula for “soothing/gentle words.”

text.greek: - "Τλῆτε φίλοι τὸν μόχθον· ἐπεὶ νύ τοι οὔτι χέρειον
text.english: “Endure, friends, the toil; for now indeed I expect that no mean wind will arise,
text.note: οὔτι χέρειον (‘by no means inferior/worse’) has an understood subject, i.e., a breeze/wind; ἀνστήσεσθαι is the epic form of ‘to rise’ (of winds).

text.greek: ἔλπομαι ἀνστήσεσθαι· ἐπιφρίσσοντα γὰρ ἤδη
text.english: for already I behold the keen Zephyros that makes one shiver;
text.note: ἐπιφρίσσοντα means ‘causing to bristle/ruffle’ (of wind on skin or sea); ἀκραῆ = ‘piercing/keen’; καταδέρκομαι = ‘I behold.’ Zephyros is the West Wind.

text.greek: ἀκραῆ ζέφυρον καταδέρκομαι· οὐδ' ἀτέκμαρτον
text.english: nor without a sign
text.note: ἀτέκμαρτον means ‘without a token/sign’ (τέκμαρ). The phrase signals that the following phenomenon is an omen of wind.

text.greek: ὕδωρ Ὠκεανοῦ κελαρύζεται ἐν ψαμάθοισιν.
text.english: does the water of Okeanos gurgle among the sands.”
text.note: κελαρύζεται (‘gurgles, babbles’) of water among sands evokes surf-sounds as a portent; Ὠκεανός is transliterated as Okeanos.

text.greek: Ἀλλὰ θοῶς ἱστὸν μὲν ἀναστήσασθε μεσόδμῃ
text.english: But swiftly raise the mast at the mid‑thwart,
text.note: μεσόδμῃ = “at the mid‑thwart” (the central bench/midships). Epic nautical term for the mast‑step location.

text.greek: λύσατε δὲ προτόνων ὀθόνας· ἐκ δ' ὅπλα χέοντες
text.english: and loose the sails from the forestays; and, bringing out the gear,
text.note: πρότονοι are the forestays; ὀθόνες = “sail‑cloths,” here the stay‑sails. λύσατε can mean “loosen/unfurl” depending on context.

text.greek: σφίγξατ' ἐπισταμένως, τοίχων ἑκάτερθε βαλόντες."
text.english: lash them firm, expertly, casting them along the bulwarks on either side.”
text.note: ὅπλα here likely “gear, tackle” (not weapons); σφίγγειν = “make fast, lash”; τοῖχοι = the ship’s sides/bulwarks.

text.greek: - Ὣς οἳ μὲν τὰ ἕκαστα πονήατο· ἐκ δ' ἄρα κοίλης
text.english: So they set about each his several tasks; and from the hollow
text.note: Formulaic: “each his several tasks.” οἳ μὲν marks their part of the action.

text.greek: νηὸς ἐπιβρομέουσα Τομαριὰς ἔκλαγε φηγός,
text.english: ship the Tomarian oak, booming, cried aloud,
text.note: Τομαριὰς = “of Tomaros,” i.e., the Dodonaean oak. ἐπιβρομέουσα = “booming, thunder‑sounding,” of a portentous cry.

text.greek: ἥν ποθ' ὑπ' Ἀργῴαισι τομαῖς ἡρμόσσατο Παλλάς.
text.english: that which once Pallas had fitted beneath Argive adze‑strokes.
text.note: ἥν … ἡρμώσσατο: the famous speaking timber from Dodona that Pallas (Athena) fitted into Argo. ὑπ’ Ἀργῴαισι τομαῖς = “beneath Argive cuttings,” i.e., under the strokes of the Argive adze.

text.greek: Ὧδε δ' ἔφη (θάμβος δὲ περὶ φρένας ἵκετο πάντας)·
text.english: Thus she spoke (and wonder encompassed the minds of all);
text.note: ἔφη is gender-indeterminate; the context (Medea) motivates “she.” θάμβος = awe/wonder “around the mind.”

text.greek: - "Ὤ μοι ἐγὼν, ὄφελόν με διαρραισθεῖσαν ὀλέσθαι
text.english: Alas for me! Would that I had perished, shattered asunder,
text.note: διαρραισθεῖσαν (aor. pass. ptcp., fem.) “smashed/torn asunder,” with με as object; the image anticipates being crushed between the rocks.

text.greek: Κυανέαις πέτραισιν ἐν ἀξείνῳ τε κλύδωνι·
text.english: among the Cyanean Rocks and in the inhospitable surge;
text.note: Κυανέαι πέτραι = the Symplegades; ἀξείνου κλύδων = the “inhospitable” surge, i.e., the Pontos (Euxine).

text.greek: ἦ καὶ νῦν ἀνάπυστον ἀϊδρείῃ βασιλήων
text.english: then even now, through the ignorance of kings, I would be unheard of,
text.note: ἀνάπυστον in the MSS is difficult beside νώνυμνον; many emend to ἄπυστον (“unheard of”). Translation follows the sense “unknown/unheard of.” βασιλῆες likely refers to ruling powers (e.g., Aeetes and others).

text.greek: νώνυμνον φορέεσκον· ἐπεὶ νῦν αἰεὶ Ἐριννύς
text.english: I would be bearing a nameless name; for now ever the Erinnys
text.note: νώνυμνον “nameless”; φορέεσκον is iterative (“I should be wont to bear”). Ἐριννύς (sing.) functions as the avenging Fury.

text.greek: αἵματος ἐμφύλοιο δεδουπότος Ἀψύρτοιο
text.english: of Apsyrtos’ kindred blood—blood that was shed—
text.note: δεδουπότος is textually problematic; sense demands “of blood that was shed/spilled.” ἐμφύλιος = “of kindred.” Ἀψύρτος (Apsyrtos) in the genitive.

text.greek: ὑστερόπους ἕπεται· στέργει δὲ τοι ἄτη ἐπ' ἄτην.
text.english: follows with tardy foot; and indeed Atê loves ruin upon ruin.
text.note: ὑστερόπους “late-footed” (of avengers who come late but surely). Ἄτη (Atê) personified as Ruin; στέργει = “loves/affects,” hence “Atê loves to heap ruin upon ruin.”

text.greek: Νῦν γὰρ δὴ λυγρῆς τε καὶ ἀργεννῆς κακότητος
text.english: For now indeed for the baleful and silvery wickedness
text.note: ἀργεννῆς (lit. “silvery, silver‑white”) modifying κακότητος is an unusual collocation; it may be purely color-epithetic (“bright/white wickedness”) or an allusion to the ‘evil of silver’ (greed). Some have suspected an emendation to ἀργυρῆς (“of silver”). λυγρός = “baleful, grievous.”

text.greek: τίσομαι ἂν νήσοισιν Ἰερνίσιν ἆσσον ἵκωμαι .
text.english: I shall exact vengeance from the Iernian islands, if I come nearer.
text.note: τίσομαι takes the dative of the party punished (νήσοισιν). ἂν with the subjunctive ἵκωμαι gives a future‑more‑vivid condition (“if I come nearer”). Ἰερνίσιν (‘Iernian’) refers to the western isles, commonly identified with Ierne (Ireland) or the British Isles.

text.greek: Εἰ μὴ γάρ μ' ἱερῇσιν ἐπιγνάμψαντες ἄκρῃσι
text.english: For unless you, by turning me in at the holy headlands,
text.note: ἐπιγνάμψαντες ἄκρῃσι: a nautical turn “to bear in toward/round the headlands.” The object μ’ (“me”) is the ship (ναῦς), here personified as speaking (cf. the Dodonaean beam). ἱεραῖσιν ἄκρῃσι likely alludes to the “sacred” promontories at the mouth of the Mediterranean (commonly identified with the Pillars of Heracles).

text.greek: κόλπον ἔσω γαίης τε καὶ ἀτρυγέτοιο θαλάσσης
text.english: the gulf within the land and the unharvested sea
text.note: κόλπος “gulf, bosom” = the enclosed sea; γαίης τε καὶ ἀτρυγέτοιο θαλάσσης “of land and the unharvested sea” describes the Mediterranean as an inner basin. ἀτρύγετος is the traditional epic epithet of the sea (“unharvested,” i.e., fruitless).

text.greek: ἵξεσθ', ἂμ πέλαγος Ἀτλαντικὸν ἐκτὸς ἵκωμαι."
text.english: you will reach—otherwise I should go out upon the Atlantic sea.”
text.note: ἵξεσθ’ belongs with the protasis (“unless … you reach”). ἂμ is textually awkward; many understand it as ἅμ’ (“at once”) or take it adverbially with the following clause. Sense: if they fail to turn in at the capes, the ship will head “outside” (ἐκτός) into the Atlantic. “Atlantic sea” renders πέλαγος Ἀτλαντικόν.

text.greek: - Ὣς εἰποῦσ' αὐδὴν κατερήτυεν· ἐν δ' ἄρα θυμός
text.english: Thus having spoken, she checked her voice;

text.greek: παχνώθη Μινύαισι διαμπερὲς, εἴτ' ἄρ' ἔμελλον
text.english: and the spirit of the Minyae grew numb through and through, whether indeed they were about
text.note: παχνώθη θυμός: metaphorical “the heart/spirits froze,” i.e., were seized with dread. διαμπερές “through and through, entirely.”

text.greek: σχήσειν λυγρὸν ὄλεθρον, Ἰάσονος εἵνεκα φίλτρων.
text.english: to incur grievous destruction, on account of the love-charms for Jason.
text.note: σχήσειν (fut. inf.) with ἔμελλον: “were about to incur/meet.” φίλτρα are love-charms/philtra; “on account of the love-charms for Jason” likely points to the dangerous consequences of Medea’s passion instigated for Jason.

text.greek: Πολλὰ δὲ μερμήριζον ἐνὶ φρεσὶ πευκαλίμῃσιν,
text.english: Much did they debate in their shrewd minds,
text.note: πευκαλίμῃσιν ("shrewd, prudent") is a Homeric-style epithet modifying phrenes (“minds”); μερμηρίζω conveys anxious, deep deliberation.

text.greek: ἤ μιν ἀποφθίσωσι καὶ ἰχθύσι κύρμα βάλωσιν
text.english: whether they should make her perish and cast her as spoil for the fishes,
text.note: ἀποφθίσσωσι (“destroy utterly”) and κῦρμα (“spoil, prey”) are strong, epic terms; the image is of making her a carcass for fish.

text.greek: αἰνολέχην Μήδειαν, ἀποστρέψωσι δ' Ἐριννύν,
text.english: dire‑speaking Medea, and so turn aside the Erinys,
text.note: αἰνολέχην (“dire‑speaking”) is a rare compound epithet of Medea; Ἐριννύς (Erinys) in the singular personifies vengeance/blood‑guilt; ἀποστρέφω here = “avert, turn aside.”

text.greek: εἰ μὴ ἄρ' ὀξὺ νόησε περικλυτὸς Αἴσονος υἱός,
text.english: had not the far‑famed son of Aison swiftly perceived it,
text.note: περικλυτός (“far‑famed”) is a standard heroic epithet; νόησε has an implicit object (“their counsel/intent”).

text.greek: καὶ τότε λισσόμενος θυμὸν κατερήτυ' ἑκάστου.
text.english: and then, in supplication, checked the spirit of each.
text.note: λισσόμενος (“beseeching, in supplication”); κατερήτυ’ is the epic contracted imperfect of κατερήτυε (“was restraining/checked”); θυμός = “spirit, heart.”

text.greek: Αὐτὰρ ἐπεί τ' Ἀργοῦς ἐτυμηγόρον ἔκλυον αὐδήν
text.english: But when they heard Argo’s truth-speaking voice,
text.note: ἐτυμηγόρον (“truth-speaking”) evokes Argo’s prophetic voice, traditionally from the Dodonaean oak built into her prow; αὐδή is the ship’s audible “voice.”

text.greek: ἧντο παρὰ σκαλμοῖσι θοῶς, λάζοντο δ' ἐρετμά.
text.english: they took their seats swiftly by the thole-pins and grasped the oars.
text.note: σκαλμοῖσι are the thole-pins (oar-pivots); ἧντο is the epic inceptive “sat down,” and λάζοντο (middle) “took hold (for themselves),” here of the oars.

text.greek: Ἀγκαῖος δ' οἴακας ἐπισταμένως ἐτίταινε·
text.english: But Ankaios skillfully kept the steering-oars taut.
text.note: oïakes = the stern ‘steering-oars’ (tillers); ἐτίταινε ‘was straining/keeping taut.’ Ankaios is the helmsman (in many traditions succeeding Tiphys).

text.greek: Πὰρ δ' ἄρα νῆσον ἄμειβεν Ἰερνίδα, καί οἱ ὄπισθεν
text.english: And the ship was passing along beside the island Iernis, and astern of her
text.note: Ἰερνίδα = ‘Iernis,’ commonly identified with Ireland; παρὰ νῆσον ἄμειβεν ‘was coasting past the island.’ οἱ ὄπισθεν = ‘astern (behind her/him),’ here rendered as ‘astern of her.’

text.greek: ἷκτο καταΐγδην δνοφερὴ τρομέουσα θύελλα,
text.english: there came headlong, with a crash, a murky, shuddering squall,
text.note: καταΐγδην is an adverb ‘headlong, with a crash’; δνοφερή ‘murky, gloomy’; τρομέουσα ‘shuddering/trembling,’ modifying θύελλα ‘squall.’

text.greek: ἐν δ' ὀθόνας κόλπωσε· θέεν δ' ἄφαρ ὑγρὸν ἐπ' οἶδμα
text.english: and it bellied the sails; and straightway the ship sped over the wet swell,
text.note: ὀθόνες ‘sails’; κολπόω of wind ‘to belly’ (make a pouch of) the sails; θέεν ‘sped, ran.’

text.greek: νηῦς· οὐ δή τις ἐσαῦθις ἀναπνεύσεσθαι ὀλέθρου
text.english: and then no one any longer hoped to draw breath again from destruction,
text.note: ἐσαῦθις ‘again/any more’; ἀναπνεῦσαι ὀλέθρου is an idiom ‘to recover breath from destruction,’ i.e., to escape death.

text.greek: ἤλπετο· δωδεκάτη γὰρ ἐπήϊεν ἠριγένεια.
text.english: for the twelfth Early-born Dawn was coming on.
text.note: ἠριγένεια is the fixed epithet of Eos (Dawn), ‘Early-born’; thus ‘the twelfth dawn.’ The goddess is implicit though not named.

text.greek: Οὐδέ τις ἔγνω ᾗσιν ἐνὶ φρεσὶν, οὗ ποτ' ἄρ' ἐσμέν,
text.english: Nor did anyone know within his own heart where indeed we were,
text.note: ᾗσιν ἐνὶ φρεσίν is the epic plural “in their own hearts/minds”; οὗ ποτ’ ἄρ’ intensifies “where indeed/at all.”

text.greek: εἰ μὴ ἐσχατιαῖς ἀκαλαρρόου Ὠκεανοῖο
text.english: save that at the uttermost bounds of turbid‑flowing Okeanos
text.note: ἐσχατιαῖς = “outermost borders.” The epithet ἀκαλαρρόου is rare/uncertain; taken here as “not fair‑flowing,” hence “turbid‑flowing,” of Okeanos (transliterated).

text.greek: Λυγκεὺς εἰσενόησεν (ὁ γὰρ τηλωπὸν ὄπωπε)
text.english: Lynceus perceived (for he was far‑sighted)
text.note: τηλωπὸν ὄπωπε is a perfect with stative sense, “he possessed far‑seeing sight”; Lynceus is traditionally famed for extraordinary vision.

text.greek: νῆσον πευκήεσσαν, ἰδ' εὐρέα δώματ' ἀνάσσης
text.english: a pine‑clad island, and the broad halls of the Queen
text.note: πευκήεσσαν is a Homeric‑type adjective “pine‑clad”; ἀνάσσης = “Lady/Queen,” anticipating the naming of Demeter in the next verse; ἰδ’ = καὶ ἴδε (“and [he] saw”).

text.greek: Δήμητρος· περὶ δ' αὖτε μέγα νέφος ἐστεφάνωται.
text.english: Demeter; and about it in turn a great cloud stood wreathed.
text.note: ἐστεφάνωται (perfect middle) has a stative value, “is/stood wreathed.” The referent of “it” (island or halls) is ambiguous; αὖτε = “in turn/again.”

text.greek: - Ὧν πέρι μῦθον ἅπαντ' ἔκλυες, Μουσαῖε δαΐφρον,
text.english: Of which you have heard the whole tale, O Musaeus, wise of mind,
text.note: δαΐφρον is vocative of δαΐφρων (“wise-minded”); Μουσαῖε is direct address. μῦθον ἅπαντ’ ἔκλυες = “you have heard the entire story.”

text.greek: ὥς ποτε Φερσεφόνην τέρεν' ἄνθεα χερσὶ δρέπουσαν
text.english: how once Phersēphonē, plucking tender blossoms with her hands,
text.note: Φερσεφόνην is an Orphic/epic form; here transliterated as Phersēphonē. τέρεν’ (< τερενά) “tender”; δρέπουσαν “plucking.”

text.greek: ἐξάπαφον συνόμαιμοι ἀν' εὐρύ τε καὶ μέγα ἄλσος.
text.english: unawares, with her kinswomen, through the wide and great grove.
text.note: ἐξάπαφον = “suddenly, unawares.” συνόμαιμοι likely stands for dat. pl. συνομαίμοισιν (“with her kinswomen/peers”); many editors so emend. ἀνὰ with acc. = “through(out).” The syntax continues beyond this line.

text.greek: αὐτὰρ ἔπειθ' ὥς μιν Πλωτεὺς, κυανότριχας ἵππους
text.english: But thereafter, when Ploteus, having yoked the dark-maned horses,
text.note: Ploteus (Πλωτεύς) is likely an epithet of Poseidon (“the Seafarer”); the “dark‑maned horses” are his sea-horses drawing the chariot.

text.greek: ζευξάμενος, κούρην ἐπεβήσατο δαίμονος αἴσῃ,
text.english: set the maiden aboard by a daimōn’s allotment,
text.note: ἐπεβήσατο with accusative (κούρην) is unusual; it can imply either sexual “mounted” or, more contextually here, “set [her] aboard/on” the chariot implied by the yoked horses. δαίμονος αἴσῃ = “by a daimōn’s allotment,” i.e., by fate.

text.greek: ἁρπάξας δ' ἔφερεν διὰ κύματος ἀτρυγέτοιο.
text.english: and, having snatched her, he bore her through the wave of the unharvested sea.
text.note: ἀτρυγέτος (“unharvested”) is the conventional epic epithet of the sea; ἁρπάζω underscores violent abduction. διὰ κύματος = “through the wave.”

text.greek: Δὴ τότ' ἐγὼν ἀπόειπον ἐπιπλώοντα νέεσθαι
text.english: Then indeed I forbade us to put back, as we bore in under sail,
text.note: ἀπόειπον + infinitive = “forbid/renounce (to do).” The participle ἐπιπλώοντα is adverbial (“as we were bearing in/under way”); the subject of the infinitive νέεσθαι is understood from context (“we”).

text.greek: νήσου ἐπὶ ῥηγμῖνα καὶ αἰγλήεντα τέρεμνα,
text.english: to the island’s surf and its gleaming abodes,
text.note: ῥηγμῖνα = “breakers, surf” (the shore-line). τέρεμνα is a Homeric word for “abodes/haunts,” often of nymphs; αἰγλήεντα = “gleaming, bright.” Some traditions read τέρμνα; τέρεμνα suits the Homeric usage (cf. Od. 13).

text.greek: ἐνθ' οὔτις σὺν νηῒ πάρα μερόπων ἀνθρώπων.
text.english: where no one of mortal men draws near with a ship.
text.note: σὺν νηῒ πάρα is an epic idiom for “come near/approach with a ship.” μερόπων ἀνθρώπων is the conventional epic periphrasis for “mortals.”

text.greek: Οὐ γάρ οἵ ἐστὶ λιμὴν νηῶν ὀχὸς ἀμφιελισσῶν,
text.english: For it has no harbor, no refuge for the double‑curved ships,
text.note: λιμὴν … ὄχος: literally “harbor, a stay/support (for ships),” hence “refuge”; the dative οἵ is possessive (“for it”); ἀμφιελισσῶν is the conventional ship‑epithet meaning “double‑curved.”

text.greek: ἀλλά γε ἠλίβατος πέτρη περὶ πάντα πέφυκεν
text.english: but rather a sheer rock, lofty, has sprung up all around,
text.note: ἠλίβατος = “steep, sheer, hard of access”; πέφυκεν “has grown/stands by nature”; περὶ πάντα “on all sides.”

text.greek: ὑψηλή· τά τε καλὰ φύει μενοεικέα δῶρα.
text.english: and it bears fair gifts that satisfy desire.
text.note: The subject of φύει (“bears/produces”) is the place understood; δῶρα “gifts” denotes the land’s produce; μενοεικέα = “desire‑satisfying,” a Homeric epithet.

text.greek: Καὶ τότ' ἄρ' οὐκ ἀπίθησε νεὼς κυανοπρώροιο
text.english: And then the helmsman Ankaios of the dark‑prowed ship did not disobey,
text.note: "ithyntor" (ἰθύντωρ) is a technical term for the steersman, lit. “straightener.” "kyanoproros" (κυανοπρώροιο) = “dark-/blue‑prowed,” a conventional epic epithet of ships; the verb “did not disobey” implies heeding a prior command.

text.greek: ἰθύντωρ Ἀγκαῖος, ἀνέτρεχε δ' αἶψ' ἀνορούων,
text.english: and straightway he ran up, springing to his feet,
text.note: The collocation ἀνέτρεχε … ἀνορούων (“ran up … leaping up”) is pleonastic for vivid sudden movement.

text.greek: σκαιὸν ὑπεγκλίνας οἰήϊον· ἐν δ' ἄρ' ἔπειθε
text.english: dipping the left‑hand steering‑oar beneath; and then he persuaded her
text.note: "oieiion" (οἰήϊον) = the steering‑oar/rudder; "skaios" (σκαιός) = left/port. ὑπεγκλίνας (“bending under”) is nautical: ‘dipping/bringing the rudder under’ to alter course. ἔπειθε (“he persuaded [her]”) anthropomorphizes the ship, i.e., ‘brought her to obey the helm.’

text.greek: μή τι κατευθὺ περᾶν, ἐπὶ δέξια δ' εἶργε θέουσαν.
text.english: not to go straight on, but held her, as she raced, to starboard.
text.note: κατευθύ = ‘straight (ahead)’; ἐπὶ δέξια = ‘to the right,’ i.e., to starboard. εἶργε θέουσαν = ‘held/kept her as she raced,’ combining restraint with speed.

text.greek: - Ἤματι δὲ τριτάτῳ Κίρκης δόμον ἐξικόμεσθα
text.english: And on the third day we came to the house of Kirkê,

text.greek: Λιγκαῖον ποτὶ χέρσον ἁλιστεφέας τε θεράπνας·
text.english: to the Lingaian mainland and the sea‑wreathed precincts;
text.note: Λιγκαῖον (Lingaion) is an obscure toponym; many take it as a local designation of Kirkê’s island (Aeaea), though some suspect textual corruption. θεράπνας here means “abodes/precincts,” and ἁλιστεφέας literally “sea‑wreathed/sea‑garlanded.”

text.greek: καὶ τότ' ἄρ' αἰγιαλοῖσιν ἐκέλσαμεν ἀχνύμενοι κῆρ,
text.english: and then upon the beaches we beached her, grieving at heart,
text.note: ἐκέλσαμεν is the technical nautical verb from κέλλω, “to run a ship aground, beach.”

text.greek: πείσματα δ' ἐν πέτρῃσιν ἐδήσαμεν· ἐκ δ' ἄρ' Ἰήσων
text.english: and we made fast the moorings to the rocks; and forth Jason
text.note: πείσματα are “moorings/warp‑cables,” a nautical term; ἐδήσαμεν = “we bound/made fast.”

text.greek: νηὸς ἀποπροέηκε μολεῖν ἐρίηρας ἑταίρους,
text.english: dispatched from the ship trusty comrades to go,
text.note: ἐρίηρας ἑταίρους is the epic formula “trusty (or loyal) comrades.”

text.greek: διζομένος εἴ τίς σφε βροτῶν ἐπ' ἀπείρονα γαῖαν
text.english: seeking whether any among mortals upon the boundless earth
text.note: σφε is the enclitic 3rd‑person pronoun used pleonastically/adverbially in epic (“there/for them”); ἐπ’ ἀπείρονα γαῖαν is the formula “upon the boundless earth.”

text.greek: ναιετάει, γνῷεν δὲ πόλιν καὶ ἤθεα λαῶν.
text.english: dwells there, and that they might learn the city and the ways of the people.
text.note: ἤθεα are the “customs/ways” (habits, usages) of the inhabitants; λαῶν (plural) is generic for “people/folk.”

text.greek: Τοῖς δ' ἄφαρ ὠμάρτησε καταντίον ἐρχομένοισι
text.english: But straightway there met them, as they came on face to face,
text.note: ōmārtēse is the aorist of homarteō in the sense “to meet, encounter” (not “to err”); katanion with the participle erchomenoisi conveys “as they came opposite/face to face.”

text.greek: κούρη ὁμογνήτη μεγαλόφρονος Αἰήταο,
text.english: a maiden, the full sister of great‑hearted Aiētes,
text.note: homognētē means “born of the same parents,” hence “full sister.”

text.greek: Ἠελίου θυγάτηρ· Κίρκην δέ ἑ κικλήσκουσι
text.english: daughter of Hēlios; and they call her Kirke,
text.note: kiklēskousi is the impersonal epic “they call,” i.e., “men call her.”

text.greek: μήτηρ Ἀστερόπη καὶ τηλεφανὴς Ὑπερίων.
text.english: her mother Asteropē, and far‑shining Hyperiōn.
text.note: The line is elliptical in apposition: “her mother [was] Asteropē, and far‑shining Hyperiōn [her father].” Hyperiōn here functions as a name/title of Hēlios (cf. “Hēlios Hyperiōn”). Asteropē is a variant mother for Kirke (elsewhere Perseis); telephanēs is the epic epithet “far‑shining.”

text.greek: Ἥ ῥα θοῶς ἐπὶ νῆα κατήλυθεν· ἐκ δ' ἄρα πάντες
text.english: She then swiftly came down upon the ship; and then all of them
text.note: ἐκ δ’ ἄρα πάντες is elliptical in Greek (often ‘up from their seats’ is understood); I render simply ‘and then all of them’ to preserve the enjambment.

text.greek: θάμβεον εἰσορόωντες· ἀπὸ κρατὸς γὰρ ἔθειραι
text.english: marveled as they gazed; for from her head the tresses
text.note: No special difficulties.

text.greek: πυρσαῖς ἀκτίνεσσιν ἀλίγκιοι ἠώρηντο·
text.english: were wafted, like fiery rays;
text.note: ἠώρηντο (‘were wafted, hung suspended’) suggests a floating or streaming motion; πυρσαῖς means ‘fiery, ruddy’.

text.greek: στίλβε δὲ καλὰ πρόσωπα, φλογὸς δ' ἀπέλαμπεν ἀϋτμή.
text.english: her fair faces gleamed, and a smokeless flame beamed forth.
text.note: Plural ‘faces’ alludes to Hekate’s triple visage in this scene. The phrase φλογὸς δ’ ἀπέλαμπεν ἀϋτμή is syntactically compressed; I translate idiomatically as ‘a smokeless flame beamed forth’ (taking φλογός as a genitive of source/description).

text.greek: Αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ Μήδειαν ἐσέδρακεν ὀφθαλμοῖσι,
text.english: But when he had beheld Medea with his eyes,
text.note: ἐσέδρακεν is an epic form from δέρκομαι (“to behold”); ὀφθαλμοῖσι is an instrumental dative (“with his eyes”).

text.greek: (λῖτι καλυπτομένην, ἑανῷ δ' ἀμφέσχε παρειάς
text.english: (veiled in linen, and with a fine veil she had drawn about her cheeks,
text.note: λῖτι is difficult; generally taken as the dative of λῖτον (“linen [garment/veil]”), hence “veiled in linen.” Many editors consider emendation to λίνῳ. ἑανῷ (“fine, thin,” esp. of clothing); ἀμφέσχε is from ἀμφέχω (“to wrap about”).

text.greek: αἰδομένη· χλωρὸν γὰρ ὑπὸ στέρνοις ἀκάχητο).
text.english: ashamed; for beneath her bosom a greenish pallor had distressed her).
text.note: αἰδομένη = “being modest/ashamed.” χλωρόν denotes the pale/greenish hue of fear; δέος (“fear”) is effectively understood. ἀκάχητο is the pluperfect of ἀκάχημαι (“to be distressed”); the subject is Medea understood, and “beneath her bosom” conveys the seat of emotion (the heart).

text.greek: Ἣν τότ' ἐποικτείρουσα προσηύδανε καὶ φάτο Κίρκη·
text.english: Then, pitying her, Kirke addressed her and spoke:
text.note: “Her” refers to Medea; Kirke (Circe) is the speaker.

text.greek: - "Ὦ δειλὴ, τί νύ τοι τοίην Κύπρις ὤπασε μοῖραν;
text.english: “O wretched one, what sort of fate has Kypris now bestowed on you?

text.greek: Οὐ γάρ τοι λελάθεσθε, ἅπερ ῥέξαντες ἱκνεῖσθε
text.english: For the very deeds for which you come have not escaped notice,
text.note: λελάθεσθε (“have escaped notice”): the sense is that their deeds are known; ἅπερ ῥέξαντες ἱκνεῖσθε “the very things for which you come.”

text.greek: νῆσον ἐφ' ἡμετέρην πανετώσιον οὕνεκα πατρός
text.english: as you make for our island—all in vain—on account of your aged father
text.note: πανετώσιον is likely from ἐτώσιος (“vain, fruitless”): hence “all in vain,” i.e., coming to Kirke’s island will not avail them without proper rites.

text.greek: γηραιοῦ κάσιός τε, τὸν ἐκπάγλως· ὀλέσαντες,
text.english: and your brother, whom in dreadful wise you slew;
text.note: κάσιος is an epic form for “brother”; τὸν functions as a quasi-relative (“whom”); ἐκπάλως intensifies (“terribly, dreadfully”); the reference is to Apsyrtos/Apsyrtus.

text.greek: οὐδὲ γὰρ ὔμμε πάτρῃσιν οἴομαι ἆσσον ἱκέσθαι,
text.english: for I do not think you will draw any nearer to your native lands,

text.greek: εἰ ἐν ἀναγνίστοισιν ἀλιτροσύναις ἀκέοντες,
text.english: even if you attempt to heal your transgressions by purificatory rites,
text.note: ἀναγνίστοισιν is a rare/technical term; probably from (ἁ)γνίζω “to purify,” meaning “purificatory.” Some take it as “unrecognized/illegitimate,” but the contrast with the next line’s “divine purifications” suggests ordinary rites versus divinely sanctioned ones.

text.greek: μέσφ' ὅταν ἐκνίψησθε μύσος θείοισι καθαρμοῖς
text.english: not until you wash off the defilement by divine cleansings,
text.note: μῦσος “pollution” (of kin-murder); καθαρμοί are technical “purifications/expiations.”

text.greek: Ὀρφέως ἰδμοσύνῃσι παρὰ κροκάλοισι Μαλείης.
text.english: through the lore of Orpheus, beside the pebbly shore of Malea.”
text.note: κροκάλοι “pebbles, shingle”; Malea is Cape Malea in Laconia; ἰδμοσύναις “expert knowledge, lore”: Orpheus’ specialized ritual knowledge effects the purification near Malea.

text.greek: Οὐδὲ γὰρ ἡμετέροιο δόμου θέμις ἐστιν ἱκέσθαι
text.english: For it is not the custom of our house to receive propitiants,
text.note: θέμις ἐστιν = “it is the (sacred) custom/right.” προστροπίους (acc. pl.) is used substantively: “those seeking propitiation,” i.e., suppliants for expiation; accusative functions as the subject of the infinitive ἱκέσθαι.

text.greek: προστροπίους· τοίῳ γε λύθρῳ πεπαλαγμένοι ἐστέ·
text.english: for you are bespattered with such gore;
text.note: λύθρον is “blood-filth, gore,” often signaling ritual miasma; πεπαλαγμένοι = “spattered, besmeared.”

text.greek: Ἀλλά μιν αὐτίκ' ἐγὼ πρόφρων ξυνήϊα πέμψω
text.english: But straightway I, with ready heart, will send provisions,
text.note: ξυνήϊα = “provisions, ship’s stores”; πρόφρων = “with ready goodwill.” The enclitic μιν is an anticipatory/pleonastic object, effectively pointing ahead to the supplies to be sent.

text.greek: σῖτον καὶ μέθυ λαρὸν ἔχειν, σὺν δὲ κρέα πολλά."
text.english: food and luscious wine for you to have, and along with them much meat.”
text.note: λάρον (laron) = “delicious, luscious” (of wine). ἔχειν is epexegetic (“for you to have”), with the beneficiary understood (sc. ὑμῖν).

text.greek: - Ὣς εἰποῦσ', ἄψορρος ἀπέπτατο· νηῒ δὲ μέσσῃ
text.english: So speaking, she flew back again; and in the middle of the ship
text.note: ἄψορρος = “back again”; ἀπέπτατο (“flew off”) hints at a divine or winged figure’s departure.

text.greek: δαιτός τ' ἠδὲ ποτοῖο τετυγμένα τεύχε' ἔκειτο.
text.english: there lay the gear prepared for a banquet and for drink.
text.note: τεύχεα here = “gear/implements” (not arms): the made-ready paraphernalia of feasting and drinking; τετυγμένα = “prepared, made ready.”

text.greek: Ἂν δ' ἄρ' ἐπειγομένοισι θέεν λιγὺς οὖρος ἀήτης·
text.english: And then, as we were pressing on, there sped a clear, favoring blast of wind.
text.note: ἐπειγομένοις is a dative of attendant circumstance (“as we were hurrying”); θέεν is epic imperfect 3sg of ‘run’ (here “sped”); λιγύς applied to wind means “clear/keen”; οὖρος = a fair/favoring wind; ἀήτης = “blast, gust,” not the proper name Aiētes.

text.greek: καὶ τότε λυσάμενοι κείνης ἀπὸ πείσματα νήσου,
text.english: And then, having loosed the moorings from that island,
text.note: πείσματα are the ship’s moorings/cables; λύεσθαι πείσματα is a set phrase for casting off from shore.

text.greek: κῦμα διαπρήσσοντες ἀνὰ στόμα Ταρτησσοῖο
text.english: cleaving the wave through the mouth of Tartessos,
text.note: διαπρήσσειν = “cleave, make one’s way through (the sea)”; ἀνὰ στόμα “through/up along the mouth.” Ταρτησσός (Tartessos) is the far‑western river/region (often the Guadalquivir); the “mouth” may poetically denote either the river’s outlet or, more broadly, the western straits.

text.greek: ἱκόμεθα, στήλαισι δ' ἐκέλσαμεν Ἡρακλεῆος.
text.english: we came, and we made landfall at the Pillars of Herakles.
text.note: ἐκέλσαμεν is the aorist of κέλλω “to bring/put in (a ship),” here with dative of place: “made landfall at.” The στῆλαι Ἡρακλέους are the “Pillars of Herakles,” i.e., the promontories at the Straits of Gibraltar.

text.greek: Ἄκραις δ' ἀμφ' ἱεραῖσι Διωνύσοιο ἄνακτος
text.english: Around the sacred headlands of lord Dionysos
text.note: Ἄκραις (dat. pl.) = “headlands, promontories”; ἀμφί with the dative is epic “around/at.” Διονύσοιο ἄνακτος = “of lord Dionysos.”

text.greek: μίμνομεν ἑσπέριοι· δαιτὸς γὰρ ἐδεύετο θυμός.
text.english: we tarried at eventide; for the spirit was in want of a feast.
text.note: ἑσπέριοι is used adverbially, “toward evening/at eventide” (not “western”). θυμός + ἐδεύετο δαιτός is an epic idiom for hunger: “the spirit/heart was in need of a feast.”

text.greek: Τῆμος δ' ἀντολίαισιν ἐγείρετο φωσφόρος αἴγλη,
text.english: Then at the eastern risings the light‑bearing radiance rose,
text.note: ἀντολίαισιν (“eastern risings”) = dawn; φωσφόρος αἴγλη “light‑bearing radiance” may allude to Phōsphoros (the Morning Star).

text.greek: ὄρθριοι εἰρεσίῃς γλαυκὴν ἐχαράξαμεν ἅλμην,
text.english: and at dawn with our oar‑blades we furrowed the glaucous brine,
text.note: εἰρεσίῃς = “oar‑blades”; γλαυκή “glaucous,” the grey‑blue of the sea; ἅλμη “brine.”

text.greek: Σαρδῶον δ' ἱκόμεσθα βυθὸν, κόλπους τε Λατίνων,
text.english: and we reached the Sardinian deep, and the gulfs of the Latins,
text.note: Σαρδῶον βυθόν = the sea off Sardinia; “Latins” = inhabitants of Latium (central west Italy).

text.greek: νήσους τ' Αὐσονίας, Τυρρηνὰς δ' ἱκόμεθ' ἀκτάς·
text.english: the isles of Ausonia, and we came to the Tyrrhenian coasts;
text.note: Αὐσονία is a poetic name for Italy; “Tyrrhenian coasts” = the western Italian littoral.

text.greek: Αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ Λιλύβαιον ἐπέσχομεν ἠχέτα πορθμὸν,
text.english: but when we made for Lilybaion’s resounding strait,
text.note: Λιλύβαιον (Lilybaion) is the W tip of Sicily; πορθμός “strait/sound”; the geography anticipates the Messina strait and is not precise.

text.greek: Τριγλώχινά τε νῆσον ἐπέσχομεν, Ἐγκελάδοιο
text.english: and we held our course to the three‑cornered island, of Enkelados,
text.note: τριγλώχινα “three‑cornered,” a standard epithet of Sicily; Enkelados (Encelados) is the Giant pinned beneath Aitna (Etna).

text.greek: Αἰτναίη φλόξ σφιν ἄρ' ἐρήτυεν μεμαῶτας,
text.english: then the Aetnaean flame held their eager rush in check,
text.note: σφιν (“them”) has an ambiguous antecedent; it likely refers to violent forces (e.g., convulsions/winds/waves) checked by Enkelados’ Aetnaean fire; ἐρήτυεν “held back,” μεμαῶτας “eager, impetuous.”

text.greek: δὴ τόθ' ὑπὲρ πρώρης ὀλοὸν περιέζεεν ὕδωρ
text.english: indeed then over the prow the baleful water closed about,
text.note: περιέζεεν “closed about/encircled”; ὀλοόν “baleful, deadly.”

text.greek: νειόθεν, ἐκ μυχάτου δὲ βυθοῦ ῥοίβδησε Χάρυβδις
text.english: from below; and from the inmost deep Kharybdis roared
text.note: μυχάτου βυθοῦ “the inmost depth”; ῥοΐβδησε is onomatopoetic (“roared/whirred”); Kharybdis is the whirlpool in the Messina strait.

text.greek: κύματι καχλάζοντι, καὶ ἱστίον ἄκρον ἵκανε.
text.english: with a bubbling wave, and it reached to the sail’s very tip.
text.note: κύματι καχλάζοντι “with a bubbling/foaming wave”; ἵκανε “reached”; the subject is the surge raised by Kharybdis, reaching the sail’s peak.

text.greek: Νῆα δ' ἄρ' αὐτόθι οἱ κατέχεν ῥόος, οὐδέ μιν εἴα
text.english: But then the current held the ship fast there for him, nor did it allow her
text.note: oî is an ethical/interest dative (“for him,” likely the helmsman/Jason) and may be left untranslated in English; mín refers to the ship (fem.).

text.greek: προπροθέειν, οὐδ' αὐτίκ' ἀναρρώσεσθαι ὀπίσσω,
text.english: to run right forward, nor straightway to spring back astern,
text.note: proprothéein is an intensive “to run/dart right forward.” anar­rṓsesthai opíssō here means “to spring back astern/backwards”; the future infinitive after “did not allow” is acceptable epic idiom of prevented action.

text.greek: κοίλῳ ἔπὶ λυγρῷ δὲ περιστροφάδην ἀλάλητο.
text.english: but upon the hollow, baleful deep she was whirled round and round.
text.note: koílō(i) … lyg­rō(i) likely with an understood póntō(i) (“upon the hollow, baleful sea”); peristrophádēn = “in whirling fashion, round and round.” alálēto is the imperfect middle of aláomai, “was being driven/whirled about.”

text.greek: Ἦ τάχα καὶ δύσεσθ' Ἀργὼ κατὰ βένθε' ἔμελλεν
text.english: Indeed, all too soon would Argo have sunk down beneath the deeps,
text.note: δύσεσθ’ = δύσεσθαι with elision; ἔμελλεν + infinitive with εἰ μὴ expresses the averted counterfactual “would have… if not.” βένθε’ = βένθεα “the depths” (of the sea).

text.greek: εἰ μὴ πρεσβίστη θυγάτηρ ἁλίοιο γέροντος
text.english: if the eldest daughter of the Old Man of the Sea,
text.note: ἁλίοιο γέροντος “Old Man of the Sea” is the traditional epithet of Nereus (also of Proteus in Homer); here the daughter is Thetis. πρεσβίστη may mean “eldest” or “most venerable.”

text.greek: εὐρυβίην Πηλῆα πόσιν λελίητο ἰδέσθαι,
text.english: who longed to behold Peleus, her husband of broad might,
text.note: λελίητο (perfect of λιλαίομαι) “was eager/longed.” εὐρυβίην is difficult; it is best taken as an epithet “of broad might” applied to Peleus by sense (“Peleus of broad might”). The form is irregular, and some emend to εὐρύβιον, but the transmitted sense is clear.

text.greek: μειλιχίη δ' ἐκδῦτο βυθοῦ καὶ ῥύσσατ' ὀλέθρου
text.english: had not, gentle, come forth from the deep and warded off destruction
text.note: μειλιχίη “gentle, kindly” as an epic epithet of a Nereid. ἐκδῦτο (middle) “came forth/emerged” from the depths.

text.greek: Ἀργῴαν ἄκατον, καὶ ὑπ' ἰλύος ἐξεσάωσε.
text.english: from the Argoan galley, and drawn it out from beneath the mud.
text.note: ἄκατος denotes a light, swift galley; here “the Argoan galley.” ἐξεσάωσε “drew out, saved from.” ἰλύς “mud,” implying the ship had grounded on shoals.

text.greek: - Δὴ τότε οἱ πλώοντες ἐπέσχομεν οὐ μάλα τηλοῦ
text.english: Then indeed at that time we who were sailing checked our course, not very far off,
text.note: ἐπέσχομεν has a nautical sense: “to heave to, check one’s way.” The object (the crag) is supplied by the next line.

text.greek: προβλῆτα σκόπελον· πέτρη δ' ἐφύπερθεν ἀπορρώξ
text.english: by a projecting crag; and overhead a rock, broken sheer,
text.note: ἐφύπερθεν = “overhead/above”; ἀπορρώξ = “sheer, precipitous.” The subject for the following participle and verb is πέτρη (“rock”).

text.greek: λισσοῖς χηραμόνεσσιν ἐπιθρώσκουσα βιᾶται
text.english: overarching with smooth ledges, forces the sea inward,
text.note: χηραμόνεσσιν is a rare/uncertain word; likely “rock-shelves/ledges.” I render “smooth ledges.” The participle ἐπιθρώσκουσα (“leaping upon”) is used metaphorically of an overhanging/overarching rock.

text.greek: πόντον ἔσω, χαροπὸν δ' ἄρ' ὑποβρέμει ἔνδοθι κῦμα.
text.english: and within beneath the grim wave makes a hollow roar.
text.note: χαροπός applied to the wave conveys a grim, grey-gleaming aspect; ὑποβρέμει = “to rumble with a muffled/hollow roar,” suited to a sea-cave.

text.greek: Ἔνθα δ' ἐφεζόμεναι λιγυρὴν ὄπα γηρύουσι
text.english: There, seated, they sing forth a clear‑toned voice.
text.note: The subject (“they”) is supplied from the next line’s κοῦραι, here the Sirens; γηρύουσι conveys “utter/sing,” and λιγυρὴν ὄπα is an epic formula for a clear, piercing voice.

text.greek: κοῦραι, ἀνοστήτους δὲ βροτῶν θέλγουσιν ἀκουᾷ.
text.english: maidens; and by the hearing of mortals they bewitch them to be unreturning.
text.note: ἀνοστήτους (“unreturning”) echoes νόστος (homecoming): the Sirens’ song prevents return. ἀκουᾷ is the dative of ἀκοή (“hearing”), used instrumentally (“by/through the hearing”); hence the sense “they bewitch mortals by the very act of listening.”

text.greek: Δὴ τότε Μινύαισιν ἐφήνδανε πύστις ἀοιδῆς
text.english: Then indeed the hearing of the Seirenes’ song proved welcome to the Minyae.
text.note: πύστις means “hearing, report, knowledge”; here “the hearing (of the song)” suits the context. Minyae = the Argonauts.

text.greek: Σειρήνων· οὐδέ σφι παραπλώσεσθαι ἔμελλον
text.english: Nor were they about to sail past the baneful voice,
text.note: παραπλῶσθαι (“sail past/by”) with φθογγή (“voice, sound”) is striking and metonymic; οὐλομένην is the epic “baneful, accursed.”

text.greek: φθογγὴν οὐλομένην, χειρῶν δέ οἱ ἧκαν ἐρετμά·
text.english: but from their hands they let the oars fall;
text.note: χειρῶν … ἧκαν ἐρετμά = “they let the oars go from their hands.” The enclitic οἱ is an ethic dative (“on them/for them”), not essential to English.

text.greek: Ἀγκαῖος δ' ἴθυνεν ἐπὶ προβλῆτα κολωνόν
text.english: and Ankaios was steering toward a jutting headland,
text.note: προβλῆτα κολωνόν = “projecting/jutting hill,” i.e., a promontory; ἴθυνεν “was steering straight (toward).” Ankaios is the helmsman.

text.greek: εἰ μὴ ἐγὼ φόρμιγγα τιτηνάμενος παλάμῃσι
text.english: had I not, shaking the phorminx in my hands,
text.note: φόρμιγξ (phorminx) is the epic lyre; τιτηνάμενος “shaking, brandishing,” a conventional performance verb for striking up song.

text.greek: μητρὸς ἐμῆς ἐκέρασσ' εὐτερπέα κόσμον ἀοιδῆς.
text.english: blended my mother’s delightful adornment of song.
text.note: ἐκέρασσ’ (“I blended/mingled”) uses the musical metaphor of mixing strains; κόσμος ἀοιδῆς “order/adornment of song.” μητρὸς ἐμῆς refers to Orpheus’ mother (the Muse Kalliope) as the source of his song.

text.greek: - Ἤειδον δὲ λιγὺ κλάζων διὰ θέσκελον ὕμνον,
text.english: And he sang, ringing clear, through a wondrous hymn,
text.note: theskelos = “wondrous, god‑wrought”; ligy klazōn = “ringing/shrilling clearly.”

text.greek: ὥς ποτέ οἱ δήρισσαν ἀελλοπόδων ὑπὲρ ἵππων·
text.english: how once they contended for the storm‑footed horses:
text.note: aellopodōn = “storm‑footed,” an epic epithet of swift horses; dērissan = “contended/struggled.”

text.greek: Ζεὺς ὑψιβρεμέτης καὶ πόντιος Ἐννοσίγαιος·
text.english: Zeus Hypsibremetes and Pontios Ennosigaios;
text.note: Ennosigaios is a cultic name of Poseidon (“Earth‑shaker”); Pontios = “of the sea.” Hypsibremetes = “High‑Thunderer,” epithet of Zeus (kept in transliteration).

text.greek: Αὐτὰρ Κυανοχαῖτα χολωσάμενος Διὶ πατρί
text.english: but Kyanochaites, angered with father Zeus,
text.note: Kyanochaites (“dark‑blue‑haired”) is an epithet of Poseidon; Diì patri = “with/at father Zeus.”

text.greek: τύψεν Λυκτονίην γαίην χρυσῆνι τριαίνῃ
text.english: smote the Lyctonian land with his golden trident
text.note: Lyctonian = of Lyktos in Crete; the golden trident is Poseidon’s weapon.

text.greek: καί ῥ' ἀΐγδην ἐσκέδασεν κατ' ἀπείρονα πόντον,
text.english: and in an instant scattered it over the boundless sea,
text.note: aïgdēn = “at once, in an instant.”

text.greek: νήσους εἰναλίας ἔμεναι· τάς ῥ' ἐξονόμηναν
text.english: to be islands in the sea; these they named
text.note: einalias = “of the sea”; exonomēnan = “they named (by name),” impersonal/indefinite subject.

text.greek: Σαρδώ τ' Εὔβοιάν τ' ἐπὶ δὲ Κύπρον ἠνεμόεσσαν
text.english: Sardō and Euboia, and, besides, windy Kypros.
text.note: Toponyms: Sardō = Sardinia; Euboia = Euboea; Kypros = Cyprus; anemoeassan = “windy.”

text.greek: Δὴ τότε φορμίζοντος, ἀπὸ σκοπέλου νιφόεντος
text.english: Then, as he was playing the phorminx, from the snowy crag
text.note: phorminx = early lyre; skopelos niphōn = “snow‑white/snowy crag.”

text.greek: Σειρῆνες θάμβησαν, ἑὴν δ' ἄμπαυσαν ἀοιδήν·
text.english: the Sirens were astonished, and they hushed their own song;

text.greek: Καί ῥ' ἡ μὲν λωτοὺς, ἡ δ' αὖ χέλυν ἔκβαλε χειρῶν.
text.english: and the one cast the lotos‑reeds away, the other the tortoise‑shell from her hands.
text.note: lotos here is the lotos‑reed used as a wind instrument, not the flower; chelys is the tortoise‑shell lyre.

text.greek: Δεινὰ δ' ἀνεστονάχησαν, ἐπεὶ πότμος ἤϊε λυγρός
text.english: Terribly they groaned, when the baleful doom of allotted death was advancing,
text.note: Subject = the Sirens (context): ἐπεὶ πότμος ἤϊε (“when doom was going/approaching”) is an epic idiom; λυγρός = “baleful, woeful.” μοιριδίου (sc. θανάτοιο) = “allotted by Moira, fated.”

text.greek: μοιριδίου θανάτοιο· σφέας δ' ἀπὸ ῥωγάδος ἄκρης
text.english: and from the cleft’s utmost edge they themselves
text.note: ῥωγάς = a rift/cleft in rock; hence “cleft’s utmost edge.” σφέας used reflexively = “themselves.”

text.greek: ἐς βυθὸν δίσκευσαν ἁλιρροθίοιο θαλάσσης,
text.english: hurled down into the bottom of the brine-roaring sea,
text.note: δίσκευσαν (from δισκεύω) literally “they discused,” i.e., “flung [themselves] like a discus,” hence “hurled down.” ἁλιρροθίος = “brine-roaring” (of the sea’s surge).

text.greek: πέτραις δ' ἠλλάξαντο δέμας μορφήν θ' ὑπέροπλον.
text.english: and for rocks they exchanged their body and their overweening form.
text.note: ἠλλάξαντο with acc. + dat. = “they exchanged [X] for [Y],” used for metamorphosis: here, body/form for rocks. ὑπέροπλος = “overweening, presumptuous,” not “well-armed.” This line reflects the myth that the Sirens, defeated, cast themselves into the sea and became rocks.

text.greek: - Αὐταρ ἐπεὶ καὶ τόνδε πότμον παράμειψε θέουσα
text.english: But when, speeding on, she had passed beyond this doom as well,
text.note: παράμειψε πότμον (“passed beyond doom”) is an epic idiom meaning effectively “escaped that peril”; θεοῦσα is a feminine participle (“speeding”) agreeing with Argō.

text.greek: Ἀργὼ, κῦμα δὲ πόντου καὶ κόλπον ἵκανε,
text.english: Argō reached the sea’s swell and a bay,
text.note: κῦμα πόντου καὶ κόλπον is likely a hendiadys contrasting open water and a sheltered inlet (“swell … and a bay”).

text.greek: λαιψηροῖς πλήθουσα κατὰ προτόνων ἀνέμοισι,
text.english: her rigging along the forestays filled with swift winds,
text.note: πρότονοι are the forestays/shrouds; πλήθουσα ἀνέμοισι implies the sails/gear are swelling with wind, though “sail” is not explicitly named.

text.greek: Κέρκυραν βαθέην ἐξίκετο, τήν σφιν ἔναιον
text.english: she came to deep Kerkyra, which the Phaeacians inhabited,
text.note: βαθεῖα (“deep”) likely = “deep‑harbored”/“sea‑deep.” σφιν is an ethical dative (“for their part/there”), here best rendered idiomatically as “which … [they] inhabited.”

text.greek: ἴδριες εἰρεσίης καὶ ἁλιπλάγκτοιο πορείης
text.english: skilled in oar-craft and in sea-wandering travel,
text.note: εἰρεσία = “oarage, rowing”; ἁλιπλάνκτος = “sea‑wandering, roving by sea.” ἴδριες = “skilled, adept.”

text.greek: Φαίηκες· τοῖσιν δ' ἄρ' ἐφημοσύναισι θέμιστας
text.english: and for them, by his injunctions, the ordinances
text.note: ἐφημοσύναι = “injunctions/behests,” a rarer term for authoritative proclamations; θέμιστες are traditional ordinances/judgments.

text.greek: Ἀλκίνοος κραίνεσκε δικαιότατος βασιλήων.
text.english: Alkinoos, most just of kings, was wont to ordain.
text.note: κραίνεσκε (iterative imperfect) conveys habitual action, “was wont to ordain”; δικαιότατος βασιλῆων is a Homeric‑style superlative formula. The king’s name is given in Greek transliteration (Alkinoos).

text.greek: Πείσματα δ' ἁψάμενοι πορσύνομεν ἱερὰ θέσθαι
text.english: And having made fast the hawsers, we made ready to offer sacred rites
text.note: πείσματα = mooring-ropes/hawsers; πορσύνω with infinitive and ἱερὰ θέσθαι is an idiom for preparing to perform/offer sacrifices.

text.greek: Ζηνὶ πανομφαίῳ καὶ ἐπακτίῳ Ἀπόλλωνι.
text.english: to Zeus Panomphaios and to Apollon Epaktios.
text.note: πανομφαῖος literally “of all-oracles”/“all-voiced,” a traditional epithet of Zeus; ἐπακτίος means “of the shore/landing,” a cult title; divine names are transliterated.

text.greek: - Ἐν δ' ἄρ' ὑπ' εἰρεσίῃσιν ἐπειγόμενοι φορέοντο
text.english: Then indeed, being urged on, they were borne along beneath the oars,
text.note: ὑπ’ εἰρεσίῃσιν (“beneath the oars”) is a Homeric formula for a ship being driven by rowing; the subject (the band) is supplied by the next line.

text.greek: νηυσὶν ἀπειρεσίαις βριαρὸς λόχος Αἰήταο
text.english: in countless ships—the mighty company of Aeëtes,

text.greek: Κόλχων Ἐρραύνων τε, Χαρανδαίων Σολύμων τε
text.english: of Colchians and Erraunians, of Charandaians and Solymoi—
text.note: The ethnonyms Erraunians and Charandaians are obscure; forms and identifications vary in the tradition. Solymoi are the Solymi of Lycia/Asia Minor.

text.greek: διζόμενος Μινύας, τόφρ' ἂν Μήδειαν ἄγοιντο
text.english: seeking the Minyae, until they should bring Medeia
text.note: διζόμενος (“seeking”) is singular, agreeing with the collective “band” (λόχος); τόφρ’ ἄν with optative (ἄγοιντο) expresses “until” with anticipated outcome.

text.greek: ὄψιν ἐς Αἰήταο πατρὸς, τίσειε δ' ἀμοιβάς
text.english: into the sight of her father Aeëtes, and that he might exact requital
text.note: Subject of τίσειε (“exact requital”) is Aeëtes; ὄψιν ἐς means “into the sight/presence.”

text.greek: σφῇσιν ἀτασθαλίῃσιν ἀδελφειοῦ κταμένοιο.
text.english: for their own reckless outrages—the slaying of her brother.
text.note: ἀδελφειοῦ κταμενοῖο (“of a slain brother”) most naturally refers to Apsyrtos, Medeia’s brother; the possessor is left implicit. σφῇσιν ἀτασθαλίῃσιν is the Odyssean “by/for their own reckless outrages.”

text.greek: Ἀλλ' ὅτε δὴ κοίλου λιμένας μυχῷ ἆσσον ἵκοντο,
text.english: But when indeed they drew nearer to the innermost recess of the hollow haven,
text.note: κοίλου λιμένας μυχῷ is syntactically awkward: one expects a genitive with μυχῷ (e.g., λιμένος) or agreement of κοίλου with λιμένας (κοίλους). Many editors emend to κοίλου λιμένος μυχῷ (“to the recess of the hollow harbor”).

text.greek: αἶψα δ' ἄρ' Ἀλκινόοιο δόμον κήρυκες ἔβαινον,
text.english: straightway the heralds went to the house of Alkinoos,

text.greek: Μηδείης λύτο γοῦνα, δέος δ' ὤχριε παρειάς,
text.english: Medeia’s knees gave way, and fear blanched her cheeks,
text.note: λύτο γοῦνα (“her knees were loosed”) is a Homeric idiom for weakness from fear; ὤχριε means “grew pale.”

text.greek: μή οἱ ἑλὼν ἀέκουσαν ἑὸν πέμψειε δόμονδε
text.english: lest he, having seized her unwilling, might send her back to her own house,
text.note: μή + optative (πέμψειε, γένηται) marks a feared outcome in past narrative. The dative οἱ is dativus incommodi (“to her hurt”). ἑὸν δόμονδε means “to her own house,” i.e., back to her paternal home in Colchis.

text.greek: Φαιήκων βασιλεὺς, ἀνάπυστά τε ἔργα γένηται.
text.english: the king of the Phaiakians, and the deeds might be bruited abroad.
text.note: Φαιήκων βασιλεύς stands in apposition, supplying the subject of the feared action. ἀνάπυστα (“noised abroad, notorious”) has Homeric coloring; ἔργα likely refers to the Argonauts’ deeds becoming common report.

text.greek: Ἀλλ' οὔ οἱ τάδε μοῖρα τελεσσίνοος κατένευσε,
text.english: But Moira, whose mind brings things to fulfillment, did not nod assent to these things for him,
text.note: τελεσσίνοος (of Moira): literally “fulfilling-minded”; κατένευσε preserves the epic image of divine assent by a nod. I take Moira here as the personified goddess (hence capitalization).

text.greek: πρὶν δή τοι Πελίαο δόμοις ἔπι λυγρὸν ὄλεθρον
text.english: not until upon the halls of Pelias a baneful destruction
text.note: τοι is an enclitic particle without direct English equivalent; ἐπὶ with the dative (“upon/against”) marks hostile direction; λυγρὸν ὄλεθρον is a formulaic “baneful destruction.”

text.greek: αὐτῷ τε κρείοντι φέροι κακὸν οἶτον Ἰήσων.
text.english: and upon the ruler himself Jason should bring an evil doom.
text.note: φέροι is optative in a πρίν-clause, hence “until … should bring”; κρείων (“ruler, lord”) in the dative goes with ἐπὶ understood; οἶτος is “doom, lot,” rendered here as “evil doom.”

text.greek: Ἀλλ' ὅτε δὴ βασιλῆος ἀπηνέος ἔκλυεν αὐδήν
text.english: But when indeed she heard the voice of the harsh king,
text.note: “the harsh king” is most naturally Aeetes; his “voice” denotes the demand conveyed by the Colchian envoys.

text.greek: Ἀρήτη ῥοδόπηχυς, ἰδ' Ἀλκίνοος θεοειδής,
text.english: Arete, rosy‑armed—and Alkinoos, godlike—
text.note: ῥοδόπηχυς (“rosy‑armed”) is a Homeric‑style epithet; θεοειδής (“godlike”) marks Alkinoos’ noble appearance.

text.greek: Ἀλκίνοος μέν ῥ' ὦκ' ἐπετέλλετο κηρύκεσσι,
text.english: Alkinoos straightway gave orders to the heralds
text.note: No special difficulty.

text.greek: κούρην ἀμφήριστον ἄγειν ἀπὸ νηὸς ἐρυμνῆς,
text.english: to bring the contested maiden from the stout ship,
text.note: ἀμφήριστος means “contested, disputed,” often of a prize; here of the maiden (Medea) claimed by both sides. ἐρυμνός of a ship = “stout, well‑defended.”

text.greek: πατρί θ' ἑῷ τίσεσθαι δίκην ἀλιτημοσυνάων,
text.english: and for her own father to exact the penalty for her transgressions;
text.note: τίσασθαι δίκην is middle “to exact the penalty”; the subject is the father (πατρὶ ἑῷ), not the maiden. Hence “for her own father to exact the penalty.”

text.greek: Ἀρήτη δ' ᾤκτειρεν ἀγακλειτὴ βασίλεια,
text.english: but Arete, the far‑famed queen, pitied her,
text.note: No special difficulty.

text.greek: μείλιχα παρφαμένη δὲ τὸν ὃν πόσιν, ὠδ' ἀγόρευεν·
text.english: and, gently addressing her own husband, spoke thus:
text.note: παρφαμένη (“speaking gently/soothingly”) is a Homeric verb of soft address.

text.greek: - "Οὐ μὲν δὴ φίλον ἐστὶν ἀπό ῥ' ὤσασθαι ὅμιλον
text.english: "Surely it is no welcome thing to thrust aside their companionship,
text.note: ὅμιλος here is taken as “companionship, consorting” (from ὁμιλέω), i.e., the couple’s union; οὐ μὲν δὴ marks the disfavored course (to separate them).

text.greek: Λέκτρα τε στορέσαι, λῦσαί τ' ἐκ πυρσὸν ἔρωτος.
text.english: but rather to spread the couch and unloose love from its torch."
text.note: The “torch” evokes both the fire of Eros and the marriage‑torch; λύσαι … ἔρωτα conveys allaying love’s fire through consummation. “but rather” renders the implied contrast with the preceding clause.

text.greek: Θυμαίνει μάλα γάρ σφι Διωναίη Ἀφροδίτη
text.english: For Dionaean Aphrodite is very wroth with them,
text.note: θυμαίνει = “is wroth, rages,” governing the dative (σφι, enclitic 3rd pl. “with/against them”); Διωναίη = “Dionaean,” i.e., of Dione, an epic epithet of Aphrodite.

text.greek: ἀνδράσιν ἠδὲ γυναιξὶν, ὅτις τάδε μήσεται ἔργα.
text.english: with men and with women, whosoever shall contrive these deeds.
text.note: ἀνδράσιν ἠδὲ γυναιξίν = dative of persons affected, “with/against men and women (alike)”; ὅτις functions as an indefinite relative (“whosoever”); μήσεται is future middle of μήδομαι (“devise, contrive”); τάδε ἔργα = “these deeds,” deictic to the preceding context.

text.greek: Ἀλλ' εἰ μὲν κούρη πέλεται καὶ ἄχραντος ἱκάνει,
text.english: But if she be a maiden and comes unsullied,
text.note: ἄχραντος = “undefiled,” with possible sexual and ritual overtones.

text.greek: οἰχέσθω πατρός τε δόμον καὶ ἐς ἤθεα Κόλχων·
text.english: let her go to her father’s house and to the haunts of the Colchians;
text.note: ἤθεα literally “haunts, abodes”; here = the homeland/realms of the Colchians.

text.greek: εἰ δέ κε νυμφιδίοις ὀάροις λέκτρῳ τε κλιθεῖσα
text.english: but if, with bridal converse and having reclined upon the couch,
text.note: νυμφιδίοις ὀάροις = “nuptial/bridal talk,” i.e., intimate wooing; κλιθεῖσα (aor. pass. part. of κλίνω) = “having reclined/lay down.”

text.greek: παρθενίην ᾔσχυνεν, ἑὸς πόσις ἄμμιν ἀγέσθω."
text.english: she has disgraced her maidenhood, let her own husband take her to himself.
text.note: παρθενίην ᾔσχυνεν = “put shame upon maidenhood”; ἄμμιν is an ethical dative (“for us/as far as we are concerned”), and ἀγέσθω (middle) = “let him take [her] for himself (as wife).”

text.greek: - Ὣς ἔφατ'· Ἀλκινόῳ δὲ περὶ φρένας ἤλυθε μῦθος·
text.english: Thus she spoke; and the word came over the mind of Alcinous;
text.note: περὶ φρένας ἤλυθε μῦθος is an idiom meaning “the word/thought came over (occupied) his mind,” i.e., it found favor; the speaker just above is likely Arete.

text.greek: Καί ῥ' οὕτω τάδε πάντα τελευτήσεσθαι ἔμελλεν.
text.english: and thus all these things were destined to be brought to completion.
text.note: τελευτᾶν here = “to come to fulfillment/consummation, be accomplished.”

text.greek: Ἀλλ' οὔ οἱ βουλὴ Μινύας λάθεν· αἶψα γὰρ Ἥρη
text.english: But the counsel of Minyas did not escape her; for straightway Hêrê
text.note: “Minyas” is a patronymic designation for Jason (a Minyan). The dative οἱ = “to her,” i.e., Hêrê; λάθεν + dative = “escaped [one’s] notice.”

text.greek: δμωῒ δέμας εἰκυῖα, θοῶς φάτο καὶ κατένευσε,
text.english: in the guise of a handmaid, swiftly spoke and nodded assent,

text.greek: νηὸς ἔπι προθοροῦσα, τά οἱ μήτιον ἄνακτες.
text.english: springing upon the ship, what the lords were contriving for him.
text.note: νηὸς is the genitive of ναῦς “ship” used with ἐπί (“upon”). μήτιον is the epic 3rd pl. of μητιάω “devise, contrive.” ἄνακτες “lords” likely refers to human rulers/princes; οἱ = “for him” (Jason).

text.greek: Δὴ τότε Μηδείη θαλάμων πορσύνετο λέκτρον
text.english: Then indeed Medeia made ready the bridal bed
text.note: θαλάμων (gen. pl.) is the epic idiom for “of the (bridal) chamber”; hence the idiomatic “bridal bed.” πορσύνετο (mid.) = “made ready.”

text.greek: πρύμνῃ ἐπ' ἀκροτάτῃ, περὶ δ' ἐστορέσαντο χαμεύνας,
text.english: at the uttermost stern, and round about they strewed ground-bedding,
text.note: χαμεῦνας = “ground-beds,” bedding laid on the floor/deck; subject of ἐστορέσαντο is implicit “they” (the comrades/attendants). πρύμνῃ ἐπ’ ἀκροτάτῃ specifies the very stern of the ship.

text.greek: ἀμφ' αὐτῇ χρύσειον ἐφαπλώσαντες ἄωτον.
text.english: spreading the Golden Fleece about her.
text.note: χρύσειον ἄωτον literally “the golden choicest (wool),” i.e., the Golden Fleece, used here as a coverlet; ἐφαπλώσαντες = “spreading over,” with ἀμφ’ αὐτῇ (“about her”) indicating the enveloping placement.

text.greek: Αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ δοράτεσσιν ἐπαρτήσαντο βοείας,
text.english: But when they had hung the oxhides upon the spear-shafts,
text.note: doratessin (“upon spear-shafts,” dat. pl. of doru) + boeias (“oxhide”) likely describes makeshift screens or a tent hung on spear-shafts.

text.greek: τεύχεά τε, κρύπτον τε γάμων αἰδέσσιμον ἔργον,
text.english: and the gear as well, and had veiled the reverend work of wedlock,
text.note: aidesimon ergon (“reverend/modest work”) is a euphemism for the consummation of marriage; krypton underscores privacy/modesty.

text.greek: καὶ τότε παρθενίης νοσφίζετο κούριον ἄνθος
text.english: then she parted with the maidenly blossom,
text.note: nosphizeto (middle) = “was separated from/parted with”; kourion anthos is the stock phrase “maidenly/virginal bloom.”

text.greek: αἰνόγαμος Μήδεια δυσαινήτοις ὑμεναίοις.
text.english: dread-wedded Medea, amid ill-omened wedding-songs.
text.note: ainogamos (“dread-/baleful-wedded”) foreshadows Medea’s tragic marriage; dysainētois (“ill-omened/ill-praised”) modifies hymenaiois, the wedding songs (with implicit reference to the god Hymenaios).

text.greek: Αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ βασιλῆος ἀμύμονος ὄψιν ἵκοντο
text.english: But when they came into the presence of the blameless king,
text.note: ὄψιν ἵκοντο = “came into the presence/sight (of).” ἀμύμονος is a traditional epic epithet, “blameless.”

text.greek: Κόλχοι καὶ Μινύαι, καὶ ἐμυθήσαντο ἕκαστοι,
text.english: the Kolchians and the Minyae, and each party spoke,
text.note: ἐμυθήσαντο: middle, “made speeches/pleaded their case.” Each side presents its claim before the king.

text.greek: ἐκ δ' ἔλαχ' Αἰσονίδης ἄλοχον Μήδειαν ἄγεσθαι
text.english: Aisonides won the decision to lead Medeia as his wife,
text.note: ἐκ δ’ ἔλαχ’ … ἄγεσθαι: “won by lot/award to take [her] as wife.” Refers to Alkinous’s arbitration that Medeia remain with Aisonides if already a wife.

text.greek: Ἀλκινόου, τοὶ δ' ὦκα λύοντ' ἐκ πείσματα νηός
text.english: by Alkinous; and they swiftly loosed the ship’s moorings,
text.note: Ἀλκινόου is genitive of agent (“by Alkinous”). πείσματα = “fastenings, moorings” of the ship.

text.greek: δὴ τόθ' ὑπ' εἰρεσίῃσι θέεν πολυηγόρος Ἀργώ,
text.english: then, beneath the oars, the much-spoken-of Argo sped,
text.note: πολυήγορος is rare; likely “much-spoken-of,” i.e., celebrated in story. ὑπ’ εἰρεσίῃσι = “beneath the oars,” epic locution for rowing speed.

text.greek: Ἀμπρακίου κόλποιο διαπρήσσουσα κέλευθα·
text.english: cleaving her course through the gulf of Ambrakia;
text.note: Ἀμπρακίου κόλπος = the Ambracian Gulf (NW Greece). διαπρήσσουσα κέλευθα = “pressing/cleaving her course.”

text.greek: - Ἔνθα τί τοι, Μουσαῖε θεηγενὲς, ἐξαγορεύσω
text.english: There—what shall I proclaim to you, Mousaios, god-born,
text.note: Apostrophe to Mousaios (Μουσαῖε), called θεηγενές “god-born.” ἐξαγορεύω = “proclaim/declare publicly.”

text.greek: ὅσσα πάθον Μινύαισιν ὁμοῦ ποτὶ Σύρτιν ἀήταις
text.english: all that they suffered, together with the Minyae, as the gusts drove them toward the Syrtis,
text.note: ἀήταις (dat.) = “by gusts/squalls”; ποτὶ Σύρτιν = “toward the Syrtis,” the dangerous Libyan shallows; ὁμοῦ = “together (with).”

text.greek: ἢ πῶς ἐξεσάωθεν ἁλιπλάγκτοιο πορείης·
text.english: or how they won deliverance from a sea-wandering voyage;
text.note: ἐξεσάωθεν = “escaped alive, won deliverance.” ἁλιπλάγκτος πορείη = “sea-wandering/sea-tossed voyage.”

text.greek: ὅσσα τ' ἄρ' ἐν Κρήτῃ πάθον ἄλγεα τετληῶτες,
text.english: and what pains they suffered in Crete, enduring,
text.note: τετληῶτες = “enduring, steadfast,” participle with concessive nuance (“though enduring”) or descriptive.

text.greek: χάλκειον τριγίγαντα δοκεύμενοι ὄφρ' ἱκόμεσθα,
text.english: as they kept watch against the bronze triple-giant, until we came,
text.note: χάλκειον τριγίγαντα refers to Talos, the bronze guardian of Crete. τριγίγαντα is a crux; often taken as “triple-/thrice-giant,” perhaps alluding to his thrice-daily circuit of the island; some have proposed emendations. δοκεύειν = “keep watch/lie in wait against.” ὄφρ’ ἱκόμεσθα = “until we came/arrived.”

text.greek: ὅς ῥά οἱ οὐκ εἴα λιμένων ἔντοσθεν ἱκέσθαι.
text.english: who would not permit them to come within the harbors.
text.note: οἱ (dat.) = “for them,” dative of disadvantage. λιμένων ἔντοσθεν = “inside the harbors.” οὐκ εἴα = “would not allow.”

text.greek: Ἠδ' ὡς στεινόμενοι βαρυηχέϊ κύματι πόντου
text.english: And as we were hemmed in by the heavy-sounding wave of the sea,
text.note: στεινόμενοι = “hemmed in, in straits”; βαρυηχέϊ (“heavy-sounding”) is an epic compound epithet of the surf.

text.greek: ῥίμφα τε κυανέῃσι βαρυνόμενοι νεφέλῃσιν,
text.english: and straightway weighed down by dark-blue clouds,
text.note: ῥίμφα = “straightway, swiftly”; κυανέῃσι (“blue-black”) evokes storm-clouds.

text.greek: ἠλπόμεθα σκοπέλοισι Μελαινείοισιν ἱκέσθαι
text.english: we hoped the swift ship might reach the Melainian crags;
text.note: νῆα θοὴν functions as the accusative subject of the infinitive ἱκέσθαι (“we hoped the swift ship would reach…”). Μελαινείοισι σκοπέλοισι probably means “the Black Rocks,” a toponym of uncertain identification.

text.greek: νῆα θοήν· Παιὰν δ' ἄρ' ἑκηβόλος ἀγχόθεν αἰέν,
text.english: but Paian, the Far-shooter, ever close at hand,
text.note: Παιὰν ἑκηβόλος = Apollo (Paian, the Far-shooter); ἀγχόθεν αἰέν = “ever at hand,” stressing his ready aid.

text.greek: Δήλου ἀπὸ κραναῆς ἧκεν βέλος, ἐκ δ' ἀνέφηνε
text.english: from rugged Delos sent forth a shaft, and by it revealed
text.note: ἧκεν βέλος = “sent a shaft,” a poetic sign/omen; Δήλου … κραναῆς = “rugged Delos,” a conventional epithet (kranaē = rocky).

text.greek: Μεσσατίων Σποράδων· Κρανάην δέ ἑ πάντες ὀπίσσω
text.english: one of the Midmost Sporades; and thereafter all call it Kranae—
text.note: Μεσσατίων Σποράδων = “the Midmost Sporades,” i.e., the central group of the scattered Aegean isles. ἑ = “it” (the island revealed). Κρανάην (“Kranae”) is a toponym meaning “Rocky.”

text.greek: νῆσον ἐπικλήσκουσι περικτίονες ἄνθρωποι.
text.english: —so the neighboring folk name the island.
text.note: περικτίονες ἄνθρωποι = “the neighboring folk/dwellers”; ἐπικλήσκουσι = “call by name.”

text.greek: - Ἀλλ' οὔ οἱ θέμις ἔσκε διαμπερὲς ἐξ ἁλὸς ἔρξαι
text.english: But it was not themis for him to destroy Aisonides outright from out of the sea.
text.note: θέμις = divine right/law; διαμπερές = ‘utterly, outright.’ The infinitive ἔρξαι with personal object (Αἰσονίδην) is elliptical (‘to do [harm] to’ = ‘destroy’). ἐξ ἁλός may mean ‘at sea’ or ‘after [he had come] out of the sea’; the sense is that such destruction was not lawful. Subject ‘he’ is supplied from 1362 (Hyperion).

text.greek: Αἰσονίδην· περὶ γάρ ῥα λύτρον φέρεν· ἆλτο δ' ὀπίσσω
text.english: For he was bearing the ransom, and baleful Fate leapt back behind.
text.note: λύτρον = ransom, expiatory payment/blood‑price; the subject ‘he’ is Aisonides (Jason), who bears expiation, hence Moira withdraws (ἆλτο δ’ ὀπίσσω).

text.greek: Μοῖρ' ὀλοή· κότεεν γὰρ ἐπιφραδέως Ὑπερίων.
text.english: For Hyperion was wroth with forethought.
text.note: Υπερίων = Hyperion (Helios). ἐπιφραδέως = ‘with deliberation/forethought,’ implying controlled, knowing anger that respects the ransom and themis.

text.greek: Ἀλλ' ὅθ' ὑπ' εἰρεσίῃς Μαλεώτιδας ἱκόμεθ' ἄκρας,
text.english: But when under oars we reached the Malean headlands,
text.note: “under oars” (hyp’ eiresiēs) is an epic idiom for traveling by rowing; “Malean headlands” refers to Cape Malea (Laconia).

text.greek: Κίρκης ἐννεσίῃσιν ἀπορρίψεσθαι ἔμελλον
text.english: by Kirkē’s counsels we were on the point of casting off
text.note: ennesiē = “counsel”; aporripsesthai “to cast off, rid oneself (of).” The sense is purification following Kirkē’s advice.

text.greek: ἀρὰς Αἰήτεω καὶ ἠλιτόποινον Ἐριννύν·
text.english: the curses of Aietes and the sin‑avenging Erinys;
text.note: ēlitopoinos = “sin‑avenging,” from alitē “offense/sin”; singular Erinys as the personified avenger (blood‑guilt).

text.greek: δὴ τότ' ἐγὼ Μινύαισιν ἐφ' ἱερὰ λύτρα καθαρμῶν
text.english: then indeed I, for the Minyans, performed holy expiatory offerings of purification,
text.note: hierà lýtra katharmōn = “sacred ransom‑offerings of purification,” i.e., expiatory rites to remove miasma; epi with acc. expresses “for, on behalf of.”

text.greek: ῥέξα, καὶ ἐλλισάμην Γαιήοχον Ἐννοσίγαιον
text.english: and I appeased Gaiēochos Ennosigaios,
text.note: ellisamen (ἐλλισάμην) = “I appeased/propitiated,” a rarer verb; Gaiēochos Ennosigaios are epithets of Poseidon (“Earth‑holder, Earth‑shaker”).

text.greek: νόστον ἐπειγομένοις δόμεναι γλυκερούς τε τοκῆας.
text.english: to grant those hastening home a return and the sight of their sweet parents.
text.note: domenai is the epic infinitive for dounai “to grant”; the addition “the sight of” renders the idiom with “sweet parents,” i.e., safe return to them; epeigomenois is a dative of advantage “for those eager for home.”

text.greek: - Καί ῥ' οἳ μὲν πλώοντες ἐϋκτιμένην ἐπ' Ἰωλκόν
text.english: And they, as they sailed toward well-built Iolkos,
text.note: The verb θῦνον (“were offering sacrifice”) in the next line governs this clause: sense = “as they sailed to well-built Iolkos, they offered sacrifice.”

text.greek: θῦνον· ἐγὼ δ' ἱκόμην ἐπὶ Ταίναρον ἠνεμόεντα,
text.english: were offering sacrifice; but I came to windy Tainaron,
text.note: Tainaron (Taenarum), the windy cape in Laconia, was famed as an entrance to Hades.

text.greek: ὄφρα κεν ἔντομα ῥέξω ἀγακλειτοῖς βασιλεῦσιν
text.english: so that I might perform cut-offerings for the very-glorious kings
text.note: ἔντομα ῥέξω is a technical phrase for chthonic rites performed by incision/slaughter (with blood offered into a pit); the “very-glorious kings” are the underworld pair, Plouton (Aïdoneus) and Persephone.

text.greek: οἵ τ' ἄρα νερτερίων βερέθρων κληῗδας ἔχουσιν.
text.english: who indeed hold the keys of the nether pits.
text.note: “Keys of the nether pits” (νερτερίων βερέθρων κληῖδες) evokes sovereign control over access to the Underworld.

text.greek: Ἔνθεν δ' ὁρμηθεὶς ἐσύθην χιονώδεα Θρῄκην
text.english: Thence, setting out, I sped to snow‑clad Thrace,
text.note: ἐσύθην is the intransitive aorist (passive in form) of σεύω, “I sped/rushed”; ὁρμηθείς “setting out.” χιονῶδεα is a Homeric-style epithet, “snow‑clad,” for Thrace.

text.greek: Λειβήθρων ἐς χῶρον, ἐμὴν ἐς πατρίδα γαῖαν·
text.english: to the land of Leibethra, to my fatherland;
text.note: Λειβήθρων is genitive plural with ἐς χῶρον (“to the land/region of Leibethra”), a Pierian/Thracian site associated with Orpheus. The double ἐς echoes the motion toward place and homeland (πατρὶς γαῖα).

text.greek: ἄντρον δ' εἰσεπέρησα περικλυτὸν, ἔνθα με μήτηρ
text.english: and I entered the far‑famed cave, where my mother
text.note: εἰσεπέρησα is an epic aorist of περάω (“to pass into/through”), here “I entered.” περικλυτόν = “far‑famed.” The ἄντρον is the specific cave at Leibethra tied to Orphic lore.

text.greek: γείνατ' ἐνὶ λέκτροις μεγαλήτορος Οἰάγροιο.
text.english: bore me in the marriage‑bed of great‑hearted Oiagros.
text.note: λέκτροις denotes the marriage‑bed; μεγαλήτωρ is a standard heroic epithet. Οἰάγροιο = Oiagros, traditionally Orpheus’ Thracian father; the unnamed mother is Kalliope in the usual myth.
